Everton told to pay Burnley £35m over PSR breach

Manchester City vs The Premier League

Meanwhile, Christian Purslow, a former Liverpool managing director and Aston Villa chief executive, who also held a senior role at Chelsea, said the City case could begin a chain of events that would be "appalling for the game".

Speaking on Radio 4's Today programme, Purslow appeared alongside football law expert Paul Gilroy KC, who described the case as a "seismic moment for world football".

Purslow said: "It's a sort of 'where does this end?' because if you look at every single season - the nine seasons which we now know Manchester City breached rules - then all of their 19 Premier League rivals in that season, to differing extents, suffered easy-to-compute loss. Whether it was a place in the Premier League - every place was worth £3m.

"Teams that came fifth who didn't make the Champions League maybe lost tens of millions of pounds - and of course teams that were relegated. Let's say the team that finished 18th would've finished 17th if Manchester City weren't there. And they, of course, suffered huge loss.

"If you add all those claims up, over nine years, and that's just in the Premier League, you can see that the potential here for this to spiral out of control is huge."

Gilroy added that, so far, four clubs have put in protective claims "reserving the right to claim compensation if City are found guilty".

The news, broken by the Athletic,, external came 1,327 days after City were charged by the Premier League in February 2023 following a four-year investigation, and 22 months after a hearing by an independent commission concluded.

No official announcement has been made by the Premier League, which has declined to comment.

Manchester City declined to comment on whether they had been found guilty, instead providing a statement which read: "Premier League process remains ongoing with significant elements to be completed, and subject to strict confidentiality.

"The club has diligently respected due process for eight years on the basis that the Premier League board and executive would behave as an independent, impartial and fair-minded regulator, free from partisan influence."

Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy has urged the Premier League to come to a quick resolution.

She told BBC Radio 5 Live: "I think most football fans will be feeling that this is not a good moment for football as a whole and I think Manchester City fans will be feeling very, very anxious about what happens next.

"It's very unsettling for football fans and I hope that it can be resolved as swiftly as possible.

"I will obviously look very closely as what comes out of this but we can't apply those rules for the Premier League. They have got to do it themselves and are going to have to resolve this as swiftly as possible - not just for the sake of Manchester City but for the sake of football."

This video can not be played

What do Man City charges mean and what happens next?

City won eight trophies in the period covered by the case, including three Premier League titles, three EFL Cups, one Community Shield and one FA Cup.

The charges cover the managerial tenures of Roberto Mancini and Manuel Pellegrini, and the first two years under Pep Guardiola, who left the club at the end of last season after 10 years in charge.

David Bernstein, who was Manchester City chairman from 1998-2003, told Times Radio he felt "absolutely awful" on hearing the news of City being found guilty - but admitted any punishment would have to be "more drastic" than a fine.

"To see all this tarnished in this way is very sad," he said.

"I feel particularly bad for the wonderful supporters of the club who've stayed with the club through thick and thin.

"This whole process has taken too long already. So the appeal process now has to be done quickly because you've got the club playing with this cloud over its head and it's just not viable.

"The appeal process cannot go on for year after year, I think that would be a disaster, not just for this particular case but for English football generally. The timing is crucial."

He continued: "I can't give a view on the punishment. If they are found, after the appeal, guilty of 115 charges, my beloved club is going to face a very severe penalty.

"All I would say is that money is not sufficient, it would have to be something, unfortunately, more drastic than that."

Meanwhile, singer-songwriter Noel Gallagher says he is "shocked" at the news and it is "quite sad" for players and fans.

"A little surprised when I heard it on the radio. Surprised because the club have assured us all along that they vehemently denied any of these charges," the Oasis star and City fan said on the Let Me Talk podcast.

"So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we've been found guilty. But really overall just quite sad really. Sad for the fans and for the players."

No Premier League appetite to strip Man City of titles - but threat remains

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 13:26:40 GMT

Manchester City won the Premier League title three times in the period covered by the investigation

It is one of the biggest talking points from the Manchester City case.

Should City be stripped of the eight trophies they won between 2009 and 2018, the period in which they were accused of breaking Premier League financial rules?

Judging by social media, many fans of rival clubs are now hoping for such an outcome.

However BBC Sport has been told there has been little appetite from within the Premier League - both the organisation and clubs - for past titles to be stripped from City

Does that put an end to it?

Not quite, as the decision will be made by an independent panel which is yet to hold a "sanction hearing". That means it cannot be ruled out, although a points deduction, huge fine or possibly even expulsion from the Premier League are thought to be more likely.

Here, BBC Sport analyses this difficult issue and decision the panel is now facing.

Man City and the 115 charges - key questions answered

Man City fans face up to reality of guilty verdict

Relegation? Titles stripped? Appeals? What next for Man City

Manchester City vs The Premier League

"I think we still have a chance to win that league… and then they have to pay me the bonus and give me the medal."

It was almost two years ago that Jose Mourinho mischievously raised the possibility that his former club Manchester United could be handed the 2018 Premier League title held by Manchester City.

Under Mourinho, United finished second to City by 19 points in 2018, his final full campaign in charge at Old Trafford.

City have always denied wrongdoing. But now we know they have been found guilty of the majority of the 115 charges, was Mourinho right?

Premier League rules do not directly make reference to such a sanction, with a fine, points deduction or expulsion listed as possible punishments. However, they also allow for a disciplinary commission panel to impose a penalty "as it shall think fit". That theoretically could include retrospectively-applied points deductions, or the stripping of titles.

Many will argue that if upheld after any appeal, the nature and scale of the wrongdoing City have been found guilty of warrants such as sanction on the basis that titles were won unfairly, and any misrepresentation of revenue and costs gave them a crucial competitive advantage.

City were accused of a wide range of rule breaches, centred around claims that they inflated sponsorship revenue from connected companies and made other "off the books" payments to circumvent football's financial rules.

So with a cloud hanging over the trophy-laden era City have enjoyed since the takeover of the club by Abu Dhabi billionaire Sheikh Mansour in 2008, could asterisks now be applied to the titles City won during the period in which they have been found to have broken the rules?

Could they be left blank? Or, as implied by Mourinho, reallocated to those teams who finished runners-up to City?

Those clubs are:

Premier League

2011-12: Manchester United

2013-14: Liverpool

2017-18: Manchester United

FA Cup

2010-11: Stoke City

EFL Cup

2013-14: Sunderland

2015-16: Liverpool

2017-18: Arsenal

Community Shield

2012-13 Chelsea

Such a move would threaten to open the proverbial can of worms, raising questions over other accomplishments.

For instance, there is now scepticism towards the various trophies Chelsea won in the 2010s, after the club were found to have made a catalogue of secret payments to agents over transfers, between 2011 and 2018.

Some will ask that if retrospective action is applied to City, should the same not happen to Chelsea?

This video can not be played

What do Man City charges mean and what happens next?

It is impossible to know exactly to what extent City benefited on the field from their rule breaches. And which players they may not have been able to afford if they had adhered to the regulations.

And what about the period between December 2018 and February 2023, when City stand accused of a failure to co-operate with Premier League investigations?

Should retrospective action be applied then too? Jurgen Klopp's Liverpool finished runners-up to Pep Guardiola's City twice during that time, by a single point in both 2019 and 2022. Last year, the German coach joked he would host a party in his garden if his former club were suddenly awarded those titles.

Some will conclude that the rule breaches between 2009 and 2018 helped City to lay the foundations on which Guardiola built on to achieve so much success, culminating in the Treble triumph of 2023.

Does that era come into scope? Where does it end?

For some, the mass reallocation of titles over such a long period would risk making a mockery of Premier League history, jeopardising its reputation and commercial viability. Others would argue that some 17 years after the first alleged breach, and with City accused of distorting the competition over multiple seasons, serious damage has already been done to the league's standing.

And while there is no Premier League precedent, such concerns have not prevented such punishments being applied before in football. Juventus had the Serie A titles they won in 2005 and 2006 revoked as a result of the Calciopoli match-fixing scandal - when five Italians teams were penalised for attempting to influence results by picking certain referees. The first title was left blank by authorities, with the second reallocated to Inter Milan.

There is also a British precedent. Elgin City won the 1992-93 Highland League, but were later stripped of the title after having been found to have fielded ineligible players.

There are examples in other sports too. In 2012, Lance Armstrong was stripped of his seven Tour de France titles by the UCI, cycling's governing body, for doping. And the reallocation of medals has become commonplace in athletics as a result of positive drugs tests that can emerge long after events have taken place.

In cases such as City's, involving financial rule breaches, the argument for such a punishment is more complicated. Many will see it as unfair that players and fans unconnected to any rule breaches should suffer by losing titles.

And with some suggesting that relations between the United Arab Emirates and the UK could be put under serious pressure by this ruling, one can only imagine the diplomatic tensions if past titles were then taken away from the club.

On Friday, former City midfielder Rodri dismissed talk of the club being stripped of some of the titles they won.

"What we did, they cannot take out of us," he added.

"It's something that is not paid by money. It's paid with effort, with the damage, with, you know, being shoulder to shoulder every day.

"I can tell you that everything was deserved, and I'm glad that I could live one of the best eras of English football in here."

Others, however, will insist the rewriting of the competition's official record is the only way of restoring justice for those clubs that competed within the rules.

In terms of retrospective action, the compensation claims for lost earnings that several clubs are known to be considering launching against City are more likely than the stripping of titles.

The ramifications could be significant. One lawyer told me, "The question isn't whether the clubs can take legal action... it's where does the line of people who have a case actually end?

"The clubs who didn't win/qualify/stay up; the players who didn't get bonuses, contract extensions; the staff who missed out on bonuses; the agents who didn't get their uplift on their player deals...

"It's endless and potentially so destructive to the whole ecosystem."

Whatever happens, more division and disruption seems guaranteed.

Met to re-examine CCTV from Jill Dando murder case

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 13:21:27 GMT

The Met Police has confirmed it will re-examine CCTV footage relating to the unsolved murder of Jill Dando, 27 years ago.

The BBC presenter and journalist was shot dead with a single bullet on her doorstep in Fulham in April 1999. Despite one of the biggest and most high-profile murder investigations in British history, the case remains unsolved.

A Met spokesperson said recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology had "provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station".

The CCTV includes an unidentified man who was seen sprinting near the scene of the shooting, 20 minutes after the event.

The Met said in the 27 years since Dando's death, the investigation had been "subject to numerous reviews", aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

It warned this latest review was part of "ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter".

The TV presenter and newsreader was born in Weston-Super-Mare, Somerset, and worked for the BBC for 14 years.

She was 37 when she died on the doorstep of her home on Gowan Avenue.

Soon after her death, a man of Serbian descent called the BBC claiming she had been executed in a revenge hit for the UK-backed Nato bombing of Serbia's state broadcaster in Belgrade.

However, Barry George, a local man, was convicted of her murder and spent eight years in jail before being acquitted at a retrial in 2008.

Dando's partner, Alan Farthing, was interviewed by the police, along with her ex-partner and BBC Breakfast news editor Bob Wheaton. Also interviewed was her agent Jon Roseman, who had written a crime novel detailing a very similar scene.

They were all ruled out as suspects.

Her killing was the subject of a Netflix documentary Who Killed Jill Dando? in 2023.

British national among six dead in building explosion close to Acropolis in Athens

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 12:47:25 GMT

Six people have died, including a British national, in an explosion that destroyed a building containing a holiday rental property in the historic centre of Athens.

The blast on Friday happened in the Plaka area of the Greek capital, a neighbourhood close to tourist sites such as the Acropolis.

Four American holidaymakers were among the dead, along with a UK national and Greek national - reportedly an elderly couple who lived in the same building.

Pictures from the scene on Saturday showed emergency service workers searching through rubble, with a gas leak the suspected cause of the blast.

All six bodies had been recovered by Saturday afternoon. Athens Mayor Haris Doukas said: "We are talking about an incredible disaster."

The tourists were confirmed to be missing when they did not arrive for their flight at Athens airport later on Friday, news agency Reuters reported citing local police.

The three-storey building completely collapsed due to the force of the blast, with neighbouring buildings damaged and debris scattered across the road.

Local media reported people were injured by material scattered across nearby streets and some buildings needed to be evacuated.

Excavators and thermal imaging cameras have been used at the scene to search for survivors.

The explosion happened on a small road situated between two of Athens' most visited sites - the Acropolis and the Temple of Olympian Zeus.

A UK Foreign Office spokesperson said: "We are aware of a suspected explosion in Athens and are in touch with the local authorities."

Prince Harry says it is 'great' to be back in Britain after six years in US

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 12:26:53 GMT

The Duke of Sussex has said it feels "great" to be back in Britain after spending six years living in California.

He told Canadian network CTV: "It's been great. It's been great to be back on British soil. The kids are happy in school and it gives me a chance to be able to really focus on the Invictus Games in Birmingham in July next year."

Prince Harry and Meghan stepped back as senior royals and began a new life in the US in 2020, before returning to live in Britain last month.

It is thought the family are basing themselves at a private property outside of London in the Cotswolds area.

The couple's children, Archie, seven, and Lilibet, five, had to be moved to a different school only days after they started over security concerns about the school run.

It is understood that the Sussexes' private security team had raised concerns about the distance and heavy traffic on the route to the school.

Harry and Meghan's return to the UK has been marked by tensions with the Royal Family.

Meghan has largely stayed out of the public eye, with few public appearances.

Harry has carried out several public engagements linked to his work with the Invictus Games.

Last week, he visited a school in Birmingham to launch an education programme inspired by the games, where he played pickleball with pupils and took part in a science lesson on prosthetic design.

The games will take place in Birmingham from 10 to 17 July next year, with 550 wounded, injured and sick service personnel and veterans from 25 nations expected to compete in 12 adaptive sports.

Harry spoke to CTV after completing a skydive in Toronto to honour a promise to a 102-year-old World War Two veteran and raise awareness of military charities.

Asked what had prompted the family's return to the UK, Harry said there were "lots of reasons" but did not elaborate.

The couple were reportedly surprised by a letter authorised by the King which reiterated that they are private citizens and set out guidance to senior government and military figures on how they should be treated.

Prince Harry and King Charles have had a strained relationship since the Duke and Duchess of Sussex stepped down as senior working royals and moved to the US.

Meanwhile, the Sussexes are waiting to hear whether they will receive taxpayer-funded security in the UK.

The committee which oversees royal and VIP security, Ravec, is set to reconsider the family's level of police protection now that they are full-time residents rather than visitors.

How long can Labour's feel-good factor last?

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 11:22:03 GMT

"He just loves being prime minister," a government insider observes.

Andy Burnham might not yet have delivered his all-important conference speech, but he has been preparing for this moment for years.

He'll lap up the inevitable whoops and cheers – not just as Labour's leader, but the kind of leader who chimes with the party's rank and file, who puts social justice at the top of his list, who is not averse to cranking up the greatest hits – whether taking a pop at Mrs Thatcher, privatisation, or the divides between north and south.

Speaking to MPs, ministers and advisers inside the party, there is no doubt whatsoever that Labour is in a much, much happier place than this time last year.

There is a very simple reason, according to one cabinet minister, fans of Sir Keir Starmer, look away now, "people like the new prime minister more than they liked the old one – that's the truth of it".

Another minister tells me: "There is no appetite for destruction – very little naysaying."

But Labour is in a position that's been all too rare for all our political parties in the last few years – there are no whispers about chucking out the leader, no-one stirring revolt.

And even those who don't like the direction of travel are labelling their opinions as a desire to be helpful, they're not trying to criticise the boss.

"The mood's good – everyone is going into conference with their ears open," one MP said, keen to hear more from the prime minister.

The feel-good factor is also driven by the party inching up a little in the polls – one senior figure says: "We're all witnessing the Burnham bounce – whether that's how you feel when you see the polls, or how we all feel when we have meetings together."

And those who work inside government also credit a more effective political operation around the prime minister. "The system's better, you get clearer decisions, better steers when you need them," says a minister.

Another government source also credits the new Downing Street operation but notes wryly, "it's unfair to compare the end of a regime which is always pretty nasty, with the arrival of a new one which is always more hopeful… these things can change".

There are whispers of announcements in the next few days on housing and defence. Some MPs also want to hear Burnham expand on themes they, and the country, have heard plenty about but that aren't specifically defined – "public control" and "re-industrialisation".

And frankly, the happy prime minister would probably be only too glad to talk for as long as necessary about those favourite subjects.

But however much he loves being PM there are also less tempting realities he'll have to confront.

"It's a new front man," says a minister, "but the song hasn't changed."

And the soundtrack to this autumn might prove to be downright miserable.

While Andy Burnham will be pressing the flesh at dozens of party events in the next few days, his Chancellor John Healey will be spending a lot of time holed up in his hotel room making decisions about the Budget which is only a month away.

The pressure on public cash is intense as the budget approaches – the choice for the chancellor doing the rounds is, "10 billion of cuts or 10 billion of tax rises," according to a well-connected senior figure.

Treasury sources say they don't recognise that simple number. However the figures shake down, the increasing cost of paying the interest on the country's debts weighs heavily.

Don't forget the rising welfare bill, demands for more defence spending. It's unusual that a party conference is happening with a budget just weeks away, and it looms over the conference, just as the state of the economy looms over Labour's current feel-good factor.

The UK can't force the US and Iran to find peace, to get traffic flowing freely through the Strait of Hormuz, to bring the oil price down. Nor can the prime minister make Putin bring his war on Ukraine to an end, with pressure on European gas supply as we enter another winter.

There are already predictions of our annual energy bills going up by £500 early next year.

You know the script – higher energy costs raise the spectre of price rises everywhere.

"We're really suffering at the hands of energy prices," says an insider.

One influential figure predicts an array of grim economic consequences, unconvinced that Burnham and his team have grasped what might be coming down the track and planned accordingly.

"The big economic challenges coming – rising housing costs, rising inflation, downward pressure on public spending because of the cost of borrowing, 500 quid on energy from January - I just don't see what the game plan is."

And there are nerves about whether the new No 10 is concentrating on getting the economy growing.

Many of Burham's priorities so far are about spending money, not helping people make it.

One of his own advisors publicly described the administration as a "traditional tax and spend socialist government with better TikTok". Ouch.

Now, the former business secretary, Peter Kyle, has very politely, but firmly, expressed concern that Burnham and his team are not thinking hard enough about helping the country make money, perhaps more focused on how to spend it. You can read more about his comments here.

He told me: "We must act with more urgency, and we must feel the need for economic growth as acutely as we do about tackling things like rough sleeping and about social care, and some of the social reforms that we want because they are inextricably linked."

Kyle is not the only person in the Labour Party who worries Burnham and Healey are more interested in spending money than helping business generate it.

And budget speculation is full of chatter around increasing taxes on property or other assets like stocks and shares.

At the other end of the spectrum there are demands on the left for the prime minister to ease the pressure on less well-paid workers.

One prominent figure warned: "Labour has a second hearing. One shot to get this right. It is beyond doubt that if they do not keep to the promises made to everyday people - workers and communities will turn their back."

Expect union leaders to renew calls for tax cuts for workers and more investment. It's a tug of war.

In the next few days, Labour are likely to look like a happy political tribe. The new chief delighted to be in charge. The rank and file relieved to have a leader they can cheer.

But one senior figure warns that what's coming could turn things sour. "The budget looks like a disaster – by Halloween we'll be looking at something else," predicting a big change in mood.

That portent of doom doesn't match the overall atmosphere around Labour right now, but there is a quiet creeping concern about whether Burnham's rhetoric of hope, and change, the classic political mantras, can be matched with people's experience.

A senior source says: "His political will needs to be more bold than the machine around him – don't write cheques you can't cash."

One minister niggles that it's easier to talk in broad terms about your long-term ambitions than to grapple with problems affecting people today, "there is comfort in dealing with some of the largest possible questions because it's a way off delivering them. But the cost of getting to work, or getting across town is expensive, going out or staying in – that's right now".

Conferences are a chance for political parties to enjoy each other's company, but also to show off to the country.

But the reality of paying the bills is, of course, more present in most people's lives, one minister tells me: "If you go into Tesco and the cereal you buy is noticeably more expensive, that has more cut through than any political clip you see on telly or Facebook."

Labour's spirits have been transformed by Burnham's soft coup that saw off Starmer.

But the minister says: "The contrast is not between now and hard times, but between the new regime and the old regime."

The question that beckons beyond the conference hall – can that carry on if hard times hit?

Rayner criticises visa rule proposals ahead of Labour conference

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 10:39:33 GMT

Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said she is concerned about Labour's proposals to change visa rules, which would make it harder for foreign workers to secure permanent residency in the UK.

In an interview with the Times ahead of Labour's annual conference, Rayner questioned Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood's plans, saying they are unfair because they "change the goalposts".

Under the proposals, most migrants would have to wait 10 years to qualify for residency - instead of the current five - while foreign workers on health and social care visas would face a 15-year wait.

Mahmood said the government would make a decision on the immigration overhaul by the end of the year.

Speaking to the Times, Rayner said she was concerned about shifting "the goalposts years down the line" for people who arrived in the UK at the beginning of this decade, expecting to secure permanent residence under the current rules.

She described the potential rule change as "very disruptive" and added: "I do have concerns about that."

During her interview with the Times, she said that the changes would impact foreign care workers who "moved their lives here to look after our loved ones".

Her remarks represent direct criticism of a policy inherited by Prime Minister Andy Burnham from his predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer.

Rayner previously served as deputy prime minister under Sir Keir, and was brought back into cabinet by Burnham in July.

It is significant that a serving cabinet minister feels able to criticise an existing government proposal on the eve of Labour's conference, albeit one inherited from the Starmer era.

It is part of a growing head of steam from some parts of the party to quash the retrospective elements of these plans.

Rayner has previously criticised the measures. In June, she said proposals to retrospectively alter the rules for migrants already working in the UK would be "wrong".

Rayner said she believed that Mahmood was aware of her position, telling the Times she has "not changed [her] view" since re-entering the cabinet.

Before he became prime minister, Burnham said he "understood" where Rayner was coming from on her criticisms of the migrant visa changes, telling reporters in June that Labour "would do well to listen to what Angela has to say".

Rayner's call for a change of approach has been echoed by York Central Labour MP Rachael Maskell, who also wants a rethink from the home secretary.

She told the Today programme that "technically and morally" what is being proposed represented "the wrong set of values" and would affect "people who have come [to Britain] to serve faithfully and are then told that they have to wait another 10 years" to secure British citizenship.

In recent weeks, trade unions have put pressure on the government to soften its proposals, and a letter to Mahmood jointly signed by dozens of Labour MPs at the start of the year described the plans as "un-British".

Lisa Nandy, secretary of state for culture, media and sport, rejected the "un-British" description of the plans.

She told BBC Radio 4's Today programme: "I don't think they are un-British because I don't think that we have ever had an automatic right to citizenship for most people who come to the UK from overseas."

Nandy said the home secretary was trying to balance respect for people "regardless of who they or where they stand" with the need for "an immigration system that people have confidence in".

Asked if Labour could change its mind on the proposals, she told Today: "We always reserve the right to change our minds but we also will reserve the right to stick to our plans if we think we are getting them right".

The culture secretary said the government will not "change the rules of the game" in a way that unfairly disadvantages migrants who have contributed to the UK.

She said it would "strike the right balance" between treating people "fairly and decently as human beings but making sure there is an asylum and immigration system people can have confidence in."

Nandy's comments are a hint the government is reconsidering. She could have given a full-throated defence of the principle of backdating the changes so they apply to those foreign workers already here.

But she did not. Instead she emphasised the principle of those "contributing" to the UK and treating them fairly.

But if the government does reverse course on applying these changes to those arriving from 2021, the large numbers who came to the UK after that date have a quicker and easier route to settlement. That is a dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK that those parties will be keen to highlight.

The home secretary faced questions about the changes during an appearance at the Home Affairs Committee earlier this month.

Mahmood said she was "very aware that a large group of people who arrived in 2022, absent any change, would qualify in February 2027" for permanent settlement.

She added: "Later this year we will set out the new policy on settlement... as well as any transitional arrangements we might decide to implement."

Could an iced coffee freeze you out of the job market?

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 10:05:36 GMT

Would you bring an iced coffee to a job interview?

The question on the internet's lips this week started life, as many do, in a TikTok video.

"Don't waltz into your interview all casual with an iced coffee, it just looks like you didn't have time to finish your coffee beforehand," said US recruiter Caitlin Wehniainen.

It's what her Gen Z job candidates are doing, she said, warning it makes it look like the interview is "just a stop on your list of errands for the day".

The post has started what Wehniainen calls the Great Iced Coffee Debate of 2026.

Some believe turning up with an iced matcha latte in hand is a cardinal sin. They say it's unprofessional, too informal, and a distraction.

Others feel this is an overreaction - distracting from how difficult it is to secure a job - or even just get an interview in the first place.

In a subsequent LinkedIn post, Wehniainen says she "was never saying that bringing coffee makes someone a bad candidate.

"My point was simply about avoiding distractions."

Hanad, 28, works for an energy supplier in London. He likes iced coffee but wouldn't bring one to an interview.

"A job interview is all about first impressions," he says. "Anything can deter the employer from employing you.

"Iced coffee is something a lot of teens drink… it would look immature and too informal."

He would never bring along an energy drink for the same reasons. But he says water or a hot coffee would be okay.

His colleague Tsvetina, 24, thinks a potential employee shouldn't be judged by what they bring to the interview, nor their dress code.

"I think we should be moving away from these traditional corporate stigmas. What matters is what the person is actually communicating during the interview."

Aisha, 28, says she would take along an iced coffee. "I think it shows that I have come early enough to get iced coffee."

She wouldn't bring a fizzy drink, however.

In general, she thinks a lot of employers like to see personality in a candidate. "It makes you stand out from other people who are coming [applying] for the job."

Katy, 25, a personal assistant in events, says she personally wouldn't turn up to a job interview with an iced coffee.

But she sees the controversy around Wehniainen's post as "a bit sexist, because it's usually girls who drink iced coffee".

"If it was a hot coffee, which is more masculine, there wouldn't be a discourse about that."

Young people trying to land their first job are facing multiple challenges.

The number of graduate vacancies in the UK has almost halved in the past year, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.

Around one in eight people aged 16-24 are not in education, employment or training - so called Neets.

Young workers in the US are also struggling with a tight jobs market as hiring slows.

Lucy Cooper is the founder of Spark, a design and branding recruitment company in London.

She says her industry - marketing - is really tough right now, and she doesn't know of any Gen Z candidates who would risk turning up to an interview with an iced coffee.

You could "seem too relaxed and a little bit flippant, like you're not taking it seriously enough, or you are interviewing the employer rather than the other way round".

"I think people at junior level are very conscious about not doing anything that could jeopardise their chances," she says.

She adds that it would be fine to accept a coffee offered by the employer, however, or drink one on a video interview.

Dan Craddock, director at Hays, says employers shouldn't rely on "snap judgements".

"It's important not to read too much into a single item a candidate brings to an interview.

"Whether that's an iced coffee, a bottle of water or a notebook, employers are ultimately assessing the skills, experience and behaviours that will make someone successful in the role."

Chris Mason, co-founder of Intelligent People - a specialist recruitment agency for the tech industry, says focusing on ice coffees alone "does seem to be an overreaction on the US recruiter's part".

He advises candidates to "try to do everything possible to project the right image and attitude".

He warns bringing snacks or specialist drinks may undermine the impression candidates will want to give - that they're "serious and focused on the interview".

He says the main issue they see with some younger candidates is a lack of preparation, not being punctual, and not researching the role, organisation or interviewer.

Murder or medical mix-up? New questions in the case of killer nurse Colin Norris

BBC News Sat, 26 Sep 2026 08:05:11 GMT

For two decades, Ethel Hall's family believed that staff nurse Colin Norris murdered the 86-year-old by injecting her with insulin while she recovered from a broken hip in a Leeds hospital.

After his latest appeal against conviction, some members of Ethel's family are having doubts.

"The evidence, it's just not sitting right to me," daughter-in-law Helen Hall told a new BBC podcast, Disclosure Investigates: Killer on the Ward.

Norris was convicted in 2008 of killing Ethel and three other elderly patients as well as attempting to murder a fifth.

The Court of Appeal rejected his challenge against his convictions last year but the new BBC podcast has reviewed medical records, looked again at police interviews and heard about new scientific discoveries.

It reveals a scenario in which the murders may never have taken place at all.

The podcast series comes a week after a public inquiry reported on the case of former neonatal nurse Lucy Letby who was convicted of murdering seven babies and attempting to murder seven others at a hospital in Chester a decade ago.

While the circumstances are very different, Norris' supporters also argue that his case hinges on disputed interpretations of medical evidence.

The story begins in 2002 when Norris, a 26-year-old nurse, originally from Glasgow, found Ethel in an hypoglycemic coma as she recovered from a broken hip.

Doctors took blood samples to find out what caused her blood sugar to drop so low.

The test results seemed conclusive - she had a massive amount of insulin in her blood.

She died 21 days later, sparking a murder investigation.

A nurse who had been on shift on the night Ethel was found told the police that Norris had predicted the 86-year-old might not last the night.

He quickly became the prime suspect.

The police operation trawled retrospectively through all the deaths on Norris's wards, looking for potential murders that may have gone unnoticed.

They identified three other cases of unexplained severe hypoglycemic deaths and one where the patient recovered.

No blood tests had been taken from these cases at the time of their deaths to be able to prove insulin poisoning but experts for the prosecution said in court that their medical charts showed persistent and severe low blood sugar readings.

They said that because this was so rare in non-diabetics that it must be murder.

When it came to court in 2007, experts called by the defence said four of the five patients had died of natural causes.

But after a five-month trial and a deadlocked jury, Norris was convicted by a majority of 11-1 and told he would not be eligible for parole for 30 years.

After the verdict, Ethel's son Stuart Hall said: "I don't think he should come out again. He's got the knowledge to commit murder but do it discreetly."

When I got involved in the case in 2009, Norris, who is now known as Colin Campbell, had just lost his first appeal against conviction.

Two years later, new scientific evidence came to light which challenged one of the key assumptions underpinning the prosecution case.

It claimed hypoglycemia - low blood sugar - in the frail and elderly is not as vanishingly rare as was once thought, suggesting the jury had been misinformed.

This new evidence was submitted for a second appeal, which took another 14 years to be heard.

During that appeal last year, experts for Norris argued that the symptoms seen in several of the patients could occur naturally in elderly, frail people.

Experts for the Crown maintained the deaths were medically distinct.

They said their blood sugar readings were refractory, meaning they kept coming back despite being given glucose, whereas naturally-occurring hypoglycemia can be easily corrected with a treatment such as a sugary drink.

They argued this distinction could only be explained by deliberate insulin poisoning.

The ultimate question in this case has always been 'what happened to Ethel Hall?', the woman whose death sparked the investigation.

Was deliberate insulin poisoning the only explanation or could she have been given it accidentally?

Doctors who first attended Ethel suspected she'd been accidentally given insulin meant for another patient.

They looked to see if anyone in the neighbouring beds were due to be given insulin in the hours prior to this discovery.

But this mix-up theory was dismissed as no-one next to Ethel was due to receive it during the time frame under scrutiny.

However, as part of the BBC investigation, we found there had in fact been a diabetic patient elsewhere on the ward who was being given insulin in preparation for an operation around the time doctors were trying to save Ethel.

Ethel had been found in a coma at 05:00 and her first injection of glucose to increase her blood sugars was given at 06:15.

The syringe was administered by the ward doctor, who had asked Norris to prepare it for them.

Our review of witness statements and medical notes shows that immediately after this, Norris was preparing another 50ml syringe of dextrose to be injected via a cannula and a 500ml bag of dextrose for a drip.

At the same time, in the same treatment room, another nurse was arranging insulin mixed with saline in a 50ml syringe for the diabetic patient.

The nurse, who had gone to another ward to get the insulin, asked Norris to check the syringe dosage and apologised for not having the ampoule they had drawn it from.

Were the syringes accidentally switched?

Initially, we discounted this scenario because we assumed medical staff would be alerted if a diabetic patient had accidentally been given dextrose instead of insulin.

However, endocrinologist Prof Joel Zonszein, an expert in diabetes, said the amount given would not have caused a severe illness.

"The answer is very different from somebody getting insulin," he said.

"Insulin is much more aggressive. Giving too much sugar does not cause a coma and it will take more that 24 hours until the person goes into a coma. It's completely different."

Prof Zonszein also said the amount of insulin Ethel may have been given accidentally would have produced the high readings in her immunoassay blood test taken five hours later.

He said the drip of dextrose would have masked the insulin, making it harder to notice, but the blood test result would still register a very high level of insulin.

If the syringes were accidentally switched, is that a mix-up rather than a murder?

That still leaves another question: what caused Ethel to fall into a coma in the first place?

Our investigation found all five patients had been prescribed medications, all were on antibiotics and two of the women were on powerful painkillers.

All of these are known to increase the risk of severe hypoglycaemia in frail, elderly patients.

It is possible that a strong opioid prescribed to Ethel for her post-op pain put her in a coma, and insulin meant for somebody else was accidentally given to her before the blood sample, which proved poisoning, was taken.

The Court of Appeal ruled last year on whether naturally-occurring hypoglycaemia could explain the medical collapse of the four patients beyond Ethel Hall but ruled the case put by Norris' team got nowhere close to undermining the safety of his convictions and rejected the appeal on all grounds.

They also rejected Norris' lawyers' attempts to go to the Supreme Court.

An application has been made to the European Court of Human Rights, by Norris' lawyers, but solicitor Rory Hearty says this "hurdle" will take many years.

West Yorkshire Constabulary said its officers worked tirelessly to get justice for the victims and their families.

A statement from the police force said: "In June 2025, the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeals, with the judges saying they had no doubt about the safety of any of the five convictions."

But some members of Ethel's family said the result had not brought them the closure they'd hoped for.

Her son Stuart's wife Helen said: "I don't think it ever will [give us closure] until we know actually, one way or the other, whether he was guilty or not.

"If he's guilty, then fine, that's it.

"But if he's not guilty and he hasn't done it, the evidence that they're trying to keep him inside for, is not enough."

Ethel's family now believe the only thing that will give them peace of mind is a re-trial.

Helen Hall said: "I'm not saying that he should walk free. I'm not saying he should stay behind bars, he should have a fair trial."

Colin Norris's mother June said she will not stop seeking what she believes is justice for her son.

"If you're a mum, you know," she said.

"You'll fight for your kids till the very end."

Additional reporting by Kate Bissell

I'd rather pay thousands on a holiday: Meet the pensioners spending the kids' inheritance

BBC News Mon, 21 Sep 2026 23:01:26 GMT

Happily retired, Sarah Moorhouse is using her private pension "to go places and do nice things at the drop of a hat".

While other retirees with a decent monthly pension income may choose to build up an inheritance for their children, Sarah, 64, and her husband Geoff are opting to spend their money on living life to the max.

"We like going to Scotland," says Sarah, a retired school administrator. "We've been down to Cambridgeshire, which was lovely. We go up to the Lake District quite regularly to a holiday cottage, and we're planning to go to Norfolk."

The couple, who live in the Yorkshire Dales, go on holiday four or five times a year, spending hundreds of pounds each time because, in Sarah's view, "you only have one opportunity at life".

They did recently sell their vintage Sunbeam Alpine sports car. But only so they could replace it with a more modern, sporty two-seater convertible, a Mazda MX-5.

"I'm of an age where I'm going to friends' and acquaintances' funerals, and I think you just need to live life and enjoy it while you can, because it's a very precious commodity," says Sarah.

Sarah and Geoff are part of a global personal finance phenomenon that has been dubbed "skiing", which stands for spending the kids' inheritance. It is challenging the notion that assets will get handed down to the next generation.

One in seven UK parents of children of all ages (15%) now plan to prioritise enjoying their money in their retirement over leaving an inheritance, according to a March report by pension provider Standard Life.

And in the US, the number of people expecting to get an inheritance from their parents dropped to 20% last year, from 25% in 2024, according to a study by financial services firm Northwestern Mutual.

Sarah and Geoff have two adult daughters. One of them, Poppy, tells the BBC that she couldn't be happier that her parents are out and about having fun.

She firmly rejects the notion that she and her sister should expect an inheritance. "To me that's wild. It never even crossed my mind that I'll get money when my mum and dad die. I'd so much rather them do what they want to do."

Mike Ambery, retirement and savings director at Standard Life, believes that the move towards skiing in the UK has been driven by the disappearance of final-salary pensions, which provide guaranteed monthly pension payments that last for as long as the retiree lives.

Instead, more people in the UK now have what are called defined contribution pension pots, which can run out. Ambery argues that it's easier to be generous with a legacy if you know your retirement income will last as long as you need it.

He also points to pensioners wanting to simply enjoy themselves after a life of working.

"It's just having a little bit of indulgence to enjoy life. Let's face it, working life can be very hard for some people."

Not all retirees are well off, of course. In the UK, 16% of pensioners live in poverty, according to the Joseph Rowntree Foundation charity.

The figure for the US is 15.4%, newly released data shows.

But at the same time, UK pensioners have seen their disposable income, excluding housing costs, increase by more than that of non-pensioners over the last three decades, according to the Institute for Fiscal Studies think tank.

Some 69% of retirees in the UK have a private pension in addition to their state one, official figures show. In the US 56% of pensioners have a private pension.

Karen Green, 60, says she has been very upfront with her children. "I have been quite explicit to say there is unlikely to be a legacy because I'm anticipating spending it all."

Originally from Berkshire, Karen has lived in Provence in the south of France for the past 11 years, and spends more than £10,000 a year on holidays.

"This year, I'm going to a yoga retreat. I did one in March in Morocco," she says. "Then in October into November I'm going to Vietnam and Laos to do a little bit of a tour."

She describes herself as semi-retired, as she tops up her private pension by still doing some business consultancy work, the job she used to do full-time.

When it comes to how much money she has per month, she says that her income is the same as when she was working full-time. In addition to her pension and income from her part-time work, she gains 40% of her funds from renting out a property.

But Karen insists she's not "crazy with money" and likes "to get a deal".

Like Sarah Moorhouse she won't get her UK state pension until she is 67. That's currently a standard £12,547.60 a year for people who reached the state pension age after April 2016, but it is due to go up next year.

As a comparison, retirees in the US get state payments known as social security retirement benefits.

The maximum annual amount starting from the "full retirement age" of 67 is $49,824 (£36,993). However, people can choose to take a lower payment from the age of 62.

Matthew Loveless, a vice president at Northwestern Mutual, based in Ohio, says retirees need to be upfront with their adult children, some of whom might be expecting an inheritance that they intend to rely on.

Back in Yorkshire, Sarah says that despite the spending, she has every intention of leaving her kids something. In the meantime she is planning her next holiday. "I've worked hard all my life and I think I deserve to have a bit of free time and to be able to do nice things."

Additional reporting by Miguel Roca-Terry

How the bare nails trend became a class issue

BBC News Fri, 25 Sep 2026 23:31:20 GMT

In recent months, Paloma Buddemeier has watched a stream of people walk into her nail salon with the goal of looking as if they'd never been there at all.

"It's crazy," the owner of Wumman Spa in London says.

These customers still get their nails filed, buffed, and trimmed. "You still do the cuticle, you do the soaking and hydrate everything," says Buddemeier, "but you just put no polish on."

Driving this, she says, is a viral craze for bare-looking nails.

In recent months, artsy shots of glossy naked nails have been flooding social media and taking over fashion runways and red carpets, which some are viewing as the latest symbol of "quiet luxury".

But critics argue the bare nails trend actually says something about class, the hamster wheel of beauty standards, and who gets to define what is considered tasteful.

Nail art's historical and creative roots are linked back to black, Latino, and Asian communities and the suggestion that bare nails are now a sign of high status could stigmatise bold manicures, they say.

"That trend really promotes blankness and this kind of sameness and erasure of culture and identity that is so important to black and brown communities," beauty journalist Kristina Rodulfo tells the BBC.

"They are often called elegant or tasteful, and these are often usually euphemisms that perpetuate white supremacist standards of beauty."

For some, though, the choice is less about a dislike of bold nails and more about simplifying their routine.

Some converts say they're ditching polish as a way of rebelling against an entrenched female beauty standard or to save time and money. Others just love the look. Then, there are some women who've long left their nails alone, amused to find their routine – or lack thereof – suddenly in vogue.

For years, Irish TV presenter Angela Scanlon marched herself to a nail salon every fortnight, a routine that started when she was living in New York in the 2000s. There, she says, manicures were so universal they felt like a uniform. But it soon became a chore.

Scanlon would have everything from thin, shiny shellac to sturdier "Builder In A Bottle" gel manicures layered onto her nails every other week without fail.

"It wasn't like I was in my head going: 'I must go because Dave from Hull is going to be disgusted if I'm on This Morning next week without a full set'," the Radio 2 presenter says. "I just added it to the list of things that we must do... in the way you would wash your hair."

Eventually, in a moment of clarity, Scanlon decided to stop going, in a bid to free up time and mental bandwidth.

"I heard myself saying to people: 'Ugh, my god, I have to go and get my nails done.'

"And I thought: 'I probably don't need to do this anymore'."

Scanlon's posts about her decision to ditch the continuous manicure blew up on Substack and Instagram earlier this year. She seemed to have tapped into a vein.

Simple nails were in the spotlight at New York Fashion Week in February, with Marc Jacobs among those sending his models out polish-less, though some fashionistas argue this is not new.

But beauty magazines have declared "All The Cool Girls Are Quietly Quitting Manicures", that "Bare Nails Are the New Status Symbol" of "Polished Women" and that "Manicures Are No Longer Classy".

And there's a never-ending stream of posts on Insta and TikTok promoting shiny, natural-looking nails, and detailing how you can get them yourself. The look has become so hyped some have gone full circle, booking in salon appointments to mimic it.

At the Wumman Spa nail salon, some of Buddemeier's clients sit in the chair for hours, as nail artists build them hyper-realistic fake nails in sheer, glossy neutrals, à la Zoe Kravitz and Zendaya.

Londoner Khadija says she was once a fan of elaborate nail art but pivoted to bare nails earlier this year.

"It's just really chic. And I love less is more, I love minimalism... less consumerism and just self-care things that you could probably do at home."

Reluctantly joining the bandwagon thanks to the rising cost of living is her friend Emmanuella. "It's just too expensive now," she says.

"I think getting [your] nails done is tacky now, because who's got an hour to waste?" one 25-year-old tells the BBC, adding, "also, I lift weights in the gym, so I don't want to snap a nail and waste money."

But there are those who think the trend - or the way it's being discussed by some - belies something more sinister.

Manicures have been whispering messages about the wearer's position in society for as long as they have existed, according to fashion journalist Suzanne E. Shapiro.

"Women's bodies - and sense of self-presentation - have always held huge political and cultural significance," Shapiro, who wrote Nails: The Story of The Modern Manicure, tells the BBC.

Even back in 13th century Imperial China, the lengthy talons grown by nobility and the delicately carved brass nail shields which usually guarded them were a symbol of a life unmarred by manual labour.

A single layer of the rose-tinted waxy salves which were popular in the 1800s was a sign of vigour and health, but two layers - in an era when cosmetics and artificial beauty were tied to virtue - was the mark of a vain or "loose" woman.

And the red at-home nail lacquer, released by Revlon in the early 1930s, was a badge of honour for modern women rebelling against that kind of oppressive judgement.

But it was women of colour who really made manicures an accessible and fashionable form of self-expression, historians say.

Entertainer Josephine Baker, disco icons Diana Ross and Donna Summer, and Olympic gold-medal-winning sprinter Florence Griffith-Joyner - whose dramatic acrylic sets often distracted headline writers from her record-setting performances - have all pioneered nail art.

And when waves of Vietnamese refugees gave rise to the nail bar in the 1970s, professional manicures were no longer the preserve of the rich.

But, like many luxuries, as they became more popular and more accessible to the masses, the wealthy began pivoting – a textbook example of behaviour known as "counter signalling", Rudolfo says.

"The same way that logo bags are considered gauche or quiet luxury is more aspirational, bare nails are considered the trend now.

"The examples are almost always white women or celebrities... [and] they'll often conflate class and taste with that bareness."

Others point out bare nails often demand their own time-consuming and costly routine.

"The irony in all this is these natural nails are not natural either," Shapiro says. "They also require a lot of grooming and sometimes pretty premiere services."

Few would argue there aren't valid feminist questions for the beauty industry to answer, around unrealistic standards for example, but the largely female-run nail sector also feels empowering for many women.

"I feel like nail care has very much had a 'for women, by women' sort of ethos around it," Shapiro says. "The first salon opened in New York City was owned by a woman, and she was a remarkably independent one... a lot of the first entrepreneurs offering product lines, opening salons were women."

Hampton admits she's saddened by the way trends have been – and continue to be - weaponised.

"We're taking the fun out of nails... Anyone should be able to wear what they like - nail polish or bare nails," she says. "Why is there an argument? Why is there beef?"

Scanlon too is a little baffled.

"For me, it's like, just stop judging ourselves and everybody else," she says. "Some people like to have the nails done, some people don't.

"I suppose the question that I was posing was, is it doing anything for you?

"The truth of it is: it's not that deep."

Your child has left home. Here's why it's time to stop checking up on them

BBC News Fri, 25 Sep 2026 23:03:51 GMT

Luke felt overwhelmed with both pride and grief after dropping his son off at university for the first time.

"It feels like a brutal adjustment," he says.

"After 18 years of seeing him every day and taking care of him, I miss him so much and I don't really know what to do with myself."

Like other parents we have spoken to, Luke (not his real name) and his wife have felt compelled to regularly check a Facebook group for parents and carers with children living in the same halls of residence, as well as a university-wide version with more than 2,000 members.

At first, being in these groups felt helpful for practical information, particularly in the weeks before his son headed to university, Luke says. But now they're feeding his anxiety.

"People will post things like: 'Is it normal to spend so much time in your room?'; 'I'm worried my daughter is struggling to make friends'; 'My child isn't replying to messages - how often are people hearing from theirs?'"

There have also been questions about Amazon parcel logistics, requests to borrow cereal bowls and what tog duvet other people's children were given.

Luke thinks these kinds of social media groups have fuelled his temptation to keep checking his son's location on a tracking app "to make sure he is going out enough and finding friends".

Because his messages and calls go largely unanswered, Luke will also watch videos posted on the university's social media accounts, hoping to catch a glimpse of his son among the throngs of Freshers. Other parents have sheepishly confessed they're doing the same.

Across universities, some enterprising parents have set up the sort of WhatsApp group chats you'd more typically find being used when children are at school. Only rather than asking after lost jumpers and what day PE is, these groups might be used to try to parent long-distance.

"Sometimes parents send their child to university and they're not even worried, but then these group chats create a worry that something might be wrong," says Rayyah Uddin, 20, a third-year student at the University of Nottingham.

She knows of WhatsApp group chats being set up by parents of first-year students at her university and has also seen parents use TikTok to share their worries about their child not making friends, and asking other parents for their help.

"These are issues the students should really be figuring out for themselves, and it is better if parents try and talk to their child rather than immediately jump to other parents," she says.

Not hearing from your child all the time isn't necessarily a cause for concern - "they might just be having a really good time and are getting absorbed into university life," Rayyah adds.

Parent social media groups can be useful, according to psychologist Charlotte Armitage, but not when they are used to share private difficulties, track movements or ask questions that the student is capable of asking themselves.

"Constant checking, tracking or intervening may soothe the parent in the short term, but it can inadvertently communicate to the young adult: 'I am not sure you can cope without me.'"

"Of course, where there is a credible safeguarding concern, a significant change in behaviour, or a known risk to their wellbeing, parents should act."

A big part of going to university is about being independent, says Manchester University student Archie Forde, 19, who has heard stories of parents "pinging phones at 3am and calling their kids 12 times a week".

He thinks parents turning to social media groups have "mostly fair concerns" but are going about things in the wrong way.

The groups can be "echo chambers where everyone just spins each other out about their kids", he says, and suggests having a proper conversation with your child about boundaries, before university starts.

Every family will have different ideas about what is overbearing, but a student shouldn't have the worry of choosing between "cutting back parents' communication and ruining that relationship, or responding to a flurry of texts at pre-drinks and detaching yourself from the social situation".

Writing a letter or sending a parcel - without the expectation of a getting a response - could be a good way to let your child know you're thinking of them, "without it feeling like a demand", says child psychologist Laverne Antrobus.

Perhaps negotiate a time to check in with them, "and be prepared to not always have long conversations," she says.

And when you do speak to your child, "make sure your curiosity is genuine, rather than half-informed by the surveillance you've been doing".

"Already knowing where they've been and what they've been up to makes for an unrewarding conversation with them and children are bright - they will know."

Rayyah says she looks forward to properly catching up when she goes home.

"If you've spent months being closely monitored it might feel as if you haven't really been away or gained any independence; it could feel frustrating."

Having seen three children off to university, Nichola McClellan wants to reassure parents that it does get easier. Based in Cheshire, she shares her experience of being an "empty nester" on social media.

"It's a huge emotional adjustment after years of your life revolving around your children, so we need to give ourselves time and permission to miss them.

"I think back to how lost I felt. I didn't know who I was without the kids.

"They're learning how to leave," she says, "but we're learning how to let go."

Rather than expect constant contact, Nichola sends "little no-pressure messages" on their family WhatsApp group.

"'Love you', 'proud of you' - things that don't require an answer."

They have a proper catch-up roughly once a week, and she has learned not to take it personally if she doesn't hear from them.

"Sometimes that is a really good sign, it means they're getting on with this new life you've spent all those years preparing them for.

"You don't stop being a parent when they leave home - but you do get the opportunity to rediscover parts of yourself that perhaps got a little lost along the way. There really is so much to look forward to."

The treasured 'eternal snow' on this tropical island is about to disappear forever

BBC News Fri, 25 Sep 2026 22:12:48 GMT

The mountains of Papua are not far from the equator, but they've been topped with "eternal snow" for centuries.

The peaks in this Indonesian region on the world's second-largest island, just north of Australia, have offered scientists countless insights into the Earth's climate history.

They're also the epicentre of the spiritual universe for many Papuans - a Mecca or a Vatican, as one activist puts it.

But now, nearly all the snow is gone.

A century ago, the 300km (190-mile) stretch of the Sudirman Range had snow and permanent ice on all four of its major peaks.

But now there are only small areas around Puncak Jaya, also known as Carstensz Pyramid, with any snow at all. These are expected to entirely disappear in a year or two.

Glacier cover around the peak has shrunk from nearly 1,900 hectares (4,700 acres) in the 19th Century to about 16 hectares (40 acres) today. Almost entire glaciers have vanished within a human lifetime.

"There is a profound unfairness in this," says Marie Šabacká, a Czech glacier ecologist who travelled to Puncak Jaya last March in a bid to be among the last scientists to study Papua's "eternal snow".

She says the tropical glaciers in Papua are unique because they are separated from other glacier systems by thousands of kilometres. Papua is home to the "last remaining tropical ice" between the Andes and Himalayas.

Ice cores taken from the slopes of Puncak Jaya preserve a record of climate history.

Scientists can use them to obtain information about atmospheric conditions in the region and understand changes in the planet's warmest ocean waters that surround the island - the tropical Pacific and Western Pacific Warm pool.

But this archive is disappearing before scientists have had time to fully study it.

The retreat of Papua's glaciers is driven by the same forces affecting ice around the world, Šabacká notes, a warming atmosphere caused by human activity, including the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas.

As temperatures rise, the freezing point moves higher up mountains, so more precipitation falls as rain instead of snow, even in places that once saw regular snowfall.

El Niño events can accelerate this process, while local factors such as cloud cover, snowfall and mountain topography influence its pace.

The mountains in Papua are just 450km (280 miles) south of the equator, where "permanent ice can survive only at very high altitudes and within a narrow range of climatic conditions", Šabacká says.

A small increase in temperature, a higher freezing point or shift from snowfall to rainfall can determine whether a glacier survives at all, she adds.

The glaciers' retreat is evidence the Earth has been warming over a long period - and their disappearance "removes both a biological habitat and part of a culturally significant landscape".

At least five groups of Indigenous people have had strong spiritual ties to Puncak Jaya for generations.

The Moni people refer to it as Mbainggela, and believe their ancestors watch over the mountain. To the Amungme people, the range is known as Nemangkawi, or the "White Arrow".

"Parents and grandparents prayed their children would have hearts like the White Arrow, never straying from the proper path," says Elfrida Natkime, a young Amungme woman. "It symbolises honesty, purity and moral integrity."

According to traditional Amungme beliefs, Nemangkawi symbolises how people should live.

Amungme environmental activist Adolfina Kum stresses how important the peak is to her people - and how traditions and cultural foundations risk being shattered as the ice melts.

"How would Muslims feel if Mecca were destroyed? How would Catholics feel if Rome or the Vatican were destroyed?" she asks. "For the Amungme people, that is what it feels like when Nemangkawi is destroyed."

For many Indigenous Papuans, the disappearance of the glacier is not an isolated event.

The discovery of vast copper and gold deposits transformed the region during the 20th Century, and the development of extractive industrial projects have reshaped parts of the landscape.

Entire mountain faces have been excavated and roads, industrial infrastructure and settlements have transformed surrounding valleys.

Papuans say the development has brought jobs, roads, education and economic opportunities, but also environmental degradation and decades of social conflict. Some have lost access to their ancestral lands as mining expanded.

The BBC has approached Freeport, which operates Papua's Grasberg mine, one of the world's largest gold and copper operations, for comment.

"Every time I see the mountains, I feel amazed, but I also feel sadness," says Elfrida Natkime. "Since the company came, I have seen the exploitation. But the development has also provided a livelihood for many people."

As local communities watch their sacred landscapes change, scientists and explorers are racing to document what is left.

Using drones and three-dimensional mapping techniques, Danish researcher Klaus Thymann and his team have created a detailed model of what remains.

From the early 2000s to 2025, the glaciated area has receded by 95%, he says. "There's almost no ice left. Those are the facts."

Thymann says glaciers are "incredibly powerful" as indicators of climate change.

"When people hear that something described as 'eternal' is disappearing, it triggers a reaction," he explains.

Adolfina Kum believes communities "lose an important source of strength" when sacred mountains, forests or ancestral places are disturbed.

"I often describe it as pulling out the roots of a tree. Once the roots are removed, the tree loses its foundation."

Copying others can help young orangutans build a broad diet

New Scientist September 24, 2026

Young orangutans who spend little time working out for themselves how to build a broad diet can partly compensate by watching how other orangutans choose what to eat.

The findings suggest that orangutans have different strategies for developing broad survival skills, says Revathe Thillaikumar at the Max Planck Institute of Animal Behavior in Germany.

Young orangutans acquire a substantial body of knowledge before they can survive independently, which they must do by the time they are 8.5 years old. The country has an ambitious list of areas it wants to master by the centenary of its founding in 2049 including AI, quantum, fusion and space, and while Leoni says it will overtake the US in some of these, it can’t hope to master them all.

Kevin Sagis at the University of Texas at Austin says the benefits of reusable rockets are simple: they’re cheap. “The cost of the Saturn V rocket in the Apollo days – that we threw away after every launch – was about a billion dollars. The SLS is about $5 billion. It’s just not sustainable,” he says.

Sagis sees strong parallels between the unfolding reusable rocket space race, and the cold war space race between the Soviet Union and the US. China has many of the same advantages now that the Soviet Union had then: a one-party government that can coral huge resources and single-mindedly chase a target unswayed by election cycles and changing leaders, a strong motivation for success and loose regulation.

See Helen Sharman at New Scientist Live 2026

SpaceX is often said to be taking a new, extremely capitalist approach – testing fast, failing often and rapidly reiterating – that’s more like Silicon Valley than traditional aerospace. But Sagis says that while this is an advantage, it’s also a return to the bold Apollo days at NASA. “It’s sort of come full circle,” he says. And he believes that it’s an approach that is paying off for SpaceX.

“What they’re aspiring to do is something audacious. Their talent and their expertise is exceptional. If you look at their track record, every mission is better than the previous one. I’d be shocked if we don’t look back at this and assess it as a success,” says Sagis.

But Sagis also sees risks in the US system. He warns that it will be important to learn from the cold war race and not lose interest or pull funding and scrap plans if the US lags behind at one point. Instead, the focus should be on the long-term benefits of advanced space travel. Russia put the first satellite into orbit, then the first animal, man and woman, says Sagis – but the US still put the first man on the moon.

“It’s the hare and the tortoise,” says Sagis.

China also has an advantage shared by the Soviet Union in that it is more tolerant of risk. An expensive failure or the injury or death of an astronaut could put an end to space ambitions, but Sagis sees that as less likely to occur in China, where politicians are less concerned with public perception and winning elections. “Space isn’t risk-free, right? If you wanna do something audacious, you have to accept some risk,” says Sagis.

Some variants of another rocket under development, Long March 10, will also be partially reusable, and a test earlier this year recovered the first stage of a Long March 10 at sea.

Ellis says that China may not be as open about its progress as SpaceX is being, perhaps distorting public perception of its capabilities. Advertisement

What you need to know here is that CRISPR stands for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. In other words, an area of DNA where there are lots of short repeated sequences separated by non-repeating DNA.

Free newsletter

Such repeats were first spotted in E. coli in 1987 by researchers in Japan and later dubbed CRISPR by Francisco Mojica at the University of Alicante in Spain. In 2005, Mojica reported that the pieces of non-repeating DNA match bits of viral DNA.

He correctly deduced this must be some kind of bacterial immune system, but it took years of research by many different teams to uncover how it works, with a protein called CRISPR-Cas9 playing a key role. The real breakthrough came in 2012 when Jennifer Doudna at the University of California, Berkeley, and her colleagues worked out how to create pieces of RNA that can hook up with the CRISPR-Cas9 protein and guide it to destroy specific sequences. This was the start of CRISPR gene editing, which has revolutionised biology.

So it is really intriguing that Claude has found a similar set of repeats in bacteria-infecting viruses. It was already known that some viruses have CRISPR systems, but this is something different that is worth studying further.

In terms of significance, however, Claude’s work is comparable to the 1987 discovery in E. coli, not the 2012 breakthrough that won a Nobel prize. And with regard to AI contributions to biology, Claude’s work isn’t even close to being in the same league as DeepMind’s AlphaFold system for predicting protein structure, which is proving to be truly transformative.

Will Claude’s discovery lead to powerful new gene-editing tools? The context here is that we have discovered many CRISPR variants, along with a few other natural systems – most notably bridge recombinases – that could be useful for gene editing.

What’s more, proteins such as CRISPR-Cas9 have now been extensively altered and evolved in the lab to make them better for gene editing. For instance, base editors – which are already saving lives – are CRISPR proteins engineered to change a single letter at a time without cutting DNA strands, as the original Cas9 protein does.

It is impressive that Claude has identified what the Anthropic team is calling array-associated reverse transcriptases, or ART. And it is possible, if unlikely, that this viral system works in a unique way that allows us to do things that cannot be done with existing genetic tools. But there is a lot more work to be done to find this out, and at best the outcome will be one more gene-editing tool in a rapidly expanding set.

See Jim Al-Khalili at New Scientist Live 2026

Mizhaev says he stumbled across the property, rather than setting out to find it, while experimenting with polyhedral surfaces in computer-aided design (CAD) software. The underlying structure isn’t entirely new – it is something Mizhaev first described it in 2020.

But the new work gives all 24 vertices integer coordinates, alongside equations that allow other mathematicians to check the shape, ensuring that the faces are flat, the surface closes properly and no parts accidentally intersect (which can be a common issue in shapes like this).

The discovery is an interesting one, but should be seen as a piece of a larger puzzle, rather than an entirely new innovation, says Lars Schewe at the University of Edinburgh, UK. “It’s more a small piece that we didn’t have before,” says Schewe. The result doesn’t overturn existing conjectures, he says, but “constructing these has always been a difficult task”.

Physicists have created a 3D shape called the cosmohedron, which can be used to reconstruct the quantum wavefunction of the universe – and potentially do away with the idea of space-time as the underlying fabric of the universe

The reason it is so difficult to construct such shapes is that there is no reliable way to do so. One brute-force approach involves writing down a huge set of equations specifying where every vertex can sit and how all the faces must fit together, says Schewe – but that approach can rapidly become practically impossible to solve.

Researchers instead often depend on computer searches, geometric intuition or even physical models. Mizhaev used ChatGPT to help with some verification calculations and to write Python scripts for the new version of his shape. But he says the original shape was developed in 2020, before he began using ChatGPT.

For Schewe, the gap between describing which parts of a shape can connect and actually building it is what makes these problems interesting. “I can tell you these are the rules,” he says. “But when I try to build it and I try to draw it, I can’t do it.”

arXiv DOI: 10.48550/arXiv.2609.17700
