The first season of Heroes is almost perfect – here’s why

New Scientist September 25, 2026

You rarely appreciate the significance of a moment while you are still living through it. But that is exactly what happened to me, 20 years ago this month, when a show called Heroes first aired.

As you may have gathered from the title, it followed ordinary people whose genes have blessed (or cursed) them with extraordinary abilities, from time travel to telepathy. Made in the wake of the Human Genome Project, it was an elaborately plotted mystery, blending comic book aesthetics with a glancing interest in evolution. And for the past two decades, it has had the dubious honour of becoming a byword for failure: after a stellar first season, Heroes limped its way through three more outings of questionable quality.

The minute I saw Heroes, I knew I was changed. It was the first TV series to set a fire in my head, at age 10. If I wasn’t watching it, I was talking about it; if I wasn’t talking about it, I was thinking about it. Chances are I was probably dreaming about it, too. But the extent of my obsession, combined with that notorious drop-off in quality, has stopped me from rewatching it or its spin-off, Heroes Reborn, in the years since.

Advertisement

The 4 best science-fiction shows of 2026 so far

That changed last month with the sad news that Hayden Panettiere, who played the show’s most iconic character, Claire Bennet, had died. Since then, I have been revisiting that almost-perfect first season – and you should do the same.

Even before its narrative spiralled out of control, Heroes had a sprawling ensemble of leads. Claire, a 16-year-old cheerleader living in Texas, was the most consequential. Her body rapidly regenerates its cells when injured, making her practically indestructible – and attracting the attention of Sylar, a superpowered serial killer. Meanwhile, geneticist Mohinder Suresh seeks to complete his late father’s work by contacting similarly gifted individuals, such as Peter Petrelli, a hospice nurse who dreams of flying, and Isaac Mendez, who can paint the future when under the influence of heroin.

Heroes, like Isaac, had a knack for striking images. Its first season is full of them: a cracked pair of horn-rimmed glasses; an office worker from Tokyo teleporting to Times Square in New York; a nuclear blast that Claire, somehow, can help prevent. “Save the cheerleader, save the world,” time traveller Hiro Nakamura tells Peter. This uncanny ability to distil essence and theme into potent symbols or phrases was the series’ own superpower. Not to mention the music: a whirling updraft of drones and chimes, featuring ethereal vocals from L. Shankar, it became a landmark score in television history.

Fabulous time travel novel is part-thriller and part-romance

It’s easy to dismiss Heroes as a Lost-alike: it was perhaps the best in a flurry of shows trying to emulate that legendary series, right down to its characteristic blend of science fiction and mysticism. But like Lost, Heroes explains a lot about what high-concept TV has become today – and has admirable qualities that its successors are thoroughly lacking.

It is a wholly original idea from creator Tim Kring, albeit one inflected with the tropes of classic comic books. It is also stuffed with action – certain plotlines, like psychic cop Matt Parkman’s collaboration with the FBI in the hunt for Sylar, could have been a show all on their own. And it proves that a show that captures true brilliance, however infrequently, will always be worth watching.

So I implore you to watch (or rewatch) the first season of Heroes. You may be averse to starting a series known to nosedive, but, as I have explained to many sceptical friends over the years, it is worth the hurt. And upon rewatching with an adult’s eyes, I have appreciated just how special Panettiere was as Claire. Her performance deserves to be remembered as one of the best of the 2000s.

Jarrod Bennett stole $2700 ring to propose before returning it to Nelson jewellery store

New Zealand Herald September 26, 2026

Jarrod Bennett has been sentenced to prison for a burglary spree that included an almost $3000 ring he had planned to propose to his girlfriend with. Photo / 123rf

A burglar who stole a $2700 ring from a main street jewellery store was sorry to upset the retail assistant, but his motives were driven by love.

Jarrod Bennett had planned to propose to his girlfriend, but when stopped by police he told them he “must have had a twin out there wearing the same clothing” and it was probably him they were after.

“He stole it because he wanted to propose to his partner. It was spontaneous behaviour,” defence lawyer Mark Dollimore said.

The 26-year-old was sentenced in the Nelson District Court to just over two years in prison for the burglary, part of a spree in which Bennett stole items worth $8000.

They included the ring, which Bennett returned but it was by then devalued by half, two brand new Samsung cellphones from a retail outlet, alcohol and cartons of cigarettes.

“I’ll pay it all back,” Bennett said via video link from a prison cell, where he had been in custody for five months awaiting sentence.

Because it would take him about 16 years to repay the amount, Judge Tony Snell did not impose a reparation order.

He said all victims were businesses likely with insurance cover, but accepted they would have excesses to cover.

Bennett had earlier admitted charges of robbery by assault and three shoplifting charges committed in March and April this year.

Dollimore said Bennett’s files showed a “chronic history” of mental health challenges, but Judge Snell said he “didn’t appear affected by mental health” at the time.

He accepted Bennett had an “enduring mental illness” but there was no link between that and the offending.

He acknowledged Bennett’s “well-crafted apology letter” was genuine.

“You make no excuses for what you did and you say that when you reflected on the victims you now recognise they were affected, particularly the woman in the jewellery store,” Judge Snell said.

Bennett’s spree began on March 31 with the theft of two bottles of brandy from a liquor store and ended days later with the theft of the ring.

On April 2, Bennett went into a central Nelson Spark retail store, asked to see two cellphones worth $5010, and fled with them when they were placed on the counter.

On the morning of April 4 Bennett stole a $949 gaming console from The Warehouse in Nelson. He asked to see it, then grabbed it and ran when the staff member brought it out from behind the counter.

Earlier that day, he stole tobacco and cartons of cigarettes worth between $1500 and $2000 from a Nelson dairy.

As the cashier tried to stop Bennett, they were smacked on the hand and threatened.

Contact the Open Justice team

The offence formed the lead charge of robbery by assault, but Judge Snell accepted there was low-level violence.

Later that morning, Bennett went to Pascoes jewellery store in central Nelson and asked to see a particular ring.

The ring, worth $2700, was placed on the counter but Bennett grabbed it and ran off.

He later returned it, but its value had halved, police said.

Judge Snell said they were “brazen thefts” of high-value goods taken by a similar method each time.

“You asked to look at the item, then fled, never to be seen again.”

Bennett would be eligible for parole after serving a third of his two-year and two-month prison sentence.

Dollimore told NZME outside court there was no word on Bennett’s pending nuptials, and that the relationship was “likely over”.

Tracy Neal is a Nelson-based Open Justice reporter at NZME. She was previously RNZ’s regional reporter in Nelson-Marlborough and has covered general news, including court and local government for the Nelson Mail.

A “strong cold front” will sweep across Aotearoa today, bringing wet, windy and – for parts of the south – snowy conditions.

MetService has warned severe gales and heavy rain are possible in central New Zealand, while heavy snow is expected in the South Island.

A raft of severe weather warnings is in place, with an orange heavy snow warning for Canterbury High Country and Canterbury Plains south of Arthur’s Pass, an orange heavy rain warning for the Tararua Range and an orange strong wind warning for Wairarapa, Tararua District and south Hawke’s Bay.

Parts of the Canterbury High Country are under a heavy snow watch, Buller has a heavy rain watch, and Horowhenua, Kāpiti Coast, Marlborough Sounds and Hawke’s Bay north of Hastings have strong wind watches.

MetService meteorologist Luis Fernandes said today is “quite busy in terms of weather in New Zealand”.

“There is a strong cold front that’s going to be sweeping over basically all of New Zealand as the day progresses,” Fernandes told the Herald.

“That strong cold front pushes across the South Island in the morning, and then in the afternoon and evening it moves across the North Island.”

Contact the Herald newsroom

With many families expected to be travelling for the start of the school holidays, NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA) warned motorists in the central South Island to prepare for road closures and weather-related delays because of heavy snow.

“Carrying warm clothing, food and water is advised on inland journeys in case of lengthy travel delays or detours,” NZTA said.

“When snow or ice is on the road, motorists are urged to reduce their speeds, increase their following distances, avoid sudden braking or turning movements and to stay as visible as possible.”

Fernandes said the snow will particularly affect South Islanders travelling inland, with snow set to drop to about 200m.

He said the cold front is expected to lose steam as it moves north, but it’s still looking like “another relatively wet and windy day” for Auckland.

The good news is the weather, for the most part, is expected to “become a lot more settled” on Monday and into the middle of next week.

While daylight saving spells the start of the spring and summer months, Fernandes said it will “take time for things to start warming up”.

“Although we have officially entered spring and daylight saving certainly makes it feel a little bit more like summer because of the longer evenings, there is a long tail to spring in the cooler weather in New Zealand.”

The cold front is set to bring extreme temperatures in some areas. Napier will have a high of 22C today and a low of 3C, while Christchurch will hit 14C after a freezing low of -1C.

Auckland faces a high of 18C and a low of 10C, Tauranga 19C and 6C, Wellington 15C and 5C, and Dunedin 11C and 6C.

Immigration NZ says Reece Salmon did not disclose UK prison sentence on NZeTA

New Zealand Herald September 26, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

A British fraudster who helped swindle elderly New Zealanders out of more than $400,000 entered the country after failing to disclose a recent prison sentence.

The case has raised questions about how much Immigration New Zealand relies on travellers to accurately report their criminal histories.

Reece Salmon entered New Zealand in July 2024 despite having served a three-year-and-nine-month prison sentence in Britain for violent offending linked to London’s Easy Cash Gang.

After arriving in New Zealand, he became involved in a British-run scam that defrauded elderly Kiwis of more than $400,000 in cash and gold.

Salmon was murdered in London this month after being stabbed in Clerkenwell, north London. He was 28.

Salmon’s case has raised the question of how someone with a recent violent criminal history was allowed into the country.

Immigration New Zealand (INZ) said Salmon did not disclose that prison sentence when applying for a New Zealand Electronic Travel Authority (NZeTA) before arriving in the country.

He also failed to declare the conviction when completing his New Zealand Traveller Declaration.

INZ director visa Sarah Clifford said his NZeTA would likely have been refused had he disclosed the conviction.

“The immigration system is inherently founded on honest and truthful self-declarations,” Clifford said.

“People seeking to enter or remain in New Zealand are expected to provide complete, accurate and truthful information.”

Clifford said INZ makes more than a million visa-related decisions each year and “cannot verify every application in full”.

She said travellers who declare a prison sentence of 12 months or more within the previous 10 years are unable to continue with an NZeTA request and must instead apply for a visa, where officials consider whether a character waiver or special direction should be granted.

INZ said it did not become aware of Salmon’s offshore prison sentence until he came to the attention of New Zealand Police.

Immigration lawyer Marcus Beveridge said he was surprised Salmon’s previous prison sentence was not detected before he travelled to New Zealand.

“Given membership of the Five Eyes security programme and all those sorts of things and the intelligence sharing, it surprises me that someone who was so recently incarcerated for that sort of term wasn’t picked up before he even got on the airplane,” Beveridge said.

According to Beveridge, a prison sentence of that length would ordinarily create significant hurdles for somebody seeking entry to New Zealand.

He said a person would generally need to apply for a visa and have immigration officials consider whether they should receive a character waiver or special direction.

Beveridge said some offenders had historically sought to evade immigration scrutiny by changing their names and obtaining new passports, although modern biometric systems had made that more difficult.

According to Beveridge, cases such as Salmon’s were uncommon and INZ’s screening system generally worked well.

“We have a pretty robust system that I think is generally very effective,” Beveridge said.

“Sure, there are a few things that fall through the cracks. But normally it comes out in the wash.”

Seal in the city: ‘Very determined’ visitor stops traffic in downtown Wellington

New Zealand Herald September 26, 2026

Onlookers were delighted to see the seal crossing the road.

A “very determined little seal” was spotted crossing the road in downtown Wellington last night, with traffic briefly coming to a halt as police ushered the creature to safety.

Wellington local Wendy said she spotted the seal on Waterloo Quay near Hnry Stadium when she was driving into the city on Saturday evening.

“I saw these flashing lights of a police car and I actually thought, ‘oh they’re doing a breath check’,” she said.

“Then I saw these young women were stepping out onto the road, and I was like, ‘well that’s a bit odd’.”

It was then that she saw a seal trying to make its way across the road towards Wellington Station.

“I was like, oh my goodness! I slowed right down and stopped. That’s when I took out the camera.

“That part of town is only really busy either before or after a game at Hnry Stadium. I’ve never seen a seal in that part of town before.”

She said the police officer used cones to try to “persuade” the seal back in the other direction towards the water, while others were acting as “seal guardians”.

“I do wonder, there must be a family of seals somewhere looking for it, but it was heading right towards the train station, and it was very determined.”

After realising she was herself holding up a bit of traffic, Wendy got back in her car and drove away.

“I don’t know if it’s a good omen, but you know there’s $10 million going on Powerball, so I did go and buy a ticket. Fingers crossed.”

Seals and other marine mammals occasionally pop up in unusual places across New Zealand.

In December last year, a heavily pregnant sea lion was found taking a snooze on a suburban Dunedin doorstep.

In 2022, a fur seal chased a cat into a Mount Maunganui marine biologist’s lounge.

The Department of Conservation has asked people to report sightings of seals, fur seals or sea lions on or near roads, which can help “map hotspots and better understand the risks”.

The hidden toll of isolation on Canterbury farm women

New Zealand Herald September 26, 2026

Anthea Rolfe says loneliness is common among farming women in New Zealand.

Rural women have a suicide rate about 1.2 times higher than women living in urban areas, but research into the wellbeing of farming women remains limited. Canterbury women shared their experiences of loneliness, isolation and the barriers to seeking help with Rafaella Melo.

Long before most people’s morning alarms have sounded, farmer Anthea Rolfe is starting her working day.

For much of the farming season, she begins at 3.45am on a large-scale North Canterbury dairy farm, where she lives and has experienced the toll of loneliness and isolation.

“Loneliness is much more common among farming women than people realise,” she told the Herald.

She said several days could pass without leaving the farm except for necessities.

“There have been periods where life became very much work, home, sleep and repeat,” Rolfe said.

“You can be surrounded by people at work but still feel socially isolated because you don’t have much of a life or connection outside the farm.”

Contact our South Island newsroom

Raised in Auckland, she knew little about farming when an opportunity brought her into the industry almost 20 years ago.

“The isolation was probably something I hadn’t anticipated,” Rolfe said.

“You can love living rurally and love farming while still finding aspects of it isolating.”

At times, she said, physical isolation, long and unsociable hours and limited interaction outside work affected her mental health, leaving her feeling “disconnected” and “stuck in the same routine”.

Connection became part of the solution.

Rolfe founded the online community Females in Farming in 2024, which now has more than 36,000 followers.

“Loneliness and isolation are definitely issues I’ve seen and heard about among women in farming through Females in Farming,” she said.

“What does stand out is how often women relate when we talk about the less glamorous side of rural life. Often the response is essentially, ‘I thought I was the only one’, which says a lot in itself.”

In a 2018 Farmstrong survey of 786 farming women, 40% said workload or trying to fit everything in had a large or greater negative impact on their wellbeing.

Fatigue or exhaustion was cited by 34%, insufficient time for themselves by 32% and not enough time off the farm by 29%.

Chief executive Gerard Vaughan said he expected many of those findings to emerge in a new nationwide study of farming women’s mental health and wellbeing being undertaken by Massey and Lincoln universities.

Although support was available through programmes such as Rural Women, Dairy Women’s Network, Farming Mums, Agri-Women’s Development Trust, and Farming Women Tairāwhiti, Vaughan believed something was still missing.

“A big gap is services that give women a break from the constant pressures of being involved in the farm, supporting their husbands and looking after children.”

Health New Zealand Mentally Well director Lisa Gestro said evidence showed people living in rural areas could face unique challenges affecting wellbeing, including isolation and longer travel distances to health services.

She said suicide rates among rural women were about 1.2 times those of women living in urban areas.

“Isolation can be a significant issue for some people living and working in rural communities, particularly where geographic distance, parenting, caring and work responsibilities, seasonal pressures or limited opportunities for social connection create barriers to seeking support.”

She said free support was available through Health NZ’s Access and Choice services, and rural residents could also access 1737 and other telephone and online mental health services when face-to-face services were not available.

“We are implementing initiatives to improve access to care closer to home.”

Farmer Lynda Brodie knows the importance of accessing help.

She grew up in Timaru and was about 30 and pregnant when she moved to her husband’s farm in Rangitata.

She went from a life where she rarely walked down the street without bumping into someone she knew to a place where she initially felt she did not belong.

“I was a townie in a rural situation,” she said.

Most women around her were about a decade older and friends and family were at least a 40-minute drive away.

Brodie would stay days in a row without leaving the farm.

People visited, but she said they were often there to see her husband, Russell Brodie.

“I think it was really easy for me to feel invisible here,” she said.

“I felt really lonely.”

Brodie would leave the radio playing throughout the day to fill the silence and stop herself dwelling on negative thoughts.

She did not recognise it as a mental health issue at the time.

Instead, she got busy.

“There was always plenty to do, so I just completely distracted myself away from any thoughts or feelings that were uncomfortable.”

Brodie remembers a sense of constant exhaustion.

“It just seemed like it was relentless and constant, and there was no time to breathe.”

Nearly 30 years after moving to the farm, some barriers to connection remained.

Phone reception inside the house can be unreliable. In winter, Brodie said she would not make a phone call in the evening as it meant standing outside in the cold to get reception.

“There are little bits ... like that that stand in the way of you actively seeking connection.”

Farm life itself could also be relentless.

“You are always on. There are no weekends or breaks,” she said.

“If you want to have time off, you have to create it.”

Brodie said it was easy for women to put themselves at the bottom of the list while caring for children, animals, the farm and their families.

She spent years reading self-development books and listening to podcasts but did not ask others for help.

“Rural women are very capable and strong, and so to actually reach out to someone for help feels like it’s kind of admitting that you’re not as capable and strong as you thought you were.”

It was not until about five years ago that Brodie discovered life coaching and began changing how she dealt with isolation and her wellbeing.

She then trained as a coach to help other women in similar situations.

“We think we are the problem because we’re unaware that our neighbours have the same challenges,” she said.

“We’re not aware of that because we’re so busy kind of surviving, and we’re not talking to each other about it.”

Brodie still lives on the same farm but now deliberately builds connection into her life.

Once a week, she drives to Christchurch to care for her 16-month-old grandson Otis, spending Wednesday night there and returning home Thursday.

“It’s my day off. It’s something that I never had on the farm before.”

She also belongs to business networking groups and has a morning routine that includes meditation, journaling, stretching and a cup of tea on her veranda.

After three decades on the farm, Brodie said she had learned to embrace more of what she has instead of looking at what she doesn’t.

She encouraged women to learn to recognise their early signs of stress and identify people they felt safe talking to.

“Often we don’t reach out until we’re right on the edge,” Brodie said.

“We can change. I’m 59 and only learned this stuff five years ago.”

Rafaella Melo is a multimedia journalist with more than 10 years’ experience in Brazil. She spent nearly two years reporting for Hawke’s Bay Today before joining the NZ Herald’s Christchurch team in 2026.

Elevate Content’s Benji Smith builds Tauranga real estate marketing business

New Zealand Herald September 26, 2026

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

This is a modal window.

Beginning of dialog window. Escape will cancel and close the window.

End of dialog window.

This is a modal window. This modal can be closed by pressing the Escape key or activating the close button.

Benji Smith left school at 17 with $6 in his bank and a camera he had just bought.

Eighteen months later, he says he’s made six figures and has enough for a house deposit.

The Tauranga entrepreneur says he is now preparing to buy his first home, with money he made through Elevate Content, his real estate marketing business.

“When my pre-approval came back accepted, and we could put an offer on the table, that was kind of a ‘s***, this is actually getting serious now’.

“Just turned 19 and put an offer on the table. A lot of people don’t buy a house till they’re 30, or ever.”

Smith started photography at school, taking photos of the rugby team, school balls, and friends.

He saw an opportunity in real estate, as agents needed fresh content for every property listing, and turned his hobby into a business.

Smith began cold-calling agents around Tauranga after his Year 12 exams and offering free content shoots.

He had no clients when he left school, but the work experience built relationships and a portfolio.

“My goal was that I just wanted to specialise in this one thing, and I wanted to do it better than anyone else.”

He soon shifted from photography to video, and Elevate Content now produces video and social media content for real estate agents and businesses.

Smith said he had worked with several of Tauranga’s major real estate brands and agents.

The business has since expanded into social media work across the North Island and has begun building AI (artificial intelligence) systems for clients. Smith saw this as the biggest growth opportunity.

This year he moved the business out of his bedroom and into an office, and began building a young team.

He has one paid staff member, an 18-year-old editor, and has taken on two other teenagers, one for work experience and another as a contractor.

Smith wanted to build a team of young people chasing their own ventures rather than conventional careers.

On his last day of school, he spent about $2000 on a camera, lens, and camera stabiliser.

“I think I left school with a screenshot of $6 in my bank account.”

Smith said he never wanted a salary or a boss, and didn’t want to go to university without a clear career path.

“I don’t want to go there and sit down and be taught by someone who hasn’t run a business how to run a business.”

He believed young people needed more visible alternatives to university and traditional employment.

Smith said he sometimes worked up to 100 hours a week during the business’ early months and went about a year and a half without seeing friends regularly.

“I didn’t really do anything apart from this. This was my life.”

These days, his role has shifted towards managing staff, meeting clients and pursuing new opportunities.

The hard work has brought its own rewards, including a small plane he recently chartered for himself and his friends.

Now Smith wants to help others find their own path.

“Jump out of school, try it, because it’s changed my life ... not in like a cocky way, but I think I’m who I wish I had [been] at that point in time.”

Harcourts real estate agent Kylee Anderson said his work stood out for its fresh approach and attention to detail.

She approached Smith after seeing videos he produced for other agents and was impressed by the quality.

“He’s definitely going ahead in leaps and bounds, which is so exciting. Obviously, as a young guy, he’s got a very bright future ahead of him.”

Anderson said Smith had produced videos for several of her properties, including a high-end Nautilus apartment that sold successfully.

Tauranga Boys’ College head of future pathways Tom Collin taught Smith in his last year and said his entrepreneurial drive was clear while he was at school.

“In Benji’s case, almost something he was born to do.”

Smith was in Collin’s Gateway class designed to prepare students for life beyond school through job-search skills, financial literacy and workplace readiness.

Collin said interest in alternative pathways was growing, with almost a third of the school’s senior students now choosing Gateway.

Smith would sometimes take business calls during Collin’s class or leave to meet potential clients.

He hoped more students would pursue entrepreneurial pathways, but warned it took a particular drive to make it work.

“Benji, I would say, to be fair, is a special case.

“You don’t get that many young people that just have the wherewithal to go out and hustle in the same way that he did.”

Priority One chief executive Dave Courtney said young people were becoming more open to creating their own career pathways.

He said technology, social media and AI had made it easier for young entrepreneurs to launch businesses and test ideas.

Programmes such as Priority One’s Instep help connect students with local businesses and entrepreneurial opportunities.

He said entrepreneurship was not necessarily replacing traditional career paths, but young people were increasingly combining study, employment, side projects, and business ventures.

“Perhaps the bigger shift is that entrepreneurial thinking is becoming valuable regardless of whether someone starts a business.

“Skills such as creativity, adaptability, innovation, digital literacy and problem-solving are increasingly important across every industry and profession.”

Zoe Blake is a multimedia journalist at the Bay of Plenty Times and Rotorua Daily Post.

On The Up: Hawke’s Bay, 10-year-old Renee Kundu wins The GreatTalk National Speech competition

New Zealand Herald September 26, 2026

Renee Kundu won The GreatTalk 2026 National Speech Competition at the grand final in Auckland on September 13.

Ten-year-old Hawke’s Bay girl Renee Kundu is a national speech competition winner.

The Year 6 student at Hastings Central School won her category in the GreatTalk National Speech competition.

Nearly 170 young speakers from across Aotearoa New Zealand took part in the competition, sharing their ideas, perspectives and personal stories.

Renee was named a grand finalist after presenting a speech in the preliminary online rounds on the topic, “What if adults had to live by school rules?”

“It was a funny speech, but the thing is I find it better when I say a persuasive speech, because I’m not funny, to be honest,” she said.

When she was selected to participate in Auckland as one of six finalists in the Year 5 and 6 category, she played to her strengths, presenting her prepared speech on “The Power of Positive Thinking”.

“I decided to do positive thinking on how I connect to people with my own personal story, because that’s what my mum taught me, that you connect better when you talk about personal stuff.”

She also presented an impromptu speech on the best invention, which she decided was books.

By winning her category, Renee has won a trip to Parliament next month, where she will debate with ministers and tour the building.

The GreatTalk facilitator Jessie Wu said Renee’s speech left a strong impression and described both her prepared speech and impromptu speech as excellent.

“She drew on her own experiences and shared her personal understanding of the topic in a very genuine and thoughtful way.

“It left a really strong impression on us.”

Renee said she started the prepared speech by talking about how she tried to stay positive when she felt nervous.

“Whenever I do go on to a stage, I always think, ‘Okay, I’m scared, but that also feels the same as excited, doesn’t it?’, so I decided to incorporate that in some way.”

Sharing such a personal story with others left her with second thoughts.

“I told my mum at some point that I didn’t want to do it and I wanted to change it to something else, but then she told me, ‘Okay, go ahead, but I’m pretty sure that if you do this it will make you feel much better about it.’

“She was right; when I finished saying my speech in front of the judges, it did make me feel really good.”

Her speech discussed her parents’ separation when she was 4, and her move to Hastings Central School this year, where she had to meet new people and find her place again.

“You connect to people when you tell the truth and when you make yourself vulnerable, like not doing it out of sympathy, but doing it out of being an inspiration.

“It catches their attention, emotionally, not just physically.”

She then used a technique suggested by her uncle.

“My uncle actually told me that I shouldn’t just have something that connects to me; I should have something that would connect to everyone in the room.

“I thought about how the All Blacks would approach their game. When something doesn’t go their way, they don’t stay stuck on that moment. They choose positive thinking and focus on what they can do next to win the game. Because with the All Blacks, there’s always a way back,” she wrote.

Hastings Central School principal Mike Winkley said Renee had grasped themes many adults hadn’t.

After listening to her talk, you would expect her to be 18 or 19, given the maturity with which she spoke, he said.

He described her as a fantastic speaker with a humble personality.

“The fact she has only just ticked over to double digits as a 10-year-old and to be able to talk about these themes that a lot of adults ... haven’t quite got in place themselves or are trying to work hard at.

“To have at her age is simply phenomenal.”

Good morning, everyone,

As I step on to this stage today, my heart races and a wave of butterflies fill my stomach.

But instead of telling myself, “I’m scared,” I choose to say, “I’m excited.” That is the power of positive thinking.

Sometimes we cannot change what we feel, but we can change how we look at it.

Today, I stand before you to tell you how I choose to think positive.

When I was just 4 years old, my parents separated. It was a big change in my life.

That’s when I realised that a positive mind can find hope in change.

And see, today, they are both here, watching me, supporting me, and cheering me on.

That reminds me that, even when life changes, there can still be love, support and happy moments.

There have been times when life has tested me. This year, I had to change schools in the middle of the year because of my mum’s work.

Starting over, meeting new people and finding my place was hard.

There were moments when I felt nervous and a little overwhelmed.

But I chose positive thinking.

I thought about how the All Blacks would approach their game.

When something doesn’t go their way, they don’t stay stuck on that moment.

They choose positive thinking and focus on what they can do next to win the game.

Because with the All Blacks, there’s always a way back. I tried to do the same.

Instead of focusing on what was difficult, I focused on what I could do next.

I joined the Bookworms Club, got to know my classmates, and worked hard to catch up with what the class was learning.

Little by little, the unfamiliar became comfortable.

That made me realise that positive thinking can turn a difficult beginning into a new opportunity.

Being positive doesn’t mean that everything is always perfect.

It means choosing how I respond when things are difficult.

For me, positive thinking isn’t just this amazing moment, standing on a stage and speaking in front of everyone.

Positive thinking is also the quiet moments.

It is when I feel sad and tell myself, “It will be okay.”

And it’s when I make a mistake and think, “It’s all right. What can I learn from it?”

I have learned that being positive doesn’t mean ignoring our problems.

It means believing that we can get through them.

So if you ever find yourself in a challenging situation, pause. Take a deep breath.

Look at how far you’ve already come.

And tell yourself, “I’m still learning. I’m still growing. And I’m still becoming the person I’m meant to be.”

Because the bravest thing we can do is choose a positive thought, take one more step, and simply keep going.

The big, fat, boozy lie that’s taken me more than 40 years to unpack

Sydney Morning Herald September 27, 2026

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Recently, I turned 60. The centrepiece of celebrations that seemed to last forever was a Blue Mountains weekend with 40 friends and family.

There were dinners, bush walks, loads of wonderful conversations, countless laughs and a fiercely contested quiz. There was also, inevitably, a lot of booze. Maybe not quite as much as there would have been a couple of decades ago, but the grog flowed nonetheless.

Not for me, however. I didn’t drink. And, as of this month, I haven’t picked up a drink for a year.

Had you run the concept of a dry birthday by me a year or so ago, I’d have thought you were taking the piss. Or on the piss. Or both.

Not having a drink on your 60th? Not giving it a nudge, bending the elbow or smashing a few cheeky chardies on the one occasion you’re given a gold-plated licence to let loose? Impossible, and, frankly, un-Australian.

But for the whole weekend I was fuelled only by mineral water and ginger beer. I laughed until my belly ached, had animated chats, went trail running and spent the entire time surrounded by people I love.

I didn’t feel like I was on the outer or being forced to endure the occasion as a sober observer. I was entirely present and, afterwards, I could remember every minute. And, best of all, there were no hangovers.

That weekend crystallised something that had been slowly coming into focus ever since I stopped drinking.

For all my adult life, alcohol has been taking undeserved credit for a whole lot of feelings and experiences. The joy of that weekend came from connecting with wonderful people. It wasn’t something that could be uncorked.

What I’ve slowly understood is that alcohol’s hold over me was built on fear, which is why giving it away has always seemed so far out of reach. There was the fear that without it I’d be less funny, less confident and less connected; that celebrations would fall flat, and all colour would be drained from life. Life’s tough enough as it is – what’s the point if you can’t at least have a drink to take the edge off?

But that could not be less true. It’s one big, fat, boozy lie. And it’s taken me more than 40 years to see through it. Maybe I’m just a slow learner.

My drinking “career” kicked off when I was about 15. Growing up in South Yorkshire in the 1980s, pub culture was at the centre of just about everything. In our small town alone there were a dozen or more boozers, with their interiors hidden from the street behind curtains and frosted glass.

The riches beyond lay tantalisingly out of reach for those of us in our early teens. Inside there was fun, laughter, connection and, of course, girls.

I can recall getting a brief glimpse inside one of these forbidden palaces when an older brother smuggled me in at the age of 12 or 13. What a revelation! The maroon velvet seats, the polished wood and brass, the haze of cigarette smoke, and all those men – mostly – drinking huge glasses of beer, talking, laughing and playing darts and pool. It all seemed impossibly glamorous and grown-up. They were clearly living their best lives, and I wanted in as soon as possible.

In the end I didn’t have to wait too long. This was well before the era of ID checks at the door. As long as you behaved yourself, didn’t look too outrageously young and stood your round, you were welcome in most pubs. I well remember the landlady of my local insisting on buying me a pint to celebrate my 16th birthday – I’d already been a regular in the public bar for a year or so.

Looking back, what strikes me most is how inevitable it was. Nobody had to persuade me to drink; the culture had already done its job. I was desperate to get on the grog.

Veronica Valli, a psychotherapist, host of the popular Soberful podcast and author of Soberful: Uncover a Sustainable, Fulfilling Life Free of Alcohol (her book and podcast have been a big part in helping me get and stay sober), says that in countries such as Australia and Britain, the assumption remains deeply embedded that becoming an adult is synonymous with starting to drink.

“Unless you grow up in a particular religion, or perhaps with a serious health problem, it’s assumed you’re going to drink,” she says. “It’s assumed you’re going to get a driving licence, get a job and drink alcohol.

“When you’re a teenager it just seems like the key to adulthood. And the consequences are deliberately obscured. We grow up in a culture that tells us the story that alcohol is the best way to have fun, excitement, belonging and connection, and to relax and reward yourself. We don’t question that.”

I certainly didn’t. From those teenage years onwards, booze was a constant.

Celebrating? Drink. Relaxing? Drink. Feeling stressed? Drink. Going out? Drink. Staying in? Drink. Feeling sad? Drink. Feeling happy? Drink.

CEO at the Foundation for Alcohol Research and Education

You get the idea – whatever the occasion, whatever the emotion, alcohol became the answer. Don’t get me wrong – I’m no wowser. It was a lot of fun. Until it wasn’t.

The point at which grog drifted from a being nice-to-have to a have-to-have is hard to pinpoint. But once that insidious shift happened, drinking rented more and more space in my head: planning when I would drink; drinking more than I intended; anxiously trying to recall what I said and did the previous night; wondering why there was a schooner in my hand at 5pm after waking up that morning with a mouth like the bottom of a budgie’s cage and swearing blind I’d take a few days off.

Then there was the endless thinking about whether I had a problem, and comparing my drinking with that of other “normal” drinkers. It was exhausting.

“People with an alcohol problem do four things,” says Valli. “They drink, they think about drinking, they think about not drinking and they recover from drinking. And the biggest one is the thinking about not drinking.”

She uses an illuminating – if quirky – analogy to drive home her point.

“People who don’t have a problem with alcohol think about alcohol in the same way that I think about sandwiches,” she says. “I might have a sandwich for lunch and enjoy it. And tomorrow I might have soup, and the next day I might have salad. And then I might be at a party at the weekend and a plate of sandwiches goes by, and I have a couple of those. And then it goes by again. I go, ‘No, I’m good’. That’s literally how much I think about sandwiches.”

I never got to the point of starting the day with a “sandwich”, but I’m convinced I would ultimately have ended up a sandwiches-for-breakfast kinda guy had I continued.

Stories of recovery are full of hair-curling “rock bottoms”. Of relationships destroyed, cars wrecked, jail time, health crises and worse. For me it was far less dramatic. My drinking had become compulsive, excessive and secretive and was only heading in one direction. I strung together a few dry days because of a serious health scare, then, out of the blue, on the day I walked out of Macquarie University Hospital feeling a million dollars after having a heart operation, I was struck by a laughably simple revelation: I didn’t have to drink.

I hadn’t realised it at the time, but on September 22, 2025, I had taken my last drink.

Deciding to quit was at once exhilarating and terrifying. Exhilaration at the possibilities of sobriety and terror at everything I was about to lose. My liver would no longer be adrift in a lake of Pinot Grigio, but would I ever enjoy life again?

Never one to do things by halves (see: “drinking”), I pitched myself headfirst into sobriety literature and sober-themed podcasts. There is something uniquely powerful about reading and listening to other people’s stories about struggling with alcohol. Every story is unique, yet at the same time every story is also the same.

Initially, I thought stopping drinking was just about, well, stopping drinking. And in those first testing days and weeks, it was. I had one job: don’t drink. And that was more than enough to cope with, especially as beer o’clock rolled around each day.

But as those weeks turned into months and I dived more deeply into the so-called “soberverse”, I began to appreciate that putting down the bottle was only the beginning.

After reaching the baseline of not drinking, I had to begin the hard work of considering why I drank in the first place, how to manage emotions without outsourcing that work to grog, and what to do with all the time I had been gifted now that drinking was no longer my No.1 occupation.

Getting sober left me facing myself with nowhere to hide. It’s a deeply confronting and uncomfortable place to stand.

And the biggest fear was how I could possibly socialise without a drink in hand.

There’s no denying alcohol is an enormously effective social lubricant. You need only witness the rising volume and change in body language at any gathering once the booze begins to hit to know that. And connecting with others is one of our most basic needs – the negative effects of loneliness on both mental and physical health have been well documented.

My first forays into sober socialising were terrifying. There was no easy way through, but gradually I got the hang of it, one sparkling water at a time. It was like reawakening a long dormant muscle, and I learnt new strategies: arrive early, leave when it starts getting messy, drive home and wake up fresh (and, maybe, just a little smug) the next morning.

And, trust me, no one ever notices you’ve slipped out the door.

Gradually, like the Russian doll I recall from my childhood on my aunt’s mantelpiece, the benefits of sobriety have unpacked themselves. Better sleep? Tick. Mental clarity? Tick. Anxiety tamed? Tick. A sense of peace and calm? Tick. Health benefits too many to list? Tick. Tick. Tick.

Will I ever go back? Hubris is one of the many enemies of sobriety. I would be a fool to say never. One of my favourite sobriety aphorisms (the soberverse loves a good saying) is that no matter how far you are down the road to recovery, you’re only the same distance from the ditch.

But I don’t want to drink again, and I have no intention of doing so. The only regret I have over this quite unexpected and delightful turn in my life is that it has come so late.

I mentioned this to Valli. “It’s never too late and you’re never too old,” she said.

And for the sober-curious, she had this advice: “If you’ve been thinking about it, give yourself a year to see what a sober life could be like. I’ve been sober 26 years and it just keeps getting better.”

A year ago I was terrified ditching the booze meant giving up practically everything I valued – fun, connection, spontaneity and even a lot of who I am.

It turns out I could not have been more wrong. I’ve given up one thing and got everything in return.

I’ll (not) drink to that.

Nick Galvin writes at: nickgalvin. net

Moses went to adult prison at 18. Now he’s voluntarily going back behind bars

Sydney Morning Herald September 27, 2026

Today, Moses Riek goes back behind bars by choice. He believes his darkest chapter is the only way to help a new generation.

You have reached your maximum number of saved items.

Remove items from your saved list to add more.

Huddled under a thin blanket, Moses Riek spent his first night in jail haunted by flashes of his mother pleading with him to be a good boy. At 18, he was now locked in an adult prison.

In the silence of a shared courthouse cell, three adult men sleeping beside him, his mind began to map the steady escalation of his teenage crimes. For perhaps the first time, he says now, he was trying to piece together how it had all gone wrong.

Over a few years, what started with low-level offending, like shoplifting from major shopping centres, had spiralled into violence, and in 2020 he was handed a four-year prison sentence for other serious crimes.

“I remember thinking, ‘oh, this is jail. I’m actually in prison’,” Riek says.

That first night in prison, he was haunted by more than his mother’s anguish. He was haunted by his own. What had happened to the kid who dreamed of becoming a pro basketballer? It was, he says, difficult to pinpoint the exact time in his life when things began to unravel.

In 2004, Riek, then just three years old, moved to Australia after fleeing with his family from South Sudan. First Egypt, then to Sydney, and finally settling in the south-east Melbourne suburb of Pakenham.

Growing up as the eldest sibling took a toll when his father left home. Riek felt the burden of being more than a brother to his siblings. Basketball, he says, became his outlet.

“I actually reached a very high level in basketball, but I lost it overnight because I suffered a pretty bad injury,” he says. “From there, I fell into the wrong crowd.”

That, he says, was when things started to go wrong.

While trying to piece together his own downfall, Riek started noticing others.

A shopkeeper in Sunshine West died in hospital after an alleged attack by a group of young people. A 13-year-old girl was allegedly murdered by a teenage boy in rural Victoria. A good Samaritan was allegedly murdered at a suburban train station as he tried to stop a fight between children.

In the year to March 2026, children were over-represented in the state’s violent crime statistics, carrying out more than 60 per cent of robberies and about half of all carjackings and home invasions.

While the most recent statistics released this week by the Crime Statistics Agency show a reduction of crime across the state – with a 2.1 per cent decrease in offences in the year to June – a report by the Victorian Auditor-General’s Office (VAGO) found the state’s current approach to youth crime prevention was not working.

Over the three years between 2022 and 2025, youth crime in Victoria increased by 40 per cent.

The report also found that the Department of Justice had overstated the effectiveness of the current Youth Crime Prevention Program when describing it as a “proven, evidence-based” intervention, and that it was reaching just 2 per cent of the state’s young offenders.

As Riek found, falling in with the wrong crowd at the wrong time can alter the course of a life. To stem that tide, and grapple with the rise in youth crime, the Victorian government late last year adopted a Scottish initiative called the Violence Reduction Unit.

Founded by former head of Strathclyde Police intelligence analysis, Karyn McCluskey, in the mid-2000s to combat rising violent youth crime in Glasgow, the unit treats youth violence like a health crisis.

As in Scotland, the Victorian unit probes how a child turns into a youth offender; their upbringing, family unit and living situation, their health, financial situation, school engagement and community involvement, and the support they receive along the way.

“Violence is a language. It tells you that something’s wrong,” McCluskey told this masthead after delivering a seminar on the program to youth workers in Melbourne.

“If you change the beginning of the story, you change the whole story.”

The over-$20 million Victorian unit includes putting youth workers in hospitals, where they can support young offenders at vulnerable moments. Former youth offenders are sharing their stories of crime and redemption with teens in custody, while new school programs are helping children spot the warning signs of grooming.

The VAGO report only touched briefly on the new VRU, saying the $27.5 million investment – which includes $7.7m for youth mentoring and $5.6 million for early intervention officers across 23 schools – was ultimately too new to judge.

“Victoria’s Violence Reduction Unit is not within the scope of this review, as it is too early to assess its effectiveness,” the report stated.

“However, applying learnings from the program could make the Violence Reduction Unit more effective.”

But while the state government continues to invest in early intervention and rehabilitation, it is also cracking down on youth crime. Labor’s Adult Time for Violent Crime initiative is backed by the state opposition, with the Liberals vowing to add to the list of offences that result in custodial sentences if elected in November.

Andrew Bruun co-founded Youth Support and Advocacy Services (YSAS) during the “heroin epidemic” of the ’90s. He understands that Victorians are growing increasingly frustrated with the rate of violent youth offending.

“These are horrible things, right? They’re all unjustifiable. But they’re explainable,” he says.

“That ends up happening when you don’t address the kind of problems that the young people have early, that escalate and manifest in those type of really horrible incidents.”

The warning signs start early, Bruun says, with the current cost-of-living crisis a major influence on why more young people are turning to crime – whether it’s for financial gain or simply a sense of belonging.

“It’s essentially one thing leads to another, and it snowballs from there,” he says. “But the kids aren’t thinking about the punishment. Sure, locking them up might make you feel good, and it keeps a certain number of people off the street. But one thing I’ve learned about kids is they’re not scared about being locked up. They’re not thinking about it when they’re doing a crime. They think they get away with it.”

Hanad Hersi, co-founder of Think Village, takes his programs straight to the kids in their classrooms. He says that youth offending is a confronting subject, but speaking to children and their families about the signs of grooming and exploitation is crucial to winning the war against organised crime.

“We know from the conversations we’re having with young people, kids as young as 12 are being recruited into organised crime,” Hersi says.

“These crime groups are tasking these kids to do firebombings, home invasions, carjackings. We’ve actually done a number of targeted sessions for parents about this, and this is the first time any organisation, any service or group has ever spoken to them about grooming and exploitation.”

Hersi says parents need help to understand when their child is a target. Being taught about the warning signs gives them the tools to intervene.

“We’ve been working with VRU to support some of those families,” he says. “These things are happening, so how do we equip the sector to be able to adapt and mobilise and get to young people before it’s too late? Most importantly, how do we support parents and young people themselves, so their kids don’t get coerced and groomed and exploited?”

Several years after his own release from jail, Riek is now trying to help at-risk teens avoid the same fate. Prison, he says, was a wake-up call, and he doesn’t want to see any more members of his community end up in a life of violence.

“I was in and around that that sort of gang culture, and I knew everything that was going on. I could see some very easy solutions to some very big problems,” he says.

Now, an average week for Riek involves regular trips to youth facilities in Little River and Parkville, as well as speaking at conferences and at schools. He tells them what his life looks like now, giving them the perspective and knowledge he wishes he had as a teenager.

“Every week I come up and talk to them about something new, and that’s where I get the most contact with all the boys in the system,” he says. “They just want that guidance, and someone that cares for them.”

While prevention is an important part of fixing the state’s youth crime problem, victims say there also needs to be real consequences for violent actions, especially where children are old enough to know what they’re doing.

Warning: Distressing content and images

On July 19 last year, Saurabh Anand picked up medication from a chemist in an Altona Meadows shopping centre just moments before a group of teens he’d never met launched an unprovoked, vicious attack.

“I had never seen them ever in my life,” Anand tells this masthead. “They just jumped on me from behind. I told them I didn’t want any trouble, and that I had nothing on me. They surrounded me completely and started looking through my pockets. That’s when one pushed me from behind, and they started bashing me.”

Anand tried to protect his head and body as the teens thrashed at him. Then, one pulled out a machete. Within minutes, one of the boys had gone for Anand’s throat, and instead sliced through his left hand, between his thumb and first finger, cutting all the way up his forearm.

Nobody intervened in the attack and it took nearly an hour for emergency services to arrive, Anand says. Another teenage boy found Anand covered in blood after the attack and ran to get help. Paramedics would later tell Anand that his hand was barely attached, hanging by a small amount of skin.

He spent hours in surgery as neurosurgeons and plastic surgeons worked desperately to save his hand. Fifteen months later, he is still unable to move two fingers, and expects a lifetime of pain.

The teenagers responsible for the attack were all arrested in the days that followed. Four were immediately released on bail. Anand said that when the case went to court, all five were released without jail and the court noted they were remorseful for their actions.

“It is a huge setback to rely on a judicial system that feels broken because there are gaps in it. It isn’t able to hold accountable these people who are actually wielding weapons and attacking people,” he says.

“And I’ll be honest with you, no matter what the age is for a teenager, everyone does have that psyche that if you jump off a wall, you might just get hurt by falling down. How is it that there isn’t then enough understanding that if you’re holding a weapon and if you use that on someone, that person may die. I think it’s that simple.”

The answer to youth violence, Anand says, doesn’t sit solely with prevention. In his experience, the kids responsible for his attack “knew” what they were doing, and mid-teen years is too far gone to rehabilitate.

“To sit someone like that in a rehab program doesn’t fix the problem,” he says. “If you’re telling me that a 14-year-old kid is going to get therapy when he has already had an experience of attacking someone, and he knows that he gets away with it every time he does that, what good will an hour a week do?

“If you are saying that you’re going to rectify that with just a rehab program, I doubt that you have enough support workers to actually fund an entire community, or entire state. Setting them free in the community is not the answer because what it is doing is giving them the licence to kill, licence to steal, licence to do anything they want without any consequences.”

Riek agrees that there needs to be accountability, but emphasises that’s what makes lived experience work so important.

“I think there are kids that think they know what they can get away with,” he said. “But they don’t actually know the real risks.”

He thinks back to the kid in the cell on his first night in custody.

“At the start, no one really jumps into the serious offending. You find yourself getting deeper entrenched in negative circles, and the people who are in the gang culture.

“I haven’t really seen any evidence that shows locking up kids is going to be the answer. But when you mix both accountability and prevention, that’s the sweet spot, really.”

Oyarzabal earns Spain Nations League win as England pay for Kane penalty miss

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 21:05:35 GMT

It was another high-profile game when Thomas Tuchel’s England let a lead slip in the second half and went on to lose. But unlike the last time, it was not one for recriminations. The England support can accept losing when their team plays with cut and thrust. More to the point, they can accept losing to Spain who, at times, played football from a different stratosphere.

England were game. They were driven by Jude Bellingham, who ran on adrenaline and played to the point of maximum expression. They had positive surges either side of the interval, especially the one towards the end of the first half when goals from Anthony Gordon and Harry Kane put them in charge, hauling them back after Lamine Yamal’s second-minute goal.

The biggest takeaway was Spain’s slickness. There is a reason why they won the World Cup in the summer. Why they won the European Championship before that. They are the best team in the international game by a distance. Nobody can live with them. England did well to stay within a puncher’s chance of a result in this Nations League opener; Bellingham was still throwing them in stoppage time. Crucially, as Tuchel and England try to look forward after the heartbreak of the World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina, there was no negativity from the Wembley crowd. Even in the face of England’s defending, which was dreadfully loose.

We were denied the chance to see how the fans would react to the announcement of Tuchel’s name when the teams were read out in the countdown to kick-off. Because, after going through the starting XI and the 12 substitutes, Tuchel’s name was not read out. But there were none of the dreaded boos at the full-time whistle.

The match turned on a Kane penalty miss in the 54th minute. Had the captain scored rather than hitting the crossbar after his standing foot gave way in the turf, England would have been 3-1 up. Shortly afterwards, they were pegged back to 2-2 by the Spain substitute Álex Baena and there was a degree of inevitability about the winner from another replacement. Mikel Oyarzabal’s dinked finish was impudently brilliant. Spain had been fantastic for the opening 30 minutes and when they went again after the Kane penalty, they had too much. It was a statement of intent from them, an illustration of their remorseless desire.

“Campeones” was the chant from the enclosure housing the travelling fans before kick-off and it is fair to say the visiting radio commentators were excited about seeing Spain for the first time since the second star was stitched on to their shirt. Their fervour went up a few notches in the early running when Lamine Yamal opened the scoring.

The goal was a personal disaster for Marc Guéhi; it was almost as if the Manchester City defender had other things on his mind. It was of a piece with England’s struggles against the Spanish press. Guéhi was facing upfield as he tried to build a move from deep but his passing lanes were blocked. So he checked back and walked straight into Lamine Yamal, who robbed him and was clean through. He made the finish past James Trafford look easy.

Tuchel had started Trafford ahead of Jordan Pickford, a major deviation from his stated intention for continuity from the World Cup. Pickford was erratic in the summer and was punished for some of his mistakes. Trafford has been outstanding for Leeds since joining them over the summer. Tuchel’s idea is to share the minutes between Trafford and Pickford during this window. Trafford could hear the knock of opportunity and he helped to keep England in the game as Spain pushed to add to Lamine Yamal’s goal.

How Spain pushed. They shimmered with menace. It was the movements, the speed of them – plus the breathtaking assurance on the ball. They had so many options in possession that it felt at times as if they had more men on the pitch.

Ferran Torres had the ball in the net only to be pulled back for offside while Trafford stood up to make a big one-on-one block against the Spain striker after Lamine Yamal had played the through-ball. England’s backline was all over the place. Torres blew another one-on-one on 28 minutes, with Trafford making himself big while Dani Olmo rifled just wide after a sumptuous Lamine Yamal flick.

England tried to throw counterpunches as they hung on. The resistance was impressive. Gordon was to the fore and so was Bellingham. They showed their personality when the chips were down. When the two combined for an equaliser that had not really been advertised, it was the prompt for a wild turnaround.

It was Spain pushing only for Nico Williams to lose his footing and then the ball to Elliot Anderson. England swept forward in thrilling style, Gordon flicking to Bellingham, getting it back and surging in on goal. The low finish was nerveless.

after newsletter promotion

Enter Kane. He was unlucky when he banged inches wide from the edge of the area after a Bukayo Saka burst. He was lucky when his header from a Nico O’Reilly cross, which Unai Simón looked to have covered, drew a panicked reaction from Marc Cucurella. The left-back jutted out his thigh to turn the ball past his goalkeeper. The fates were against Cucurella. When his mishit cross on 45 minutes sailed over Trafford, the ball came back off the far post.

Bellingham appeared particularly determined to leave his imprint. The Real Madrid midfielder was in the mood for bragging rights back in La Liga. It was the power and directness of his running; the smoothness of it, the quickness of his moves. Spain could not contain him. It was his persistence after yet another surge that led to the penalty.

Gordon played the pass back inside from the left and Bellingham got there before Rodri, who invited trouble when he hung out a leg. Down went Bellingham and after a review, it was decided that the contact trumped the feeling that the England player had tried to engineer it. Kane could not convert.

Back came Spain. Lamine Yamal pushed a shot wide after a give and go with Baena, whose backheel was beautiful. Then Baena equalised after O’Reilly gave away the ball and Olmo quickly shifted it to the edge of the area. Baena bought himself the space for the shot with an expert drop of the shoulder.

Saka curled just wide at the other end after more good work by Bellingham but the tide had turned. You could not take your eyes off Lamine Yamal while Luis de la Fuente’s attack-minded changes worked. It was Oyarzabal who made the difference from a Baena pass. England could have no complaints.

Republic of Ireland’s Gavin Bazunu boycotts Israel match ‘as a person of principle’

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 20:18:05 GMT

Bolton goalkeeper issues statement after withdrawal

Ireland players will wear black armbands in match

The Republic of Ireland will fulfil their fixture against Israel in Hungary on Sunday night, but only after lengthy deliberations between the players resulted in a “significant majority” voting to play. The Bolton goalkeeper Gavin Bazunu, however, will not be involved, after pulling out in protest.

After a week in which the Irish team and officials have come under increasing domestic pressure to boycott the match due to Israel’s military actions in Gaza, training was delayed by five hours on Saturday while the squad discussed whether to go ahead.

“This morning, a player expressed their discomfort with fulfilling this fixture to the head coach and indicated their intent to withdraw from the squad,” said the FAI’s chief David Courell, referring to Bazunu.

“What proceeded was another four hours of conversations, predominantly amongst the players themselves, but also at times with the coaching staff and the executive. Ultimately we carried out a vote amongst the squad ... and it was a significant majority that was returned with the intention to continue.”

Courell said the squad had also agreed a number of measures to signal their unease with the fixture taking place. Players are to wear black armbands “in recognition of all the lives lost in the conflict” he said, adding that there will be “elements of the pre-match ceremony” that will “not be partaken in by the Republic of Ireland” players, namely the pre-match handshake and exchange of pennants.

Bazunu, writing on Instagram, said: “Representing my country means everything to me. I have the utmost respect for every single one of my teammates, the manager, his staff, and the Irish people.

“However, I have reached a decision that I have not taken lightly. I am a man of strong faith, and try my best to be a person of character and principle, therefore I feel it would be wrong to participate in the upcoming fixtures against Israel.

“My decision is based purely on my personal belief that the killing of innocent people is wrong. It is important to note that my stance is not in opposition of the Israeli people or the Jewish community, but against the atrocities in the region.

“There are a few times where you get a chance in life to stand up for something bigger, and I strongly believe that this is one of them.”

The Republic’s head coach, Heimir Hallgrímsson, meanwhile, said “nobody is comfortable playing these games for many reasons” as he was once again put under pressure over remarks in which he described his team as “playing against genocide” earlier this week.

If a player chooses to play in the fixture “he is not supporting or agreeing with anything in Gaza” Hallgrímsson said. “We are not playing with that word, we are playing against it.”

The leadership of the Israel team used their press conference to read a statement congratulating Ireland on their decision to play. “What we have seen today is that football has won,” it read. “The separation between football and politics must continue. Anything else spells chaos and creates consequences for the game we love. The Irish took the right decision in agreeing to this. Even if it took longer than it should, it was welcome.”

Israeli officials said they would engage in all of the pre-match formalities with the head coach Ran Ben-Shimon confirming: “I will shake hands with Hallgrímsson.”

The Israel FA will also appeal both yellow cards awarded to Saied Abu Farchi during Thursday’s defeat to Austria. Farchi was given a second yellow after he celebrated scoring an equaliser by uprooting the corner flag, an action interpreted by officials as mimicking the firing of a rifle.

Israel dispute this interpretation. “Anyone familiar with him knows it was an imitation of a snooker player, like the legendary Ken Doherty,” their spokesperson said.

I was focused on becoming the first Aboriginal tennis champion. Then one remark changed something in me

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 20:00:46 GMT

As a teenager in Sydney, the would-be Wimbledon champion was working towards a singular goal when an act of racism shattered her naivety

It was a regular match. Until it wasn’t. In 1969, I was 17 and had been living in Sydney with my tennis coach, Vic Edwards, and his family for several years. I had left my home town of Barellan – on Wirajudjuri country in the Riverina region of New South Wales – to pursue my tennis dreams in the big smoke.

The year before, I had finished high school at Willoughby girls high – where I was the only Aboriginal student – and I was doing my secretarial course in the city. The Metropolitan Business College where I studied was conveniently located near the headquarters of the Foundation for Aboriginal Affairs.

The idea for the foundation was to give city-based Aboriginal people a cultural hub where we could come together and find support. I was spending more and more time there with my friends Isabel and Bob, the latter whom I was casually dating.

Isabel and Bob were young and lots of fun but they were also acutely aware of the politics of being Black. I was naive to the injustices of Australia – and the world – and I learned a lot from Isabel and the guys at the foundation.

At the time, I was focused on a single goal: to become the first Aboriginal tennis champion. To achieve that goal, I had to shut myself off from everything other than tennis. That included politics.

I was training for my upcoming European tour, and part of program included playing doubles with Vic Edwards’ daughter, Trisha, at the White City badge competition twice a week. Trisha and I had been playing together for years and were quite the pair. We were the “tennis twins”, in our matching dresses, at tournaments.

It was during our usual doubles game at White City against two older women that something happened. Trisha and I convincingly won against our opponents, and we went to the net to shake their hands. As we reached over the net, though, one of the ladies turned to her partner and said, “That’s the first time I’ve ever been beaten by a n*****r.”

The N-word. I had never been called it before. I went into shock.

The word took a moment to sink in. At first, I thought I had misheard. But then Trisha responded with a cutting comment and I knew it was real. Still, the moment felt far away, as though it was happening to someone else.

The older women left and I remained at the net with Trisha. Suddenly, we were crying. We both stood in the centre of the court, hugging and sobbing. The word had wounded me like a paper cut, innocuous at first, then stinging. I’m not sure why that single word had such a dramatic effect on me. It wasn’t even an Australian slander. The N-word was a cheap, American slur that reminded me of fake soap-opera trash talk. But when it was directed at me, it felt very real. Was this the way it was going to be out there in the mean streets of tennis?

Still sobbing, I called the first person I thought of: Isabel at the foundation. Through tears, I told her what happened. “You jump in a taxi and get here right now,” she said.

When I arrived, I was greeted by Isabel and Bob. They held me and patted my back as I cried in their arms. Isabel said she had never seen me so upset. We sat around and drank cups of coffee for hours, talking it over. “It’s OK,” Bob told me, kindly. “These things happen to us all the time. You just have to deal with it, and you can. You’re strong.”

Something had irrevocably changed within me. My naivety had been broken. The protective bubble my family and the Edwardses had built around me had been smashed. I would move on but I would never be the same innocent young girl.

When I got back to the house hours later, Trisha had already relayed the events to Mr Edwards. I was glad to have missed his initial fury at the incident. Mr Edwards – who was quick to anger – was remarkably matter-of-fact. He had informed the NSW Lawn Tennis Association over the phone and was in the middle of writing an official complaint. “We have to deal with this in the proper manner, through the correct channels,” he said.

I don’t know what happened as a result of the call or the complaint. But I never saw the woman at White City again.

After that, I spent more and more time at the foundation. My friends there reminded me of my people but not in a way that made me homesick; instead, they gave me a sense of feeling good about being Aboriginal. Proud – that was it! They made me feel proud to be Aboriginal.

When I went on to win my first Wimbledon singles tournament two years later in 1971 – becoming the first Aboriginal woman to claim the title – the win was for all Aboriginal people.

I like to think I was doing my part in my own way – by breaking new ground, taking up space and inspiring the next generation of hopeful Aboriginal athletes.

I hope I have paved the way for our young ones, and that the road is a lot smoother these days.

This is an edited extract from Only Ever Evonne by Evonne Goolagong Cawley with Alley Pascoe (Allen and Unwin), out 29 September
