I hoped my children would have epiphanies while visiting my homeland; my father suggested we go swimming instead

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 20:00:45 GMT

I brought my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. When I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege, we enjoyed our final days doing as locals do

As I stepped out of Penang international airport, the humidity hit me like I was peering into a just-opened rice cooker. The air carried whiffs of exhaust fumes, fried food and something earthy. It felt thrilling and familiar because I was born in Penang and lived there for six years before I moved to Australia. I looked back at my three children who were visiting for the first time. They were draped over their suitcases like wilted lettuce. “Welcome to Penang,” I said, wiping sweat off my brow.

It was July 2026. It had been 13 years since I last visited Penang, when my father had hosted a lavish wedding dinner featuring a champagne fountain and swan-shaped ice sculpture for me and my new husband. For my white, Australian husband, it was a trip of firsts: his first Chinese tea ceremony; his first 10-course banquet; the first time he met my extended family. But for me, it had been the last time I’d spoken Mandarin and the last time I had seen my grandmother before she died.

As my parents grew older, I worried my Chinese heritage would be lost for ever. My children spoke only English and spent their Saturdays playing sport rather than attending Mandarin lessons and calligraphy classes like I had. When Gong Gong (maternal grandfather) spoke of his childhood, the children smiled indulgently but thought he was exaggerating when he said his only toy was a discarded bicycle tyre and he’d had to share one apple with his five siblings.

I wanted to bring my children to Penang to immerse them in the places of their grandparents’ stories. My father, who lives in Perth but travels there frequently, booked his flight the night I floated the idea to him.

On the first morning of our trip, my father met me, my husband and our children at our hotel in central George Town. He gazed at the gleaming marble floors and wood panelling of the Eastern & Oriental Hotel and said: “When I was young, I never dared to set foot in this hotel. Only rich Europeans stayed here.” Now we were the rich tourists – a fact that made me feel guilty and grateful – and to the man dressed in a khaki colonial outfit and safari helmet who held a door open for us, my toddler sang a cheery: “Thank you!”

We began our trip gently, letting the children luxuriate in an air-conditioned mall and paw through racks of fast fashion before we ventured outside to explore George Town on foot. “It’s not every day you get to walk through a Unesco world heritage site,” I chirped. But the heat was intense and the children’s interest in colonial architecture and street art evaporated in the afternoon sun.

In the evening, my father led our search for dinner through a labyrinth of alleyways, shepherding us off the road when cars and motorbikes rumbled through. At the first restaurant, there were no free seats and the air was sulfurously pungent from a nearby durian stall. In the second place, the smoke billowing from the satay grill triggered my daughter’s asthmatic cough. Finally, we found a place that dished up barbecued pork on springy egg noodles coated in a sticky soy sauce. We fell upon our food in a frenzy. Later, we walked back to the hotel along the esplanade, marvelling at the sunset that lit up the clouds like smears of mandarin sorbet across the sky.

Towards the end of our trip, we visited my father’s childhood home. We drove along a winding road that hugged the contours of the hills in the island’s north. On one side, verdant rainforest towered above; on the other side, past the guard rail, was a sharp drop, with dizzying glimpses of the houses in the valley below. When we reached Tanjung Bungah, the suburb where my father had lived, the children scowled from the backseat. My 10-year-old hissed: “When can we go shopping?” The toddler pleaded to return to the hotel’s infinity pool, which was fringed by palm trees and overlooked the Andaman Sea. Undeterred, my father stopped by a truck piled high with coconuts. A shirtless man used a machete to hack one open and stuck a plastic straw in it. My father handed it to my son, who spilled it on to his lap.

We continued down a narrow dirt road and stopped at a small weatherboard house with a red tin roof. The house was empty and neglected but my father still had a key. We squeezed past two bedrooms and shuffled to the kitchen at the back. The electrical wiring was exposed and the concrete floor was gouged with holes. There were no ceilings; sunlight filtered in through the holes in the roof. The toilet was outside. The entire house was smaller than our two hotel rooms. I pictured my father, who was one of six children, living there with his family.

“How did you fit all eight of you in this tiny house?” I asked.

“Fourteen,” he corrected me. “With my grandparents, three uncles and one aunty.”

“Woah,” my eldest daughter said, her eyes wide. Perhaps she was thinking of her bedroom at home, which was spacious enough for two bookcases and a double bass, and had a door that she slammed for privacy. The toddler began to cry and I picked her up, wondering if she finally understood the grim poverty that her Gong Gong had endured.

“I want to go back to the pool,” she sobbed.

My father ushered us back into the minivan and we drove back to the hotel. I thought he might be disappointed in the children’s behaviour but, instead, he urged me to take them for a swim. I realised that I’d expected too much of them; what child could resist leaping into cool water on a muggy day or lying on a sun lounger eating ice-cream? I stopped lecturing them about gratitude and privilege and we enjoyed our final days doing as Penang locals do: shopping and eating. On one occasion, when I ordered food in faltering Mandarin, my toddler stared at me with wonder and exclaimed: “Mum, you can speak Spanish!”

Our trip did not, as I had hoped, inspire epiphanies in the children about their heritage or their grandparents’ early struggles. Perhaps these will dawn on them as they grow up. For now, it was enough that they shared some experiences that featured in my earliest memories – they’d sweltered in tropical humidity and sat on red plastic stools, slurping noodles. And their Gong Gong had hugged them goodbye in a hotel lobby where he’d once believed he did not deserve to step foot.

The moment I knew: My late fiance’s favourite song was playing – and Billy said ‘Jamie’s here, isn’t that nice?’

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 20:00:45 GMT

After the death of his partner, Anthony Nocera had almost given up on love. Then Billy walked through the door

Find more stories from the moment I knew series

In 2024, about 18 months after my fiance Jamie passed away, I decided I was lonely and horny and so put myself out there on the apps. I’d placed Jamie’s ashes on the TV cabinet in the living room, so he was smack bang in the middle of his two favourite places: his spot on the couch and his coffee machine. It also meant he was in the centre of the house, which made dating hard.

I had a guy over for a hook-up one night and he kept fixating on the urn. “So … He’s dead?”

“I hope so,” I said. “Otherwise the urn was a mistake.” “Wow,” he said, not getting the joke. “You’re so brave. I don’t know how you do it.”

Nothing kills a boner faster than someone thinking you’re brave. When someone thinks you’re “brave”, you stop being flesh and pulsing blood and hot salty saliva and start being something coolly observed. Being a “brave widow” makes you desirable in theory. Not practice.

When the urn didn’t ward off potential suitors, my cat Freyja – or Miss Freyja, as Jamie called her – did. She appointed herself my fluffy protector in Jamie’s absence. Each night, she camouflaged herself on the charcoal-grey carpet outside my bedroom and kept watch while I slept. Two emerald eyes scanning for threats.

When I did have a visitor, she sprung into immediate, hostile action. She yowled and hissed when a semi-closeted doctor, who had came over for a blowjob, tried to pick her up. One guy didn’t see her flattened into the carpet and accidentally kicked her across the room. She responded by clawing his shin.

After that, I figured that what I experienced with Jamie was so real and pure and true that I’d used up all the love I was allocated in my lifetime. Or that maybe Freyja was secretly homophobic and only put up with me because I was the one who fed her.

I’d spent months in self-imposed celibacy, when a guy named Billy, with gorgeous green eyes and a crooked smile, messaged me. He asked about my day and I sent him a picture of a painting I’d hung up. He asked to see it in person. I said yes. When he arrived, he spotted Freyja, and before he even said hello to me, he crouched down to her level and said: “Hello Miss!”

As if some muscle memory kicked in, she waddled over to Billy and flopped on her back, presenting her belly for patting while she purred. “Oh Miss Freyja!” he said, when I told him her name. When he was done, he kissed me.

He didn’t mention the urn until hours later – and when I told him the story of me and Jamie, he said, “Sounds like a great guy.”

Freyja wove between our feet and vibrated her tail when he kissed me goodbye. As he drove away, Freyja waited by the door and let out a melancholic meow. Don’t go. I agreed.

Late one night we walked past a club having a 90s party. Madonna’s Ray of Light, Jamie’s favourite song, blared out on to the street. Billy turned to me smiling, his pointy canine tooth glinting in the moonlight, and said: “Jamie’s here, isn’t that nice?” and then he squeezed my hand. I felt flutters all through my body and fell head over heels in love in a way I never thought I would again.

It takes a special person, like Billy, to look at the shoes of a past lover and not try to fill them; to leave them be and plant their own next to the ones left behind. To carry something as heavy and slippery as a loss that doesn’t belong to him. To see that the pair of Jamie’s glasses I keep next to my bed are dusty, and clean them as if it’s nothing at all, even though for me it feels like the most generous thing you could do for another person.

Billy is funny, patient and kind. He’s smarter and more handsome than he realises. I find it hard to think of things in terms of “forever” now, because I know how quickly things can be taken away. But I look at Billy, and think I’d be happy doing this day by day, for a long time – with Miss Freyja by our side and Jamie watching over us all.

Anthony Nocera is the writer of the Log Boy, which runs from 1-10 October at Adelaide College of the Arts, Main Theatre. Presented by State Theatre Company South Australia.

Messi’s exit leaves Argentina with impossible task of replacing their superhero

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 19:00:43 GMT

When things are going awry, the Albiceleste will no longer be able to rely on their ultimate get-out clause

It isn’t quite over yet. Lionel Messi will return a week on Wednesday for his formal farewell in a friendly against Benin, but, before that, Argentina face two games when they will begin to experience a future without the most potent get-out-of-jail-free card football has known.

Messi’s international career falls into two distinct halves. There was the first decade when there was a sense that he didn’t quite fit, was somehow insufficiently Argentinian, didn’t care for his country. That was always absurd and can be recognised now as a manifestation of the Argentinian public’s frustration at their trophy drought despite the presence in their forward line of one of the best three to play the game.

Then Messi retired, distraught after a missing a penalty in the shootout against Chile in the Copa América final in 2016. Suddenly, Argentina, rather than just lashing out at their biggest star, was forced to confront what it would mean to live without him. The prospect was so appalling it provoked a mass campaign to encourage Messi to reverse his decision.

Since then he has been loved and, despite a shambolic World Cup in 2018, has delivered with two Copas América, a World Cup and another World Cup final. His career was dogged by the accusation that he never matched Diego Maradona’s achievements in a national shirt; he ended up having won more.

This retirement will not be overturned. Messi is 39. Those who persuaded him to change his mind in 2016 were perhaps imagining – hoping for – six more years: they got 10. There will be no second thoughts this time. The rupture is real. No longer when things are going awry will Argentina be able to turn to the superhero in their midst and ask him to fix it.

The best example came almost at the end, when Argentina trailed Egypt 2-0 with 11 minutes of their World Cup last-16 tie remaining. Barcelona youth team coaches used to speak of the teenage Messi “getting the face on”, at which point he would be unstoppable. It happened in Atlanta: it was as though Messi simply decided that wasn’t going to be his last World Cup game. Argentina won without needing extra time.

Optimists will draw solace from the fact that Argentina’s best performance under Lionel Scaloni probably came in their 4-1 victory against Brazil in a World Cup qualifier in March 2025, when Messi did not play. Even allowing for the odd tactical choices of the opposing coach, Dorival Júnior, Argentina were exceptional. Leandro Paredes anchored a midfield as Alexis Mac Allister and Enzo Fernández linked exhilaratingly with Rodrigo De Paul and Thiago Almada on the flanks and Julián Alvarez at centre-forward.

But football is not just about when things are going well. Even in the bleak times, the years of doubt under Edgardo Bauza and Jorge Sampaoli, when games were spiralling out of control, there was always the possibility Messi would put things right. But Argentina now have to deal with a future without that get-out potential.

The post-Messi future begins next week with games against Bolivia and Burkina Faso. Scaloni, has hinted he will sign a contract extension that would take him through to the 2028 Copa América with an option to the 2030 World Cup. That, at least, would provide a measure of stability, but there is little disguising the fact that a new cycle is beginning, just as Scaloni instituted a new era after the 2018 World Cup.

Other than Messi and Nicolás Otamendi, who are retiring after the Benin valediction, Scaloni named a 35-man squad. Of those, 20 were at the World Cup; given Paredes and Nahuel Molina are serving lengthy bans, that represents a remarkable degree of continuity, although Nicolás Tagliafico, at 34, is also understood to be considering his future. But 12 of the squad had played three internationals or fewer and De Paul and Giovani Lo Celso, who are in their thirties, will play only against Benin, giving the new cohort space to impress in the first two friendlies.

The biggest opportunities, at least in the short term, look to be at the back. Cristian Romero and Lisandro Martínez, both 28, look likely to be the first-choice central defensive pair, but Valentín Gómez of Real Betis and Tomás Palacios, on loan at Estudiantes from Inter, are competing to be back-up.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

With Molina suspended, Tagliafico ageing and Gonzalo Montiel injured, the real interest, though, is at full-back, where a pair of 22 year olds could stake a claim to be the future: Agustín Giay of Palmeiras and Román Vega of Zenit.

In Messi’s absence, there remains a question of formation. Although that Brazil game demonstrates what is possible through inter-movement even without a huge amount of overt creativity, it maybe that Scaloni opts for more traditional wingers. Again there are young options: Leonel Flores of Boca Juniors and Roma’s Matias Soulé are likely to make their debuts over the next few days.

And replacing Messi? That’s just not possible, either at a tactical level or, perhaps more significantly, in terms of what he meant for the spirit of the team. It’s not that Argentina need Messi to play well. Indeed, a purist could even argue that Argentina played better in that game that they ever could have played with Messi (or at least the pedestrian Messi of late), because of his lack of movement and the way the game had to be built around him.

That is always the danger with individualists, but Messi was so spectacularly consistent that the percentage option was to rely on his extraordinary genius, the true extraordinariness of which was how reliable it was.

No matter how well-organised an opposition defence, there was also the possibility – the probability even – that he would find an opening, no matter how badly things were going, there was always the chance he would get the face on and sort everything out single-handed.

Plenty of sides have found a new fluency, a more team-based dynamic, after a major star has moved on. Argentina’s ceiling could conceivably rise, but Messi offered a reassurance, a possibility of salvation, that will be sorely missed.

Wakefield stun Wigan to storm into their first Super League Grand Final

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 18:40:28 GMT

Semi-final: Wigan 6-33 Wakefield

Wakefield face Warrington at Old Trafford next Saturday

The corridors of Wakefield’s famous Belle Vue ground are lined with black and white photos of the halcyon days of the 1960s, when this grand old club were last a rugby league force. Days like these could not have seemed further away in 2023 when Daryl Powell was appointed by their new owner, Matt Ellis, with an initial remit to secure promotion back to Super League.

But Ellis, the local kitchen magnate who has followed Wakefield all his life, had much loftier goals for the club he had just purchased. He delivered Powell a clear message, something the Trinity coach recalled this week: “When I came, Matt said to me: ‘I want you to turn black and white into colour’.” There is only one colour on this club’s mind right now though: gold.

This is one of the great sporting stories of recent times. Two years ago this weekend, Wakefield beat Doncaster 72-6 in front of just under 5,000 supporters in the Championship. Next weekend, they will walk out in the Super League Grand Final for the first time. There are rapid rises, and then there is this particular story.

The club have spent the majority of the Super League era and the decades before it languishing in the lower reaches and light years away from clubs like Wigan – who they dismantled here with one of the most complete playoff performances you are ever likely to find. Now, one of rugby league’s true sleeping giants are alive, and within one win of a first league title since 1968.

How they did it defies description. Few gave them a chance of beating a Wigan side seemingly on an unstoppable run to an historic treble; surely not even the most optimistic of Trinity fans would have suggested a victory of this margin. The turning point was Wigan’s Adam Keighran being sent to the sin-bin early in the second half, during which time Wakefield scored 16 unanswered points.

That turned a slender 8-6 half-time lead into a commanding 24-6 advantage. But even when Keighran returned, Wakefield were the superior team. It never really looked like Wigan could launch any sort of comeback, meaning it is Trinity who now stand on the verge of history with Warrington – the club who sacked Powell in 2023 – standing in their way.

“Our mentality was always we thought we could come here and win despite what people said,” Powell said. “We were superb. This is a special group of boys and we have a great opportunity ahead of us next week.” This is a seismic moment for the game too; next week will be the first Grand Final not to feature any of Leeds, Wigan or St Helens.

And the Warriors could have no complaints, in truth. They did go ahead through Brad O’Neill’s try but that was a false dawn. By the break, Tom Johnstone’s score and two goals from Max Jowitt nudged Wakefield ahead – and they didn’t relent after half-time. Keighran’s yellow for a tip tackle on Isaiah Vagana was the semi-final’s defining moment, though.

By the time he returned, Corey Hall, Jack Sinfield and Johnstone had all scored tries to make it 24-6. Nobody, not even this Wigan side, can overturn a scoreline like that in a game of this magnitude. “Wakefield were outstandingly good,” Wigan’s coach, Matt Peet, conceded. “We were outplayed and out-coached: they beat us all ends up. The night belongs to them.”

Peet, as magnanimous as always, is correct. This was their night, underlined by Ky Rodwell’s try after Keighran returned which just emphasised further the gap between the teams on the night. Mason Lino’s drop goal and a late Jowitt penalty were mere cherries on top: by then, the 5,000-strong travelling support – the same number that used to watch them at home - were celebrating.

We often say there are incredible stories and historic moments to be written at Old Trafford. Next Saturday, that is categorically the case as Wakefield Trinity finally aim to write a new, colourful chapter in their illustrious history.

Belfast court injuncts decision to allow Orange Order march down Garvaghy Road

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 17:48:38 GMT

Andy Burnham calls for calm as fears of unrest grow after request for countermarch in mainly nationalist area

A controversial loyalist parade down a nationalist street in Portadown has been temporarily injuncted after a high court judge urged all sides to “step back from the abyss” and take responsible decisions for “the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland”.

The ruling was made amid rising fears that a parade could unleash fresh sectarian violence, 28 years after the parade route was banned due to disorder.

After a five-hour hearing at a special sitting of the high court, Justice Smyth issued an order temporarily suspending the parade, which was due to take place at 8am on Sunday, until a judicial review application can be fully heard.

She has also suspended the determination by the Parades Commission on Friday that the event could take place, albeit with restrictions on numbers.

However tensions remain with an appeal against her decision by loyalists to be heard at a second special hearing on Saturday night.

Smyth arrived at her conclusions after several attempts to coax the parties, the Loyalist Orange Order and the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition, to reach a voluntary agreement.

After it was clear that was not possible, she said: “The level of mistrust between residents and Portadown Loyalist Lodge cannot be overstated. Neither side accepts any of the reassurances of the other.”

The march down Garvaghy Road has been banned for 28 years due to widespread sectarian violence in 1998 outside Drumcree church.

“It is also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland,” Smyth said.

The court was sitting on Saturday after a last-minute legal challenge by the Garvaghy Road Residents Coalition.

Smyth urged the parties to reach a voluntary agreement to delay the march, given few had time to digest the reasoning behind the commission’s decision.

It was important “to reach an agreement for the sake of everyone in Northern Ireland, not just for your sake” to have the issues “properly aired” so that “everybody knows they’ve had a fair hearing”.

“Be big enough to step back from the abyss,” she told the parties in court.

This followed a high court ruling quashing the restrictions on the annual parade route.

The Portadown loyalist Orange Lodge was not represented at the hearing. But after a request from the judge for its view through the individual who had sought permission for the parade, the lodge made it clear it would not agree to suspending the procession.

The SDLP leader, Claire Hanna, said the parade plan was “provocative”. She told residents she was “so sorry” that some “bad faith actors” were “intent on reopening the hurt and the traumas of the past”.

Fears of clashes increased on Saturday after a request to the commission for permission for a countermarch, a protest that, it was estimated, could be attended by up to 5,000 people, the court heard. That was later revised to 300.

On Friday night, the British prime minister, Andy Burnham, appealed to leaders to “work calmly” through the weekend while the Northern Ireland secretary, Chris Bryant, called for “cool heads”, saying Northern Ireland had “withstood many moments of sharp disagreement over the years” and must do so again.

Before her ruling, Smyth asked the parties in court, including the Police Service of Northern Ireland and the Parades Commission, to “consider carefully the very important issues to our society” raised in this case, and the importance that they were dealt with properly given the “importance of this case to community relations”.

She also noted that the issues of judicial review were of “such fundamental importance” that it could be unwise to hold a full hearing without all the facts.

Delivering her ruling, Smyth said: “The level of mistrust between the residents and the Portadown Orange lodge cannot be overstated.

“Neither side accepts any reassurance provided by the other or that there’s any genuine reason for the stance adopted by the other.”

She added: “It’s also clear to me that this particular long-running dispute has the potential to escalate within Northern Ireland.

“Against that background I am thoroughly of the view that the issues of all three parties must be properly ventilated so that whenever an ultimate decision is made by this court the parties know they were heard.”

Democratic Unionist MP Carla Lockhart insisted nationalist residents on the road had “nothing to fear” from the march on Sunday, but Sinn Féin leader Mary Lou McDonald described the decision as “utterly reckless”.

The Parades Commission has placed a number of restrictions on the procession, including an 8am start and limiting the number of participants to 35 people, but not placing any restrictions on the route.

‘Charming and disarming’ … how Meta’s technology-packed Muse harnesses the power of cuteness

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 17:09:28 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

The tech giant has launched a cute ‘little guy’ that can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop

After the recent backlash against Meta’s so-called “pervert” smart glasses, this week Mark Zuckerberg launched a much cuter alternative: the Muse “charm” device.

With a screen that shows a cutesy little avatar, it has drawn comparisons with Tamagotchis. “We’ve packed a lot of technology into this little guy,” the Meta founder told the San Francisco audience.

The “little guy” could fit, like a Labubu, on to a keychain or bag. But unlike a Labubu, the interactive AI assistant will have significant capabilities, including the ability to have live conversations. It can answer emails, book travel or do your weekly food shop.

According to Katie Seaborn, a Cambridge associate professor who has been researching cuteness – creating the science of cute voices within the context of computing – it’s cute because it “basically looks like a baby”.

For Joshua Paul Dale, professor at Chuo University in Tokyo and author of Irresistible: How Cuteness Wired our Brains and Conquered the World: “It’s really significant that along with the wearable charm, Meta also introduced a new pair of smart glasses with no camera. Everyone hates cameras in smart glasses. But if the camera is contained in a charm you wear around your neck, it shifts the agency. Suddenly, you’re not recording people. It’s just a cute little animated avatar looking out on the world.”

An individualised, customisable, and in this case adorable, AI companion, it tracks with Zuckerberg’s commitment to the idea of personal, wearable super-intelligence that you can chat to. As well as a broader shift towards cute technology, cited by forecasters WGSN as a top trend for 2026.

“Clearly,” says Dale, “what Meta is trying to do is make Muse into a companion. And it’s doing it in the simplest possible way … It’s using a very simplified, tiny 2-inch screen to encourage you to anthropomorphise the figure on it so that you treat it as if it’s human even though you know it’s not.”

Its cuteness is, according to Seaborn, “strategic”. “It’s very natural to emerge from this controversy with a technology that uses cuteness because … it’s so weak. Don’t worry about it. You can trust us.”

To try to harness the power of cuteness, according to Seaborn, “makes sense, especially from a big tech perspective because maybe people are getting wise to the ways of current strategies when it comes to people’s attention, their personal data and what have you. And now they’re trying new things that may or may not work”.

Seaborn, who has just moved to the University of Cambridge from Japan, points out that “this is something that is very normal in Japan. So the first thing you notice when you go there is that every single thing has a mascot. The government organisations, the media companies, the businesses, they all have a cute mascot”.

Seaborn has studied the “impacts cuteness can have on people”. “We’ve been seeing cuteness applied as a design strategy for different purposes. We know [that it] has certain impacts on people.” For one thing “cuteness is a way for certain social interactions to take place or to be smoothed over”.

There is also a “natural link between cuteness and deception … I call it ‘charming and disarming’, because one of the things cuteness does to us unconsciously, it’s just how our brain processes it, is lets down our guard. We can’t really help it.”

Whether Muse will catch on when it is released in December, or whether such a blatant attempt to gain trust via an on-screen avatar with cheeks you want to squish will land, remains to be seen. But different generations are likely to react differently. “That’s so AI!” is the phrase gen Alpha are using to dismiss anything they think is inauthentic.

For many gen Zers who are au fait with having a cuddly toy hanging from their bags, most typically in the form of a Labubu, it might feel less of a wrench. For older generations there will be nostalgic associations given its resemblance to older technologies. Embedded in it, says Seaborn, “[is] this legacy of these cute kind of gamified pet sort of things like Tamagotchi and Pocky Pikachu”.

Plus different cultural contexts will affect how it is received. Seaborn’s research has found that “Americans were actually less likely to be deceived compared with Japanese people … Because in Japan robots are heroes, they’re like babies”. Whereas “in western culture they’re often presented in the public imagination as kind of scary, potentially broken, sinister devices”. In UK focus groups, people reported a “gut feeling” that something was wrong when cuteness was part of a deceptive design idea. “People felt like something was off, but they couldn’t articulate what it was.”

But the picture, says Seaborn, is changing. “Because cuteness [or kawaii] has been a cultural export of Japan and other nations for a while now … there might be a slow cultural shift happening in terms of how we orient ourselves towards cuteness and what we accept as adults.”

While Dale is “not rushing out to buy one”, he “will say, however, that when I’m 80 years old I’ll definitely want one of these things. I want to wear it around my neck always, and I want the camera on all the time, so it can tell me where I left my glasses.”

Gloucester’s Dewi Lake in full flow with two tries in emphatic win at Exeter

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 16:37:22 GMT

Exeter 24-45 Gloucester

Ben Loader also scores two tries in bonus-point win

Gloucester are determined to make significant progress up the Prem table this season and here was a hugely promising first step. The Cherry and Whites had a bonus point on the board before half-time on a breezy afternoon in Devon and had more than enough in the tank to build on a 14-point interval lead and secure a morale-boosting early away victory.

Considering they claimed just one league win on the road in the whole of the 2025-26 campaign, this seven-try fusillade was a big plus, spearheaded by their new Welsh reinforcements Dewi Lake and Jac Morgan. Lake was the deserved player of the match, scoring two tries and adding significantly to Gloucester’s efforts in both the set pieces and the maul.

This performance was also a tribute to the summer input of Gloucester’s new forwards coach Brett Deacon, defence coach Joel Tomkins and technical director Chris Boyd, albeit helped by a distinctly off-colour Exeter display described as “baffling” by Rob Baxter, the Chiefs’ director of rugby. There was a touch of illness in the home camp this week but that did not wholly account for the visitors’ overall supremacy.

In addition to a couple of tries for left wing Ben Loader there was considerably more cohesion and focus to Gloucester’s game, not always consistently evident on their travels in recent seasons. And crucially, they now have a central pillar around whom they will be keen to rally. In contrast to the south-west’s depleted reservoirs, this newly arrived Lake is already making a significant difference to Gloucester’s level.

The visitors, in their pink change strip, certainly made the most of the wind behind them in the opening 40 minutes. There were two very similar tries from little chip kicks out to the left wing which gave the talented Loader plenty of time and space to outflank the cover but the real secret of Gloucester’s improvement was the all-round balance to their game.

Rather than chucking the ball around like headless chickens there was much more solidity to their set piece and more control generally. Their defensive appetite was also impressive, forcing the Chiefs to work overtime for any tangible reward in their opponents’ 22.

Aside from a forward rumble by Josh Iosefa-Scott and a compelling surge down the left by the forceful Ethan Roots, Chiefs were visibly lacking their usual verve and energy. Seb Atkinson should not have been first to Caolan Englefield’s chip in behind but, for whatever reason, Exeter’s rearguard were caught ball-watching.

Lake, throwing his lineout arrows straighter than Luke Littler and galvanising everyone around him, was already a central figure even before he dived into the left corner to score his side’s fourth try just before the break. There was a certain inevitability when the former Osprey burrowed over for his second five minutes after the restart and Chiefs’ pain soon deepened further.

Again, there seemed little obvious danger when Will Joseph received the ball wide on the right around the halfway line, only for the younger brother of the former England centre Jonathan to score a quite brilliant weaving solo try to help push Gloucester out to a 20-point lead.

With Freddie Thomas sent to the sin-bin, though, Gloucester had to survive the final 10 minutes with only 14 men and Exeter’s replacement hooker, Louie Gulley, collected a try on his Prem debut to secure a try bonus point. ‘I can deliver’: Burnham pledges radical change on eve of Labour conference

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 16:35:27 GMT

Exclusive: UK prime minister says delivering fiscal stability would be ‘crucial’ to be able to fix bigger problems

Andy Burnham has said he can deliver on his promise of radical change for the country despite severe economic headwinds, telling the Guardian: “There’s always things you can do; it’s just whether you’re prepared to do them.”

The prime minister acknowledged public finances were “challenging” ahead of next month’s budget but said delivering fiscal stability would be “crucial”, because only then would the government be able to focus on fixing bigger problems.

A series of global economic shocks, including the Iran conflict, has put the UK economy under intense inflationary pressure and pushed up borrowing costs, leaving the government limited room for manoeuvre.

Ahead of his first Labour conference as prime minister, however, Burnham sought to reassure voters he was willing to make tough decisions to deliver change and show the markets he could ensure fiscal stability while preparing the groundwork for more substantial change ahead.

Speaking to the Guardian on the eve of his first conference as Labour leader, he said: “The public would have more respect for us if we go and grab something difficult … and say, ‘Right, we’re going to do something here’, rather than constantly playing the political game before fixing the problems.

“It’s challenging, definitely, but there are still things that you can do. Always in politics, there are things that you can do. The question is sometimes: Are you prepared to do them? Yeah, I am prepared to do them.”

When asked about the need for a large fiscal buffer against shocks, he said the key thing was stability, indicating that he understood the need to reassure the markets, but that more radical transformation of the state would follow.

“I do think it is crucial to have stability and to show that there’s a willingness to face up to the reality of some of these difficult things. But actually from that stability, the permission can come to make bigger change that, in the end, could put the country in a stronger position in relation to the public finances,” he said.

“You have to have stability, but you have to do what you can within that. You can’t pursue a major programme of change, which is what I believe the country needs, in a chaotic situation.”

After ruling out holding a snap general election before 2029, Burnham said he wanted to set out a clear path for how the country could move to a better place – and that he hadn’t been spending his time “sitting politicking and strategising” but instead was focused on fixing problems.

His ambition to give people “a bit more belief that things can improve” across the country, he said, would not come from “endlessly running elections and referendums”.

He denied having had discussions with his senior team about whether to call an early election. “The speculation in no way matches the internal discussion because there isn’t one,” he said, rejecting claims he did not have a mandate as the public had voted for the Labour party.

However, Burnham acknowledged he was hemmed in on tax and the fiscal rules of Keir Starmer’s manifesto commitments, and suggested he would have done it differently had he been in charge at the time.

“I’ve inherited those positions and, as I say, I think the main thing for me is to focus on the here and now for people, not to be self-serving about ‘oh, what would suit me?’ and playing politics. That’s not where my mind is, and possibly would have framed it different, but we are where we are, you know, and that’s the reality.”

Burnham played down speculation that Labour may give more support for energy bills, with the price cap set to soar from January. “I think people need to remember that measures have already been taken,” he said, referring to VAT on electricity bills being scrapped from next week.

The prime minister also reiterated that while he thought the welfare bill was too high, the will among Labour MPs was “not there for crude cuts” because they would push people into crisis, so a longer-term approach to reform was required.

After warning of the risks, as well as the opportunities of artificial intelligence at the UN last week, Burnham admitted to concerns about rogue AI agents attacking state institutions in the UK, after the Australian medicare system was hit.

Burnham addressed the presence of far-right protesters on the streets of Britain, accusing Daniel Thomas, who has led black-clad anti-migrant vigilantes on the streets of some English towns, of “creating fear” but did not go as far as Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, who accused him of being an “outright racist”.

Speaking of Thomas’s masked gangs, he said: “I mean that’s not Britain. That’s not what we want to see in people’s communities. There’s legitimate concerns about issues, and then there is intimidation – and that is intimidation,” he said.

The prime minister also addressed political funding, which has been in the spotlight since Reform UK received two record-breaking £36m donations from cryptocurrency billionaires, saying that – contrary to reports – he would not rule out a domestic donations cap.

“You know I think we do need to continue to have a cross-party discussion about how do we uphold trust in politics? How do we not give the impression that politics can be bought and that people are, if you like, unduly influenced?”

He was also open to looking at election spending limits, he said, which are now being examined by the Electoral Commission, adding that he has “real concerns” about crypto-fuelled politics.

An emotional Burnham revealed that the death of his father, Roy, last week had made him more determined to deliver. “I’m in this job for what I can do for people, not for what it can do for me … to make the changes that my dad, for instance, long pushed me to make,” he said.

“It’s been a hard thing, if I’m honest, coming into this position in the last three months when I also knew in my heart that I was starting this journey as my dad was ending his.

“Although that’s hard, and I’m not seeking sympathy in saying it, I say it because the coming together of those two things increases my determination to make a difference on the things that I’ve long said I want to fix.”

With political courage expected to be a focus of his speech to Labour’s conference in Liverpool, Burnham said he was willing to be honest with the public about what needed to happen, even if it was difficult to hear.

“I think the public want to see, number one, honesty about things. So not spin or putting things a certain way that’s self-serving. They want honesty, and then they want, I think, difficult but real decisions,” said Burnham.

“Not difficult decisions and making a fetish out of that, but actually grasping nettles and then moving things forward. I don’t think politics has been prepared to do that enough in recent times.”

Burnham criticised previous governments for failing to tackle difficult issues such as social care, housing supply and youth unemployment, saying longer-term reform was needed because there were no “easy or quick wins”.

He revealed there would be a new help-to-buy scheme aimed at giving first-time buyers who cannot rely on the “bank of mum and dad” the keys to their own home. It will be funded by reallocating existing budgets, although it is unclear which ones, rather than through extra borrowing.

Burnham also said he wanted to deliver significant progress on social care reform – a manifesto commitment – before the next election. “Who is going to do something to actually make it real? I’m saying to you that I am going to address this directly.”

Zoe Harrison rescues Red Roses with thrilling last-gasp try against New Zealand

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 16:18:55 GMT

WXV: England 26-19 New Zealand

Interception score arrives with clock in the red

If anyone thought a noise at Twickenham would not reach the decibel levels of the full-time whistle of the Rugby World Cup final last year then they were firmly wrong. Zoe Harrison’s last-gasp winning try against New Zealand was met with ear-bursting cheers and brought 59,871 fans to their feet with their hands in the air.

It was extra sweet for the Red Roses fly-half who had moments earlier missed a match-clinching penalty, but as the Black Ferns looked for their own victory moment, Harrison intercepted the ball to put her name up in lights.

The Red Roses ability to continue their unbeaten streak mimics how Neo dodged bullets in the blockbuster the Matrix. Last Saturday they drew against an impressive Canada team looking to avenge last year’s World Cup result and against New Zealand at a hot and humid Twickenham they pulled off a comeback win.

The Black Ferns, the last team to beat England, back in 2022, held a half-time lead after a display of resilient attack, but their rivals had an extra edge in the second 40.

Maddie Feaunati was a highlight for the Red Roses. The No 8 is ever dependable for John Mitchell but at HQ she sparked attack with lengthy breaks and turned over the ball in defence. Marlie Packer, promoted from the bench just before kick-off because of an injury to Sadia Kabeya, also had a good outing before being forced off with an injury of her own.

New Zealand were in great form heading into the match, winning their past eight games, and had a positive first half but discipline let them down in the second including a yellow card for Veisinia Mahutariki-Fakalelu. Despite losing to England for the fourth time in a row there were bright sparks which lit up this Test match, namely Amy Du Plessis. The centre was hugely physical in defence and imaginative in attack, her first-half try the best score of the game.

This was a barnstorming Test match, one that fans could not take their eyes off with the teams matching each other pound-for-pound. The New Zealand captain, Georgia Ponsonby, described the game as an “absolute tussle, the Test match of our dreams”. The tension started before kick-off as the haka was met by a response from England who stood in a V shape facing New Zealand before walking towards them to form a united line.

In the early stages it was all New Zealand but Ayesha Leti-I’iga had an early try ruled out after repeated Black Ferns attacks. Their inability to capitalise on momentum meant England were the ones to break the deadlock. A huge attack, initially inspired by a 40m break by Feaunati, ended minutes later with a great run-in by Claudia Moloney-MacDonald.

Jess Breach stopped a certain try with a powerful tackle on Leti-I’iga a metre from the line and England twice turned over Black Ferns ball in the 22, but a piece of individual brilliance from Du Plessis got New Zealand on the board. She caught a long ball from Lucy Packer and responded with her own kick from the halfway line and chased it. No one from England was covering the back left corner and Du Plessis scored, the stands of Twickenham falling silent.

That set a fire under New Zealand who scored through Leti-I’iga next and for the second time in this WXV Global Series England headed into half-time down at the break. To start the second, Ellie Kildunne and Breach connected well to see the star full-back over.

Braxton Sorensen-McGee slotted the penalty to even the score at 19-19 but Harrison made sure it wasn’t another draw with an excellent read to rescue the win.

When asked about the winning trying, Harrison said: “Obviously the kick didn’t go the way I wanted it to. I felt I had to make up for it somehow. That last bit was a bit shit or bust. They had an overlap and I had to stop it somehow, so I just thought I had to get in their eyeline and grab the ball, score a try.”

England march on to Canada, where they will play two Tests next month, with their unbeaten record now stretched to 41 games. New Zealand will look to get their wins back on track when they host France in October in a three-Test series.

Hundreds of thousands of people lined the Avenue des Champs-Élysées in ⁠Paris on Saturday to attend an open-air mass with Pope Leo, on the second day of his visit to France.

The Vatican estimated 700,000 people turned out for the outdoor mass with the 71-year-old American pope – about 100,000 more than the number of people who had registered to attend.

It took place at the Place de la Concorde, the site of bloody executions by guillotine during the French Revolution – when Louis XVI’s staunchly Catholic rule was overthrown – and now the centre of the secular republic.

The choice of the site, a symbol of the French republic to many, was criticised by supporters of France’s strict legislation separating church and state in public life.

But cheers rang out in the crowd as the pope thanked ‌God in his homily for the chance to ‌visit France on a whirlwind four-day, three-city tour to promote Catholicism and its teachings.

It is the first official papal visit to France in 18 years.

Pope Leo asked those in the crowd not to keep their faith to themselves. “Let it overflow, so that those you meet may be refreshed and their thirst satisfied,” he said. “From this beautiful city of Paris, I pray fervently that the living water of the Holy Spirit may flow throughout France.”

He told Catholics that only their faith, and not material things, can provide true happiness.

“Only God can fill the emptiness within us,” he said.

The security zone for the event – the biggest of the papal tour – stretched about 1.4 miles (2.2km), shutting down road traffic in central Paris from the Place de la Concorde to the Arc de Triomphe and beyond.

Chanting “Leo, Leo” and “Long live the pope”, crowds of people waved French and Vatican flags as the pontiff rode slowly down the grand boulevard of the Champs-Élysées aboard a popemobile – a specially designed, partly open vehicle used during public appearances.

He stopped frequently along the way as babies were lifted out of the crowd and brought to him to receive a papal caress on their heads. The city centre was sealed off for the service, with helicopters circling overhead and snipers positioned on rooftops.

About 14,500 police officers, gendarmes, military personnel and firefighters were deployed to the event, which was attended by 2,400 priests and deacons, and about 100 bishops.

Marie-Élisabeth, a 44-year-old nun from Burgundy, told a reporter for France 24: “This event is a way for us to say loud and proud that Christians are here.”

Speaking to reporters from Agence France-Presse, Sylvie Leclerc, a 51-year-old teacher, also said she and her fellow Christians want to share their fervour for their faith. “You don’t hear much from us Catholics, but now we’re going to make some noise!” she said. “But to proclaim love, peace, joy.”

Jill Dando murder: technological advances allow police to review CCTV 27 years later

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 15:15:47 GMT

BBC broadcaster was shot in 1999 in case detectives have previously said may never be solved

Technological advances are allowing police to review old CCTV footage in the unsolved murder of the BBC broadcaster Jill Dando, Scotland Yard has revealed.

Advances in CCTV enhancement technology have allowed detectives to return to 27-year-old footage of Putney Bridge Underground station, Scotland Yard said. But detectives stressed that the review was part of existing inquiries – not a new investigation.

The former Crimewatch presenter was 37 years old when she was shot and killed outside her home in Fulham, west London, on 26 April 1999. An unidentified person, referred to as “Man X”, was captured on camera near Putney Bridge station – about a mile from Dando’s home – shortly after the attack.

A driver had seen a man “running for his life” on Fulham Palace Road around the time of the shooting, the Mirror reported. She later picked out Man X in the station CCTV as the person who had been sprinting.

A Met spokesperson said: “In the 27 years since Jill Dando’s murder, the investigation has been subject to numerous reviews, aiming to identify whether matters could be progressed with advances in technology and forensics.

“Recent advancements in CCTV enhancement technology have provided investigators with the opportunity to re-examine original footage from Putney Bridge train station.

“The review of CCTV footage forms part of ongoing inquiries and should not be interpreted as a significant line of inquiry nor as a new investigation being opened on this matter.”

Outside her work on Crimewatch, Dando was also seen during the 1980s and 1990s on BBC shows including travel show Holiday and The Antiques Inspectors.

She began as a reporter at her local paper The Weston Mercury in Weston-super-Mare, Somerset, before moving to the morning programme Breakfast Time, which later became BBC Breakfast.

In 2019, the detective who led the inquiry into Dando’s murder expressed doubt the case would ever be solved. Speaking in a BBC documentary to mark 20 years since the television presenter’s shooting, Hamish Campbell said he did not think any new suspects would ever be brought to court.

“Do I think somebody will come back to court? Probably not, no. Sometimes, I felt we were a day away from solving it and other times, I thought: ‘No, we’re a long way away’. Senior officers were asking: ‘What are the likelihoods of this case being resolved?’

“We had over 2,000 people named as potential suspects or responsible. Some actions to trace and eliminate one person might take a day. One action might take two weeks. But there’s thousands of them and that’s the issue of managing stranger homicides.”

News broke on Friday that City had been found guilty on all but one of the 115 charges laid by the Premier League in February 2023, charges the club have always strenuously denied.

The club did not comment on the verdict until Saturday afternoon when Al Mubarak said on social media: “While some people have been quick to reach their own conclusions, and there is so much noise swirling around us, nothing has changed. We have faced challenges together before and have prevailed. There remain many who want to undermine the momentum of our club. We will not give them that opportunity.

We travel to Anfield in a fortnight and then host Paris Saint-Germain in the Champions League back at Etihad Stadium – moments that give us an opportunity to celebrate the strength of the Manchester City family. Earlier, City’s manager, Enzo Maresca, posted a cryptic message on social media reading “I know nothing”.

On Saturday morning, Maresca was approached for comment about whether he is seeking reassurance from the club on their continued stance of innocence. The Guardian was sent by his representatives a screenshot of a quote attributed to Socrates, the Greek philosopher, which Maresca posted on Instagram.

The quote reads: “The only thing I know is that I know nothing.” Maresca also wrote: “Time to breathe. Time to analyse. Time to learn.”

Elsewhere, there wwere contrasting reactions to the outcome of the Premier League investigation. Oasis’ Noel Gallagher, a longtime City fan, described his shock at the news, while the club’s former chair David Bernstein believes any potential punishment should not be only financial. The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, described the case as unsettling.

“So it was a bit of a shock to find out that we’ve been found guilty of all but one. But really just quite sad. Sad for the fans and for the players.”

Asked if it changes the context of moments like Sergio Agüero’s title-winning goal in 2012, Gallagher said: “Our focus as fans is always on the pitch and we know what we saw.

“Whatever goes on in the boardroom, it’s nothing to do with the supporters or the players. The players won that game and won that title on the pitch. Whether some of those players should have been there or not, that’s nothing to do with the fans.

“Does it taint it? I suppose in the eyes of everybody else in England it would, but I know what I saw and I know what I felt.”

Bernstein, City’s chair from 1998-2003, told Times Radio: “I felt absolutely awful, I felt in shock yesterday. You’ve asked me on the programme because of my time as chair of City and the FA, but basically I’m a fan of Manchester City and have been a fan for 70 years.

Bamber did most of the rest, finishing with five for 52, including the spectacular dismissal of Ben Green, plucked by Will Young at third slip with an outstretched left hand, like a tumbling leaf from an autumnal tree.

Ian Holland(23) and Tom Scriven (49) ensured the players would have lunch, but Bamber wrapped things up seven balls afterwards to rapturous shouts of “You Bears”. Trump rejects Iran’s seven-day peace deal to reopen strait of Hormuz

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 12:38:46 GMT

US president is said to expect renewed strikes after midterms

US president Donald Trump has said he has rejected an Iranian proposal to reopen the strait of Hormuz within a week and resume nuclear talks in return for the lifting of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports.

“They made a proposal but I reject it,” he told reporters at the White House.

The US president was earlier said to be privately sceptical Iran would meet his demands to dismantle its nuclear programme, according to unnamed US officials cited by the Wall Street Journal.

Trump has told aides he expects to resume bombing Iran after the November midterms in the US, the newspaper reported.

Meanwhile, on Friday evening, he published a post on his Truth Social platform with a graphic showing a map with the strait of Hormuz renamed as the “Trump Strait”.

During a three-hour meeting at the UN general assembly in New York earlier this week, Iran had proposed reopening the strait, which would have relieved pressure on global energy markets, and restarting talks on its nuclear programme within seven days.

In return, as well as lifting its naval blockade, Iran wants the US to permit the release of some of Iran’s frozen assets, restore the waiver that lifted sanctions on Iran’s oil exports and observe a “ceasefire on all fronts”.

That would involve the US president convincing Israel to end its attacks on Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon, a tall order, and allowing the strait to reopen largely on Iran’s terms, with the new route predominantly going through Iranian waters.

Saudi Arabia is also said to be concerned that the route deal is bilateral between Iran and Oman, and not with the Gulf states as joint signatories.

Reports of the rejection came as Iranian state media reported on Saturday morning that the Iranian president, Masoud Pezeshkian, was on his way back to Tehran from New York.

After a meeting with UN secretary general, António Guterres, Pezeshkian said: “Iran has not walked away from the negotiating table, but given past experiences, it no longer trusts the United States.”

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, said ⁠late on Saturday that ​Tehran had seen ⁠an initial reaction from ​Trump ‌to ‌its proposal ‌but had yet to receive a response through mediators.

Iran ‌was waiting for the mediators ​to convey the definitive US position ⁠and would ​make a ​decision ​based on ​it, he added.

Earlier, a US official had ⁠said discussions with Iran through mediators were “positive and constructive” and, on Friday, Araghchi, had detailed the proposal to reporters outside the UN security council.

He said the seven-day timeline to open the strait and resume talks could start as soon as the US accepts Iran’s proposal. The initial steps would take about four to five days to complete, the strait would be opened on the sixth day and talks on the nuclear programme would start on the seventh day, he said.

This would include a protocol to allow UN nuclear inspectors back in to look at Iran’s damaged sites and the stockpile of highly enriched uranium.

The US naval blockade is putting intense pressure on the Iranian economy, while the seven-month-old conflict in the region has disrupted oil flows through one of the world’s most critical shipping lanes and is increasing the cost of living around the globe.

Pezeshkian, in an interview with the CBS show Face the Nation, said Tehran was ready for talks on its nuclear programme and other issues, but would not accept “bullying or coercion”.

“Iran is not seeking war, but will defend itself against pressure, threats and attacks,” Pezeshkian said, adding that it had already agreed that “we’re not supposed to develop nuclear weapons”.

Previous attempts at diplomacy have failed ‌to end the war, which began on 28 February with US and Israeli attacks.

Since then the conflict has alternated between pauses and renewed strikes, killing thousands while degrading Iran’s conventional forces and damaging its already ailing economy.

Iran and its allies have retaliated by extending the conflict throughout the region. Iran has struck US allies in the Gulf with drones and missiles while its Houthi allies in Yemen have targeted Saudi interests. Iranian-aligned militias in Iraq were blamed for a pipeline attack that temporarily took more Saudi oil off the market.

The violence in Yemen has prompted a new humanitarian crisis, the UN children’s agency said on Friday, reporting a rise in acute malnutrition among children.

Trump has previously said he was in no rush to reach a deal, even as high oil prices fuel inflation. On the Iranian side, there are questions as to whether the hardliners who dominate the security forces would accept compromises championed by moderates such as Pezeshkian.

Diplomatic efforts surrounding the UN general assembly underscored the global stakes in the conflict.

Marina Dunbar contributed. With Reuters and AP

Kamala Harris is belatedly courting progressives. Is it too little, too late?

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 12:00:35 GMT

As she mulls another presidential run, the former VP is building bridges with progressive and Arab American leaders

Does Donald Trump secretly want Republicans to get annihilated in the midterms? Because he’s certainly acting that way. He continues to brush off concerns about the cost of living, saying last week that high gas prices are a very “inexpensive price to pay” for the war on Iran.

And, of course, the president seems to have no plans to end that disastrous war, apart from making vague threats about blowing the entire country up. Trust me, he keeps saying, everything will get better after the midterms. But by the looks of his dismal polling numbers, not many people are swallowing his empty promises anymore.

Still, despite the mess the Republicans have made of the country, I wouldn’t feel too optimistic about the Democrats returning to power: the party is famous for snatching defeat from the jaws of victory. Instead of evolving, it has a tendency to do the same thing over and over again, expecting different results.

See, for example, the fact that there are once again loud murmurings that Kamala Harris plans to run for president in 2028. The former vice-president hasn’t made any sort of official announcement yet – she told voters in Detroit this week that she’s still deciding what to do – but she seems to be testing the political waters through midterm campaigning.

This week she flew to Michigan, one of the states she lost to Trump in 2024, to join the Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed at a roundtable focused on Black maternal health. Harris will also be campaigning with the senator Jon Ossoff in Georgia next month and attending an event in Las Vegas with the Nevada attorney general, Aaron Ford, for his gubernatorial bid.

Harris’s appearance in Michigan wasn’t some spur-of-the-moment attempt to be helpful; it was a highly calculated move designed to put her back on the national political stage.

The New York Times reported this week that Harris’s aides had circulated a donor prospectus in July “that showed how she would try to maintain her influence atop the Democratic Party as she considered another run for president in 2028”. The document, which solicited funds for campaign travel, explained how Harris could boost midterm candidates. It also asserted that the current moment is “uniquely suited to Vice President Harris and a broad coalition already in motion”.

But not everyone agrees it’s Harris’s time to shine. Numerous Democratic candidates have publicly stated that they don’t want Harris’s toxic brand anywhere near their elections.

El-Sayed, meanwhile, seems to have decided that an alliance with Harris is mutually beneficial. It gives the progressive candidate an inroad into the establishment and might help him win more support with Black voters.

Harris, who alienated many progressives and Arab Americans by her stance on Gaza, clearly thinks that associating with El-Sayed might improve her reputation among that cohort of voters. El-Sayed has said he opposes military aid to Israel and termed the situation in Gaza a genocide – as have numerous human rights groups and genocide experts.

El-Sayed isn’t the only progressive that Harris appears to be trying to build bridges with. Last year, Harris offered only the most lukewarm of endorsements for Zohran Mamdani, stating: “He’s the Democratic nominee, and he should be supported.” Now that it’s clear that Mamdani embodies the political zeitgeist, she’s a lot more keen to be besties. In early July, Axios reported that Harris called up the New York mayor a couple of days after three leftwing candidates he’d endorsed won their primaries over establishment-backed candidates.

In fact, Harris has been working the phones pretty hard. The same Axios piece noted that she’d reached out to a number of pro-Palestinian activists and Arab American leaders including James Zogby, founder and president of the Arab American Institute. He told Slate this week that the two had had a “long talk”, which he felt good about.

In 2024, the Democrats took progressives for granted. They assumed that young progressives would show up to vote blue no matter who, even when the party treated them with disdain. Instead many of these voters stayed home.

The Democrats are still loath to admit that Gaza was a factor in their defeat: a 2024 autopsy report released by the Democratic National Committee did not mention the issue once. However, it looks like Harris is waking up to the realization that her almost unconditional support for Israel hurt her in the previous election and is something she will have to rectify if she wants to run again. Particularly since polls show a record 60% of US adults now have an unfavourable view of Israel and the vast majority of Democrats support an arms embargo.

Is all this too little too late for the former nominee’s brand? I don’t know. But it’s certainly too late for the tens of thousands of Palestinians the Biden-Harris administration were complicit in killing.

Is it possible they were maybe just mucking around? Or have the friendly really skies been taken over by a dastardly coalition of furries?

I wrote about the Last Ditch drama here.

“The future is already here – it’s just unevenly distributed,” the science fiction writer William Gibson once said. And that is very true of AI. “We don’t have to wait to see how AI will bring about unprecedented death and destruction, because we’ve already witnessed its unleashing,” Granate Kim and Mohamed Hussein write in the Guardian.

Lian Yunzhi is reportedly “the first female speedcuber to average under 4.5 seconds”.

Sitting in her tent, warding off rats, Alaa watches videos of her three children, killed in an Israeli airstrike, on her cracked smartphone. She gave birth to a new baby boy, Waseem, shortly after the Guardian published this piece.

A hilarious development in the Ed “I’m not complicit in genocide” Sheeran tour story. Even the weather is sick of hearing him whine.

Arwa Mahdawi is a Guardian columnist

Oxford lets OpenAI train its AI models on Bodleian Library

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 11:00:36 GMT

University staff voice concerns over reputational risk of partnering with company behind ChatGPT

The University of Oxford has allowed the company behind ChatGPT to train its AI models on historical texts from its Bodleian Library, as tech companies scour academic institutions for fresh data.

The Bodleian material digitised by OpenAI has been used to “populate the OpenAI training set”, according to internal documents.

Oxford announced a partnership with the company in March 2025, using OpenAI software to digitise texts from the university’s world-famous library, which it said would make the content more widely available for students and researchers.

However, the announcement did not state the material would be used for training OpenAI’s models, which are trained to recognise patterns in words – and thus “learn” to write complete sentences and perform other cognitive tasks – by being fed vast amounts of data.

An OpenAI spokesperson said the company was “proud” to ensure “the AI models of today preserve the world’s historical knowledge for the future”.

“With more than a billion people using this technology in everyday life, it’s important it reflects different cultures, histories and perspectives,” they added.

Meeting minutes at the University of Oxford, obtained via a freedom of information request, record concerns from staff, including members of the Bodleian governance committee, about the reputational risk of partnering with OpenAI and the effect on the university’s environmental commitments of striking a deal involving an energy-intensive technology.

Booksellers have also reported a spate of orders for obscure titles such as a guide to agricultural implements in 18th-century Africa or biographies of 1950s car drivers. Secondhand bookshop owners have speculated that because the titles are unlikely to exist online in digitised form, they represent fresh data that can be consumed by the next generation of AI models.

Scraped websites are increasingly saturated with AI-generated material, making them less useful for training models, and developers have turned to physical, often historical, book collections.

OpenAI has struck similar agreements with US research libraries such as Boston Public Library, Caltech, MIT, and the University of Michigan under a project called NextGenAI. Oxford is the only UK member of the project.

By June 2025, 125,000 images scanned from historical dissertations had been shared with OpenAI from the Bodleian collection, including PhD theses from European and American universities written in the 19th and 20th centuries. Other texts scanned include a rare collection of 10,000 16th-century “broadside ballads” containing song lyrics and musical notes that were once circulated on Tudor street corners. Staff have also discussed digitising of 18th-century Irish state papers, the private letters of Irish novelist Marie Edgeworth, and Dorothy Hodgkin’s penicillin notebooks.

The OpenAI contract with Oxford also raises the prospect of the mass digitisation of the Bodleian’s collection consisting of 23m items. The minutes also discussed the creation of an “Ask the Bod” chatbot.

A spokesperson for the University of Oxford said the amount of text being digitised was “modest in scale” and covered only out-of-copyright material. The Bodleian keeps the rights to the scans and will begin publishing them openly online within months, the spokesperson said.

after newsletter promotion

They rejected the suggestion that the machine-learning element had been hidden from the public and students. Digitisation was the university’s primary interest, said the spokesperson, but staff had been open that the project would also contribute training data.

The Bodleian’s collections remain intact under the deal, unlike with secondhand book acquisitions elsewhere that are being pulped after scanning. Anthropic, OpenAI’s close rival, has spent tens of millions of dollars acquiring books and slicing off their spines so their contents can be scanned before having them pulped. Anthropic has said it does not buy and destroy rare and antiquarian books.

A tech news site, 404 Media, also placed a tracking device inside a secondhand book order and traced it to an Amazon facility in the US, where the books were also dismantled and scanned.

The Oxford spokesperson said: “The material digitised through the project with OpenAI is modest in scale, out of copyright, and OpenAI’s use of the material is not exclusive.

“The Bodleian libraries also retain the rights to make the digitised material available themselves, and the library will begin to publish these materials openly online in the next few months, as we do with outputs from other digitisation partnerships.

“The project will in fact allow the Bodleian to make the material more accessible to a wider number for people, who might otherwise have found it difficult to access.”

Raye’s I Know You’re Hurting urged me to confront a lifetime of depression

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 11:00:35 GMT

I had always ignored my anguished mental state or tried to push it aside, and CBT didn’t work for me – then one song seemed to articulate my pain

Six months ago, I was driving past John Lewis on the M40 with my wife and stepdaughter, Raye’s I Know You’re Hurting playing on the stereo, when I realised I was crying. It was the third time I’d listened to the song, but it was the first time I’d really heard it. It was as though the lyrics were speaking directly to me: “I can see you standing on the edge … You give when you have little left to give.”

Music had made me emotional before, but only ever because of the melody or the arrangement or the orchestration. I have worked in music since I was 21, and as a recording and mix engineer, I’ll listen to a song all day, taking it apart to work out how to make it better. After listening to a song 200 times, it inevitably loses its meaning, and over the years, I’ve become desensitised to the power music can have. But this time, for the first time, it was the lyrics that brought me to tears.

I had been struggling with my mental health for two decades – almost half a lifetime. But I hid it, scared to admit it to my family, even to myself. As Raye sings: “And you hide it so well, you do.” The last few years had been especially difficult with Covid, a divorce, becoming a stepfather to teenagers and turning 50. I’d invested so much time into my career – working 80-100-hour weeks at its peak – but I questioned what my legacy would be when I look back on my life. I’d sit in silence, a face of thunder, wallowing in self-pity. My family would ask: “What’s wrong with you?” And I’d bite my tongue, not knowing what to say, just knowing I needed to do better.

I had tried cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) many times, but I found I’d just talk without acting on the steps. Still, when my wife suggested speaking to the GP about antidepressants a couple of years ago, I was reluctant, thinking it would kill my creativity. I Know You’re Hurting unlocked something in me, though. Hearing my pain articulated by Raye finally allowed me to accept that I was struggling. It gave me permission to admit it. Two months later, I made an appointment with the GP, who prescribed antidepressants. After Raye’s music spoke to me that day, I also decided to start music therapy. Exploring my thoughts through music, something I instinctively connect with, has been much more effective for me than CBT ever was.

In her lyrics, Raye urges the listener to “stop trying to be so strong all alone”, and “If you need two more arms to hold these burdens, I’m here”. I realised I didn’t have to continue struggling on my own. Help was available and I had people who could support me.

A couple of weeks ago, I got a tattoo to commemorate the impact the song has had on my life. The line “close your eyes and let this music get to working” summed that up for me – the way that music can be medicine. I messaged the producer, who sent me the score, and I got the musical notes of that line tattooed on my forearm. It’s a reminder that I’m not alone, a reminder of where I am now compared with where I was. I just look at it and it makes me feel good.

Around that time, my music therapist suggested I write a song. The lyrics just poured out of me – I wrote it in an hour. I’ve got an urge like never before to make music. I feared that antidepressants would kill my creativity; instead, they opened up the space for me to access it.

Raye’s song told me it was going to be OK, and I still return to her perfect album This Music May Contain Hope in moments when I need to be reminded that hope can be found. One of the final tracks on the album is called Joy, which feels fitting because that’s also where I’ve ended up.

Four months into taking antidepressants and starting music therapy, I argue less, I let things go more. I’m a better husband and a better father to my son and stepdaughters. My family have noticed the change in me, often saying how much happier I seem.

In the UK, the charity Mind is available on 0300 123 3393 and Childline on 0800 1111. In the US, call or text Mental Health America at 988 or chat 988lifeline. org. In Australia, support is available at Beyond Blue on 1300 22 4636, Lifeline on 13 11 14, and at MensLine on 1300 789 978.
