We followed five people in Gaza from dawn to dusk – this is what the headlines don’t tell us

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 11:00:34 GMT

Behind the stories of bombings and mass deaths, the everyday challenges facing Palestinians living under siege portray a quieter tragedy we rarely hear

What does it take to make a morning cup of tea in Gaza?

For Alaa Hessi, in her final month of pregnancy, this small ritual begins with a calculation of gas rations. Her family gets a ration of 6kg of gas every three months – enough to heat a pot for 18 precious minutes a day. That’s needed for cooking – so for tea, a fire must be built instead.

For 12-year-old Ramadan, the process begins with a hunt for anything flammable, in an environment where there is almost no wood left. He scouts through the sand dunes where he lives, snaps off a few twigs from a thorn bush, and feeds the flames with pieces of discarded plastic that wash up on the beach.

Before you boil the kettle, though, there is the matter of the water – with none running, the question is whether a water truck visits your area that day, and if not, how far you must walk to find it. Then there is transporting that water – how will Ramadan store it, given all of his family’s large water containers have been chewed through by rats? And how does a small boy carry the weight of it – enough liquid for a family to wash, brush teeth, cook with and drink through the next 30C summer day?

Finally, the water is boiling, but still there is the question of whether you even have tea or coffee or sugar to brew. Holding the paper bag of rationed sugar sparks a memory of what those goods have sometimes cost to acquire. Crouched over the teapot, Ramadan recalls last year’s famine, when aid points became death traps, and he and his brother risked everything to sprint for a bag of flour or sugar. He remembers the boys he saw shot beside him, because they moved too soon or too late.

Most of the headlines we encounter about Gaza are the extreme events: bombings, mass deaths, targeted assassinations. These demand attention.

There are some things, however, that rarely make the headlines, but have come to define life in Gaza. They are grinding, cruel realities that only really emerge when you inspect the minutia of a day – like a cup of tea. Over the course of this week, we documented the daily routines and mundane tasks of five ordinary Palestinians: a child, a pregnant woman, a teacher, a skateboarder and a grandmother. We followed them from sunrise to dusk, through the small, ordinary moments that rarely make international news – and through them, hoped to get a different, deeper understanding of what life is like now for Gaza’s people.

There is a lot you can understand from the anatomy of a day in Gaza. One thing that comes sharply into focus is the effect of dismantling or withholding those things – higher education, books, arts, museums, hobbies, musical instruments – that take human life beyond pure survival.

Israel continues to control everything that passes into Gaza, deciding how many calories it will allocate to its citizens, how much gas can be eked out to heat a minimum of hot meals.

Along with restricting the essentials required for life, the blockade bans a plethora of ordinary objects from entering Gaza, classing them as “dual use” items that could be used by Hamas. The blacklist and its criteria are opaque, arbitrary and ever-changing. At various times they have blocked the import of ventilator machines, medications for cancer, wedding dresses, sewing machines, toys, musical instruments, spices, dates and crutches.

From the story of Rajab al-Reefi’s day, we learn how the ban on skateboards has reverberated through his life. The 30-year-old has spent the past five years running Gaza Skate Team, a youth club that teaches children how to skateboard. During the war, their weekly gatherings became a lifeline and outlet for displaced children. Even after their skatepark was demolished, the team continued, posting videos of landing tricks on the rubble, kickflips executed on collapsed beams of concrete and tangled metal pylons.

But skateboards only have a lifespan of a couple of years: one by one, their layers snapped, wheel bearings wore out, parts salvaged from one broken board could no longer be fitted to another. With none left, the club went on a salvage mission, to dig some equipment from the rubble of a bombed building. Now, they have a handful of working boards again, and the girls are back to skating. But even these boards are on their last legs. When they wear out, there is nothing coming to replace them.

A skateboard is not essential to live – its absence will not make headlines like the systematic deprivation of food. But their absence illuminates the nature of the blockade in a fuller way: its random cruelties, the curtailing of opportunities for lightness, fun, self expression.

Still, against the odds, each person finds ways in their day to keep hold of the things that make them feel human. Prof Mahmoud Seydam wires a solar panel to power a laptop, uploading lectures over WhatsApp and taking oral presentations instead of written exams – battling to provide an education with no paper, no notebooks, no university campus. Alaa Hessi does her best to prepare a safe crib for her baby, in a tent pitched above the rubble where her three children were killed in a strike. Mansoura Ibrahim Mohammed Abdel Dayem, living in the back of a truck, tells her grandchildren stories of their history. Ramadan watches the ocean and dreams of becoming a lifeguard.

You can read all five of their days here.

London transfer: is it time to kill off the Heathrow Express?

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 11:00:33 GMT

With fares high and passenger numbers low, plans for a third runway could bring the train’s future into question

If Heathrow finally builds its third runway, Londoners can expect hundreds more planes flying overhead each day. But greater congestion on the ground will be a problem too. Under Heathrow’s £33bn expansion plan, 100,000-200,000 more passengers would eventually be travelling to or from the airport each day.

The most eye-catching problem has been moving part of the UK’s busiest motorway, the M25, to make space for a new 2.2-mile (3.5km) runway. A thornier one may be getting motorists out of their cars, and finding more sustainable ways for the extra passengers – and thousands of staff – to travel to and from Heathrow.

Although ride-sharing, coaches and buses can play a part, scaling up rail is the clear alternative. Space on the existing line is, however, at a premium, and the Elizabeth line, built with a promise of connecting business travellers swiftly and directly from Heathrow to the City and Canary Wharf, only has limited paths. With everything up for negotiation, transport experts are asking: has the time come to kill off the Heathrow Express?

The obvious airport train, as unwary visitors often find out too late, may not be the best one. The Heathrow Express, which charges a whopping £26 for a 15- to 21-minute one-way hop, was long one of the most expensive airport connections around (at least until it was overtaken by the Luton Dart). It is, as advertised, technically the fastest way to central London, though passengers travelling beyond Paddington may reach their destination more quickly on the Elizabeth line or even the tube on a direct route.

For those who value the speed – in addition to TV news, a toilet and a luggage rack – it may be the perfect service. But the Heathrow Express was only used by 4.5 million passengers last year, a figure that represents, at best, less than 6% of Heathrow’s air passengers, with the number bolstered by airport staff on heavily discounted tickets.

Transport for London (TfL) has signalled its belief that the service’s time is up, as the government consults on its Heathrow expansion national policy statement. MPs must approve the statement for the runway to go ahead. That no longer seems automatic: Andy Burnham’s long-term scepticism over a third runway, along with the loss of Rachel Reeves in No 11 as a champion of expansion, makes Downing Street support look ambivalent at best – even given the new chancellor’s belated assertion that the “economic case stacks up”.

The Sunday Times reported this weekend that airport bosses have told ministers the third runway will not now be operational until 2039, a four year delay.

However many runways the airport has, TfL said it was “worth reviewing [the Heathrow Express’s] future in the context of determining the optimal mix of services on the Great Western mainline to make the most effective use of the limited capacity available”.

For TfL, the Elizabeth line, going deeper and cheaper into the heart of London, is “a more compelling service”. At the moment, only two Elizabeth line trains an hour serve Heathrow’s Terminal 5, which handles about 40% of the airport’s passengers. That means a passenger who does not carefully judge the timing may face a journey from the City or Canary Wharf to T5 of more than an hour. The frequency is due to double next year but more space into Heathrow could still be freed up.

Alex Williams, the chief customer and strategy officer at TfL, told MPs at a select committee hearing this month that the Heathrow Express was “taking up valuable paths that aren’t actually well used. There’s a way of repurposing that to be more affordable, more attractive, and carry more public transport users.”

Surface access, or getting people between central London and Britain’s biggest airport, underwent a step change with the Elizabeth line. Previously, the little-advertised offering Heathrow Connect joined the dots at the likes of Hayes & Harlington on a slower train to Paddington, serving many airport workers, if not international travellers. Fares were then about a third of the price of the Heathrow Express – a gap that is now less significant given that the Elizabeth line charges £15.50 to reach any of its central London stations. And for those who are able to book and plan a month ahead, the Express advance tickets can prove less expensive at £10.

TfL’s cheaper but slower alternative, the Piccadilly line (£5.90 into central London), is also due to get an upgrade of signalling and trains, increasing capacity.

Two additional rail schemes have been mooted – Heathrow Southern Railway and a Western Rail link – as ways to connect into the wider national rail network, and the Elizabeth line itself could be extended to Staines – all of which would encourage many more from the suburban commuter belt to take the train rather than drive to the airport.

Rebooting the railway now would coincide with the end of Heathrow Express’s operating agreement with the Department for Transport, which gives the service access rights to the national railway until June 2028. The DfT says no decision has yet been made on the future operation.

after newsletter promotion

It’s complicated: the actual operator, the FirstGroup-owned Great Western Railway, is due to be nationalised this December and become part of Great British Railways next year. Meanwhile, Heathrow owns the stations and five miles of railway from the airport to the mainline, part of its original £1bn investment in the Express in the 1990s.

The service brought in revenue of £48m for the first six months of 2026, according to a Heathrow spokesperson. They said: “It operates without taxpayer funding and helps keep airport charges down. Passengers don’t want fewer choices – Heathrow Express remains an important part of the competitive connectivity, convenience and flexibility they expect.”

But many question whether enough is being done – or if there will be enough pressure on Heathrow to avoid gridlock on the roads. The mayor of London, Sadiq Khan, warned that the taxpayer could be left picking up the bill for public transport improvements “left undefined and unfunded in the current proposals” for expansion – estimated at up to £9bn by TfL, a figure Heathrow said it did not recognise.

Most passengers go to the airport by car. And while Heathrow is funding new car parks – with plans to boost its parking space capacity from 21,000 to 36,000 – and its rerouting of the M25, it has not pledged any of its £33bn expenditure on improving the trains, Williams told the select committee, adding: “If you make it easier for people to park very near the terminal, how will you encourage them to get on the train?”

Without clear demands for a mode shift to public transport – as existed in the previous expansion plan, as well as in the planning permission for Gatwick’s recently approved second runway – the policy statement was “a step backwards”, Williams said, adding that in 2017 “there was a commitment or an aspiration from Heathrow to get no extra traffic. That is gone.”

A DfT spokesperson said: “We are carefully considering responses to the consultation, which sets out the key requirements any future planning application for expansion would have to meet, including public transport targets.”

A legal mandate could happen, a source said. But so far these are just targets: at the most stringent, 55% of airport passengers using public transport, and only when Heathrow’s third runway is fully operational.

For Anthony Smith, the former passenger watchdog who now chairs the Heathrow Area Transport Forum, it seems a curious timetable. He told MPs: “If you’re trying to shift people out of cars in 20 years’ time, when you’ve got 130 million passengers, it’s just harder, harder, harder.”

‘Refusing to meet Trump was an easy no’: Colin Kaepernick on being ‘blackballed’ for taking the knee, racism, and why he’s still ready to play

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 10:59:33 GMT

Ten years ago, the San Francisco 49ers quarterback refused to stand for the national anthem. He was accused of disrespecting the flag, the game, and America. In a rare interview, he talks about inspiring a global gesture of civil rights

Colin Kaepernick still gets up at 4.30am every morning to train. “Strength training, speed training, position training – still do all of the same type of workouts I did while I was playing,” he says cheerily. “And then go about the rest of my day.” It is almost 10 years since Kaepernick last played a game of top-flight football. His career was abruptly and cruelly cut short just as it was peaking, after the National Football League (NFL) effectively closed ranks and shut him out for being too political. Now, at 38 years old, he is well aware that his chances of a return are dwindling by the day, but he remains as game-ready as ever. “I stay relentless at it,” he continues in his easy drawl. “I look at it from the perspective of, ‘What are the things that I can control?’ And what I know I can control is being prepared for when opportunity knocks, and to also continue knocking, on my end, looking for ways and opportunities … just staying resilient and focused and disciplined – that is what’s gotten me to this point in my life.”

Kaepernick’s story is defined by the events of late 2016, when he repeatedly refused to stand for the pre-game national anthem – resulting in a chorus of booing on the pitch, insults and outrage off it, and exclusion from the sport he still loves. He was one of the biggest names in the game at the time; quarterback for the San Francisco 49ers, a national celebrity, sponsored by major brands, and looking back, his actions fed into so much that has happened since: the rise of Donald Trump, the Black Lives Matter protests and a global reckoning with racism, then the backlash against what is now being called “Woke 1.0”, and the resurgence of a white nationalism that the US complacently assumed was in the past.

Through all of this, Kaepernick has largely held his silence. He has rarely spoken to the media and restrained from making public statements. Why so, I ask. Surely there must have been times he’s wanted to speak out?

“Oh, absolutely,” he replies. “But I go back to, like, what am I trying to accomplish by doing so?” The temptation to rebut all the lies, the bad takes, the accusations was great, he admits, but, “I realised that, coming out of the protests in 2016, there was a lot of movement and effort made to try to make it as if I was the singular voice in this space doing work, and I was the person solely leading this movement, and that’s just not the reality.”

In person, Kaepernick is friendly and relaxed, speaking on a videocall from his agent’s office in New York (understandably, he doesn’t like to disclose where he lives or spends his time). Even when he’s talking about the worst moments in his life, which is most of the time in our 90-minute conversation, his face defaults to a smile and he’s quick to laugh. He’s looking as dapper as ever: black dress shirt, top button done up; neatly trimmed facial hair; his voluminous afro a work of tonsorial topiary.

The reason Kaepernick is talking now is because he has a new memoir: The Perilous Fight, which details his upbringing, his illustrious sporting career, and the events leading up to and from that pivotal moment in his life. This is not Kaepernick closing off a chapter of his life, he insists, he just felt that now was the time to speak up: “It’s important for where society is, where we’re at as a country, and some of the direction that the world’s heading in, to be able to continue to move things forward.” Also, he says, “we’re coming up on the 10-year anniversary. So a lot things just naturally aligned.”

He doesn’t need to clarify the anniversary he’s referring to. Kaepernick’s decision to protest was the culmination of “a lifetime of experiences of being Black in America,” he says. But in the moment, it was also spontaneous: “It is not something I discussed with anyone else. It was a personal belief and conviction, and originally I did it not knowing or thinking anybody would see or ask about it,” he says. He didn’t even tell his then fiance (now wife), Nessa Diab. The first three times he did it, hardly anyone noticed. At the 49ers’ preseason game in Santa Clara, California, on 14 August 2016, Kaepernick did not take the knee; he simply sat on a cool box during the pre-game Star-Spangled Banner. He was recovering from injury and not dressed for the game, so he was inconspicuous. He did the same thing for the next two games.

By the third time, NFL Network reporter Steve Wyche (who is Black) had clocked it, and spoke to Kaepernick about it. Wyche had also noticed that Kaepernick had been posting all year on his social media about Malcolm X, Martin Luther King Jr, Muhammad Ali, Black Panther co-founder Huey P Newton and Tupac Shakur. That January, for example, he had posted a quote from Dr King: “He who accepts evil without protesting against it is really cooperating with it.”

Kaepernick had certainly been on a journey in terms of his Black history education, partly thanks to Diab – who, a few years earlier, had given him a copy of Malcolm X’s autobiography and told him he’d be “for ever changed”. But his decision to act was also motivated by recent police killings of innocent Black men: Mario Woods, shot and killed by five officers in December 2015 in San Francisco, where Kaepernick was living at the time, using what was later judged “unnecessary force”; Alton Sterling, shot and killed in Louisiana in July 2016; Philando Castile, shot and killed in Minnesota the day after Sterling’s death.

“You then get to a point of, if you understand the problem and you understand the reality and you understand the experience, you either look at yourself in the mirror and say, ‘I’m gonna take action and try to do something about it’, or, ‘I’m not going to, and I’m going to be complicit in this’,” he says. The reality had become clear to him: that “the United States is not a representation of my ideals and my beliefs and has not been representing myself or the Black community. And that has been true since its inception.”

By the time Kaepernick took the knee for the first time, at the suggestion of his team-mate Eric Reid, who knelt alongside him, the issue had become a global news story. He, Reid and others continued to kneel through that season, often to boos and chants of “USA! USA!” Opponents accused Kaepernick of disrespecting the flag, the country, the military, and law enforcement, repeating the familiar mantra that politics should be kept out of sport. People began selling T-shirts outside football stadiums showing him in the scope of a rifle or telling him to, “Shut up and stand up!” Social media posts against Kaepernick turned vicious and racist. He began to receive death threats, including letters sent to his home address. Unfamiliar cars would park outside the entrance to his and Diab’s house, within a gated community. He temporarily moved out, for their safety.

Trump, then a presidential candidate, seized on the controversy: “I think it’s a terrible thing. And maybe he should find a country that works better for him,” he told a radio interviewer. Steve King, at the time a Republican congressman, invoked Diab’s Egyptian heritage to argue that “this is activism that’s sympathetic to Isis”. President Obama’s response was different: “I think he cares about some real, legitimate issues that have to be talked about,” he told reporters.

Kaepernick felt largely supported by his immediate teammates; less so by the NFL as an institution. By the end of the 2016 season, by which time dozens of other players had joined in the knee-taking, it had become clear to him they were “trying to get rid of me”, he believes. In February 2017, the 49ers’ new coach and general manager gave him a choice: he could opt out of his contract now, or they would cut him later – knowing that if he left later, his chances of signing for another team would be greatly reduced. In other words, they were pushing him out, but wanted to make it look like he was leaving of his own volition. “It was a cowardly way for them to handle it,” he says.

Kaepernick was “both surprised and not” by the response. “History tells us that a reaction like this is likely to take place. At the same time, because I have a belief that people are fundamentally good and want to do right, I was amazed at how visceral the response was to saying we shouldn’t be killing Black people. It is almost unfathomable to me that that is something that’s a debate in this country. And on the back of that was a realisation of: good, we need to have this conversation. It made it very clear where a lot of people’s beliefs lay, which then became a much more honest place to be. And there really wasn’t a whole lot of middle ground.”

It must have been an alienating experience, I suggest. Were there times when it all got to him?

“The same way it revealed a lot about society at large, it also revealed a lot about the people around me,” he replies. He talks of how it led to deeper relationships, new friendships, an expanded community. “So while a lot of the immediate reaction is, ‘Oh here was all of the backlash and all of the things that were difficult’, it’s also, ‘Here are all of the great things that came out of this.’ Both of those exist, but we have to put things in perspective. Maybe that’s the eternal optimist in me: I like to look at things through the lens of ‘these are opportunities to get better’.”

You are relentlessly positive, aren’t you, I say to him. He laughs. “I try to be! That’s not to say that that negative thing doesn’t exist, but I don’t want to just live in that negative thing. I think there’s always a solution, and a way forward.”

If there is any middle ground to occupy when it comes to race issues in the US, Kaepernick could make a pretty good claim to it. His racial identity is more complicated than it appears. He was born to a Black father and a white, teenage mother, and was adopted at five weeks old by a white family from Wisconsin (he has never met his biological parents). Rick and Teresa Kaepernick were conservative, church-going, Republican-leaning. Rick was a manager for a cheese company. They already had a son and a daughter, but had lost two sons due to heart defects and were eager to have another one, irrespective of race. So Kaepernick grew up in predominantly white communities, first in Wisconsin, then, from age four, in Turlock, California.

As such, his early experiences of being Black in the US were largely as an isolated individual, often made more acute by his parents’ lack of understanding or even awareness of his racial difference. “They came in with a perspective of, ‘Hey, if we do things the same way we did with my brother and sister, everything will be OK’, and that just wasn’t the case.”

Growing up Black in a white community had its advantages, he says. “You get to see and experience a lot of things that otherwise may not reveal themselves. There was a level of comfort there of like, ‘Oh well, if this Black boy is in this white family, he must have assimilated into some of the white perspectives and cultural elements. That makes it OK for us to talk freely and openly in front of him.’ You get a lot of valuable insights into people’s true perspectives, and it gives you a better understanding of how to be able to navigate that.”

But he was often treated very differently when strangers did not realise he was his parents’ son. In his memoir he recounts how, aged eight, he was tied to a tree by some older white kids in his neighbourhood, who called him the N-word and told him to “go back to Niger”.

Kaepernick’s youthful attempts to connect with Black culture did not always go down well with his parents, either. When he first got his hair braided in cornrows, like his hero, basketball star Allan Iverson, they told him: “You look like a thug.” They were happier when he brought home a white girlfriend than when he brought home a Black one. There were a lot of arguments, he says, over his taste in hairstyles, clothes, music. “But what I will say is, the areas that there was no question around were the idea of being a moral person and doing the right thing and treating people well … The foundational piece is, I know my parents love me as their son.”

Sport was one route to connecting with his racial identity. He was outstanding from a young age – as talented at pitching a baseball as throwing a football, and a pretty good basketball player, too. As he ascended the ranks of school and college football, he came into contact with more Black peers. He also experienced the US’s racially charged law enforcement first-hand. As a teen he was pulled over and given a ticket driving his mother’s convertible with three Black friends – “driving while Black”, he jokes. Another time, at college, the cops pulled guns on his Black roommates, who were helping someone move; they had assumed it was a burglary.

But Kaepernick’s discipline and commitment began to pay off: by the time he turned pro, in 2011, he was already a clear talent. The following season he led the 49ers to the Super Bowl (they lost to the Baltimore Ravens). He was one of the best “dual-threat” quarterbacks in the league – as effective running with the ball as he was passing it. In many respects, before 2016, he was living the footballing dream: he was rich, famous, one of the biggest stars in the game. He had a glamorous girlfriend (Diab was hosting a hip-hop radio show and appearing on MTV), big-name sponsors like Nike, was on the cover of magazines. “Suddenly, I was everywhere all at once,” he recalls.

As much as he still loves the sport, Kaepernick’s protest changed his relationship to it, almost irreparably. And as much as he sought to expose racism in policing, he exposed it within football. More than 70% of NFL players are Black, but historically, team owners and coaches have been overwhelmingly white, and there have been mechanisms in place to keep it that way. In his book, Kaepernick likens the NFL’s scouting combine, where college players are assessed by NFL teams with a series of physical tests and demeaning medical assessments, to a slave market. He recounts how commodified players often are, how their injuries are often glossed over in the interests of short-term results, even how Black players’ baseline intelligence is assumed to be lower than that of white players, which makes it harder for them to claim medical benefits for brain injuries later on. “It is something that historically we will look back on as a society like, how did we ever let that fly? The same way that we ask, how did we ever allow slavery or Jim Crow to happen?”

After he left the 49ers in 2017, no other team picked him up. Other players who protested had similar experiences, including Reid, even as scores more continued to take the knee. Trump, by then president, told a rally that he’d love to see NFL owners respond by saying: “Get that son of a bitch off the field right now. Out! He’s fired.” Many of those owners were his people: white, Republican-leaning billionaires. Some were friends and direct supporters, including New England Patriots owner Robert Kraft, the Dallas Cowboys’ Jerry Jones, and Miami Dolphins’ Stephen Ross (who held a fundraiser for Trump in 2019).

Kaepernick believes the NFL made an example of him: “By blackballing me, denying me employment because of fighting to create a better society and fighting to keep people alive, there’s very real implications about who they are as an organisation and what they believe. I think, largely, the community and society knows it and sees it,” he says.

In October 2017, he sued the NFL for “collusion” in shutting him out in retaliation for his activism. The NFL settled out of court in February 2019 for an undisclosed sum. Kaepernick has signed a non-disclosure agreement so cannot go into details, he says, although he would be “very open to the NFL releasing all the documentation and letting society decide”. But he clearly regrets the way things panned out: “I was not protesting the NFL; I was protesting what was happening directly in communities and Black people being killed by police. And the NFL inserted themselves within that conversation and took a side.” (NFL Commissioner Roger Goodell has denied Kaepernick was blackballed, saying personnel decisions are made by individual teams.)

As well as being the 10th anniversary of Kaepernick’s protest, it is also, of course, 10 years since the arrival of Trump on the political scene. Their fates seem intertwined: Trump capitalised on Kaepernick’s protest to whip up political support, then his associations with NFL owners helped shut Kaepernick out of the sport. What would Kaepernick say to Trump if they met?

“Well here’s the funny part,” he says breaking into a broad grin. “My lawyers got a phone call with him asking for me to come in to a meeting, I believe it was 2017 or 2018.” There was not a lot of clarity around why Trump wanted to meet him, but it was “a very easy no”, he says. “I am willing to work with anyone who has a genuine interest in creating a better environment and a more equitable society. I do not think that is the case there. I would be curious why there would even be a call and what the topic would be beyond trying to do a photo op.”

Within a few tumultuous years, Kaepernick’s stance began to look less controversial. The Black Lives Matter movement had already begun before he started kneeling, but by 2020 the catalogue of police killings of innocent and unarmed Black men, many of them captured on video, had become intolerable. The murder of George Floyd, in Minneapolis in May 2020, was a tipping point, sparking huge anti-racism protests worldwide. As a consequence, players began taking the knee across US sports – football, basketball, baseball, soccer, hockey – at every level, from high school upwards. In England, football players began to take the knee before kick-off for every game, including the national team. Sportspeople and public figures across the world joined in. Where Kaepernick had once knelt virtually alone, now he had inspired a global gesture. He takes no credit for what happened, simply observing that, when it comes to highlighting police brutality, “there are people that have been doing work on the ground directly in communities for years and decades, and a lot of this bubbled up and came to fruition and got elevated during this moment”.

In terms of the so-called “racial reckoning” that ensued in the immediate aftermath of 2020, he observes that “people and organisations were pledging large sums of money to address everything but police brutality. A lot of it became about businesses using the moment to further their interests.” There was some radical reassessment of racial attitudes on all levels – societal, political, corporate – but there was also a lot of political virtue-signalling, such as house speaker Nancy Pelosi, Kamala Harris and other Democrats taking the knee in the Capitol in June 2020, scarves of kente cloth around their shoulders. The then Labour leader Keir Starmer and deputy leader Angela Rayner also performatively knelt, as did many others. Even some progressive politicians cringe at the recollection now. We are speaking shortly before Alexandrio Ocasio-Cortez gave her assessment that “Woke 1.0 was crazy” – suggesting that progressives went too far, post-BLM. This comes on top of ongoing efforts by Trump to roll back all manner of civil rights and inclusion advances: removing high-ranking Black officials from the military; allowing immigration officials to target Black and brown people; effectively operating a whites-only immigration policy. It is sometimes difficult to see what progress has been made. What does it say, for example, that Trump is still in power, a decade on?

“It says we have a long way to go,” Kaepernick acknowledges. But as ever, he accentuates the positive: “I also think, within that, it has created such a clear and stark reality for so many people that they are rejecting the politics of the administration and looking for something that actually serves everyone.”

This is where Kaepernick’s energy is focused: building the movement. He may have been quiet but he has been busy over the past decade. His Know Your Rights Camp tours the country teaching young people “not just how to survive but also how to thrive”. His charity funds legal assistance and independent autopsies for those who need it (including the family of Nolan Wells, the Black Mississippi teenager who died in mysterious circumstances on a trip with his white friends this July). He runs a publishing company, and has donated over $1m to community projects. He’s thinking in terms of Ella Baker, the relatively unsung activist who laid the foundations for America’s civil rights movement, from the 1930s onwards. “That was centred around: yes, we need strong leaders, but we need strong people, and how do we elevate more people to become leaders so this truly becomes a movement?”

Progressive politics is making a comeback, he says, especially within younger generations. “When we think about gen Z and gen Alpha, they’re very much coming from a perspective of, ‘Do you represent my beliefs? Do you represent who I am? And if you don’t, we’re not going to support you’ … As more and more pressure is able to be exerted from the ground up, I think those high-level conversations and positionings are going to start shifting and swinging as well.” He has a four-year-old daughter now, he adds, describing her as “relentlessly fierce”: “Being a father heightens the sense of urgency.”

Given all this, isn’t Kaepernick more an activist than a sportsman now?

“I look at myself as multi-faceted,” he says. “I still love playing football. I still train for it, make sure that I’m ready and prepared. I also care deeply about people. And if that gets framed as being an activist, by all means, great, let’s do that. But at the core of it, I think people should be able to live, they should be able to thrive, they should able to have dignity, have justice, and that should extend to everyone.”

Kaepernick was always mindful of the roll call of Black sportspeople who took a stand for civil liberties and paid a price for it, he says. “That was something I was aware of prior to ever protesting.” Muhammad Ali refused to be drafted into the Vietnam War and was stripped of his heavyweight boxing title. Tommie Smith and John Carlos raised their fists in Black Power salutes on the podium at the 1968 Olympics, which effectively ended their sprinting careers. Curt Flood challenged the “reserve clause”, which prevented baseball players from choosing their own fates, in 1969, and forfeited his career. More recently basketball player Mahmoud Abdul-Rauf, refused to stand for the national anthem throughout the 1995-96 season, for similar reasons to Kaepernick, and was suspended and fined by the NBA as a consequence.

Kaepernick has had a few tryouts with interested teams, most recently in 2022 with the Las Vegas Raiders – their head coach told him, “You look bigger, faster, stronger than when I last saw you,” Kaepernick says. But the longed-for return has not happened. Is there a part of him that accepts his sporting career may be over? “We don’t have to accept that as the reality,” he replies. “There’s an opportunity to change that … so that when an athlete or when someone speaks up to try to create a better life and better future for a people, for a community, for society, they aren’t met with exile, but they’re actually embraced and people say, ‘You know what, you’re right. Let’s take the actions to actually make this better.’ When we can lay that foundation, that creates significant opportunity for change.”

So he will continue to train, he says. “I will not let go of that as a discipline, as part of who I am.”

If he was back on an NFL team again, would he still take the knee for the national anthem?

“Absolutely,” he says. “The work still needs to be done. More people need to be brought into that work and into that conversation. And more people need to be taking action around it. And I will continue to do the work. I will continue to protest because, quite literally, people’s lives are at stake.”

The Perilous Fight by Colin Kaepernick is published by Grand Central. To support the Guardian, order your copy from guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

The truth behind Donald Trump’s ‘biggest oil deal in world history’

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 10:00:33 GMT

The US’s oil deal with Venezuela faces multiple legal and logistical problems, including questions about whether it can be implemented

Donald Trump has long coveted the oilfields of other nations and declared an agreement with Venezuela to be “the biggest oil deal in world history”. But the agreement, reached after the US seized Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro, is almost certainly doomed to collapse amid a wide array of legal and logistical issues, a Guardian investigation has found.

The US president first mused about taking oil from Iran in 1987, when he told ABC’s Barbara Walters that Iranian attacks on American shipping during the Iran-Iraq war required an extreme response. “Why couldn’t we go in and take over some of their oil, which is along the sea?” he asked. Over the ensuing years, he has returned frequently to the idea that the US should seize oil from other countries after military conflict, from Libya to Iraq.

Earlier this year, Trump finally got a chance to enact his plan – at gunpoint. US forces stormed Venezuela in January and seized Maduro, who was quickly shuttled to a federal holding facility in the US and replaced by the compliant Delcy Rodríguez. Trump told the Atlantic in the days following the raid: “If [Rodríguez] doesn’t do what’s right, she is going to pay a very big price, probably bigger than Maduro.”

Then in August, Trump announced that the office of strategic capital (OSC) at the Pentagon, which he has rapidly transformed, would own a third of the second-biggest private Venezuelan oil firm, North American Blue Energy Partners (Nabep). Trump said the deal means he’ll soon refill the US strategic petroleum reserve, which dropped to a longtime low after the US invaded Iran.

But virtually everything Trump and his cabinet have said about the deal is false and misleading, according to the experts and officials who spoke with the Guardian. The Venezuelan law governing oil development does not allow for 100-year deals, or anything longer than 25 years. The OSC isn’t authorized by US law, experts say, to own shares in companies. Moreover, they say, the deal as structured won’t bring new capital to Venezuela’s oil sector.

And contrary to Trump’s claims, the Venezuelan oil will not help refill the US strategic petroleum reserve any time in the near future.

There is also a curious figure at the center of the deal: Alejandro Betancourt López, the affable Venezuelan with a complex background who is becoming a partner of the US government as the owner of Nabep.

Betancourt, 46, went to college in Massachusetts and has homes in Spain, the UK and New York City. He has a history in Venezuela’s energy and oil sector, owns a sunglasses company and once had Rudy Giuliani as his lawyer.

Betancourt, who has been drawn into multiple international investigations in connection with Venezuelan corruption allegations, was brought into the deal by a private associate of Marco Rubio, according to three people who know him. Betancourt has never been charged with or convicted of any crime.

The Guardian has learned that Venezuelan government officials who are now in charge once hired investigators and hackers to dig into the source of Betancourt’s money.

Experts are ultimately skeptical the oil deal can hold together. “The deal is like the big beautiful wall that Mexico will pay for,” said former US diplomat John Feeley.

It was less than a month after the January US raid that toppled Maduro that Exxon’s CEO, Darren Woods, said the country was “uninvestable” because of the “legal and commercial constructs and frameworks in place today”.

Two people familiar with the process said Trump began looking for a way to make sure the US had “skin in the game” – financial ownership that would put investors at ease. The potential answer became the US stake in Betancourt’s firm, North American Blue Energy Partners.

Though the White House and defense department say it has 35% ownership, the Pentagon told lawmakers on the congressional armed services committee in a written briefing seen by the Guardian it has “warrants” in Nabep: rights to purchase shares, rather than the shares themselves.

The state department, the administration says, will also have a right to buy 20% of all the oil Nabep pumps, at cost – meaning it should be able to buy it cheaper than the market price.

“The Departments of State and War have negotiated a historic opportunity to secure US majority control of more than 65bn barrels of proven oil reserves in Venezuela at zero taxpayer cost,” a Pentagon spokesperson said.

It’s unclear how the US would buy crude oil, or what the process would be. The state department, for its part, insists: “This is a private deal with a private company. It’s not a deal with the interim government of Venezuela and there was not a political process included in the negotiations.”

That appears to be at odds with Trump’s initial announcement, which said: “The United States of America has just entered into an Agreement with the Country of Venezuela.” The administration says a majority of the board of Nabep, which is incorporated in Barbados, will be US citizens.

The Pentagon ownership has been one of the most puzzling parts of the deal, because the idea that the Department of Defense could own more than a third of a Venezuelan oil company, or any oil company, would have been unthinkable in any previous US administration. Prior to Trump, the defense department had never operated like a private equity fund that could directly own percentages of foreign companies.

But the Pentagon has been transformed. The OSC is under the authority of the deputy defense secretary, Stephen Feinberg, a powerful billionaire who wields the real financial power in the Pentagon and has surrounded himself with former employees from the private equity giant Cerberus, as the Guardian has reported. Feinberg installed a former Cerberus employee, David Lorch, as the head of the OSC.

The Trump administration is using a 1950s law called the Defense Production Act to allow the Pentagon to become a kind of giant investment fund. “It has turned them into a vehicle for ownership of substantial domestic and international companies,” said the former official.

A former Pentagon official familiar with the project said Feinberg and Lorch structured the financial end of Trump’s Venezuela deal. “It is absolutely a Feinberg project,” said the former Pentagon official.

However, the law that created the OSC actually didn’t authorize it to make equity investments, and the Pentagon’s spokesperson told Reuters: “The Office of ​Strategic Capital (OSC) ⁠does not take equity stakes in private companies” in August.

“Congress clearly doesn’t believe that it has given the power to OSC to make equity investments,” said Ashley Deeks, the vice-dean of the University of Virginia law school, who has written about US government ownership stakes in companies for the Harvard National Security Journal.

Since the OSC is not authorized to invest in shares of private companies, the Nabep ownership will be held by an entirely different Pentagon office, called Industrial Base Analysis and Sustainment (Ibas), according to the former Pentagon official.

But the mission of Ibas has nothing to do with oil. Its job, as it says on its website, is solely to “strengthen the US Defense Industrial Base”.

That incongruity is just one of the reasons major oil companies and investors privately say they are keeping clear of this deal, said Phil Gunson of the International Crisis Group, who has been briefed on the problem. “They are concerned about the irregularities. They are concerned about the terms of the deal. It’s the opacity of the agreement that has serious investors concerned,” he said.

“Whether the Pentagon has the authority to act in this way is debatable,” he added.

The White House directed questions about whether the OSC is authorized to own shares to the defense department. The department didn’t answer emailed questions about the matter. In a statement, a representative merely repeated some prior claims by the administration: it’s a “historic opportunity”, with control over most of Venezuela’s oil reserves.

The length of the deal also doesn’t appear to be as long as the administration claims. Venezuelan legal expert Jose Ignacio Hernández says Venezuelan law is crystal clear that this is impossible, and Venezuela’s government itself has said the deal is for 25 years, not 100.

“This is all just propaganda,” said Ignacio Hernández. “It cannot be implemented as announced by the administration.”

Those who have met Alejandro Betancourt say he is remarkably pleasant and obliging. “He was a really nice guy,” says Lev Parnas, the former Giuliani associate who broke from Maga after his arrest in 2019, and who traveled with Betancourt. “I don’t like too many people but I like him, his wife, his family.”

“Betancourt, he’s a good sales guy,” said another American who has known him for years. The US secretary of state, Marco Rubio, told an interviewer in early September that Betancourt had a “track record” of producing oil.

Some view him as an effective businessman who can deal with a variety of administrations and has experience both in energy and oil deals.

In 2012, Betancourt bought El Alamín castle in Spain, a vast estate with its own tennis court and soccer field, according to aerial photos. The castle has become a venue to host meetings with prominent business leaders and politicians, El País reported.

Betancourt has been a subject of scandal for well over a decade. Public scrutiny of him first emerged in the US in 2013, when a former US ambassador to Venezuela, Otto Reich, laid out a series of allegations in a civil lawsuit, including violations of the Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations (Rico) Act, which targets organized crime, and defamation, in New York federal court. Along with his partners in a company called Derwick Associates, Betancourt made his money in building electrical plants in contracts he won by kickbacks, according to Reich’s complaint. The Rico claims were dismissed when the court found that Reich failed to establish a legal “pattern of racketeering”, and the defamation claims were rejected for lack of jurisdiction.

In a letter to the Guardian, Betancourt’s lawyer Vel Freedman wrote: “Neither Derwick nor Mr Betancourt ever asked, directed, or encouraged anyone to pay a bribe.”

In 2018, Betancourt’s cousin, a business partner also affiliated with Derwick, was charged in a $1.2bn money-laundering case in federal court in Miami. An affidavit submitted by an agent with Homeland Security Investigations cited an unnamed “conspirator 2”, who he said received hundreds of millions in laundered funds with the cousin, who is still a fugitive in the case.

The Miami Herald reported it was Betancourt. In a letter to the Guardian, Betancourt’s lawyer wrote: “Mr Betancourt has never been charged with a crime in the United States. He has never been named as a defendant. The United States government has never sought his extradition, and the United States government has never publicly identified him as a target, as an unnamed co-conspirator, or as any numbered conspirator in any charging instrument.”

Marco Rubio told a Venezuelan radio interviewer that Betancourt was not the subject of a US probe. “There was no investigation within our system against him.”

In the height of Trump’s first term, Betancourt hired Giuliani, then Trump’s personal lawyer, as his own lawyer.

His relationship with Venezuela’s government has seesawed over the years. According to two people familiar with the situation, Venezuelan authorities were so concerned over allegations about Betancourt’s finances that they hired a team of lawyers and investigators that began an intense investigation to try to track his money.

Betancourt’s attorney said the businessman never misappropriated money.

The investigators hired by Venezuela even used hackers to try to trace his funds. A source familiar with the hacking project said their intrusion was extensive. “His WhatsApp,” they said, “‘His accountants, his lawyers, everything.”

Corporate computer hacking was a well-known investigative tool, though usually illegal, at the time. A 2021 document obtained by the Guardian, prepared by a group of hackers, shows a list of Venezuelan targets. It lists Betancourt as a “secondary” target.

Betancourt’s lawyer didn’t confirm the hacking, but he said that Betancourt was a major supporter of the interim opposition government backed by the US. If it happened, he said, any hacking effort “belongs in the context of Mr Betancourt’s opposition to the Maduro regime”, rather than as a legitimate financial investigation.

The Venezuelan ministry of communications and information did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

By 2024, Betancourt was involved in drilling again in Venezuela, with Nabep, the company he owned at the time with Harry Sargeant, an American oil executive. The company started small, at just 23,000 barrels per day, according to recent statements by Venezuela’s interim president.

In September 2025, Spanish police descended on his castle in connection with a money-laundering investigation, according to Spanish press accounts.

But at about that time, officials in the Trump administration were already in touch with Betancourt about the pressure on Venezuela’s government, according to a former official, as well as a businessman who was aware of it. Betancourt’s lawyer wrote that the Spanish investigation “has never resulted in any charge against Mr. Betancourt”. The Guardian was not able to confirm the status of the investigation.

By 3 January, when Maduro was arrested in the US raid, a source who was involved said Betancourt played a crucial role in negotiations with Delcy Rodríguez. Betancourt’s lawyer wrote to the Guardian that Betancourt functioned as a go-between. “There was no established channel of trust between Venezuela’s interim government and the United States. Both sides spoke with Mr Betancourt, because each knew him and each was prepared to rely on him, and he facilitated communications between them.”

What many people familiar with Venezuela’s recent history question is why the US government is going into business with Betancourt given his substantial baggage.

“The only discernible winner in any of this is Betancourt,” said a businessman who has spent years on Venezuelan issues.

For Trump, the issue is simple. “It was a war, but it’s perhaps the biggest deal ever made,” he told the United Nations this week. “To the victor belong the spoils. You’ve all heard that.”

Amazon’s Ring wants to replace local WhatsApp groups. It’s a recipe for curtain-twitching disaster

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 09:00:31 GMT

Do we really want a slick digital message board overseen by Amazon? It’s the neighbourhood nonsense we treasure

Ring, the Amazon subsidiary of camera-enabled doorbells fame, wants to be an even bigger part of your neighbourhood. Next month in the UK, it will be launching Neighbours, a community app that seeks to replace the now traditional neighbourhood Facebook or WhatsApp group. It will be available inside the Ring app, free to everybody, including people without Ring products, and will include a community requests feature wherein the police can ask for footage from residents living near reported crimes, who can then choose whether or not to share it.

My first thought was that this is curtain-twitching culture gone mad. If you must have a Ring doorbell (and my instinctive feeling as someone without one, a feeling I will no doubt have until I get one and decide it’s great, is that it’s narc-coded behaviour) then: OK. But does Amazon need to be in charge of a digital village messageboard too?

The selling point, Ring thinks, is that posting will be anonymised, and posters will have to conform to strict guidelines on what they are allowed to post. It would, in other words, be very unlike the lawless badlands of a neighbourhood WhatsApp.

Maybe people really did want these groups replaced by something more centrally managed. I asked around people I knew about the WhatsApp communities that they were in, and the kinds of behaviour they had witnessed. Some of it, naturally, demonstrated an ugly dislike of homeless people, fear and loathing of door-to-door salespeople, racial profiling of local youths, and the view that everyone not personally known to the residents was a criminal in waiting.

Some of what people encountered on these groups was just strange: a north London WhatsApp group of more than 500 people having to disband because someone was giving away a Hewlett-Packard printer and another person said that shouldn’t be allowed because of BDS; a woman forced to recuse herself from a neighbourhood group because she saw a toad get squashed by a car, and was inundated with local volunteers who wanted her to set up and run a toad protection squad in case there were other vulnerable toads in the area; a man with a vendetta against a local couple who were feeding the foxes that went on to rip up his garden taking to his local chat to respond with witty bons mots such as “they are as stubborn as the foxes themselves but lack their intelligence”; repeated reports about a “sick cat” that people familiar with the animal had to confirm was “just ugly”; and this is leaving out the party poopers, bin police and other assorted oddballs.

But then there were the wonderful stories, too: the organisation of a funeral procession for an older woman who died on the street with no immediate family; borrowing laptop chargers and camping equipment; taking in people who had locked themselves out. And all of these led me to feel a little envious.

I’ve just moved, but for four years before that I lived on a street in south London. One time, I witnessed something insane happen. My flatmate was at home one Saturday afternoon and heard an altercation on the street, and looked out the window to see what was going on. He was, in his way, curtain twitching. A neighbourhood cat, a friendly local celebrity who always greeted you as you passed, had been mauled to death by an XL bully being walked past the house where it lived.

The cat’s owners were, understandably, furious and upset. The noise my flatmate heard was them trying to detain the person with the dog so they could be held accountable. Later that week, signs appeared on trees on the street inviting anybody who knew the departed cat to gather outside the family’s home for drinks. My flatmate and I looked at this sign and became anxious that nobody would go. I was moved almost to tears at the image of this grieving family, including two young children, with their trestle table of prosecco and nobody to serve it to.

We needn’t have worried. Dozens of people showed up, with flowers and wine and stories of giving little pieces of chicken to the cat. At this memorial, I looked around and thought: God, it is actually quite strange and perhaps reflects poorly on all of us that most of us had never met. Our street, as far as I know, had no WhatsApp group. If it had done, I would have known these people already. Community, especially in big cities, can be hard to come by, and is precious to people when it’s found. After that cat memorial, we invited two of our newfound neighbours over for drinks. We’ve since become friends. I felt, for the first time, part of my local area.

Neighbourhood WhatsApp groups can be a way to create that feeling. But. But! They are also places where people exercise their worst small-time cop impulses, demonstrate their smallmindedness, allow the little annoyances of life to induce them to send people they hardly know crazed screeds about recycling etiquette. Would you give up the latter if you had to give up the former as well, though?

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Here’s a comment Dave Ward, Ring’s managing director of international, gave to the Guardian about what they want to do. “We are going to coach people to make sure they’re creating the right sort of post, asking them if that’s really something they want to write or whether it really needs that descriptive term, to help stop the type of content no one wants to see and make it more community focused. That’s very different to other places [such as WhatsApp groups].”

So Ring wants to streamline things, moderate, vet, polish. I have worked my way around to feeling, however, that the problem here isn’t just Ring wanting to connect us all up to the police, encouraging the darker side of local message groups, that micro-nation surveillance state tendency, or even it wanting to induct more people into local groups that can so often be irritating. It’s that the rough edges of these groups are the spice of life. You don’t have to participate in a neighbourhood WhatsApp group, but if you choose to be in one, the price for the moments of kindness and connection you can find within them is the nonsense.

Imogen West-Knights is a writer and journalist

‘We left Ireland because there wasn’t work – and we wanted to get the hell away’: Trespasses author Louise Kennedy

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 08:00:30 GMT

Her Troubles-set debut became a hit TV series starring Gillian Anderson. Now the novelist has returned to her teen years for a follow-up. She talks about her journey from chef to author, and how her cancer diagnosis inspired her to write

Louise Kennedy’s life has hardly wanted for dramatic events, but the recent past has been spectacularly busy, even by her standards. You wouldn’t know it to look at her, as we chat in the sitting room of the house in Sligo that she shares with her husband, son and daughter, but this is the home that she once thought would be repossessed. The couple bought it “for stupid money” in 2007, when they also opened a restaurant, initially so successful that the only way seemed to be up. The following year, financial mayhem descended on Ireland, their customers ebbed away, and the Celtic Tiger years morphed into a country racked with job losses, bankruptcies, apparently endless debt. “I didn’t think I’d ever be able to keep the house,” she says, glancing around an elegant room dotted with beautiful objects and plants, but nonetheless relaxed and comfortable. “I’d say we only got out of negative equity about a month ago. There are probably arguments for moving now, but I’m so proud that we managed to hold on to it, I’m not going anywhere. I’m going to be carried out of here in a box.”

Kennedy had been a chef for 30 years, working all over the place from Dublin to London and, for two years, Beirut, before ending up in Sligo, on Ireland’s west coast, not far from the border with her native Northern Ireland. Crucially, she had never given a thought to writing, not since a teacher had admired a poem she wrote when she was seven. Now, she is about to publish her second novel, Stations, which follows a collection of short stories, The End of the World Is a Cul-de-Sac, and her debut, Trespasses, which was shortlisted for the 2023 Women’s prize for fiction and won other prizes in Ireland and the UK in 2022 and 2023. Last year, Trespasses gained further acclaim when it was adapted for Channel 4 in a production starring Gillian Anderson as the mother of Cushla, the young Catholic teacher who falls in love with Michael, an older, married Protestant lawyer, in 1970s Belfast.

Trespasses fired readers’ imaginations because it gave an already complex love story a terrifying, high-stakes backdrop; Michael and Cushla’s relationship wasn’t simply clandestine because it was extramarital, but because they came from communities pitted against one another in an occupied country. And to recreate the detail, texture and jeopardy of Belfast at the time, Kennedy had to look no further than her own upbringing.

She relates it so vividly and, at times, so humorously, that you have to remind yourself how intensely difficult it must have been. Kennedy’s Catholic family ran pubs in Belfast. One day, her grandmother was on her way to bank the takings when a bomb exploded in a building she was walking past and a chunk of glass pierced her jugular vein. “Some off-duty British soldier, a young fella who was down the town, held her neck together to stop her from bleeding to death until the ambulance came,” Kennedy recalls, before adding that her grandmother’s life was saved by the fur coat she’d been wearing. Throughout the ordeal, she wouldn’t let go of the handbag full of money, nor stop insisting she had to go and fetch her daughter from school.

“There was a lot of scarring on her face because she’d been cut by glass, but already, even in 71, the plastic surgeons in the north were just brilliant at patching people up. She just had very fine lines where the scarring was. She was really lucky.” What about psychologically? “She was a complete walking trauma case. She never talked about that. She wouldn’t even have known the word trauma. But if there was a loud noise, she’d go to pieces.”

Meanwhile, Kennedy’s father had experienced intimidation at work, in a factory in East Belfast where he was the only Catholic. He had been followed home, and one of their Catholic neighbours had been killed in a loyalist “romper room” – essentially, an interrogation and murder site, the slang taken from a children’s TV programme. Now, her father was training to become an accountant through evening correspondence courses, simultaneously studying and minding the children while his wife went to work in the pub. One night, Kennedy’s mother, grandmother, two uncles and a policeman found themselves standing in a tunnel opposite the building when it was blown up, an attack that found its way into Trespasses. “It was a crazy thing to happen. And I think that that was the thing about the north: you know it’s not normal, you know it’s mental, but yet it is normal because this is how you have to live. You just have to go on about your business, because otherwise you’re going to be freaking out left, right, and centre. ”

Kennedy’s skill at conjuring the past without succumbing to the shorthand of nostalgia was one of the qualities that made for the success of the adaptation of Trespasses, which was written by Ailbhe Keogan, who also worked on Bad Sisters. “Ailbhe is not from the north, she’s from Kerry, and she was very open to me. I wanted the dialogue to be authentic to the north, but not just to the north. It also had to sound like 1975, and that’s quite easy for me to remember: the voice in my head is of a child in the north of Ireland in the 70s. And people don’t speak the same now as they did then. The place is really different. It was quite a complicated location shoot for that reason, because a lot of the place was wrecked and a lot of rebuilding has been done since that. It was pretty tricky to try and find a bar that hasn’t changed at all. The book is set in Holywood, County Down, where I grew up, but Holywood doesn’t look like it did in the 70s, so it was filmed in Portaferry, a village in County Down.”

In 1979, life changed again. Kennedy was 12, and in her first year at grammar school, when her parents decided they’d had enough and uprooted the family to Naas, then a small town not far south of Dublin. She hated it. “From my point of view, it was really crap.” She lost her pals, it took two years to get the phone connected, and even worse, there was only one television station, “so all of my cultural references had been wiped out”. Six weeks later, they went back to Belfast for a visit, and Kennedy was shocked to find how strange a friend’s accent sounded to her. “I just thought ‘Oh my God! I don’t belong anywhere.’ I didn’t belong to either place, and I still feel that now. When you leave a place, it goes on about its business, but for me it’s frozen in time.”

Back then, though, she didn’t have that perspective. “I was an atrocious adolescent. I was really angry that we’d had to leave and move to a place where there was one TV channel.” And it’s this dislocation that she’s mined for her new novel, Stations, in which two misfit teenage protagonists, Róisín and Red, cleave together to create some version of belonging. But as the story progresses from the early 1980s to this century, moving from Ireland to London, it becomes apparent that only one of them will thrive.

It’s a portrait not only of teenage alienation, displacement and small-town Ireland, but of one of the waves of Irish emigration that have characterised its history. Remembering her own time in London, Kennedy says that you could walk into a pub on Sunday mornings in the 1980s and 90s and feel like you were at mass. And you could also feel that you were in flight: “We left because there wasn’t work, but we also left because it was a closed, judgmental, shithole theocracy that we were living in, and we wanted to get the hell away.” It’s that historical precision that has led Anne Enright to say of Stations that “it holds a national sorrow”, describing it as a “work of mourning and reclamation”.

And in Róisín, Kennedy gave herself permission to write a “pain in the arse” character, unpopular, temperamental, self-centred, in contrast to Cushla whom, she says, readers found so likable. “I ran into a friend of mine recently who was in school with me. She was asking what the book is about and I said a character who moved from the north, and everybody in school hates her. She was like, is it a memoir?”

Back to that wild pivot from cooking to writing. How did all this happen? Put simply, Kennedy was still trying to keep her ailing restaurant on its legs back in 2014 when she found herself ambushed into going along to a new creative writing group set up by the writer Una Mannion. “Why would I be doing that?” she asked the friend doing the persuading, visual artist Niamh Mac Cabe, whereupon Mac Cabe just turned up and plonked her in the car. “I thought it was the most hilarious thing I’d ever heard in my life,” Kennedy remembers. But at that first meeting of eight or so people, Kennedy found herself committing to writing a piece over the next few weeks. “From the minute that I started trying to write this mad little short story – I didn’t even know what a short story was really – I just thought: I don’t really care what happens as long as I can find a way to keep doing this.”

Sign up to Inside Saturday

The only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.

after newsletter promotion

That story, which eventually found its way on to national radio, drew on a family memory, and told of a young girl in the 1920s who gets into a world of trouble when she writes Rudolph Valentino’s name in the list of that month’s deaths at church. When she read it to the group, “I fully expected everybody just to laugh or to very politely move on from having to talk about my crap story, but they were wildly enthusiastic. So I thought, ‘OK, I’m going to try to write another one.’”

Partly, she was enjoying the distraction. At work, Kennedy and her husband were constantly firefighting to stave off creditors and make sure staff got paid. “We were skint. Everybody was, and I suppose the thing is that if the whole country is like that, it means that the people who in the past you might have been able to go and borrow a couple of bob from didn’t have any. They were all up the shit as well.” When the restaurant finally closed, a few months after she had joined the writing group, “I just thought, I don’t care. I could sit and fart around trying to write something for two or three hours and I wouldn’t even have thought about the business.”

After that seismic change, her writing life began to blossom; she accumulated short stories, did an MA and then started a PhD at Queens University in Belfast, where she was supervised by the writer Garrett Carr, and began to publish in magazines. She acquired an agent, Eleanor Birne, who was building a list of Irish writers, and who told her that her work might be more attractive to British publishers if they thought a novel was coming. “I had lied to her and said, ‘Oh yeah, I’m kind of working on a novel’, but I wasn’t really.” She told Carr the same. But in fact, the idea for Trespasses was beginning to brew.

And then, another curve ball arrived, in the form of a diagnosis of melanoma: a mole on her shoulder blade had mutated into cancer, and subsequently, the cancer had spread. First, there was the prospect of surgery and, later, immunotherapy. She didn’t, she says, want to be thinking about cancer all the time, but she knew she wouldn’t be working as she had been. “So I just rigged myself up a sling. I sat here, off my tits on really strong painkillers for a few days and watched all three series of Call My Agent. But I couldn’t really do anything, so I thought, OK, the only thing I can do is sit at the kitchen table and try to write 1,000 words a day of something that might be a novel, and see what happens. So by the time I went back to work, I had 64,000 words of something. It wasn’t really a novel. It was a pile of shite. But when I did actually go back to it, there was something on the page to fix.”

Kennedy subsequently endured various complications and resurgences of her original cancer, including damage to her pituitary gland that caused sudden menopause and severe endocrine problems. She has spent several years tailoring her life around treatment – during our conversation, an alarm reminds her to take one of her many daily pills – but she’s on far more of an even keel nowadays. I ask her whether the next book will follow a chronological pattern and anchor itself in the 1990s; the answer is yes, and she’s working on it.

Although she says she prefers the doing to the being when it comes to literary life – in other words, writing rather than talking about it – she’s established herself enough to rule out a return to the kitchen. At least, not professionally: before I leave, she ushers me to the table and produces, with zero fanfare, a homemade quiche, homemade bread, homemade paté and, finally, a vast homemade raspberry and lemon curd cake. Every mouthful is delicious. You can entirely imagine that, had a global financial crisis not wrecked her career as a restaurateur, she would still have been cooking up a storm: good news for diners, but a major blow to readers.

Stations by Louise Kennedy is published by Bloomsbury. To support the Guardian, order your copy at guardianbookshop. com. Delivery charges may apply.

Manchester City verdict: what happens next, will club appeal and could they be relegated?

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 07:00:30 GMT

We analyse what City must do to appeal, why even that might not be the end of the legal wrangling, and the potential penalties if the verdict is upheld

Manchester City have been found guilty of the vast majority of the 134 disciplinary charges brought against them by the Premier League.

In keeping with the history of this case which has been conducted exclusively in private and with every party sworn to secrecy, there is a lot we don’t know. We do not even have an official confirmation that the three-person judicial panel has reached a verdict. All of football is acting as if they have, however, and that reports of a big win for the Premier League are correct.

If these assumptions are accurate, and neither party have formally denied them at least, then the immediate thing to watch out for is news of an appeal. Under Premier League rules, City would have 14 days from the announcement of the verdict to submit an appeal and the process that follows should be completed in less than 12 weeks from then. Once the appeal has been heard – which should happen in one block of no more than five days – and a verdict reached, the appeal panel are also expected to publish written reasons behind their decisions. We should also see the written reasons from the original judicial panel too, but the unique scale of this case has meant that normal procedures have not always been followed, and the date of publication for these reasons remains unknown.

The club would be submitting an appeal based solely on the decision and not any resulting punishment, which is yet to be determined. In hoping to make the case that the judicial panel were wrong in their observations, City would be allowed to submit new evidence, providing it had not been previously available to them, and make new oral presentations. Once the hearing is concluded, a verdict would be expected in 30 days.

According to Premier League rule W.97, “the decision of an Appeal Board shall be final”, but even this is subject to one final route, that of arbitration. This would mean appearing in front of another panel of eminent legal figures, but the criteria for any hearing would be a lot stricter and successful arbitration only possible in the main if the judicial panel or appeal board was found to have abused the legal process. City have recently been through the arbitration process with the Premier League over its rules related to associated party transactions and, after an initial verdict challenged two applications of the rules but otherwise found them to be sound, City and the Premier League reached a settlement which stopped the case from going to court.

Sign up to Football Daily

Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football

after newsletter promotion

If City managed to overturn the verdict, there would of course be no sanction. If City’s appeals failed, there are a number of measures available to the panel. They start at fines and end at complete expulsion from the league, with a variety of sporting sanctions including point deductions falling in between. Given the magnitude of the verdict, City can expect to receive a punishment at the sharper end of the scale should any appeal not prove successful.

It seems unlikely. Premier League clubs and those who have been relegated from the division are understood to have been assessing any financial losses they may have incurred during the period City were winning and, appeal pending, breaking the rules. A wave of lawsuits is likely to follow, with Manchester United, for example, having finished second behind City in 2017-18 and potentially denied a record-breaking 21st league title in the process. It is possible that clubs who were relegated could argue that they were sent down because of points denied them by a City side subsequently found to have cheated. Premier League clubs reportedly lost their appetite for legal action after an estimated £50m cost to the competition last season, but if the verdict against City revealed this week is ultimately upheld, a new wave of lawsuits will surely follow.
