In his final UN speech, Macron may have given other leaders a valuable parting gift: the guts to stand up to Trump

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 06:00:29 GMT

The French president’s resolve seems to have rubbed off on the leaders of other ‘middle powers’

On the first day of the United Nations general assembly this week, two world leaders outlined competing visions for the future. Donald Trump’s speech was disturbingly familiar to those he’s given before: a litany of false boasts and odd tangents, peppered with grim military threats against a variety of nation states. Discussing his seven-month war with Iran, he mused over whether to “annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly”.

In Trump’s eyes, the world is there to be ruled – and ruled only by the US, whose economy is “the envy of the world” and military is “the most powerful on Earth”.

A couple of hours later, Emmanuel Macron took to the podium to offer an alternative. In a full-throated defence of international law, multilateralism and the rules-based order, the French president said we were living in a “new era of barbaric acts”. He directly criticised Russia and Israel, but much of it was clearly aimed at Trump. “They say might is right … but we will not yield,” he argued. “We cannot simply accept this new order of impunity which some are trying to erect … Do we want to live under … the law of the jungle or do we want to live in a civilised international society?”

Importantly, he also acknowledged the west’s “permanent temptation to espouse double standards”. “How many times have we heard that people’s sovereignty has value in Europe, but if we look at the Middle East and Africa, it is less valuable,” he asked. “No, that is unacceptable … A life is a life. Peace and security are indivisible, and everyone has a right to them.”

Over the past decade, Macron has consistently been one of the only western leaders with a morally intelligent analysis of what Europe and the world should look like. As Trump, Vladimir Putin and Benjamin Netanyahu have ushered us into an age of impunity, he has defended the rules-based order and, in recent months, been at the forefront of attempts to forge new alliances to support the crumbling old ones.

He has pushed the idea of European strategic autonomy more than anyone else, understanding that while Europe is an economic power, it is yet to fully realise its potential as either a military or geopolitical force. During Trump’s first term, Macron was the only major leader willing to publicly acknowledge that Nato could no longer rely on the US, leaving the alliance all but dead.

And yet the big speeches have rarely led to any substantial change. His ambitious call for EU reform in 2017 went nowhere, in essence scotched by Angela Merkel, who praised his “passion” and “verve” but failed to back the substance. Likewise, in New York this week, while his analysis was sound, the solutions were slight.

This isn’t necessarily all Macron’s fault. He came to power in May 2017 as the new world order was crumbling. The EU was in crisis: one of its largest members had just voted to leave, while the remaining member states were still fatally split over the fallout from the eurozone crisis earlier in the decade and the migration wave in the summer of 2015. France’s two biggest European allies have been on the slide during his time in office. He has had to work with three German chancellors, the most recent two less popular than their predecessors, and is now on his sixth British prime minister.

More urgently, Trump had taken office four months earlier, signalling the start of the break up of the rules-based order that had guided the west since the end of the second world war. Had Macron had the chance to work with Barack Obama, Angela Merkel at the peak of her popularity and a British prime minister committed to the EU, things might have turned out differently.

Macron’s domestic woes have increased his impotence on the world stage. He has in effect been a lame duck for the past two years, since his disastrous snap election in 2024 left him without a majority.

But his speech in New York, his final UN address before he steps down as president next spring, may have a more lasting impact. It certainly set the tone for the week. Over the following days, a procession of leaders of the so-called middle powers defended the principles of the UN and offered coded criticisms of Trump. Many of those who would have been scared of speaking out last year feel more emboldened now.

The Australian prime minister, Anthony Albanese, warned that “the UN mission cannot be entrusted solely to the great powers, or the biggest countries, or even the loudest voices alone”, while Spain’s PM, Pedro Sánchez, said he sought to “defend what so many are trying to destroy” and called for countries to come together to fight “political actors and governments that want to take us back to a dark past”.

The middle powers are united in their opposition. The question is whether they can agree on what they’re for. The events of the past few weeks suggest that process is under way. New alliances based on values, not geography or size, are being formed – a reinvention of multilateralism, rather than a simple defence of the old model.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

So far this month, the EU and Canada have discussed the idea of “associate membership”, while the UK has formed a new coalition of middle powers to impose sanctions targeting Israel’s unlawful occupation of the West Bank.

Another new group was created at the UN this week, with Finland and Norway launching a call for an international body to oversee the safety of AI models. It is a direct challenge to Trump, who has called concerns about AI safety a “hoax” – nonetheless, 27 world leaders signed up, including Macron, Canada’s Mark Carney, Germany’s Friedrich Merz and Albanese.

What ties all this together is the idea of “values-based realism”, an argument first put forward by the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, and echoed this week by Carney, who arguably lit the “middle powers” spark in Davos earlier this year when he spoke of the “rupture” in the world order caused by Trump. The new world Carney, Macron and others are trying to build will be one of different, sometimes overlapping alliances of like-minded states.

There will be an ongoing question here for Andy Burnham and Ed Miliband. Which of these groups do they join, which do they try to form themselves and which do they politely decline? Despite Burnham’s desire to lead the push for new global AI standards, the UK has so far not joined the Finnish AI group, perhaps for fear of invoking Trump’s wrath. Another issue emerged this week: how to respond to Trump’s desire to invite Putin to the G20?

Each middle power will face the same conundrum: when to fight back and when to sit on the sidelines. At least now the middle powers have understood that fighting back is an option.

Steve Bloomfield is the former international editor of the Observer

15 great small hotels, inns and restaurants with rooms for an autumn stay in the UK

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 06:00:28 GMT

From a cosy Cornish inn with open fires to a boutique hotel in Northumberland, these new and revamped boltholes tick all the right boxes

From the chequerboard restaurant chairs to the disco ball-glittered bar and leopard print-cushioned bedrooms, this 41-bedroom hotel has more than a hint of Alice’s Adventures in Wonderland about it. The 2026 winner of Visit England’s gold award for best small hotel, the Tempus recently opened eight wooden cabins overlooking the estate’s lake, and runs stargazing breaks in partnership with nearby Kielder Observatory. This month sees the launch of wellness experiences, combining gentle yoga and sound baths, while foraging workshops celebrate the estate’s wild bounty. Alnwick, Bamburgh and kipper-smoking Craster are close by. Doubles from £121 B&B, thetempus. co. uk

You can walk, cycle, swim or kayak straight from the door of this pub and bunkhouse on the banks of the River Spey in outdoorsy Aviemore. This mellow gastropub serves smoked haddock chowder and Caribbean lamb curry pies along with Cairngorm Brewery’s ales – and you’re likely to catch some live folk music too. Fresh from a recent revamp, its seven vintage-inspired bedrooms are decorated in autumnal shades of gold, green, rust and teal. Ranging from simple dorms to en suite doubles and family rooms, they come with access to a shared kitchen and dining room for DIY dinners and breakfasts. Family rooms for up to five from £80 room-only, oldbridgeinn. co. uk

Food is the big draw at this new pub with rooms in the South Downs. Run by farm-to-fork restaurateurs the Gladwin brothers, the 12-bedroom inn is their first venture outside London, and their first with accommodation. One thing they are deeply familiar with is local producers – not least their own family. Beef comes from their farm, wines from their vineyard, Nutbourne, and some of the pub’s artwork has been painted by family matriarch Bridget. Stay over and you can wake to breakfasts of homemade brioche with just-laid eggs, farmhouse sausages or trout gravadlax. Stroll around the village, with its castle hotel and pottery, or hike over to Arundel then catch a train back to Amberley. Doubles from £125 B&B, blackhorse-pub. com

Pembrokeshire is home to spectacular beaches, but if an autumn storm blows in, it’s great to have galleries, cafes, pubs and cinemas where you can take cover. That’s where Fishguard comes in. This small harbour town has quietly blossomed over the last couple of years. The latest opening is the Abergwaun, a bistro with rooms launched in July by the folk behind the nearby Red Onion cafe. Feast on locally line-caught seabass with kelp beurre blanc, then drift off to sleep in one of five smart, latte-coloured bedrooms. The next day, take in a pottery workshop at Tŷ Clai, hike along the Pembrokeshire coast path for a Sunday roast at the Sailor’s Safety, or catch a gig at Ffwrn. Doubles from £140 B&B, theabergwaun. co. uk

Malham is one of the Yorkshire Dales’ great hiking hubs, with Malham Tarn, the amphitheatrical cliffs of Malham Cove, and Janet’s Foss and Gordale Scar waterfalls within easy reach – and staying in the village became a little easier this summer with the opening of Lister Farmhouse. Its 13 bedrooms pair smart taupe, olive and blueberry fabrics with warm wood and leather. Part of the expanded Lister Arms, which includes rooms at the inn itself and at a nearby barn conversion, the new farmhouse bedrooms are two minutes’ walk away, beside sister pub the Buck Inn. For breakfast, stroll across a packhorse bridge to the pub. Doubles from £135 B&B, listerarms. co. uk

Formerly the George & Dragon, when this Test valley pub with rooms opened in June, its name was changed to the Great Decoy in a nod to the area’s second world war history, when the surrounding countryside was used as part of a network of decoy sites to draw enemy bombers away from strategic targets. These days, a tempting mix of pub bangers (venison steak frites, wood-fired pizzas), plump-pillowed bedrooms and affordable rates is luring a more peaceful crowd. The pub is a low-beamed, candlelit haven and its eight bedrooms mix antiques with bright modern art and jauntily striped, scalloped headboards. Doubles from £90 B&B, thegreatdecoy. co. uk

It was in Ross-on-Wye in the late 18th century that the artist and writer Rev William Gilpin set the blueprint for British tourism. Popularising the picturesque, he encouraged travellers to explore the local landscape for pleasure, helping to establish the idea of the British scenic escape (albeit infamously suggesting that “a mallet judiciously used” might improve the ruined charm of Tintern Abbey). More than two centuries later, five elegant new bedrooms have just opened at the Riverside Inn, giving modern-day visitors a suitably comfortable base from which to explore the area’s antiques and salvage shops, and stroll the leafy riverside pathways around Symonds Yat. Named after Charlie Mackesy characters, the rooms are decorated with finds from Baileys Home Store and other local businesses. Doubles from £180 B&B, riversideinn-wyestreet. com

On the edge of the Burghley estate, along one of Stamford’s cute-as-a-bonnet Georgian streets, this treasured hotel underwent a major renovation two years ago. Named after Lord William Cecil, chief advisor to Elizabeth I, the 18th-century building is home to 26 bedrooms decorated in Bridgerton-meets-Babington chic, all chalky pink and sage green stripes, ginghams, velvets and chintz. The latest addition is Wild Floral, a botanical-inspired room launched this summer in collaboration with Lincolnshire designer Sophie Allport. Head out to explore the copper-flecked parkland of Burghley House, then return for pheasant kiev and blackberry tart at Milly’s, the in-house bistro. Doubles from £155 B&B, thewilliamcecil. co. uk

It was no surprise that Corsham was chosen as a backdrop for the recent TV dramatisation of Jilly Cooper’s Rivals – the market town is a primetime destination. Wild peacocks roam its Georgian streets, a “secret” garden unwinds behind stately Corsham Court – home to one of Wiltshire’s finest private art collections – and independent shops and cafes rule. In the centre of it all is Corsham House, a new brasserie and bottle shop with rooms that opened in July. Once a bank, it’s now profiting from the town’s “Bath in miniature” credentials, serving its signature Corsham chips with chicken salt alongside fat rump cap steaks, and putting guests up in 11 small but daintily designed bedrooms painted in shades of rose, damson and beech. Doubles from £111 room-only, corshamhouse. com

Just off the A387, between Plymouth and Looe, this riverside pub with rooms is worth detouring off the beaten Cornish track for. Recently taken over by the couple behind Lydford’s award-winning Castle Inn, its 17th-century core has been elegantly refurbished. Fill up on fish tacos or the catch of the day, then head upstairs, or into the cottage just behind the inn, to slumber in one of eight earthily coloured, softly lit bedrooms (the cottage rooms are the quietest). The following morning, wake to a full Cornish before hiking a loop through the woods of the Seaton Valley or strolling a section of the South West coast path over to Looe. Doubles from £100 B&B (two nights for £160 from Sept-April), copleyarms. co. uk

Just across the road from its namesake waterfall, this former coaching inn reopened last year after a major overhaul, offering visitors a comfortable and affordable base for exploring Eryri national park. Its 38 bedrooms are painted in warm, muted shades and bookended by floral wallpapers, tongue-and-groove panelling and bright, metro-tiled bathrooms. Family rooms come with sturdy wooden bunk beds and, downstairs, you can order lasagne or sausage and mash in a space framed by fringed lampshades, floral curtains and mossy green paintwork. From the inn, you can follow a riverside trail into the village of Betws-y-Coed or soak up the autumn colours on one of the waymarked paths in the nearby Gwydir forest park. Doubles from £76 B&B, inncollectiongroup. com

Estate-to-plate dining is the cornerstone of this sunshine-hued Tudor inn between Bury St Edmunds and Ipswich. One of several Suffolk pubs and hotels owned by the Nedging Hall estate, who completed a sympathetic makeover this spring, it has 13 smartly understated new bedrooms. It’s fully plugged into the estate’s homegrown supply chain; the owners also operate a butchery, kitchen garden and East Anglia’s oldest brewery, Mauldons (for which they grow malt barley). Head out on a gentle three-mile loop walk to neighbouring Chelsworth, then take a seat by the dining room’s open fire to feast on treacle-cured pork ribeye with garlic croquettes, and deliciously wibbly Basque cheesecake. Doubles from £195 B&B, thebildestoncrown. com

A hop, skip and jump (or 30-minute train ride) north-west of Glasgow, this stylish new hotel sits at the western end of the Forth and Clyde canal. Well-placed for towpath walks and cycles, it’s a grand reimagining of what was built in 1790 as the customs house for Bowling harbour. There are seven tweed-hued bedrooms in the main building, each with a view of the water and each named after a different cargo, and a floating lodge suite was added this summer, along with a sauna and cold plunge. When the restaurant opens in a neighbouring building next year, it will operate as a full-service hotel but, for now, staff are only on site during the day; evening arrivals are self check-in and continental breakfasts self-serve. Doubles from £120 B&B, thecustomshousebowling. co. uk

Close to the RSPB reserve at Snettisham and the nature reserve at Holme Dunes, this stretch of north Norfolk coastline is a prime destination for spotting waders and waterfowl as they stop to rest on their way south, and is similarly restorative for humans. Follow a day of beach walks and sky-gazing with dinner at newly renovated gastropub the Ancient Mariner – menu highlights include Barsham’s beer-battered fish and chips, and cheeseboards ripe with local favourites Norfolk Dapple and Binham Blue – before walking across to sister hotel Le Strange Arms to sleep. Its more affordable standard rooms have yet to be updated, but recently renovated self-catering lodges and apartments put a modish mustard and navy spin on seaside chic. Doubles from £91 room-only, lestrangearms. co. uk

Open fires? A scene-stealing, carved wood bar? Plates of buttery chicken and chips? Double Diamond ale on tap? If you were Pinterest-boarding the fantasy Cotswolds pub after a yomp through the fields (or along the river – the Thames Path starts 10 minutes’ drive away), it would be something like the Wild Duck. Just south of Cirencester, this 16th-century gardeners’ cottage turned coaching inn has been stylishly overhauled by local hospitality luminaries Sam and Georgie Pearman. Reopened in March, it now has five bedrooms above the pub and 14 others in a new wing, each decorated with heritage wallpapers, Edward Bulmer paints, antique finds and custom-designed rugs. Doubles from £150 B&B, countrycreatures. com

Prices are for October-November and were correct at time of publication

‘The weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets’: Trump lashes out as his power wanes

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 06:00:27 GMT

Trump tries to dominate at the UN as his approval ratings plummet and even some Republicans stray from the script

Donald Trump stood before the United Nations on Tuesday and threatened to “annihilate” Iran. Yet even as the most powerful man on the planet flexed his military muscles, he was powerless to keep the gravitational pull of domestic politics at bay.

Heading into the UN building in New York, the US president was questioned by Kaitlan Collins, an anchor at CNN, which he had banned from the White House before a judge ruled against him. “I’m surprised that CNN is here covering me,” the 80-year-old snapped. “You should not be here covering me.”

The lashing-out was a reminder that even Trump, who has expanded executive power and dominated the national consciousness, finds some things beyond his control. Indeed, 20 months into his second term, there is a widening gap between the president’s self-perceived invincibility and the reality of his waning influence.

Federal courts are reining him in. Congressional Republicans are straying from the script. Poll numbers are tumbling to historic depths, driven by persistent inflation, rising fuel costs and an increasingly unpopular war in Iran. For the first time since his improbable political resurrection, Trump’s aura of authority is fading.

Rick Wilson, a longtime Republican strategist, prophesied: “This is the beginning of the end. This is the decline. As powerful and transgressive as he’s been, the country does not have a positive outlook right now. In fact, the negativity and pessimism among voters has reached a point that is unparalleled since Jimmy Carter.”

Trump’s self-belief never wavers. He faced four criminal cases and two assassination attempts before winning the 2024 election. He has lived by a mantra of “it will all work out well in the end” while his supporters wear hats that state: “Trump was right about everything.”

Yet he has had a rough month. The Federal Reserve defied him on interest rates. The supreme court blocked his administration’s attempt to impose new restrictions on mail-in ballots for November’s midterm elections. One judge prevented him adding his name to the Kennedy Center, prompting him to threaten the national arts complex with demolition; another judge blocked his ban on three news outlets from the White House grounds, ordering the administration to “immediately return, reinstate and restore” their access.

Now even Trump’s dependable power base, the Republican party, is showing cracks amid fears that he will cost them seats in November. In Florida, his home state, gubernatorial candidate Byron Donalds quietly scrubbed most Trump references from his campaign website, while the congresswoman María Elvira Salazar ran campaign advertisements openly declaring that federal immigration enforcement had gone “too far” and asserting that Latino voters “feel betrayed”.

Wilson, a co-founder of the Lincoln Project, an anti-Trump group, sees a herd mentality among congressional Republicans and compares the current mood to a wildlife documentary.

“It needs a David Attenborough voiceover,” he said. “It’s like the gazelles wandering the savannah. They’re sniffing the wind now and they smell something in the wind. They know it’s a predator but they don’t know what to do about it yet. What they haven’t realised is that the predator has been among them all along. The risk factor that they face now is Trump.”

For nearly a decade, elected Republicans maintained a posture of submission, fearful of drawing a primary challenger or a scathing post on Truth Social. But with the elections looming and control of Congress hanging in the balance, self-preservation is rapidly overriding loyalty to the president.

Wilson said: “Now it’s reached the point where the magic doesn’t work any more. There’s no political upside from a president who is at 29% approval rating in some polls, has presided over a disastrous war, and has ended up raising energy prices and food prices – all the things that they can’t spin away.

“The voters now have very much put that together. They associate the war with Trump. They associate the gas prices with Trump. They associate the grocery prices with Trump.”

This creates a vicious circle, Wilson argues. “The more he becomes a liability, the more he acts out. The more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it, the more he demands loyalty from people and doesn’t get it. Everything was handed to him for a decade by that party and, now that they’re paying the price, they’ve decided this has got a little too hairy.”

Faced with shrinking authority and a hostile economic landscape, Trump has reverted to his trusted playbook: manufacturing spectacle, picking cultural fights and raging against the press. His recent decision to ban the news outlets CNN, MS Now and Politico from the White House campus following critical coverage was viewed by critics not as a display of strength, but a symptom of deep frustration.

The administration rejects such charges and insists that the president’s agenda is succeeding. Davis Ingle, a White House spokesperson, said in an email: “President Trump is the unequivocal leader, best messenger, and unmatched motivator for the Republican Party, and he is committed to maintaining Republican majorities in Congress.

“The president signed the largest working-class tax cuts in history, lowered the cost of prescription drugs, sealed the border, drove violent crime to the lowest level in nearly a century, unleashed an energy revolution, added more than a million private-sector jobs, and sent Americans’ 401(k)s climbing to record highs,” he added. “The choice has never been more clear: doubling down on President Trump’s winning, commonsense agenda or the Democrats’ extreme liberal policies and obstruction.”

But the trend lines are only set to worsen for Trump. If Democrats gain control of the House of Representatives, they plan to launch investigations into how he has allegedly abused his office to enrich his family, grant favours to supporters, hollow out the federal government and carry out expensive construction projects. The attention economy, meanwhile, will inexorably shift to the 2028 presidential race and the question of succession.

Bill Galston, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution thinktank in Washington, said the inevitable shift of focus toward potential candidates – such as the vice-president, JD Vance, or the secretary of state, Marco Rubio – will be cause for friction.

“Nothing will drive him crazier than the shift of the spotlight away from him,” said Galston, a former domestic policy adviser to Bill Clinton. “The prospect of passing the torch, giving up the spotlight, is intensely painful for him. It’s his oxygen. Will he be able to breathe, spiritually and emotionally speaking, without it?”

Trump is not the first president to run into trouble after winning re-election. From Richard Nixon’s Watergate downfall to Clinton’s impeachment and George W Bush’s quagmire in Iraq, second terms have historically served as the graveyard of presidential ambition.

Allan Lichtman, author of a new book, Great American Presidents: The Twelve Who Transformed the Nation, calls it “the second term curse”. He noted: “Second terms have been remarkably difficult for presidents.”

Lichtman, a history professor at American University in Washington, believes that Trump is driven by two things: money and glory. “He cannot stand not being the centre of attention and that’s dangerous,” he said. “I don’t care much about his verbal lashing-out; I don’t think that helps him at all. But who knows what crazy things he might do to reassert attention on him? And that’s frightening.

“Never underestimate the power of the president. Just because Republicans are criticising him, his poll numbers are low, prospects for Republicans look dim, doesn’t mean he doesn’t have enormous power – and he is certainly quite willing to use that power unconstrained. He doesn’t care about the courts and doesn’t care about the Congress.”

From this perspective, Trump’s last refuge will be the unchecked use of executive authority, a politicised justice department and a sweeping pardon power. With nothing to lose in his final two years, he could go out all guns blazing.

Charlie Sykes, a conservative author and broadcaster, said: “Donald Trump fears irrelevance more than anything and he’ll rage against it as long as he can. The notion that he will go quietly would be incredibly naive.

“We’re headed for a collision between a lame duck who has no respect for the constitutional norms and an opposition that may have some power to hold him accountable. The paradox is the weaker he gets, the more dangerous he gets.”

From Sense and Sensibility to Kill Jackie: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 05:00:29 GMT

Guardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link. Learn more.

Daisy Edgar-Jones dons the bonnet in Georgia Oakley’s take on the Jane Austen classic, and Catherine Zeta-Jones battles assassins in a madcap action caper

Sense and SensibilityOut now Daisy Edgar-Jones has a big bonnet to fill in the role Emma Thompson made her own in Ang Lee’s Oscar-winning version of Jane Austen’s romance. But let’s not compare: Blue Jean director Georgia Oakley’s take sees a fresh cast place new emphasis on the bond between sisters Marianne and Elinor.

Her Private HellOut now Professional provocateur Nicolas Winding Refn returns with another slice of the outre, this time in a science fiction mode. It’s the tale of a young woman, Elle (Sophie Thatcher), who encounters a supernatural killer in diamond-encrusted gloves in a mist-shrouded city.

RemakeOut now Taking on the devastating subject of the death of his own son, revered documentary-maker Ross McElwee makes the film that no parent would want to make. Using his own home video and family archive, he creates a bereavement memoir that traces a life from infancy to adolescence to an adulthood marred by addiction.

Heart of the BeastOut now Training Day screenwriter David Ayer directs this thriller about one man and his dog attempting to survive in the wilderness after a plane crash. But not just any man and dog: he’s an ex-special forces officer and the dog is a retired combat dog. Curiously, it stars Brad Pitt where you might expect Jason Statham. Catherine Bray

Jill ScottLondon, 28 September; Birmingham, 29 September; Manchester, 1 October; London, 13 & 14 October; touring to 14 OctoberThe R&B and soul legend heads out on tour in support of To Whom This May Concern, her first album in 11 years. Expect classics, specifically from 2000’s Who Is Jill Scott?, alongside her dextrous, genre-hopping new material. Michael Cragg

Wagner’s Parsifal Royal Opera House, London, 1 to 17 October It grapples with good and evil, love and violence, life and death – so no wonder Parsifal lasts upwards of four hours. Acclaimed director Evgeny Titov makes his Royal Opera debut with this new production conducted by Jakub Hrůša. The high-wattage cast includes Stanislas de Barbeyrac, Christian Gerhaher and Ekaterina Gubanova. Flora Willson

Xhosa Cole Scarborough Spa, 26 September Contemporary and classic jazz sax maestro Xhosa Cole reworks the music of Thelonious Monk at the 23rd Scarborough jazz festival – Soft Machine, Alan Barnes and star vocalists Ian Shaw, Liane Carroll and Brigitte Beraha also enhance the event’s usual classy bill. Cole also plays London’s Vortex on 29 & 30 September. John Fordham

HomoblocDepot Mayfield, Manchester, 26 SeptemberBilled as a “Queer block party for all”, the late-night celebration returns to Manchester with a typically stellar lineup, including German pop star Kim Petras. Elsewhere, DJ-producer Honey Dijon goes back-to-back with underground house maverick Derrick Carter, while LSDXOXO, Erol Alkan and DJ Paulette will also be popping up. MC

This Is Still Not a Pipe: The Afterlife of MagritteGagosian Grosvenor Hill, London, to 12 DecemberIt may not be a pipe but it is an exhibition, one dedicated to the great surrealist master René Magritte and his enduring influence on art. Some major loans will hang alongside works on paper, photography and sculpture.

Beverly BuchananSpike Island, Bristol, to 31 January Five decades’ worth of sculpture, painting and earthworks are packed into the first European survey for this artist who died in 2015, leaving behind a vast body of work about the US’s troubled south.

Olivia BaxYorkshire Sculpture Park, nr Wakefield, to 14 March Twenty new, heavily textured, multicoloured and very strange sculptural assemblages by this young London-based artist, filled with salvaged materials and gloopy neon references to BMX parks.

Evelyn Taocheng WangGoldsmith’s Centre for Contemporary Art, London, to 13 DecemberExpect an outsider’s portrait of Britain in this debut UK institutional exhibition for Evelyn Taocheng Wang, taking a heavily conceptual look at what makes us so uniquely us (humour, reserve, period dramas) through sculpture, painting and installation. Eddy Frankel

The Standard of LivingTheatre Royal Haymarket, London, to 12 DecemberJames Graham has an uncanny way of combining character and country. His latest play stars Rory Kinnear and is about the radical economist John Maynard Keynes, set against the backdrop of a Britain reeling from the first world war. Directed by Nicholas Hytner. Miriam Gillinson

Rhys James 30 September to 15 May; tour starts FolkestoneYet to achieve household-name status, 35-year-old James is widely considered one of UK standup’s master craftspeople. His new show Chop Logic combines a relentless stream of ingenious gags with the story of his circumcision. Rachel Aroesti

Murder Before EvensongWatermill theatre, Newbury, to 14 NovemberRev Richard Coles’s cosy crime novel is adapted for the stage. It’s 1988 in the peaceful village of Champton, where life centres on the church, but a shocking murder changes everything and the rector is pulled into the investigation. MG

Thick & TightTuesday to 28 November; tour starts Newcastle upon TyneThe Guardian’s best dance show of 2025 goes on tour. A hilarious, subversive, offbeat treat from uncategorisable duo Thick & Tight and guests, Natural Behaviour mixes dance, text, lip-sync and silliness in surreal sketches. Subjects include the writer James Baldwin, lesbian seagulls and the dust in Quentin Crisp’s flat. Lyndsey Winship

Kill Jackie Prime Video, 2 OctoberCatherine Zeta-Jones goes full madcap camp – and even gets to keep her native Welsh accent – in this big, bonkers crime caper about an ex-con art dealer whose past catches up with her. Daniel Ings, Raff Law and Sidse Babett Knudsen also star.

WarSky Atlantic & Now, 2 October, 9pmIt’s Sienna Miller v Dominic West in this deluxe new thriller from George Kay (Lupin, The Long Shadow). A film star and tech titan face “the biggest divorce trial in British legal history”, meaning their respective teams of lawyers, including Nick Mohammed, will stop at nothing in order to come out on top.

East of Eden Netflix, 1 OctoberZoe Kazan follows in her grandfather Elia’s footsteps with this adaptation of Steinbeck’s 1952 opus. Florence Pugh gets her teeth stuck into one of fiction’s most notorious antiheroines in Cathy Ames, whose author described her as having a “malformed soul”. Christopher Abbott plays her abandoned husband.

Break ClauseChannel 4, 1 October, 10pm A former couple – promising young architect Lil (comedian Lara Ricote) and directionless graduate Ben (Samuel Bottomley) – are forced to cohabit in a London flat due to a watertight rental contract in this sweet and goofy will-they-won’t-they (get back together) comedy from Jess Bray. RA

Nivalis NightsPC; out 29 SeptemberA cyberpunk life-simulation where, instead of running around with a futuristic pistol and getting caught up in gang wars, you are just trying to make a living. Starting out with a food stand, you can eventually own the night through a network of bars, restaurants and clubs – and learn everything about the city from your loose-lipped patrons.

The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt – RemasteredAll platforms; out 29 SeptemberOutcast monster hunter Geralt of Rivia gets caught up in the dark machinations of phantom huntsmen and warring kings in this updated and complete version of an all-time great role-player. If you have somehow yet to play this eastern European dark fantasy masterpiece, you really have run out of excuses. Keza MacDonald

Blondshell – ViolinsOut nowAfter Sabrina Teitelbaum’s first pop-leaning incarnation as BAUM imploded in 2020, the New Yorker morphed into alt-rocker Blondshell. While the musical backdrop is heavier and more guitar-based, that pop nous still runs through this third album, especially on the galloping Fur Elise.

Julia Jacklin – The GemOut nowNamed after her local pub, the fourth album – and her first for the much-loved label 4AD – by Melbourne-based songwriter Julia Jacklin is full of lovingly crumpled rock. Exploring reinvention, longing and excavation, songs such as The Hardest Thing and I Wish are full of unforgettable melodic nuggets.

Tinashe – PopstarOut nowAfter getting lost in the major-label system, US bop-maker Tinashe has thrived as an independent artist. On her eighth album she dabbles in hyperpop elasticity via the undulating Melatonin, while the low-slung Crash Out adds trap and R&B to the mix.

M83 – I Wrote You a LetterOut nowThe French synth-pop outfit, led by Anthony Gonzalez, return with their 10th album, and first in three years. Worked up from demos recorded in 2024 as a way of capturing the spirit of the band’s earlier work, it opens with the blown-out alt-pop of the cinematic Blister Sunrise. MC

90 Minutes or Less Film FestPodcast Host Sam Clements programmes his dream film festival lineup in this charming series celebrating the art of well-edited cinema. Picks include Godard’s Breathless, as chosen by director Richard Linklater, and Jackass, as selected by Steve-O.

DeconstructedYouTube Detailed 3D animations dissect some of history’s most complex machines and structures on this fascinating channel. Discover the inner workings of an ancient Greek water clock and the unusual design of the Eiffel Tower elevators.

Mapping India: The World’s Largest CountBBC World Service, 26 September, 12.06amIndia is undertaking one of the largest counting exercises in the world: a census of its 1.5 billion inhabitants. This astounding documentary follows the logistical challenges of the process, from Delhi streets to Himalayan mountains. Ammar Kalia

Of course you can be English if you’re not white. So why can’t the right leave the question alone?

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 05:00:27 GMT

Even Jacob Rees-Mogg pushes back on defining Englishness in exclusively ethnic terms. But the endurance of this discourse is still deeply troubling

Can you be English and non-white? It’s a question that keeps stubbornly resurfacing in our political discourse.

Last weekend, the former prime minister Rishi Sunak gave his view in a column in the Times, arguing that national identity should not be turned into a DNA test. After leaving office, Sunak, the UK’s first prime minister of colour, was subject to claims by a prominent podcaster that he was not English because he was a “brown-skinned Hindu”. Reflecting on this, Sunak described it as a “reverse Tebbit test”: the sociological concept measuring the loyalty of immigrants – and their children – in the UK depending on which cricket team they supported in international matches. “Once we say that this or that person isn’t really English or British because they are not white,” he wrote, “then we are on a very slippery slope. Some people will argue that English is an ethnic identity and British a civic identity. Though if you think those nuances are heard by most people, I fear you are being rather – perhaps even wilfully – naive.”

Sunak is right that this conversation isn’t really about nuanced distinctions between ethnic and civic identities. The questioning of one’s Englishness is deeply insidious, as it is not solely articulated through supposed “legitimate concerns” about the pace of immigration, crimes committed by migrants or ethnic minorities, or anxieties around jobs and access to public services. Instead, it is presented as a question of first principles: whether you are a “good” or “bad” minority, a citizen or non-citizen, your ancestry or skin colour means you will never truly belong. Your claim to belong in this country, and that of your descendants, will always be implicitly lesser than those who could, at least theoretically, trace their ancestry back to Oswald of Northumbria. That idea is deeply uncomfortable for many, rejected both by those who hold progressive views on immigration and community integration, and those who otherwise hold conservative views of national belonging and hardened borders.

There is growing concern among sections of the British right about increasingly “ethnonationalist” impulses emerging on its fringes and entering mainstream political debate. That has particularly gathered steam with the rise of Rupert Lowe’s hard-right Restore Britain. These beliefs belong to what the Financial Times’s Robert Shrimsley described as the right’s own “woke wing”, which fusses over “the great replacement theory and the betrayal of the west”. More moderate conservatives will want to distance themselves from these views as much as they will from the black-clad far-right mobs that descended on Portsmouth and Dover this summer.

There are indications that some of these views are gaining greater public legitimacy. An analysis by the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) last year found that the percentage of those who believed “Britishness” was something you were born with had almost doubled in two years (from 19% to 36%). But there are reasons for those on the right to worry that the popularisation of these once-fringe views could alienate them from the majority, who still reject them. According to the IPPR analysis, only 3% of people believe that being a “good” British citizen requires having white skin, while at least 74% of English people believe that Englishness is not defined by ethnicity. The hard right’s attachment to a politics of ethnicity also threatens to upend a project that the broader conservative movement has been at pains to build over the years: a multi-ethnic coalition that can hold anti-immigration views without the Englishness or Britishness of its own members being called into question. That means maintaining a definition of national belonging that minorities can actually attain.

So it may feel curious to see the Tory traditionalist Jacob Rees-Mogg, no ally of Sunak, release a series of videos on X stating that “everyone who has a British passport is equally British or English” and positing that the English are “a mongrel people, not an Aryan master race”. But the desire to openly define Englishness, and Britishness, in exclusively ethnic terms remains relatively fringe, and it is not a politics that yet finds a broad coalition. Perhaps unsurprisingly, two of Sunak and Rees-Mogg’s lead opponents were minority politicians on the hard right: Reform spokespersons Suella Braverman, who insists that she cannot be English, and Zia Yusuf, who recasts the argument in familiar culture war terms about those who have “betrayed” our country, and insists that “people are furious about what Rees-Mogg and Sunak are saying”.

That preoccupation over ethnic nationalism isn’t purely a feature of the modern hard right; in 1701, the English writer Daniel Defoe wrote The True-Born Englishman, a poem to defend William III, born a sovereign Prince of Orange, from xenophobic attacks disparaging his lack of ethnic “Englishness”. Defoe wrote: “Thus from a mixture of all kinds began, / That het’rogeneous thing, an Englishman”, referring to the English, as Rees-Mogg did, as a “mongrel half-bred race”. That speaks to something that is worth remembering when questions about who gets to be English recur: it has never been a property passed down intact from one generation of ethnically pure Englishmen to the next. Instead, it has continually been remade through migration, assimilation, conquering, marriage, conversion and settlement.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

Attempts to impose a simplified ancestry-based definition quickly become absurd, as Lowe saw when, in August, he could not answer whether or not he would consider King Charles, whose father was born in Greece and who has German and Danish ancestry, a “white Briton”. But even a more inclusive civic-nationalist definition of Englishness raises questions with no settled answer: is it defined simply through citizenship or through language, accents, behaviours, “values”, culinary preferences or sporting affiliation? For those who believe that it is an ethnic identity based on ancestry, how many generations back must you be able to trace your lineage?

Even if ethnonationalist views are stymied by more moderate voices on the contemporary right, the surfacing of these discourses is still deeply troubling for many ethnic minorities. Its traction may, for now, be limited, but it still risks contributing to a “common sense” assumption that there is something like a pure English ethnicity determined by race. Interestingly, ethnic-minority adults themselves are more likely to view Englishness as tied to heritage, and prefer an identification with Britishness. I can’t speculate on each individual’s reluctance, but it doesn’t displace a simple truth: there is no single, historically fixed population from which today’s “English” have descended. From the Celts, the Romans, the Anglo-Saxons, the Vikings, the Normans, the Huguenots, Jewish and Irish communities – England is ancestrally mixed. That waves of arrivals over the past century have been Caribbean, African and South Asian has only made this more observable.

For those who believe Englishness is threatened and marginalised by demographic change, it is precisely this process that has allowed it to endure: continued participation and attachment, not bloodlines and biological inheritance. Even if the ethnonationalist right wants to project a future based on a kind of racial nostalgia, English history itself offers very little support for it. It is a politics with nowhere to go.

Jason Okundaye is an assistant Opinion editor at the Guardian

Look again – there’s more to Europe’s election trends than far-right success

The Guardian Sat, 26 Sep 2026 04:00:25 GMT

Defeatist narratives abound. Yet Germany’s latest elections suggest voter dissatisfaction is benefiting the left as well as the right

Germany held three regional elections this month and, although each of them had a unique result, much of the media and political commentary reduced them to: “German chancellor clings to power after latest loss to far right. Since 2016, the year of Brexit and Trump, “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” has become the overarching narrative about Europe. But while these elections were important, this reductive take both oversimplifies the complexities of contemporary European politics and drives a defeatist “end of democracy” narrative.

Saxony-Anhalt’s election on 6 September was a global news event – understandably, given Germany’s history, economy and place in Europe. The international media had speculated for months about an outright majority for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD). The party came close, setting a record score with 43.8%, but it has so far failed to form a government, despite the amenable position of the “left-conservative” Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance.

Two weeks later, the AfD came in first again, in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, with 38.2% of the vote. International media interest was much less pronounced this time, maybe because it was the second of the three ballots, but more likely because the party was not close to reaching a majority. Moreover, the far-right success was overshadowed by the dramatic defeat for the Christian Democratic Union (CDU) of Chancellor Friedrich Merz. For the first time in the history of the Federal Republic of Germany, the party did not make it into a state parliament. The relatively modest loss of the governing Social Democratic Party (SPD), on the other hand, was barely discussed.

Finally, in the Berlin state election on the same day, the Left party (Die Linke) scored a stunning victory, gaining almost twice as many new votes as the AfD, which came in only third. Berlin will most likely now be governed by a Left-Greens-SPD coalition, headed by Elif Eralp, the daughter of Turkish political refugees. Perhaps most striking was that a clear majority of young women (54%) voted for the “far-left” party, representing a broader leftwing trend among young women that continues to be ignored by most media and politics representatives.

Whereas the Saxony-Anhalt election was often generalised as the story of Germany, if not Europe as a whole, the Berlin election is, at best, flattened out to a story of capital cities: uniquely cosmopolitan metropoles inhabited by highly educated progressives and immigrants. No matter that Saxony-Anhalt’s population, at 2.1 million, is just slightly over half the size of Berlin’s, and is among the oldest and whitest in the country. Moreover, Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, a state that is much more like Saxony-Anhalt than like Berlin, will most likely also be governed by a Left-Left-Green government – a striking fact that again has gone largely undiscussed.

This is not to say that the success of the far right and the defeat of the established parties in Germany are not important or alarming, but they are not the only notable features of these elections. Actually, the fact that two of the three states will have leftwing governments is in many ways more newsworthy, given that purely leftwing governments are increasingly rare in Europe. On a similar note, global media attention on Sweden waned as soon as it was clear that the left bloc was likely to succeed in creating a new government and the far-right Sweden Democrats would not enter the government.

Reducing the many complexities of contemporary politics to an “embattled mainstream threatened by emboldened far right” narrative is not only problematic because it ignores significant other developments; notably, important transformations within major cities, where multicultural electorates are moving left rather than right (seen recently in, among others, Copenhagen and New York). But more importantly, and dangerously, it also strengthens the far-right’s populist narrative, which portrays politics as a struggle between “the elite” (that is, all the mainstream parties) and “the people” (allegedly represented by the far right).

Sign up to This is Europe

The most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environment

after newsletter promotion

Similarly, some media have been keen to adopt the “horseshoe” theory of politics, prominently and strategically used by Merz, in which the liberal-democratic mainstream is squeezed from both sides, by the far right and far left. This conflates two very different challenges though. While it is true that established parties are challenged by new(er) parties, particularly because younger voters vote less for the established right and left, this includes liberal democratic parties like the Greens, too.

Moreover, while the far right does threaten liberal democracy – and the AfD even threatens democracy per se – the so-called far left rarely does. Like Die Linke, most parties that are considered “far left” are former communist parties which have become significantly more moderate over time, presenting an ideology that reflects the social democracy of the 1970s much more than the revolutionary socialism of the former communist world. In fact, few “far left” parties are still even populist these days.

So, while both the far right and “far left” threaten the established parties, only the far right threatens liberal democracy. It makes political sense for established politicians such as Merz to equate liberal democracy with the established parties, but the media should not uncritically share these claims. Surveys continue to show evidence of what the US political scientist Robert Dahl termed “a democratic paradox”: where very high support for the system of democracy is combined with very high dissatisfaction with the state of real, existing democracy.

By highlighting the complexities of contemporary politics, in particular the frustration of the young (women) who are looking for liberal democratic alternatives to established parties, both the far-right populist binary of “establishment versus far right” and the defeatist “end of democracy” narrative are weakened. Hopefully this will give space to liberal democratic parties, old and new, to move beyond the self-defeating strategy of catering again and again to the same stereotypical voter with “legitimate concerns”, and instead mobilise and represent different groups of dissatisfied democrats.

Cas Mudde is the Stanley Wade Shelton UGAF professor of international affairs at the University of Georgia, and author of The Far Right Today

Five Great Reads: A week in Gaza, the queen of toddler TV, and bunkering down

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 22:05:30 GMT

The Guardian’s weekend wrap of essential reads from the past seven days, selected by Jacqui Housden and Miles Herbert

Get this in your inbox every weekend. Sign up for Five Great Reads here

Hello and welcome to the weekend.

This week, we could not look away from the series Gaza: a week in the life. In the story linked below, a Palestinian mother recounts how she is rebuilding her future in the ruins and fragments of the past she lost. Across the rest of the reads in this newsletter, there is hope, resistance and rebirth in the history that continues to define our present.

I hope you enjoy them all as much as we did.

As the war in Gaza approaches its fourth year, this week the Guardian followed five ordinary Palestinians going about their daily lives. Each piece tells the story of their day, revealing the conflict’s terrible toll. On day one of the series, Alaa Hessi brought readers into her world. Hessi lives in a tent pitched on the ruins of her house, which was destroyed by an Israeli airstrike that killed all three of her children.

Life in the rubble: Gaza holds the memory of Alaai’s lost children, and she finds beauty in the ruins that surround the tent. In the late afternoon, Alaa scrolls through old photos and videos to hear their voices.

Notable quote: “I do not tell nurses at the clinic about my circumstances and my children who died, because even the healthcare workers are emotionally exhausted. They are unable to offer comfort or psychological support. My story is not unusual in Gaza. Many women here have lost their children.”

How long will it take to read: About three minutes.

Further reading: A week in Gaza day two, day three and day four.

You may not be familiar with the process of “cuckooing”. It’s where a drug dealing gang takes over the home of a vulnerable person, usually exploiting them to use their home as a base from which to operate. In the past couple of decades it has been increasingly used as a way for gangs to avoid detection. And just as it sounds, it’s grim and dangerous. But as the author and journalist Max Daly writes here, the reality is complex.

From misery to an unusual “friendship”: Daly’s friend Duncan, a musician, artist and father, ended up opening his doors to drug gangs – not once but twice – but his two experiences turned out to be completely different. The first brought him only misery; the second, in his telling at least, brought him a strange kind of friendship. Did it save him? The answer to that is perplexing.

How long will it take to read: 13 minutes.

Further reading: The history and the victims of cuckooing.

Rachel Accurso, better known as Ms Rachel, has become a global star in the world of children’s entertainment. Accurso has been labelled a “toddler whisperer” and racks up billions of views on YouTube with her catchy videos. Having signed a deal with Netflix, Ms Rachel dolls, rattles, talking toy phones, books and pyjamas are now all available. But statements on everything from Gaza to LGBTQ rights have prompted criticism as well as support.

Why get involved in politics? In the beginning, Accurso was advised to keep quiet about political issues. She was told that if she avoided controversial topics, more viewers would follow, and she would eventually be able to help more kids. But after watching footage from Gaza and speaking to families on the ground, Accurso says, she doesn’t understand why anyone would not do all they can to stop the violence: “How could we not want to help everyone?”

Notable quote: “We’re the grownups of this world and we’re meant to keep children safe. And the fact that we are not is horrific.”

How long will it take to read: almost nine minutes.

Further reading: Matching Macklemore, and the TV event of the year.

Sign up to Five Great Reads

Each week our editors select five of the most interesting, entertaining and thoughtful reads published by Guardian Australia and our international colleagues. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Saturday morning

after newsletter promotion

Having made its debut on Broadway in 1935, the play Till the Day I Die found itself at the centre of controversy in Australia when it was banned by the federal government at the request of the Nazi party. Written by the US playwright Clifford Odets, the play is about a communist who was arrested by the Nazis for producing leftwing political pamphlets. But the ban created a groundswell of support, leading to a creative production being performed on the back of a truck in Melbourne. Ninety years on, it’s being staged again.

A symbol of rebellion and resistance: Theatre-makers Mark Wilson and Katie Sfetkidis were inspired by that surreptitious production, which took place in the bed of a pickup 90 years ago. Wilson and Sfetkidis view their modern-day production as “as an act of leftist solidarity with the past and a spur for future activism”.

Notable qoute: “The work is long and the work is ongoing, and fighting against the forces of fascism is going to be much larger than anybody’s lifetime.”

How long will it take to read: less than two minutes.

Further reading: When a theatre becomes a culture war.

Across the Nordic countries of Finland, Sweden and Norway, something is happening underground. Bunkers made during the cold war now have a new purpose as Russia’s war in Ukraine revives old fears of conflict across Europe. These once disused bunkers remain ready for a crisis.

“It was a debate before, but thanks to Putin, it no longer is”: For years, the legacy of underground shelters was viewed as a costly one. Jukka Lehtiranta, the head of Helsinki’s Civil Defence Association, who continues to train volunteers for wartime, says that has now changed. In addition to their renewed use as a civil-defence system, these spaces designed for conflict have become a part of Finnish everyday life. Across Helsinki, underground bunkers now contain a 300-metre karting track, a popular axe-throwing club, garages and a shooting range used by reservists.

Can you oppose a datacentre if it is underground? Sweden has found a different use for their neglected shelters. The cold war spaces beneath Stockholm have been transformed into datacentres. Deep beneath the earth, rows of servers stand beside granite walls lined with green vegetation.

How long will it take to read: about two minutes.

Further reading: The super-rich “preppers” planning to save themselves from the apocalypse.

The Guardian view on Trump and Xi: a show of friendship, but no real attempt to address the tensions

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:53:49 GMT

The Chinese leader’s visit to Washington appears to have done nothing to shift the stalemate in bilateral relations

Within days, two high-profile Chinese visitors will arrive in the US – envoys of friendship, as Xi Jinping described them when he met Donald Trump at the White House this week. The giant pandas, Ping Ping and Fu Shuang, will be hosted at Atlanta zoo. Beijing dispatched the first panda pair to the US in 1972 following President Richard Nixon’s landmark visit to China. It uses the animals to indicate satisfaction or displeasure with other nations. But it also charges heftily for their lease: reportedly, around $1m a year per pair. Americans’ views of China have warmed from a pandemic nadir, but are unlikely to be shifted much by two animals, however charming. These days they are more of a token gesture than a striking symbol.

It is telling that the announcement was one of the main takeaways of Mr Xi’s visit to Washington. Expectations were low after May’s stalemate summit in Beijing, but this meeting still struggled to meet them. The US president gave Mr Xi a lavish welcome – unusually, travelling to meet the “strong, vibrant and fit” Chinese leader off the plane. He insisted that they had “never gotten along better”.

In a sense that is not surprising. Mr Trump admires and envies authoritarians with untrammelled powers. Chinese state media were welcome at the White House, unlike CNN, MS Now and Politico. Since he rarely pays even lip service to human rights, the treatment of Uyghurs or jailed Hong Kong activist Joshua Wong – facing another lengthy sentence for his international advocacy – were never likely to figure large, whatever the hopes of protesters outside.

Mr Trump told Mr Xi that any Chinese help for Iran is unacceptable; Mr Xi said that the US should adhere to the “correct position” of opposing Taiwanese independence. Beijing wants Washington to shift from the long-held stance of “not supporting” it. That would be a grave mistake, but Mr Trump has given worryingly mixed messages on Taiwan.

It is striking how little of consequence has emerged from the summit given that this is arguably the most consequential diplomatic relationship in the world. A two-month extension of the trade war truce was announced as Mr Xi arrived in the US. China’s curb of rare earth exports has checked Mr Trump’s appetite for an economic offensive; Beijing is anxious about its struggling economy. But if they are more wary of the fallout, they are also more fearful of the other side gaining ground. AI is central to this battle. Mr Trump has resisted all calls to restrain development because “Whoever wins AI, wins.” Mr Xi said it had to be managed responsibly, but Beijing has attacked “threat narratives”, fearing that the US wants to prevent it catching up.

CNN last week highlighted the dangers: the US military reportedly prepared to intercept a Chinese ship in the Middle East after an intelligence report said it was carrying nuclear weapons components – only for officials to realise that the partially AI-generated analysis had misidentified the cargo. Controls on development are desperately needed, but neither side is willing to accept them. Even the limited AI dialogue and “notification hotline” for AI safety proposed by Scott Bessent, treasury secretary, seem to be rather less than meets the eye. This summit should be viewed with alarm not because it saw substantive developments – but because it illustrates the dangers of drift.

The Guardian view on the 2026 Booker shortlist: what it takes to be a man

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:52:33 GMT

All the contenders for this year’s prize are a reflection of the crisis in masculinity

Jarvis Cocker, one of the judges for this year’s Booker prize, has expressed surprise that the shortlist, announced this week, contains four male authors and only two female writers, because, “generally speaking, the male-written books weren’t as good as the ones written by women”.

The Pulp frontman might be on to something. Over the past 10 years, however, seven Booker winners have been men; the number of women boosted to four by the controversial joint win between Bernardine Evaristo and Margaret Atwood in 2019. The 2024 Booker shortlist was the first to have five female authors in the prize’s history. Last year’s winner Flesh, by British-Hungarian author David Szalay, stripped what being a man means down to its bones.

This year’s contenders all approach the same question through wildly different forms: historical, domestic, dystopian and comic fiction. The novels by female authors both have male protagonists: a reluctant medieval monarch in Rebecca Perry’s May We Feed the King and a 57-year-old history teacher in contemporary Massachusetts in The Things We Never Say by Elizabeth Strout.

The Disappearers by Marlon James and John of John by Douglas Stuart, both previous Booker winners, show young men confronting their sexuality in the repressive climates of late 20th-century Jamaica and the Outer Hebrides, respectively. In The End of Everything from science-fiction giant M John Harrison, the central character is trying to survive in a post-apocalyptic Britain under invasion from ambiguous entities (AI is never explicitly mentioned). In Black Bag, by Luke Kennard, an out-of-work actor lands a job in which he has to wear a black bag all the time, based on a 1967 social psychology experiment in which a student was asked to wear a big black bag for a whole semester. “It’s a statement about being a man,” one character says of the eponymous bag. “There’s a whole contingent of men who are lost and dissatisfied.”

All the male characters in these novels are walking around in metaphorical black bags, flailing awkwardly in the dark, unknowable to those closest to them. Whether set in medieval times, Donald Trump’s America or a nightmarish near future, the 2026 shortlist is a reflection of current anxieties about masculinity.

Publishing is just catching up. Thanks to the so-called Sally Rooney phenomenon, the book world (if not the Booker) has been dominated by novels written by and about young women, a long overdue pushback against generations of swaggering fiction by men. The male gaze has finally shifted. As Szalay has said, “you can’t write like Martin Amis or Norman Mailer or Philip Roth now”. Notable exceptions such as Szalay and Ben Lerner, whose novel Transcription was a surprise omission from the longlist, have been steadily chronicling 21st-century manhood. But some feared that male writers and stories were being overlooked altogether. Last year, the independent publisher, Conduit Books, was set up exclusively for male authors.

The shortlist shows a renewed confidence in narratives about men. Here are fathers and sons, husbands and lovers, kings and losers, none of whom conform to male stereotypes. All of the novels are about a longing for purpose and connection. In a world where the strongman myth is mighty, the characters show vulnerability and uncertainty. As the lyrics of a 1998 Pulp song have it, they make us “start to wonder what it takes to be a man”.

How Labour can reform Britain’s pensions triple lock

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:37:08 GMT

Readers offer solutions to the thorny problem facing the government, in response to an article by Gaby Hinsliff

Gaby Hinsliff (Britain needs cash and everyone knows we should break the pensions triple lock. Where is the courage?, 22 September) is right that public policy should not subsidise wealth without limit, but breaking the triple lock is a poor way to target affluent pensioners. Most pensioners are not affluent. Indeed, a quarter of pensioners require benefits in addition to the state pension just to survive and keep a roof over their heads.

If the aim is to stop subsidising wealth, a more direct target is the generous tax treatment of private pension savings. A taxpayer contributing £100 to a pension can receive £40 or £45 in tax relief if they pay higher- or additional-rate tax, compared with £20 for the basic rate. Tax and national insurance contributions relief on private pensions costs the government a staggering £84bn a year.

Most of this money (almost three-quarters) goes to the wealthiest 20% taxpayers because they can afford to save the most and receive the highest rate of relief. Instead, a flat 20% rate of tax relief on private pensions would preserve the incentive for basic-rate taxpayers while reducing the additional subsidy concentrated among higher earners. It’s also fair because when pensions are drawn down, much less tax is recovered by the Treasury, making the net cost of this relief over £50bn a year.

This could raise billions more than breaking the triple lock. The triple lock’s 2.5% floor was only significant during the period when both earnings growth and inflation were close to zero. When inflation and earnings growth are above 2%, as they are now and are expected to be over the coming years, the difference between the triple lock and a conventional uprating mechanism becomes irrelevant.

The policy challenge therefore is to avoid the economically irrelevant, politically damaging and socially divisive red herring that is breaking the triple lock and instead reform the far more regressive support given to large private pension pots. Stephen RichardsonGrange-over-Sands, Cumbria

Gaby Hinsliff makes the point that retirees of the future are likely to have smaller cushions to fall back on than baby boomers. But it is precisely this that justifies maintaining the triple lock as a bulwark against poverty. Young and middle‑aged workers do indeed face the prospect of an impoverished old age. As highlighted in the Pensions Commission interim report, according to 2025 figures, 43% of working-age people are undersaving for retirement, with just 25% of Bangladeshis and Pakistanis of working age participating in a pension scheme.

The pensions crisis is likely to grow, given the rise in the numbers of self-employed people – the group least likely to be saving for a pension. Millions of workers in their 40s and 50s face the prospect of poverty in retirement, given the rise of precarious working and continuing age discrimination in employment.

We do need a new deal to achieve generational fairness, but breaking the lock will leave millions facing poverty. The alternative must be keeping the lock, but tackling the reasons that justify its existence – low incomes, insecure employment and the high cost of housing. Chris PhillipsonEmeritus professor of sociology and social gerontology, University of Manchester

There is a simple tweak that would improve the affordability of the triple lock. The goal of the triple lock is to ensure that the value of the pension keeps up with both price inflation and wage inflation. But the way it has been implemented allows pensioners to do much better than this.

Between 2011 and 2026, prices rose by 60% and earnings rose by 66%, but pensions rose by 89%. This happens because in some years prices rise more than wages, but in other years wages rise more. So the pension does better than both of them.

The fix is to smooth out the earnings link. Instead of looking at wages growth over the last year, we should look at growth over the past five years, for example. Pensioners would still be protected against price rises, and would maintain their current position in the wages league table. But they would no longer rise up it. Bob VickersTwickenham, London

Gaby Hinsliff claims that “Every serious party needs billions of pounds to fund their promises, and everyone knows there’s an obvious place to find the money, but nobody wants to be the first to say so. And so a deferential silence shrouds the pension triple lock.” The problem is that everybody might think they know this, but that does not mean it is right.

If we do need to find money, it is within the government’s power to create it. And if it refuses to use that power, it can look elsewhere within the pension system for funds. For example, the pension tax relief given to the highest-earning people in this country, at rates above the basic level of income tax, costs at least £15bn a year – vastly more than costs attributed to the triple lock.

We have a cost of living crisis and a pension poverty crisis. So why is everyone looking at punishing some of the most vulnerable people in our society when the rich continue to have their ever-increasing wealth subsidised by the state at a cost of many billions of pounds a year?Richard MurphyEmeritus professor of accounting practice, Sheffield University

Along with my state pension, I receive two small pensions from the Ministry of Defence and the NHS. If my husband should die before me, I don’t know how I would survive financially. We have a small cottage and downsizing wouldn’t result in a significant profit.

My “inheritance” from my parents disappeared when my mother had to go into care with Alzheimer’s; her house had to be sold to pay for her care.

In a week when the billionaire tax avoider Jim Ratcliffe badmouths the country, Gaby Hinsliff makes no reference to the tax system and how the very rich can get away with paying very little.

She also makes no reference to why the UK is doing so badly financially or why young people are struggling – my son can’t afford a house – after a decade of Tory misrule, a decade of Brexit wilderness and the legacy of Thatcherism. Removing the triple lock won’t solve the now endemic financial challenges the UK is facing. Ingrid MarshNewton Abbot, Devon

Gaby Hinsliff is right about the triple lock: it has done its work in raising the ratio between the state retirement pension and average earnings from 18% in 2010 to about 30% now. Two problems remain: what should replace it and how to stop an opportunist opposition from playing politics with the issue?

There is no need to decide this matter now. Far better to announce the end of the triple lock in the forthcoming budget and refer the question of a replacement to a time-limited, cross-party commission. The state pension should not become a political football or part of a short-term fiscal fix. David PurdyCausewayhead, Stirling

Arts Council England doesn’t need ‘swagger’, it needs reform

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:34:28 GMT

Reader Chris Hodgkins proposes a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music

The interview with the new chair of Arts Council England (ACE), who says she wants the organisation to “get its swagger back”, misdiagnoses the crisis facing England’s cultural system (‘I want us to be loud’: Arts Council England’s new chair aims to reconnect young people with culture, 18 September). Swagger is not what is missing. What is required is contrition, honesty and structural reform.

Eighty years after its creation, Arts Council England remains built on a 1946 architecture that privileges opera and classical institutions while systematically marginalising jazz, folk, world, brass, choral and grassroots arts and music. This is not a matter of confidence or energy; it is a matter of structural imbalance. The Review of Jazz in England (2025), Margaret Hodge’s review (2025), and ACE/Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s 2026 responses all identify bureaucracy, mistrust and inconsistent decision‑making – yet none confront the deeper failures: lottery funding misuse, national portfolio organisation dominance, regional inequity, governance opacity, and the collapse of grassroots infrastructure. These problems are not recent. Every major review confirms the same pattern: ACE’s centralised model reproduces historical privilege and suppresses contemporary cultural practice.

International evidence shows that modern cultural systems – in Scandinavia, Ireland and Australia – are built on devolved delivery, direct investment in artists, touring infrastructure, and integrated cultural‑education policy. England has none of these. ACE’s legacy architecture cannot deliver the government’s growth agenda, cannot support regional cultural economies, and cannot unlock the high‑growth potential of grassroots arts and music.

What is needed now is not swagger but a new organisation. I propose a dual‑pillar system that safeguards national institutions while establishing a dedicated body for grassroots arts and music, with transparent allocation formulas, restored lottery funding, art form‑specific policy and a national touring infrastructure. Swagger will not fix England’s cultural system. Structural reform will. Chris HodgkinsEaling, London

New map projections don’t make the Mercator wrong

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:31:30 GMT

The transverse Mercator projection was created for European sailors – and it worked for their world, writes Paul Harwood

The subject of projections is incredibly complicated and you did a good job of navigating the discussion (‘A map is never neutral’: meet the cartographers who took on centuries of western bias, 18 September).

However, suggesting that transverse Mercator is inherently biased is not fair (if it is possible to be unfair to an equation) to both the projection and the cartographers.

Mercator et al just did the job of creating maps that were useful for the European sailors they were working for. The fact that everyone carried on using it was our laziness and not their bias.

The Equal Earth projection is a much better representation for what we use maps for now, but that does not make the Mercator wrong.

You say “A London-centric worldview has long dominated how world maps are presented.” But I can think of almost no maps that have London at the centre. The international coordinate system (ie latitude-longitude, which is unchanged by this resolution) is based for arbitrary historical reasons on a meridian drawn through Greenwich.

However, the “centre” of this coordinate system is not London but a point in the sea off west Africa. No map or representation has to use this as the centre and the current best practice – called UTM – has 60 different zones (thus 60 centres) to represent all parts of the globe.

Even the UK Ordnance Survey mapping system is not “centred” on London. As far as you can say it has a centre, it would be somewhere in Lancashire. Paul Harwood London

The dark art of maths and the AI revolution

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:28:05 GMT

Bev Littlewood reminds us that mathematics has been the prime driver of the rise in AI, in response to an editorial

You report in your leader that some mathematicians feel discomfiture at the AI solution to a Navier-Stokes problem (The Guardian view on AI v mathematicians: humans are still vital to the field, but tech firms refuse to see that, 20 September). I fear that they have been hoist by their own petard: mathematics, after all, has been the prime mover of the AI revolution.

As a somewhat lowly mathematician, let me remind others of the famous quote of Augustine: “The good Christian should beware the mathematician and all those who make empty promises. The danger already exists that the mathematicians have made a covenant with the devil to darken the spirit and to confine man in the bonds of hell.”

While the accuracy of the quote, and Augustine’s meaning, are in some dispute, its appropriateness here is too good to waste. Bev LittlewoodEmeritus professor of software engineering, City St George’s, University of London
