England v Spain, Azerbaijan GP and county cricket finale – follow with us

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:27:53 GMT

Here’s how to follow along with our coverage – the finest writing and up-to-the-minute reports

The Premier League may be on a break but there is no slacking at our essential gateway to the weekend’s football action. Front and centre, we will have the latest news on Manchester City’s legal battle. Plus England’s mouthwatering confrontation at Wembley with the world champions, Spain, on Saturday evening, the hosts’ first match since that semi-final freeze against Argentina. At 2pm, a new era for Scotland commences as Sébastien Pocognoli’s side kickstart their Nations League campaign away to Slovenia. We will not be forgetting Leagues One and Two either, and if the National League is your passion and you are travelling to a match, we would love to hear from you. You will be a lot of things, but one thing you will not be is bored. Emillia Hawkins has all the breaking news and more.

As the campaign rushes to its conclusion, Tanya Aldred keeps those on tenterhooks updated with all the highs and lows, wickets and runs. Champagne corks are planned to pop at Warwickshire who are striding toward clinching the County Championship title against relegation-threatened Leicestershire at Edgbaston. A win would guarantee a first pennant since the Covid-shortened 2021 campaign, with second-placed Somerset faltering against Surrey. In Division Two promotion hopefuls Kent are battling rock-bottom Gloucestershire at Canterbury. Northamptonshire, just four points behind second-placed Kent, need to step up against Middlesex. Why not join the conversation?

Azerbaijan is marking 10 years since its first F1 race but this year’s event is a little different. The grand prix is taking place on a Saturday because Sunday is a national holiday, Remembrance Day. The Baku City Circuit hosting Saturday’s race is about 105 miles from the nearest point on Azerbaijan’s southern border with Iran, yet the turmoil of the regional conflict that has accounted for other motor sport events has not shunted this fixture off the F1 calendar. Two other world championships governed by the FIA have abandoned plans to race in the Middle East this year. The World Rally Championship last week scrapped its season-ending event in Saudi Arabia after travel concerns from teams. The World Endurance Championship cancelled races in Bahrain and Qatar in July and replaced them with European venues. Azerbaijan has been less directly affected by the Iran war than the Gulf nations, many of which host major US military bases and were targeted by Iranian strikes. So, F1 racing will go on, as Kimi Antonelli commands a vast 81-point lead over his Mercedes teammate George Russell. Baku is where Oscar Piastri’s title challenge started to crumble a year ago but Antonelli’s lead is more than double the biggest advantage the McLaren driver had last year and he is coming off back-to-back wins. Dominic Booth covers the race lap-by-lap. Giles Richards reports.

So to the first of Saturday’s two big games. In an extended international break, the Scots face the Slovenians twice, Switzerland and North Macedonia as they strive to get out of League B. Enter Sébastien Pocognoli, tasked with building on the groundwork laid by Steve Clarke, under whom Scotland qualified for three major tournaments, including this summer’s World Cup in North America. “We arrive in the timeline of the Scotland national team [where], in the natural way, you will have some changes. But I don’t see this as a bad challenge, I think it’s a needed challenge,” the former Union Saint-Gilloise and Monaco manager said in the buildup. Those Scotland followers of a jaded nature might say t’was ever thus: a challenge. Maybe it will take a Belgian to take this generation of players to a higher level and provide some cheer for the longsuffering Tartan Army. Barry Glendenning live blogs the match, with Ewan Murray reporting from Ljubljana’s Stadion Stozice.

Spain’s visit to Wembley is a painful reminder to England of what might have been, and Thomas Tuchel needs a positive response to silence criticism of how the Three Lions’ World Cup fizzled out against a snarling, brutal Argentina. Had England held out for the final five minutes plus stoppage time in their semi-final two months ago, they would have met Spain in the final. Instead Tuchel’s players wilted, conceding twice after he had attempted to batten down the hatches with a series of defensive substitutions. The German coach admitted to being left “unfulfilled” by failing to achieve his target of a second star on the England jersey. Bukayo Saka went even further in midweek by revealing “there’s still a scar in us” over what happened in Atlanta. Time to start healing those wounds against the best international team on the planet. It is a tall order, particularly with a string of high-profile withdrawals. Rob Smyth will keep the blog updates flowing while our top team of David Hytner, Barney Ronay and Jacob Steinberg provide reports and analysis from the national stadium.

Matchday live returns with more buildup, breaking news, good vibes and reader comments, with Billy Munday, Will Unwin and Yara El-Shaboury keeping it all flowing. There will be the latest updates on Manchester City v the Premier League and wash-up from England and Scotland’s Nations League clashes, as well as looking forward to Sunday’s key clashes: Israel v Ireland, Denmark v Wales, Serbia v Netherlands, Germany v Greece and Norway v Portugal. There is no better place to start your footballing day. Join the conversation by emailing your thoughts and queries to matchday. live@theguardian. com

Rob Smyth and Tim de Lisle have over-by-over coverage of the third ODI after Sri Lanka levelled the series in thrilling last-over fashion at Headingley on Thursday. England were cruising to a target of 322 while Tom Banton (73) and Ben Duckett (67) shared a first-wicket stand of 143. Sri Lanka had been hammered 3-0 in a preceding T20 campaign but Dunith Wellalage dragged them back by removing both openers and captain Harry Brook to reduce England to 157 for three. The left-arm spinner finished with figures of three for 49 after captain Kusal Mendis hit a fine century. The teams now head to London for a series-decider at the Oval. In the aftermath Brook insisted this was just what England needed before next year’s 50-over World Cup in southern Africa. “We’ve got a great opportunity now to try to win this series, and a great opportunity for 12 months’ time,” he said. “In pressure situations, like the one that awaits us at the Oval, it will be great to see where we are as a team.” Our cricket correspondent Ali Martin reports.

The season’s final day – will it be Warks? Or will Somerset gatecrash the pennant party? Tanya Aldred is back to steer the live blog as the domestic campaign hurtles to the grandest of grandstand finishes. Join her for all the latest developments.

Renée Slegers’ unbeaten Arsenal face their derby rivals at Stamford Bridge after draws against Crystal Palace and Manchester United. However, only two goals and five points from three WSL matches is a telling indication of their season so far. Yet Tuesday’s 1-0 Champions League victory over HB Køge was achieved while several first-choice players were rested. They should be back in red and white for one of the campaign’s blockbusters as the two most successful clubs in the WSL era collide. Chelsea recorded their own Champions League success in midweek, with Wieke Kapteina’s strike securing 1-0 win over Austria Vienna, having struggled to impose themselves over Birmingham City last weekend. Will Unwin hosts the live blog, with Sophie Downey reporting.

Buckle up, NFL fans: Graham Searles’ rolling blog is the best way to follow all the unfurling action on a Sunday evening. He’ll be focusing on two of week three’s key games: Dolphins v Chiefs and Bills v Chargers. Miami lost to San Francisco 49ers last time out – unraveling in the second half of an eventual 35-13 defeat – and face another tough challenge when the three-time Super Bowl MVP Patrick Mahomes and the Kansas City Chiefs visit. The Chiefs are off to a 2-0 flyer, thanks largely to a balanced offence bolstered by the former Seattle running back Kenneth Walker III. The reigning Super Bowl MVP began the season with consecutive games of more than 175 scrimmage yards, creating room for Mahomes to have more success through the air. The Chiefs are averaging an NFL-best 457.5 yards through two games, which is about 137 more than their per-game average last season. Likewise, Buffalo are rolling after two straight wins, while the Los Angeles Chargers are winless as they hit the road for Sunday’s game.

John Brewin has rolling coverage of Sunday evening’s big internationals, and he’ll be zeroing in on the Republic of Ireland’s troubled clash in Hungary. The Irish face Israel before a designated “home” game in Serbia on 4 October, amid protests and calls for a boycott over Israel’s war in Gaza. The country’s strong support for the Palestinian cause dictates there will be no Irish supporters in the stadium, no home match in Ireland, and no pundits or Irish commentary on television. The game is being staged in Debrecen because Israel cannot host international matches. Ireland’s manager, Heimir Hallgrimsson, raised tension levels last week by saying that many of his squad were uncomfortable about taking part, adding: “We’re not playing with genocide, we’re playing against genocide.” Those comments drew a furious response from the Israel Football Association, which accused Hallgrimsson of “hypocrisy and stupidity”.

The makers of the 7 Up series set out to prove a point about class. What they achieved is far more profound

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 16:10:14 GMT

The epic documentary series reveals much about the shifting social attitudes of the last 60 years – and much more about the quiet mystery of human life

For an hour or two this week, I’ve been in the company of people whose lives I’ve seen unfold, almost from the beginning, almost to the end. They are people whom, with one exception, I’ve never met. And yet I’ve shared in their triumphs and disappointments for decades.

They are the group who, in 1964, when they were seven years old, were the subjects of what was initially a single, 40-minute ITV documentary, but which flowered into a work that is quite magical. Returning to those same boys and girls every seven years, watching as they turned first into shy and awkward teenagers, then into husbands and wives, then into parents and grandparents, the 7 Up series has become a document of our times – but also something larger and far more revealing. This week the broadcaster aired what it says will be the final chapter: the seven-year-olds are now 70.

The original aim of the show, made under the World in Action banner, was sociological and transparently political. It wanted to expose the entrenched nature of the British class system. And so it watched a trio of pre-prep school boys singing verses in Latin, contrasting them with the cheeky East End kids living just a few miles and a world away. While the posh trio could name, even then, the specific Oxbridge colleges their parents had in mind for them, Paul, raised in a children’s home, asked: “What does university mean?”

Sure enough, we have seen how those born into money keep it, while those with less have less – though what the programme missed was the huge and expanding group in between. By focusing either on foxhunting John at one end or cabbie Tony at the other, it largely left out what would turn out to be the story of these decades, namely the sprawling growth of the middle class.

Indeed, it’s the programme’s early assumptions that often turn out to illuminate most sharply how much society has changed. In 1964, the researchers only thought to include one child who wasn’t white: Symon. In a later episode, we hear the director, the late Michael Apted, ask him about being “illegitimate”, until Symon gently sets him straight: “We’re living in different times.” Apted is also admonished for his sexism: why, says Jackie, does he always ask the women about marrying and settling down, but not the men?

We get glimpses of the politics of these years. Lynn was a devoted children’s librarian, until successive rounds of budget cuts hacked away at the service to which she had given much of her life. We hear Tony complain about immigrants enjoying easy access to benefits, including housing – except that footage is from the 1970s, a reminder that the current debates are anything but new. We see that Bruce, who as a seven-year-old aspired to be a missionary in Africa in order to help the neediest, is now a lifeboat volunteer for the RNLI. Aware of the recent assaults on that organisation, we suspect he’s still doing God’s work.

Perhaps most striking is the shifting view of mental illness. When 28 Up aired in 1984, much of the nation was shocked by the fate of Neil, who as a wide-eyed seven-year-old had dreamed of being an astronaut, and who was now found lonely, wandering and homeless. There is vague talk of a “nervous complaint” and Apted asks him, “Can you lick it?”, as if a stiff upper lip and cold shower might do the trick. Now, Neil speaks directly of a lifelong battle with depression, naming it at last.

It’s not wrong to speak of “much of the nation”, by the way. 7 Up came of age in the era of terrestrial, limited-choice TV when the audiences were enormous and major programmes were collective experiences. The medium had weight and a kind of patience, so that a six-decades-long project like this one was at least conceivable. In the age of YouTube Shorts and Instagram Reels, there won’t be another. (Though before we romanticise the olden days too much, 70 Up self-critically notes that the children’s parents never gave anything that we would recognise as consent.)

Still, it’s not here – in the charting of shifts in society or broadcasting – that the magic lies. If the original ambition was to examine class in modern Britain, the series very soon transcended that to becomebigger, to become, like the best works of art, both timeless and universal. As Peter, now retired from teaching, says, “It’s a film about living a human life.”

We see the compromises that real people in real situations have to make. Bruce was once “the only socialist in the village” who, on principle, taught maths at an inner London school to kids who had none of the privileges he had known as a boy. At 49, we found him in a master’s gown at a public school, facing accusations from old friends that he had sold out. But life, we realise, is not political theory. Sometimes it just takes a different course. There are events you cannot plan for, including, of course, the lottery of health and the random intrusions of mortality. You know it’s coming, but it stops you all the same: two of the seven-year-olds of 1964 are dead.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

after newsletter promotion

Those who remain are very clear on what matters. One after another, they say they now understand the centrality of family. At 70 and a retired lawyer, Andrew offers an age-old lament when he wonders if, perhaps, he should have forsaken those extra hours in the office that seemed so important at the time, and gone instead to his children’s school play or sports day. Apted overlooked this dimension, too, often asking his subjects about their career disappointments or the apparent modesty of their achievements, failing to see what he eventually recognised as the “power” of the families they had built.

We hardly need to be told that, because we see it for ourselves. We see again and again how these people were shaped, yes, by class but also by the family situations they were born into, and especially by what was missing. So many of them devoted themselves to avoiding the mistakes of their parents, to ensuring their own children enjoyed the stability they had lacked.

Perhaps the most vivid example is Symon. At seven he was in care; now aged 70, it still gnaws at him that he never knew his father. In the 1964 film, the kids visited an adventure playground: Symon and Paul, both raised in the same children’s home, immediately set about moving planks and bricks. They were trying to build a house. In the latest film, we learn that Symon and his wife became foster parents, not just once or twice but, over the decades, to a staggering 130 children. As Symon said of his own children when he was 28, “They’ve got everything. They’ve got a father.” The animating premise of each of the Up films was the old Jesuit saying: “Give me a child until he is seven, and I will give you the man.” There turns out to be great truth in that, a truth far more profound than the political point the film-makers first set out to prove.

As Nick, a boy who dreamed of exploring the moon and went on to become a nuclear physicist, says, we are moved when we see time-lapse photography of a single flower, watching it “blossom and then fade away”. How breathtaking then to see the full span of a human life, several of them at once – the quiet, ordinary mystery of it. How breathtaking and how beautiful.

70 Up is available on ITVX

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist

I love a drink in the stands, but Burnham’s beer proposal feels out of step with modern football

The Guardian Fri, 25 Sep 2026 14:00:08 GMT

Focusing on the right to drink at your seat is an odd place to start when discrimination in the game runs much deeper

Andy Burnham is right that football fans have historically been treated differently from other sports fans. But if we’re going to talk about discrimination in football, the ban on drinking at your seat feels like a strange place to start.

The rule may have its roots in a very different era of football, but for many fans today, being able to take a pint to your seat may not be top of their list of changes they’d like to see in the game. Especially at a time when discrimination is very much present elsewhere in football.

The legislation, introduced under Margaret Thatcher in the 1980s as part of a crackdown on football hooliganism, was rooted in the idea that football fans needed to be treated differently from the supposedly better-behaved crowds at rugby and cricket – which smacks of classism and the stereotyping of working-class fans. But football has changed since then, and so has drinking culture. Fans have adapted to the restrictions and built a matchday ritual around them. A good fan concourse pint is up there with an airport pint or a beer-garden pint on the first day of summer.

Fans have got used to this routine, and one of the biggest concerns of lifting this ban now seems to be the Boxpark-ification of football: the dreaded performative beer throw when anything good happens.

Even when it’s not performative, it does raise a problem of logistics. With no cup holders, when a 95th-minute winner goes in and you’re suddenly off your seat with your limbs in the air, a pint is unlikely to remain where you left it. There will be people walking back and forth from the concourse during the game for another pint or the toilet, too. It used to happen before, of course, but it would still be a new irritation that fans would have to adapt to. And, most importantly, it isn’t a change many fans seem to have been asking for.

As a fan of both men’s and women’s football, I’ve experienced the Women’s Super League’s successful trial of beer at your seats, as well as drinking at non-league games, and it was a nice change. It has even become a distinct part of the matchday experience in leagues where the atmosphere is different and the crowds are smaller. But the women’s game is not simply the men’s game with fewer people in the stands. The matchday experience is different – and that’s important when we talk about what works.

Watching Everton Women with a beer in hand can be lovely. So can spending a long day at the cricket with a pint. But I was also at the game in which Chloe Kelly scored the winner for England against Germany at Euro 2022, and was immediately swallowed up in the chaos of the celebrations, being thrown around by the people around me. Having a pint in my hand in that moment would have been less than ideal. Beer and football can clearly coexist, but what works at one level of the game, or in one kind of crowd, doesn’t necessarily translate neatly to another.

But this is where Burnham’s argument starts to feel out of step with the reality of football now. At a time when working-class fans are being priced out of their season tickets, racist, sexist, homophobic online abuse is ever-present, and figures at the very top of the game – such as Jim Ratcliffe – use their platform to push deeply divisive politics, it feels out of touch to make the right to drink a pint in your seat a headline example of football discrimination.

And that’s not to deny discrimination of working-class fans, but this is a problem that runs much deeper in the game. And if the old assumption is that football fans are uniquely likely to cause trouble when alcohol is involved, lifting the ban doesn’t automatically remove that belief. It’s possible these biases will show up in how games are policed, with a heavy pre-emptive police and security presence.

If the ban is lifted, there’ll be teething problems, there will be beer showers, complaints and no doubt a bunch of stories in the press making an example of any issues of violence held up as evidence that football fans can’t be trusted with a pint. Eventually, though, fans will adapt, security will relax and, for the most part, it will probably become normal.

Sign up to Matters of Opinion

Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more

after newsletter promotion

But that’s precisely why Burnham’s argument feels like such an odd intervention. There are serious questions about class and access in football that deserve to be scrutinised as discrimination. If Burnham wants to tackle the ways football fans are treated unfairly, there are plenty of other places to start.

Football fans have every right to drink their beer wherever the rules allow. But sometimes a pint is just a pint – and football has bigger battles to fight.

Marva Kreel is a broadcaster and football content creator

Nor’easter Live Updates: Heavy Rain and Wind Batter Northeast, Bringing Coastal Flooding

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Source: Tomorrow. io.

The storm flooded low-lying areas, knocked out power for thousands and forced the cancellation of several major events and hundreds of flights. Wind gusts exceeded 50 miles per hour in places.

Judson JonesNazaneen GhaffarAmy Graff and Francesca Regalado

Fierce winds and rains from a strengthening nor’easter lashed the Northeast on Saturday as the storm crawled up the coast, flooding low-lying coastal areas, knocking out power and canceling flights and events.

The combination of strong winds and exceptionally high tides caused flooding in coastal areas of New Jersey and New York City, submerging streets, cars and the first floors of some buildings.

In Edgewater, N. J., the Hudson River flooded, forcing emergency workers to evacuate people from a waterside hotel. Hamilton Beach, a neighborhood of bungalows near Kennedy Airport, also saw streets filled with flood waters.

Wind gusts exceeded 50 miles per hour in several places on Saturday morning, reaching 62 m. p. h. in Nantucket.

The high winds were already downing power lines and causing outages. Nearly 28,000 people lost electricity in New Jersey. In Suffolk County, Long Island, about 17,000 people were without power on Saturday afternoon, and officials expected the number to double in the next 24 hours, the county executive, Ed Romaine, said.

The storm caused headaches for thousands of airline passengers. More than 250 flights were canceled at Boston Logan International Airport, which is about a quarter of the airport’s traffic, according to the online flight tracker FlightAware. Hundreds of flights were also delayed at the three major airports serving New York City, but there were few cancellations.

Forecasters had predicted from two to six inches of rain would fall on Saturday across a swath of the East Coast stretching from Atlantic City to Boston.

The center of the storm was off the coast of Delaware as of 2 p. m. on Saturday, inching north. The threat of coastal flooding remained high because of the storm’s strength, its slow pace and exceptionally high tides because of the full moon.

The storm’s center was expected to stay offshore until late Saturday evening, and then take a turn west toward New Jersey on Sunday. It will most likely linger there until Monday and then move northeast, the National Weather Service said in an advisory early Saturday morning.

The Weather Service has issued coastal flood warnings effective until Sunday evening for northeast New Jersey, southeast New York and the Massachusetts coast, including Cape Cod and Nantucket.

Here’s what else to know:

Latest forecast: Meteorologists say the heavy rain could lead to some flash flooding, mainly in coastal Massachusetts, some of Rhode Island and eastern Long Island. Though the tip of Long Island could see the brunt of the heavier rain and higher winds, significant rain could also fall toward the west, including across New York City, said Joe Pollina, a meteorologist with the Weather Service.

Rainfall total: One and a half to three inches of rain was forecast over the weekend for cities including New York, Philadelphia and Atlantic City. Around four inches was predicted for parts of Long Island and Connecticut, with totals as high as six inches possible around Boston and Cape Cod.

El Niño effect: This is likely to be the first of several East Coast storms to follow this path over the next few months, driven by a developing El Niño weather pattern.

Hilary Howard

In New York City, a 56-year-old man was killed by a falling tree on Saturday while walking near a playground in East New York, Brooklyn, according to the police. It’s the only recorded death amid the nor’easter.

Heather Beasley Doyle

The Quincy Market in Boston is bustling. The food hall is crowded, and people are shopping at the wooden stalls. The rain seems like a side note, just another part of an autumn trip to New England.

While parts of New York City and Long Island have been spared from heavy downpours so far, dangerous wind has emerged as a more immediate risk. Just before 2 p. m., the National Weather Service issued a high wind warning covering large portions of Long Island and areas of Connecticut. Winds are expected to 25 to 35 miles an hour with gusts as strong as 65 m. p. h. The advisory will remain in place until midday on Sunday.

A similar wind advisory is in place in parts of New Jersey, including Eastern Monmouth, the Atlantic Coastal Cape May, the Coastal Atlantic and other watery areas.

A potent nor’easter will continue to roil coastal areas of the Northeast on Saturday, with the highest threat of flooding and strong winds stretching from New Jersey to Massachusetts.

The center of the storm was off the coast of Delaware as of 2 p. m. on Saturday and inching north. The combination of the storm’s strength, slow pace and the exceptionally high tides caused by the full moon have exacerbated the flooding threat.

The powerhouse El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is making itself felt on two sides of the nation for the first, but probably not last, time this year.

The nor’easter lashing the East Coast this weekend followed a path that can become more common for storms during El Niño, the climate phenomenon that originates in the tropical Pacific and goes on to influence rainfall, temperature and storms around the globe.

A continent away, Hurricane Nolo, which is threatening to soak the Big Island of Hawaii with rain, is being fueled by El Niño-warmed waters in the Pacific. Since August, a parade of hurricanes has battered Hawaii with an intensity that has caught even scientists off guard.

“I lived in Hawaii for 24 years and this is the craziest summer, the craziest fall, I’ve ever seen,” said Mark Merrifield, an ocean scientist and former director of the University of Hawaii Sea Level Center.

El Niño is part of a natural cycle in the Pacific Ocean that recurs every few years and brings a cascade of weather effects across the planet. Its strength typically peaks late in the calendar year. By some metrics, this one is already the strongest on record, an indication of how significantly it is likely to upend many regions’ normal weather patterns in the coming months.

People around the world are already dealing with the consequences. Indonesia is living under a haze of toxic smoke from wildfires worsened by drought. Crops have withered under dry conditions in India, Central America and parts of eastern Africa. Sea levels are rising on the coast of California, giving a leg up for storms and waves to flood homes and erode beaches.

And Hawaii is confronting an extraordinary spate of hurricanes, which are drawing strength from the thick layer of warm water that El Niño produces at the surface of the central and eastern Pacific.

Besides providing more energy for Pacific hurricanes, El Niño also creates conditions in the atmosphere that help them stick around and intensify, said Kim Wood, an associate professor in the department of hydrology and atmospheric sciences at the University of Arizona.

Hawaii has been threatened by such storms before, but never in rapid succession like this year. “It is quite unusual to get that kind of back-to-back-to-back experience,” Dr. Wood said. “And with how mountainous those islands are, the rain threat is just that much worse.”

When moist air hits mountains, it is forced upward, causing it to cool and release precipitation.

Before this year, only six hurricanes over the past seven decades had been recorded as passing within 50 miles of the state, according to Michael Lowry, a hurricane expert for WPLG-TV in Miami. Hurricane Nolo could become the third one to do so this year.

Scientists are working to understand whether human-caused global warming might be leading to more frequent, strong El Niños. They haven’t reached a clear consensus, though one thing is certain: The gyrations that El Niño brings are coming on top of an ocean and atmosphere already warmed by greenhouse gas emissions. That means the effects of an El Niño — whether downpours, wildfires or droughts — can potentially be more severe than they would have been in an earlier, cooler time for the planet.

El Niño’s influence on storms around the United States this year might just be getting started. Come winter, it is likely to help deliver more drenching rain to California. During some past El Niños, the perennially water-stressed state has received one and a half times its usual amount of precipitation, often through winter storms that recharge groundwater but can also cause flooding.

For the Northeast, El Niño doesn’t directly feed storms like the one pounding the coast this weekend, though nor’easters appear to be more frequent in El Niño years. One possible reason? El Niño causes the Pacific jet stream, or the band of air moving west to east at high altitudes, to shift south. That provides a supply of energy and moisture for storms that can take shape off the Southeastern United States then swing north.

The saving grace for eastern states is that El Niño generally leads to quiet Atlantic hurricane seasons. The shift in atmospheric patterns over the Pacific also increases upper-level winds over the Atlantic, making it harder for storms to spin up into hurricanes there.

So far this year, not a single storm in the Atlantic has managed to become a hurricane.

The couple replanned their wedding in a matter of days, finding a new, mainland venue, florist, D. J. and accommodations for guests as all ferries to Block Island were grounded. Ferry services to Nantucket, Martha’s Vineyard and parts of Massachusetts were also suspended this weekend.

All that remains of the wedding the couple had long envisioned on Block Island, where Mr. MacDougall spent summers as a child, is their handmade arch.

The East Coast of the United States hasn’t experienced a hurricane this year, but the storm trudging up the Northeast this weekend may feel like one in some places.

This storm is technically a nor’easter, a type of storm that more commonly stirs visions of heavy snow and plunging temperatures.

So what’s the difference, and why is this a nor’easter if it’s not going to snow?

“Nor’easter” applies broadly to storms that move along the Eastern Seaboard with winds that blow from the northeast. These types of storms typically occur between November and March. A nor’easter in September is relatively early, but not unheard of.

A nor’easter gets its energy from colliding air masses, like cold, dry air and warm, moist air. On satellite images, it often looks like a large comma. The long tail is the cold air wrapping around the storm’s center — that’s what causes thunderstorms to form — while the comma head is where the warm, moist air wraps around. These storms can be enhanced by the jet stream, a ribbon of very strong winds at the cruising altitude of commercial airplanes.

Often, the National Weather Service will avoid using the word “nor’easter” entirely if the storm doesn’t have a major snow component, because residents in the Northeast so strongly associate the term with snow. Dominic Ramunni, a meteorologist with the Weather Service in New York City, said that the local weather offices and the national centers of the Weather Service had a call Thursday and agreed to all use the same term for this storm so there wasn’t confusion in the media. So, they all began using nor’easter on Friday instead of coastal storm, because nor’easter was already being widely used.

Mr. Ramunni said that while weaker than some systems this past year in terms of precipitation and winds, the coastal flooding could rival some of the worst events in the past several years.

A hurricane is different: It is fueled by warm ocean temperatures and requires a calm atmosphere to intensify. At times, these storms can be hybrid versions that begin as hurricanes before morphing into more typical storms. A famous example is Hurricane Sandy, which started as a hurricane but then became what is called an extratropical storm — another name for a typical storm system found across the United States.

One way meteorologists monitor a storm’s strength is through its pressure. The lower the pressure, the more intense the storm.

Sandy reached an intensity of 940 millibars before it began to transition into an extratropical storm. That transition spread Sandy’s damaging winds out farther than they were as a hurricane. The storm surge had already built up over several days and pushed inland with hurricane force.

The storm was essentially a concoction of the worst hazards from both types of systems.

This weekend’s nor’easter is not Sandy. Its intensity is peaking around 992 millibars. (For context, a strong nor’easter this past February reached 965 millibars.) This doesn’t diminish this weekend’s potential for coastal erosion, strong winds and rainfall, but the Northeast coast has seen worse.

This storm isn’t even named, which is standard for anything other than a hurricane. Sandy only had a name because it was a hurricane first. The National Weather Service does not name winter storms.

In Europe, storms that could cause potential damage are routinely named. In the United States, some private organizations and media outlets choose to name winter storms unofficially.

Perhaps the most pronounced element of the nor’easter will be the wind.

“We’re already starting to see strong winds across the area,” Mr. Ciemnecki said early Friday afternoon. But wind gusts will strengthen into the afternoon and evening, and could reach speeds of up to 55 miles per hour across Long Island and 50 miles per hour in New York City.

New Yorkers can sign up for the city and state alert systems NotifyNYC and New York Alert, while New York City and New Jersey residents can follow @NotifyNYC and @ReadyNJ accounts on all major social media platforms.

It was raining. That was what first startled Alyssa Atwood when she stepped off the plane on Christmas Island in August.

Torrential downpours had already turned the dirt roads into impassable waterways, leaving her research team questioning whether their trucks could even reach their lodge.

When she finally waded into the Pacific Ocean, it wasn’t quite as she remembered it.

“You almost don’t want to wear a wet suit, it’s so hot,” said Dr. Atwood, a paleoclimate scientist at Florida State University who recently returned from the island, a remote coral atoll that sits in the Central Pacific at the geographical bull’s-eye of El Niño.

The typical winter peak of El Niño is months away. Yet on Christmas Island, also known as Kiritimati, the ocean was already at least two degrees warmer than average, hovering between 30 and 30.5 degrees Celsius, and the reef was actively bleaching. It was an ominous sign of what forecast models suggest could become a record-breaking El Niño, and stark proof that the ocean had already entered uncharted territory amid what some have called a “super El Niño” or even a “Godzilla El Niño.”

It has already helped make this the hottest summer on record in the United States and boosted Pacific hurricane activity with rare, damaging storms near Hawaii. At the same time, it has kept hurricanes away from the Atlantic, making parts of the Caribbean drier than usual. And as winter approaches, experts are closely monitoring what El Niño’s most intense phase will mean for the day-to-day weather.

The dire warnings may leave everyday people around the world with a central question: How concerned should they be?

First, a brief explanation: El Niño is a natural weather pattern that comes around every few years. It typically develops in the spring or summer, gets stronger through the fall, and peaks in the winter. It doesn’t, by itself, mean a wetter winter in California or a warmer Christmas in New York, but more often than not, when El Niño arrives, that’s what tends to happen. A stronger El Niño like this one can make it more likely.

Emily Becker, a climate scientist at the University of Miami, explained that seasonal forecasts, like the ones making headlines as the off-the-charts scale of this year’s pattern became clear, represent shifting probabilities rather than precise predictions. A winter forecast can offer a strong signal that December, January and February will likely be above or below average, she said, but not when a single storm will hit and how bad it will be.

Think of the El Niño pattern as a dance between the ocean and the atmosphere. As winds in the tropical Pacific weaken, a pool of warm water that otherwise would have stayed in the western Pacific near Indonesia instead sloshes east, dragging the ocean’s primary zone of thunderstorm activity with it. This shift acts like a boulder dropped into a stream, rippling upward through the atmosphere to alter the jet stream and disrupt weather patterns worldwide.

“I see El Niño as an artist that is providing some broad-brush preliminary sketches on what to expect for upcoming seasons,” said Michelle L’Heureux, an El Niño expert at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration. “But the details of the final portrait will be determined by events we cannot predict months in advance.”

California, being on the Pacific, is often the first land mass affected by this new pattern. The state gets most of its annual precipitation in the winter, so an El Niño year leads to the kind of storms that live on in popular memory for decades. That’s what happened in 1997, when relentless storms left more than a dozen people dead and caused a half-billion dollars in damage.

But while a strong El Niño loads the dice, it does not offer a guarantee.

In 2015, another “Godzilla El Niño” year, forecasters expected winter storms to help break a multiyear megadrought. But the storms were forced around California by more regional weather patterns.

“Our return interval in California is two-thirds,” Dr. Becker said. In other words, California sees above-average rainfall in only two out of every three El Niño seasons. So there’s a one-in-three chance that the winter stays dry.

This time around, weather experts believe California is more likely to end up with more rain, said Jon Gottschalck, who works at NOAA’s Climate Prediction Center. But that forecast is based on the similar statistics used in 2015, and even Mr. Gottschalck cautions that California is often more difficult to predict with certainty than other parts of the country during El Niño.

Parts of the South, too, are likely to end up with more rain this winter, Mr. Gottschalck said. The jet stream routinely pins itself across the southern United States during El Niño, delivering a steady conveyor belt of Pacific moisture across Texas, Oklahoma and Kansas.

That could be a good thing, said Weston Anderson, a crop scientist.

“This El Niño may actually bring some needed relief to the area, with increased precipitation in the Southern U. S.,” Dr. Anderson said, noting that winter wheat crops in Kansas and Oklahoma stand to benefit significantly after years of La Niña-driven drought.

Unlike in California, the signal El Niño provides for above-average winter rainfall across the Gulf Coast, the Southeast and up the Eastern Seaboard of the United States is among the most reliable seasonal forecasters can read.

“The probability there’s pretty high,” said Ben Kirtman, a climate scientist at the University of Miami.

While it’s extremely likely that there will be more storms, and that they will move up the East Coast as they do every winter, those systems don’t always translate into snowfall as they move into the Northeast, as they might in a year without El Niño.

Why? Because the northern half of the United States leans toward significantly warmer temperatures during El Niño. That means potential snowstorms often shift into rain or ice in the major Northeast cities, because it’s not always cold enough for snow to fall or accumulate.

“There’s a reasonably strong relationship between El Niño and a warmer winter throughout the northern tier,” Dr. Becker said.

But don’t put your winter coat back in the attic quite yet. A generally warm northern winter does not rule out sudden, severe blasts of Arctic cold.

Amy Butler, a research scientist at NOAA’s Chemical Sciences Laboratory, explained that El Niño frequently triggers what weather people call “sudden stratospheric warmings” high above the North Pole. These warmings can push the cold Arctic air farther south.

If you’re in New York, for example, it wouldn’t be impossible to be enjoying a warmer than usual Christmas Eve, only to need that heavy parka by the time the New Year rolls around.

As global temperatures continue to break records, scientists are grappling with how climate change, caused primarily by the burning of fossil fuels, is altering El Niño itself.

“El Niños have been acting like a stair step,” said Dr. Kim Cobb, a climate scientist at Brown. Global temperatures tend to spike during an El Niño, and when the cycle winds down, temperatures drop — only never back to the previous baseline. “That’s what frightens me about El Niño,” she said.

Dr. Cobb works with Dr. Atwood on Christmas Island, where they are watching corals bleaching before El Niño has even reached its winter stride. Super El Niños are recurring on tighter timelines, and fragile ecosystems no longer have sufficient time to recover between shocks.

That acceleration concerns her. “People should be planning for worst-case scenarios,” she said.

Dr. Michael McPhaden, the director of a NOAA buoy network that has monitored El Niño conditions since the 1990s, offers a different framing.

“Ignorance is the foundation of fear,” he said. “El Niño should not be feared. It should be understood for what it does, what it can do, and what you can do to prepare for it.”

That preparation is being tested like never before. Historical statistical models are fed data on past El Niño patterns to predict how the next one will behave. They have struggled to keep up with the extreme heat of the ocean this year.

There’s another type of projection, called a dynamic physical model, which calculates atmospheric physics based on current data rather than relying on past examples. Those models are forecasting a much stronger, more disruptive El Niño period.

“We are very much in uncharted territory,” Dr. Kirtman said. “What I feel completely confident in is that things are going to happen that are entirely unanticipated — things we didn’t even think of.”

Hilary Howard

An unusual early fall nor’easter is expected to deliver a slate of weather hazards over the weekend, with coastal areas of New York City and Long Island at particular risk of flooding. Some areas of eastern Long Island could also see more than three inches of rain, while totals over an inch will be more widespread.

Meteorologists said that high winds, choppy seas and the coincidence of a storm surge with the abnormally high tides that accompany Saturday’s full moon were likely to produce waves of up to 10 feet, rip currents and beach erosion all along the Eastern Seaboard through Sunday evening.

As with any forecast, however, there is still uncertainty about how much rain will ultimately fall in New York City, but the National Weather Service has said that the area is looking at a slight risk of “excessive rainfall.”

New York City’s sewers and subways, which were built more than 100 years ago, were not designed for the fast and furious deluges that have become routine with climate change. Many of the roadways surrounding the city, where storm water tends to pool during these extreme rainfall events, are low lying and were built over wetlands.

Precipitation intensity

Note: Times are Eastern. Source: National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration via Iowa State University William B. Davis, Joel Eastwood and Bea Malsky/The New York Times

By the end of this century, the city could see 150 percent more days with more than an inch of rain. Nuisance flooding and waterlogged commutes — and the headaches that come with them — are becoming the new normal, along with life-threatening flash flood events.

Here’s how New Yorkers can prepare.

As New York grows hotter because of global warming, the atmosphere is able to hold more moisture, which means heavier downpours.

Most of New York City’s sewer and drainage network is designed to manage a maximum capacity of 1.75 inches of rainfall per hour. When extreme weather or “cloudbursts” drop more, the system becomes rapidly overwhelmed, leading to street and basement flooding.

It is easy to forget that New York City is coastal. It sits near the Atlantic Ocean and is cut through with several brackish rivers that rise and fall with the tides. As climate change increases sea levels, which then push up groundwater tables, the earth underneath our buildings, streets and sidewalks will be less able to absorb the water that pools beneath them.

This means that storm water will drain more slowly and contribute to flooding, particularly in low-lying and subterranean areas, like basements and subway stations. Parts of the subway system, including much of Manhattan’s west side, are below the groundwater table, requiring the Metropolitan Transportation Authority to pump about 14 million gallons of water a day from the tunnels, even during dry weather.

Government officials encourage all New Yorkers to sign up for the city and state alert systems, NotifyNYC and New York Alert.

The alerts announce extreme rain, roadway closures and flash flood watches and warnings. Warnings are the more serious of the two. If you receive such an alert, it means that flooding is imminent and that you should follow official guidance immediately. This could include moving to higher ground if you are in a basement apartment or a low-lying area. The National Weather Service also updates local forecasts throughout the day and night.

First things first: Straphangers should bookmark the M. T. A. website or download its app. The authority provides updates in real time about train delays and stoppages, as well as the reasons behind them, along with information on alternate routes.

During extreme rainfall, excess water can enter the system from the street, from underground and from backed‑up storm drains.

Though recent videos on social media have shown waterfalls on train tracks and storm water gushing down subway entrances, a spokesman for the M. T. A. said flooding in the subway is still rare.

But passengers who find themselves in such a situation should listen to announcements and follow the instructions of station personnel and train crews, the spokesman said. When leaving flooded areas, passengers should use the handrails near the exits for support and move slowly, he added. More guidance around flooding and public transit can be found here.

Many cars can be swept away in just one or two feet of flooding.

“The guidance is simple: Turn around, don’t drown,” said Aries Dela Cruz, a spokesman for the city’s Office of Emergency Management. “You cannot reliably tell how deep the water is, how fast it is moving or whether the road beneath it has been damaged or washed away.”

The floodwaters could also be covering dangerous debris, electrical hazards or other risks, he added.

If you do find yourself stuck, roll down your window, get out of the car immediately and move to higher ground — perhaps onto the car’s roof — and call 911. Step-by-step instructions for how to escape a car in floodwaters can be found here.

“If you live near water, in a low-lying area or near city storm drains, you are on the front lines of flooding,” said Dominic Ramunni, a meteorologist with the National Weather Service. New Yorkers can learn more about their flood risks by plugging their locations into the city’s storm water map.

In New York City, basement and ground-level apartments are especially at risk. When signing up for NotifyNYC, residents can select a special basement apartment alert option to receive additional guidance for extreme rainfall.

Water flows downhill, so if you are in an area that dips, is at the bottom of the hill or along the coast, chances are that you will experience flooding. And since New York City is covered in asphalt, it lacks the porousness of natural areas with soil, which can ease drainage. This means that flooding can crop up anywhere when infrastructure becomes overwhelmed or storm drains become clogged.

The nonprofit Rebuild by Design offers an interactive flood map based on 311 data it has collected. The map invites New Yorkers to share their flooding stories, including video. Visitors to the site can click around to find out which neighborhoods have been hardest hit by which kind of flooding, such as clogged storm drains or basement water.

Knowing and understanding the geography of where you live and work is helpful. The website Welikia. org shows what the city used to look like before it was developed, including where marshes and streams once sat. If you live atop a paved-over wetland, swamp or body of water, it could be prone to flooding.

Many neighborhoods have community groups, some on Facebook, that monitor and organize around extreme weather. Sign up and get involved.

Install a flood sensor in your basement. You can get one for free every spring and summer, when the city’s Department of Environmental Protection holds flood preparation town halls in low-lying neighborhoods. After the sessions, officials distribute the free sensors, as well as free pumps and inflatable flood barriers.

In the hours leading up to a storm, residents should try to clear storm drains of trash and vegetation. Though the city cleans storm drains, debris can accumulate fast, and there is only so much territory that workers can cover at the last minute. New York City Emergency Management offers a guide for flood preparation here.

Finally, if you live in a low-lying area and the forecast looks particularly dangerous, arrange to stay with friends or family members, or at a shelter or hotel on higher ground. Develop a plan, including a go bag, so you can leave your home quickly. NotifyNYC and city leadership will often announce which shelters are open during dangerous weather events.

Max Bearak contributed reporting.

The president said the deal was not “acceptable” and demurred on whether he would restart military strikes after the midterm elections.

By Zolan Kanno-Youngs

Reporting from Washington

President Trump said on Saturday that he turned down Iran’s latest cease-fire proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz and restart talks on the country’s nuclear program in exchange for U. S. concessions.

“They made a proposal, but I rejected it,” Mr. Trump told reporters as he left the White House on Saturday morning.

Mr. Trump demurred when asked if he expected to restart military strikes after the November midterm elections, saying Iran wanted “to make a deal where they open the strait immediately because they’re losing so badly.”

Mr. Trump’s rebuff was the latest turn in what has been a cycle of bombings, peace proposals, grandiose threats and conflicting messages throughout the nearly seven-month U. S.-Israeli war against Iran. Mr. Trump’s public rejection of Iran’s offer came after his aides held a three-hour meeting with Iranian officials at the United Nations General Assembly earlier this week in New York.

In his speech at the United Nations, Mr. Trump issued an ultimatum to Iran, saying its leaders could strike a deal with the United States or risk annihilation.

“Will a deal be made with Iran that lets them rebuild and create a far greater country than it ever was before — maybe one of the greatest in the Middle East or even the world?” Mr. Trump asked in speech on Tuesday. “Or do I annihilate the Islamic Republic and do it quickly, never giving them a chance to kill and destroy people and countries again?”

Mr. Trump also suggested Iran was dragging the war out to the midterm elections in the hopes of politically damaging Mr. Trump and Republicans. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz, a key shipping route for oil and gas, has surged energy prices across the globe.

Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, told reporters on Thursday that the seven-point proposal that Mr. Trump rejected closely mirrored the commitments laid out in a so-called memorandum of understanding that was struck between the United States and Iran in June but quickly unraveled.

Mr. Araghchi added “it would be better” if a deal were reached before the U. S. midterm elections.

He said that the proposed agreement would end fighting for seven days, including in Lebanon, and require the United States to release Iranian frozen assets estimated to be at least $12 billion, waive sanctions on Iranian oil and lift the naval blockade on Iran. Then, on the last day, the Strait of Hormuz would be opened.

After the seven days, negotiations over Iran’s nuclear program would restart.

Mr. Trump on Saturday said he was still open to negotiating with Iran.

“They want to make a deal, and I think that’s fine, I like making a deal too,” Mr. Trump said. “But that deal would not be acceptable.”

Zolan Kanno-Youngs is a White House correspondent for The Times, covering President Trump and his administration.

Connections: Sports Edition

Connections: Soccer Edition

Connections Coach

The longtime Democratic insider has emerged as a behind-the-scenes force in his party’s push to win back Congress. After that, he’ll think about the next presidential race.

Rahm Emanuel, the former Chicago mayor and chief of staff to President Barack Obama, has been recruiting Democratic House candidates and helping to guide their campaigns. Credit... Lexi Parra/The New York Times

Supported by

By Shane Goldmacher

Shane Goldmacher is a national political correspondent.

At a private dinner of branzino and salad at Centrolina in Washington this month, Rahm Emanuel offered a dozen of the top Democratic recruits for the U. S. House some guidance for the final fall sprint.

The role was familiar for him. Twenty years ago, Mr. Emanuel led House Democrats’ campaign arm when the party made big gains in red corners of the country.

Now he ticked through how the current environment was “eerily similar” to 2006.

“Unpopular war: check, check,” Mr. Emanuel recounted in a later interview. “Unpopular president: check, check. Massive corruption throughout the system: check, check. Spiking energy prices: check, check.”

As Mr. Emanuel, the longtime Democratic insider, not so quietly explores a run for president in 2028, he has emerged as a behind-the-scenes force in his party’s push to flip the House this fall.

He has made calls to recruit candidates, traveled for events in swing districts, offered private guidance to candidates on campaign ads, events and messaging. He has rolled out alliterative slogans — “greed, grievance and grandeur” is his latest about President Trump — and policy proposals alike. And he speaks regularly with Representative Hakeem Jeffries of New York, the minority leader, serving as an informal sounding board for the potential next speaker.

“We’re in frequent communication at least every other week,” Mr. Jeffries said in an interview, noting that Mr. Emanuel sometimes provided readouts of how candidates were performing on the trail. “Rahm’s perspective is always thoughtful, frank, insightful and helpful.”

Mr. Emanuel, 66, has as long and varied a résumé as any Democrat. He served in the Clinton White House in the 1990s, as a key congressional lieutenant for Speaker Nancy Pelosi in the 2000s, as the first White House chief of staff for President Barack Obama and later as Chicago mayor.

On Tuesday, Mr. Emanuel is set to host a fund-raiser in Chicago for five women in the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee’s “Red to Blue” program. He said he hoped to raise $60,000 to $75,000 for each of them this election cycle.

But while Mr. Emanuel has campaigned for multiple House candidates in swing seats, few seemed eager to get on the phone to discuss his exact role.

Denise Powell, a Democrat trying to flip a House seat in Nebraska, said in a statement that she appreciated Mr. Emanuel’s visit with her on a picket line. “Having the support of experienced Democratic leaders like Rahm — people who know how to win tough fights — has been invaluable,” she said.

Some progressives cast doubt on any insights from a Democrat who is the opposite of a fresh face and who works for a Wall Street firm.

“He’s like the political equivalent of Windows 95 — an operating system without an application in the modern era,” said Maurice Mitchell, the national director of the Working Families Party, a progressive group. “I don’t know what counsel he has to offer people who are running in competitive elections in 2026.”

For his part, Mr. Emanuel said he had a history of winning. And while he did not shy away from the fact that fresh alliances he is forging in these House races could help him if he does, in fact, run for president in 2028, he was also clear that his efforts were not driven by higher ambitions.

“When I got up in Western Michigan to fly out to Summit, N. J., at 4:30 in the morning — that ain’t what it is,” he said of appearing with battleground House candidates like Sean McCann in Michigan and Rebecca Bennett in New Jersey. “I’m not saying it’s zero. But it is not a hundred percent. It’s not even 50 percent.”

When Mr. Emanuel returned from a stint as ambassador to Japan under President Joseph R. Biden Jr. in early 2025, he reached out to Mr. Jeffries and offered to help recapture the House in any way possible.

“It’s very simple,” Mr. Emanuel said. “We win the House and it’s the first day of the end of the Trump presidency, and it is the most important thing to do.”

Right now, he projected that Democrats would pick up a “low end” of 10 to 12 seats this fall, and on the “high end, 15 to 17.”

“Independents are breaking our way,” he said. “There’s a low turnout among Republicans. That is a chemistry for a wave. That’s the law of physics. That is what determined ’94. That is what determined ’06. That is what determined ’08. That is what determined 2010. That is what determined 2018.”

He is tapping an unrivaled Rolodex to ensure Democrats maximize their chances, estimating that he texts and talks with, on average, around 70 people a day. “It can go three figures,” he said.

The interactions often put a premium on efficiency.

“Talking to Rahm, it’s like middle-age married sex,” said John Anzalone, a Democratic pollster who has known him for decades. “It’s focused. You know what you’re going for. And it’s short.”

At times, speaking with Mr. Emanuel can feel like watching a comedian workshop his material, making sure the lines land just right.

“He gets an arch — and you can’t afford a meal at the Golden Arch.”

“He gets a $450 million plane — you get $4.50 of gas.”

Then Mr. Emanuel explains why he phrased it exactly that way.

“You’ve got to drive the corruption and the greed into people’s own wallet,” he said of how Democrats should frame the Trump agenda. “It’s not just that he’s getting rich. You’re getting poor.”

Other potential 2028 candidates would begin the race with clearer constituencies. He hasn’t won an election since before Mr. Trump’s first term — and it was for municipal office. Still, few can match the sheer number of Mr. Emanuel’s reps in the political game.

The first of his nearly 4,000 appearances in the pages of The New York Times came way back in 1987, when he made a cameo in an article as a young strategist for House Democrats’ campaign arm. He was advising political action committees on where to send their money.

“Yes, people could graduate, I suppose,” he said of his enduring passion for working on House races. He added: “Maybe this is my postdoctoral work. Maybe I did my B. A. and I’m working on my postdoctorate?”

So what part of politics does he like the most?

“I like it all,” Mr. Emanuel said, before stopping himself. “I mean, I don’t want to say that.”

But he just did?

“No,” Mr. Emanuel corrected. “I cut myself off.”

Mr. Emanuel’s disdain for his party’s left flank is palpable. Democratic socialists, he said, don’t even belong in the party until they reverse their positions on key issues.

“Some people want to do oligarchy tours,” he said, nodding to the rallies held last year by Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez of New York. “I want to do majority tours. That’s what I’m doing with my time.”

For months, Mr. Emanuel has been unveiling plans — either for his party to take up or, maybe, for him to promote during a presidential run.

Some aim to tap into the same populist anger the left has sought to harness, minus the progressivism. He called last year for the United States to ban social media for those under 16. And in Texas this past week, he released a five-point plan to counter corruption in Washington (the proposals included no stock trading, no prediction-market trading, and mandatory retirement at 75).

Mr. Emanuel has also rolled out a series of education proposals, including on early childhood reading and higher education, hoping Democrats can reclaim their traditional edge on the issue.

He has honed catchphrases, too.

In May 2025, he wrote that Democrats could win against Mr. Trump by focusing on “three C’s: corruption, chaos and cruelty.” A few weeks earlier, Mr. Jeffries had used similar wording — “chaos, cruelty and corruption” — at a news conference about the administration’s first 100 days.

“Let’s just say there was creative tension,” Mr. Emanuel said. “I used it on CNN once, but I’ll let — it’s his, he’s a leader.”

Both men have since moved on. Mr. Emanuel now has his “greed, grievance and grandeur” line. For his part, Mr. Jeffries said, “The phrase that we’ve been using from the beginning has been cost, care and combating corruption.”

Mr. Emanuel, when told by a reporter that he seemed to be constantly tinkering with his message, replied, “Who doesn’t?”

But few do it this much.

“Well, OK, I have a degenerate — I’m on the spectrum, OK?” he said. “I’m self-aware. I am on the spectrum!”

And with that he was off to his next appointment.

Shane Goldmacher is a Times national political correspondent.

With Storms on 2 Sides of the U. S., El Niño Shows Its Might

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Hurricane Season

Advertisement

Supported by

Hurricanes near Hawaii. A nor’easter on the East Coast. The ocean phenomenon’s influence on storms around the country may just be getting started.

By Raymond Zhong

The powerhouse El Niño in the Pacific Ocean is making itself felt on two sides of the nation for the first, but probably not last, time this year.

The nor’easter lashing the East Coast this weekend followed a path that can become more common for storms during El Niño, the climate phenomenon that originates in the tropical Pacific and goes on to influence rainfall, temperature and storms around the globe.

A continent away, Hurricane Nolo, which is threatening to soak the Big Island of Hawaii with rain, is being fueled by El Niño-warmed waters in the Pacific. Since August, a parade of hurricanes has battered Hawaii with an intensity that has caught even scientists off guard.

“I lived in Hawaii for 24 years and this is the craziest summer, the craziest fall, I’ve ever seen,” said Mark Merrifield, an ocean scientist and former director of the University of Hawaii Sea Level Center.

El Niño is part of a natural cycle in the Pacific Ocean that recurs every few years and brings a cascade of weather effects across the planet. Its strength typically peaks late in the calendar year. By some metrics, this one is already the strongest on record, an indication of how significantly it is likely to upend many regions’ normal weather patterns in the coming months.

People around the world are already dealing with the consequences. Indonesia is living under a haze of toxic smoke from wildfires worsened by drought. Crops have withered under dry conditions in India, Central America and parts of eastern Africa. Sea levels are rising on the coast of California, giving a leg up for storms and waves to flood homes and erode beaches.

And Hawaii is confronting an extraordinary spate of hurricanes, which are drawing strength from the thick layer of warm water that El Niño produces at the surface of the central and eastern Pacific.

Besides providing more energy for Pacific hurricanes, El Niño also creates conditions in the atmosphere that help them stick around and intensify, said Kim Wood, an associate professor in the department of hydrology and atmospheric sciences at the University of Arizona.

Hawaii has been threatened by such storms before, but never in rapid succession like this year. “It is quite unusual to get that kind of back-to-back-to-back experience,” Dr. Wood said. “And with how mountainous those islands are, the rain threat is just that much worse.”

When moist air hits mountains, it is forced upward, causing it to cool and release precipitation.

Before this year, only six hurricanes over the past seven decades had been recorded as passing within 50 miles of the state, according to Michael Lowry, a hurricane expert for WPLG-TV in Miami. Hurricane Nolo could become the third one to do so this year.

Scientists are working to understand whether human-caused global warming might be leading to more frequent, strong El Niños. They haven’t reached a clear consensus, though one thing is certain: The gyrations that El Niño brings are coming on top of an ocean and atmosphere already warmed by greenhouse gas emissions. That means the effects of an El Niño — whether downpours, wildfires or droughts — can potentially be more severe than they would have been in an earlier, cooler time for the planet.

El Niño’s influence on storms around the United States this year might just be getting started. Come winter, it is likely to help deliver more drenching rain to California. During some past El Niños, the perennially water-stressed state has received one and a half times its usual amount of precipitation, often through winter storms that recharge groundwater but can also cause flooding.

For the Northeast, El Niño doesn’t directly feed storms like the one pounding the coast this weekend, though nor’easters appear to be more frequent in El Niño years. One possible reason? El Niño causes the Pacific jet stream, or the band of air moving west to east at high altitudes, to shift south. That provides a supply of energy and moisture for storms that can take shape off the Southeastern United States then swing north.

The saving grace for eastern states is that El Niño generally leads to quiet Atlantic hurricane seasons. The shift in atmospheric patterns over the Pacific also increases upper-level winds over the Atlantic, making it harder for storms to spin up into hurricanes there.

So far this year, not a single storm in the Atlantic has managed to become a hurricane.

Raymond Zhong reports on climate and environmental issues for The Times.
