It’s Time for the W. N. B. A. to Pick Sides

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Guest Essay

By Roxane Gay

Ms. Gay, a contributing Opinion writer, is an author.

The W. N. B. A. is having a moment.

As the league celebrates its 30th anniversary, the audience is growing exponentially, and the number of teams is expanding. After years of fighting tirelessly for fair wages and a successful strike authorization vote, the players’ union earned a collective bargaining agreement; for the first time, star players in the league have secured million-dollar contracts; the league minimum salary is now $270,000; and there are higher salary caps for teams.

For anyone watching the W. N. B. A. blossom over the past three decades, this has all been a long time coming, hard-earned and richly deserved. But alongside the growth and increased public attention, the league is also facing a pair of crises, not necessarily of its own making: how to welcome trans women, if and when it becomes necessary, and a rise in racism directed toward Black players. How the league and the players navigate that will determine its future, one made possible by a loyal fan base that is largely composed of the very people most vulnerable to those ideological attacks.

As L. A. Sparks courtside ticket holders, my wife and I take in as many games as we can each season. The W. N. B. A. athletes are fascinating both on and off the court. Unlike their male counterparts, many players are openly gay or bisexual. Some have dated one another and broken up, and their romantic dramas play out off the court but in the public eye. This year’s All-Star Weekend was particularly spicy. All of it only endears the W. N. B. A. to me more.

The players are generally progressive and willing to voice what they stand for. That is especially noteworthy because professional athletes, like musicians, actors and other celebrities, are often told to “stay in their lane,” to not be political.

Over the years, W. N. B. A. players have expressed support for Black Lives Matter, eradicating gun violence, gender equity, reproductive freedom and L. G. B. T. Q. rights. In an interview with Harper’s Bazaar, the veteran player Nneka Ogwumike, a fierce champion for her fellow players and for social justice throughout her 15-season career, said, “Our league is made up of the people that require more rights in this world and our society.” Most players are keenly aware that they cannot just parcel out pieces of themselves in service of their professional lives.

The league, however, does not exist in a bubble. The former N. B. A. players Enes Kanter Freedom and Royce White, in a bid to be provocative, declared in August for the 2027 W. N. B. A. draft. In doing so, they stated that they were going to identify as trans women so they could be eligible to play. Freedom has continued this farce, appearing on conservative media, desperately seeking the attention he was unable to garner in the N. B. A.

Freedom has mostly pushed the league to provide a definition of “woman,” a tired conservative talking point, presumably because he and White think they are cleverly revealing some flaw in inclusive logic. The W. N. B. A. has indicated that neither Freedom nor White is eligible, but the question of how to craft a fair and reasonable policy for trans women remains.

The Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham was vocal earlier this year about her beliefs that trans women shouldn’t play in the W. N. B. A. “I want to protect young girls in a locker room, or young girls in sport who shouldn’t have to go against biological men,” Cunningham said in an ESPN interview. Her claims exploit one of the most popular attacks against trans women — the idea that women and girls are not safe around trans women.

Cunningham supporters have staged small anti-trans protests at Indiana Fever games in several cities, presumably in solidarity with her and to keep the issue in the news. The White House press secretary at the time, Karoline Leavitt, even weighed in on Cunningham’s statement, amplifying the ambient transphobia now encircling the league.

Every once in a while, the outgoing league commissioner, Cathy Engelbert, has made a tepid statement about intolerance, but the league she leads, as an organization, seems to address politically charged issues without the vigor or moral courage of many individual players. Thus far, there has been only one openly trans W. N. B. A. player — the talented Layshia Clarendon, who retired after playing for 12 seasons, and also identifies as nonbinary. Thus far the controversy has been entirely manufactured by people with no real connection to the trans community.

Pressures on the league can also rise from within. In 2024, two stars joined the W. N. B. A.: Angel Reese, playing for the Chicago Sky, and Caitlin Clark, for the Indiana Fever. Reese and Clark, a Black woman and a white woman, have been pitted against each other as rivals on and off the court since their college days. Since they’ve become professional athletes, their style of play, penchant for fouling one another and professional rivalry have been used to amplify some of the stark cultural divides that have shaped American life for the past decade or more.

Clark, who was popular as an N. C. A. A. player with the University of Iowa, has brought a legion of new fans to the game. But even two years in, many of them seem willfully unfamiliar with who makes up the W. N. B. A. About two-thirds of W. N. B. A. players are Black, and many of the women are queer. Some of Clark’s fans seem to want to change, through the sheer force of their will, this reality by making Clark the only face of the league. These fans give the impression that they are more attached to Clark’s whiteness than her talent.

When Clark doesn’t receive an accolade that her fans think she deserves, like a spot on the 2024 U. S. women’s Olympic team, there is an immediate outcry as if she were the only talented player. Some of her fan base has taken to harassing on-court rivals online after referee calls that don’t favor Clark. It all draws from an unholy miasma of racism, homophobia and, of course, selective misogyny.

Clark’s contributions to the W. N. B. A. are undeniable, even as her on-court efforts — like defense — have been uneven. She has an excellent three-point shot. She also has a real temper when things don’t go her way. Like soccer players, she flops dramatically when other players make contact with her. But most people are willing to overlook all this because she has brought unprecedented attention to the game. Unfortunately, much of that attention is neither good nor welcome.

In July, 11 Republican lawmakers, led by Representative August Pfluger of Texas, sent a letter to Ms. Engelbert demanding the league account for fouls against Clark and warning that they would support a Department of Justice investigation if the league’s response revealed discrimination. It was ludicrous, but it was also a perfect example of how unhinged and far-reaching efforts to protect her have become. To Clark’s credit, before the lawmakers’ letter was sent, she disavowed a lot of this nonsense. “Harassment, hate, none of that is OK,” she said after a particularly tense game against the Phoenix Mercury.

Despite the excellent basketball being played in the W. N. B. A., it often seems like the loudest conversations are about everything but basketball. It is a profound disservice to the players, coaches and professionals running the league. Given this country’s political fractures, there should be no ambiguity or compromise when it comes to what is right for the players, the fans or the country. This is not the time to move toward the imaginary middle or political neutrality.

The W. N. B. A., as a league, should lead the charge for making space for trans women in women’s sports. They should do more to honor the identities of the players and protect them from bad-faith attacks, death threats, harassment and other racial animus that players like Reese, Alyssa Thomas, Dearica Hamby and Chelsea Gray have been subjected to.

Surely, a league made up of such smart, dedicated players, coaches, general managers and executives can come up with a way forward that is fair to everyone involved. But not enough of the current conversation is focused on progress, compromise or actionable solutions. Instead, politicians, cranks and conservative pundits are trying to remake a diverse professional league into something small, empty and exclusionary.

Their ambitions are not inevitable, though. The W. N. B. A. has an invaluable opportunity right now; the league can be a reflection of the world as it could be, not merely as it is.

While there is definitely a nuanced conversation to be had about trans athletes, conservative attacks on trans girls and women provide cover for attacks on ALL girls and women. The Trojan horse of “protecting girls and women” is being used to narrowly define acceptable roles, presentation, and behavior for girls and women and push us out of the public square and rob us of opportunities for self determination. Whenever conservatives says they want to “protect” girls and women”, they really mean “confine, control, and police.”

Great article, and long needed, thank you. I’m a long-time WNBA fan who started out loving one team (Go Storm!) and now enjoy watching every team and every player - and am so looking forward to the playoffs in spite of my beloved team not being part of it. We also are women’s college basketball fans and love seeing the talent emerge. It’s been frustrating to see media focus on just a few players, when there is so much incredible talent across the league. I have faith (and hope) that the league will continue to grow, thrive, and be a strong voice for social justice.

I'm a big fan of the WNBA. I watch most of their games. While you offer fair points in your analysis of the league's current atmosphere, you don't mention the most important imperative that all of these WNBA players share: their fierce competitiveness on the court . They want to win, and win fairly. They don't seek out or enjoy the other distractions (created by the media and fans) that take away or diminish their great athletic abilities. May the WNBA continue to grow, and I for one will continue to enjoy watching.

Roxane Gay is a writer in residence at Harvard Medical School and an author.

Antiwar Veterans Group Spends Millions to Elect Democrats, Shaping Midterms

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

The organization, founded in 2006 to back Democratic veterans opposing the Iraq war, is pouring huge sums into this year’s elections amid intense voter antipathy for another conflict in the Middle East.

By Annie Karni

Reporting from Washington

The Democratic primary for Iowa’s open Senate seat presented exactly the kind of scenario that Jon Soltz, the co-founder of VoteVets, is always searching for: one where his organization could play an outsize role in shaping a race.

Two little-known Democrats were vying for the nomination, in a contest where no outside group was spending. So Mr. Soltz poured money into the campaign of Josh Turek, a state legislator and a former Paralympic gold medalist, who did not serve but was born with spina bifida after his father was exposed to Agent Orange in Vietnam.

The first infusion of cash from VoteVets — $825,000 in March — was more than Mr. Turek’s opponent, Zach Wahls, had on hand at the end of 2025. (VoteVets entered the race only after Nathan Sage, a veteran of the Iraq war, dropped out of the primary.)

And VoteVets kept spending, totaling an eye-popping $9.7 million on digital and television advertising, as well as direct mail, in a race that Mr. Turek won and is now viewed as within reach for Democrats.

The group is shoveling an additional $4.5 million into ads hitting his Republican rival, Representative Ashley Hinson, for her support of the war with Iran. (Ms. Hinson this week called for an “immediate end” to the war after voting a half-dozen times against directing President Trump to halt it.)

It is the starkest example of the extensive role the organization, formed in 2006 to support Democratic veterans running in opposition to the war in Iraq, is playing in shaping this year’s midterm elections as a different conflict in the Middle East has again soured voters on the party in power.

“Iowa is in play because we helped put it in play,” Mr. Soltz said in a wide-ranging interview this month. “If Democrats take back the Senate, it could be because of Iowa, and if that happens, then I can sit here and say this is the most successful cycle VoteVets has ever had.”

Overall, VoteVets plans this year to spend $60 million on 331 Democratic candidates nationwide — 20 House and Senate candidates and 311 down-ballot races — the most since it was founded. That makes it one of the most substantial single-issue advocacy groups operating in the midterm cycle, and one of the main groups spending the most to support Democratic candidates.

The only other such organization that comes close is the United Democracy Project, the super PAC associated with the American Israel Public Affairs Committee that has spent about $54 million so far this cycle and is likely to spend much more.

VoteVets operates independently, but its interests often align with those of the Democratic congressional leaders. It also coordinates with other outside groups on endorsements and then bundles money under its own umbrella. While the majority of the group’s money comes from individual donors, a substantial portion comes from big labor unions and corporate PACs, including those associated with Honeywell, General Motors, General Dynamics and Elevance Health.

“I call candidates all the time, and they can send me donors,” Mr. Soltz said. “Perhaps another organization cares about a race, but we’re the better brand.”

Over the years, the group has expanded its mission beyond supporting veterans to elevating candidates with national security backgrounds as well as people like Mr. Turek, whose lives have been shaped by a family member’s service and who understand a different facet of the human cost of war.

Mr. Soltz, who served in multiple tours in the Iraq war and other deployments overseas, is currently out to elect a new slate of Democratic veterans, including many women, at a time when opposition to the war in Iran is dragging down Mr. Trump’s approval ratings and bringing Republicans with him.

It is happening as democratic socialist candidates have received outsize attention for defeating establishment contenders in primaries across the country.

But VoteVets’ millions could be a more decisive factor in some of the critical races in which Democrats are looking to unseat Republicans to win control of the House.

In upstate New York, the group has spent $1 million on behalf of Cait Conley, who served in combat in Iraq and Afghanistan, in her race to unseat Representative Mike Lawler, a major infusion of cash for a House race. In Arizona, the group has money on hold to put behind Jo Mendoza, a former Marine drill sergeant running against Representative Juan Ciscomani. In New Jersey, the group is spending $1.2 million for Rebecca Bennett, a Navy veteran looking to unseat Representative Thomas H. Kean Jr. And in Virginia, the group is planning to spend to back Elaine Luria, a Navy veteran, against Representative Jen Kiggans.

VoteVets also played a significant role in financially boosting Luke Bronin, the former Navy intelligence officer who defeated Representative John B. Larson, the 78-year-old Democrat who was seeking a 15th term in his solidly blue district.

“We have no issue with Larson,” Mr. Soltz said. “It’s about the fact that we can get a veteran into Congress for the next 30 years, to be the chairman of the House Veterans Committee or Foreign Affairs. That’s our interest. If you only work in flippable seats, then when the wave comes in, you will lose.”

Special interest groups have long played a prominent role in elections, but some ethics experts said that an organization as powerful as VoteVets could potentially eclipse the candidates themselves.

“It’s a broader trend where outside groups are coming to just dominate the most competitive races and increasingly competitive primaries,” said Daniel Weiner, the senior director of the Brennan Center’s Elections and Government Program. “That is risky when they start to drown out candidates.”

Still, Mr. Weiner said that VoteVets was the exception in an arena increasingly dominated by outside groups that seek to hide how they are influencing elections, because it runs ads on the issue it actually stands for and has a clear agenda that voters understand.

“That is increasingly not the norm,” Mr. Weiner said. “The norm is more shadowy groups where voters don’t know what it stands for or who is behind them.”

Andrew Mayersohn, a researcher for the watchdog group OpenSecrets, said that he classifies VoteVets as “partially disclosing” its donors, meaning that more than 5 percent of its money comes from dark sources that are not disclosed. That is because it has its own nonprofit set up under the 501(c)(4) section of the tax code whose donors are not required to be publicly disclosed.

The group has had some setbacks this cycle. It heavily backed Maura Sullivan, a Marine veteran, in a New Hampshire primary she lost to Stefany Shaheen, the daughter of Senator Jeanne Shaheen, a political powerhouse in her state. And in one of Michigan’s most competitive districts, VoteVets backed Matt Maasdam, a former member of the Navy SEALs, in a heated primary he lost to William Lawrence, a progressive activist and co-founder of the Sunrise Movement.

When VoteVets was founded 20 years ago, it was still uncommon for Democrats to attack Republicans on military issues, which had long been seen as one of the G. O. P.’s strongest suits.

The organization burst onto the political scene with a searing ad that showed a mannequin dressed in the body armor given to soldiers in Iraq getting shredded by bullets, and targeted Republicans who voted against a Democratic proposal to provide $1 billion to outfit U. S. troops with more modern equipment.

Representative Pat Ryan, a New York Democrat who completed two tours in Iraq, credits VoteVets with providing the financial and political support for him to win a 2022 special election that many in his party thought was out of reach.

“This linking of military service and fighting for core American freedoms as a thing that the Democratic Party should absolutely, unabashedly own and dominate on is a huge value-add to the party,” Mr. Ryan said in an interview.

“In 2003, I desperately wish there had been leaders who could say, ‘I fought for the country; this is going to make us less safe, less prosperous’ — and to do it right out of the gate,” he said. “I’m super proud that we as vets, with VoteVets driving that, stood from Day Zero of this war in Iran and said, ‘This is bad.’”

Senator Tammy Duckworth, the Illinois Democrat and former helicopter pilot who lost both of her legs in the Iraq war when her aircraft was hit with a rocket-propelled grenade, was the first candidate VoteVets ever backed, in her first race in 2006, which she lost. She now refers to herself as “Candidate Zero” for the organization.

Ms. Duckworth said the organization has been key to her political success ever since. When opponents have tried to brand her as overly sympathetic to Syrian refugees posing a national security risk, or have raised questions about the circumstances of her injuries in the Iraq war, VoteVets has been there to defend her.

“You’re weak when you have to defend yourself,” Ms. Duckworth said in an interview. “They come in with a very strong message that just penetrates in a way that no one else knows how to do.”

Mr. Soltz is already eyeing how he can shape the 2028 field. He said he speaks regularly with Senators Mark Kelly and Ruben Gallego of Arizona and Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, as well as former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — all of them veterans or people with national security backgrounds. He is not ready to pick a favorite just yet.

“The only thing that could overtake this year,” he said, “is if we help elect a Democratic veteran president.”

Annie Karni is a congressional correspondent for The Times.

‘Zombified’ C. D. C., Hobbled by Cuts, Struggles to Fulfill Scientific Mission

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Trump Administration

Advertisement

Supported by

The agency has lost its independence and nearly a third of its staff, as Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and associates have tightened control.

By Apoorva Mandavilli

For decades, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention was the undisputed global leader in public health. Its scientists helped train health officials worldwide. In the United States, it was the primary source of guidance for prevention and treatment of diseases, including diabetes, H. I. V. and the seasonal flu.

But after a year and a half in the cross hairs of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr.’s drive to remake public health policy, the agency is a skeleton of the powerhouse it was.

The Trump administration’s widespread layoffs in early 2025 cut 18 percent of the C. D. C.’s staff. But new personnel data, compiled by a group of former federal scientists and reported here for the first time, indicate that the agency’s staff has dwindled far more, as large numbers of employees retired or resigned. As of May 2026, the C. D. C. had 30 percent fewer employees than it did before the layoffs, the data show.

Interviews with more than 30 current and former employees reveal the agency is now tightly controlled by Mr. Kennedy and his associates, and its scientists are finding it increasingly difficult to do their jobs effectively. (Some of them spoke on the condition of anonymity because of a fear of retaliation from the administration.)

Note: Data obtained by The New York Times from a group of former federal scientists.

Arfa Momin/The New York Times

The changes have hindered the C. D. C.’s ability to respond to outbreaks as measles spreads at home and Ebola abroad, and to issue timely guidance on vaccinations as cooling temperatures kick off the respiratory season, according to current and former employees. State and local health departments, which rely on the C. D. C. for resources and technical advice, have been stymied by delays. Entire divisions have been shuttered, including teams that worked on smoking, sexual violence, child abuse and falls among older adults.

Even some areas central to the Trump administration’s priorities have been gutted. Despite Mr. Kennedy’s focus on chronic diseases and autism, the C. D. C. centers that aim to prevent chronic diseases and birth defects are at half their previous size, according to the new data, compiled by the Public Data Observatory from the Office of Personnel Management, the Department of Health and Human Services, and the employee union.

The layoffs spared the agency’s infectious disease centers. But even so, the center for emerging and zoonotic diseases, which manages Ebola and hantavirus, among others, now has nearly 300 fewer employees than in March 2025, and the respiratory disease center has lost nearly 200 — about 17 percent in each case.

Beyond staff reductions, there is a leadership vacuum. Only one of the 11 center directors from March 2025 remains at the agency. Most of the other centers are being run by acting directors, some of whom were elevated from jobs one or two levels below.

“It’s a zombified C. D. C. where you have all the bits and pieces — like the body’s there, the substance is there, but it’s not acting like how an agency like that should act,” said Dr. Demetre Daskalakis, who led the respiratory disease center before he resigned in August 2025.

Despite a series of high-profile disease outbreaks, C. D. C. workers have had little contact with the World Health Organization, with members of Congress and even, for a time, with their partners in state and local health departments, some employees said. Statements to the media about health crises are also tightly controlled by H. H. S.

Even basic functions have broken down. Travel approvals take months; upkeep of bathrooms and vacuuming of offices have been disrupted, some current employees said.

One senior official said it felt as though the agency was being held together with bubble gum and duct tape, with employees running from crisis to crisis, and nothing working the way it is supposed to.

The Department of Health and Human Services did not respond to a series of questions about the C. D. C.’s work, staffing and independence. “C. D. C. continues to protect the health and safety of the American people and communicate clearly about the importance of vaccination,” the department said in an emailed statement.

But several former officials disagreed with that assessment, noting that the C. D. C. has offered little leadership or clear communication even as, in just a few months, the nation has grappled with record cases of measles, cyclosporiasis and rabies.

“Imagine losing a third of a city’s firefighters and then wondering why downtown is burning,” said Dr. Jonathan Mermin, who led the agency’s center for H. I. V. and sexually transmitted infections till April 2025, and is now the dean of the Columbia University Mailman School of Public Health.

From the very first day of Mr. Trump’s second term, when he withdrew the country from the W. H. O., his administration has sought to upend the nation’s health policies and align them with his political priorities.

In past administrations, just two or three political appointees had purview over the C. D. C. Now, there are nearly 20 political appointees from H. H. S. who communicate with C. D. C. staff members, sometimes directing them to spend time and funding on dubious theories outside the agency’s scope, according to several officials.

Last year, an H. H. S. official directed the C. D. C. to award a no-bid contract — a rarity for the agency — to Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute to explore whether immunizing pregnant women would lead to autism in their children, a theory that Mr. Kennedy has espoused but that has been debunked by numerous studies. To pay for the research, the C. D. C. took $362,000 from a program that provides free vaccines to about half of American children.

In an email viewed by The New York Times, Stuart Burns, a political appointee, asked C. D. C. employees to pull together details of every measles case since 2010, including patients’ underlying medical conditions with diagnostic codes; that information is not collected routinely, they told him. Mr. Kennedy has falsely argued that measles only causes death in children who are already ill with other conditions.

Dr. William “Reyn” Archer III, another appointee who previously oversaw the C. D. C., repeatedly asked agency employees to work on screwworm, a disease that mostly affects cattle, even though the C. D. C.’s mission is to protect human health, said Dr. Daniel Jernigan, who headed the agency’s emerging disease center before resigning in August 2025. Dr. Archer did not respond to a request for comment.

Mr. Kennedy’s associates outside the administration have also been allowed direct access to senior C. D. C. staff members. Dr. Ben Edwards, a physician in Lubbock, Texas, who treated children while he was infected with measles and whom Mr. Kennedy had praised as an “extraordinary” healer, asked senior C. D. C. officials to look into cod liver oil as a treatment for measles, citing “historical references dating back to the 1700s,” in an email viewed by The Times.

“We just would have to run around constantly to be responsive to all of these strange asks,” recalled Dr. Daskalakis, the former head of the respiratory disease center.

Numerous other instances of political interference in the C. D. C.’s activities have already been reported. Most notably, Mr. Kennedy openly overruled the C. D. C.’s scientists in imposing strict quarantine measures for people exposed to hantavirus. Dr. Jay Bhattacharya, who led the agency for six months in the absence of a Senate-confirmed director, squashed publication of a study on the effectiveness of Covid vaccines.

Some observers had hoped the C. D. C.’s new director, Dr. Erica Schwartz, a physician who has pledged to “follow the science,” would provide a bulwark against political interference. But one month into the job, she has made no public statements about the importance of childhood vaccines or corrected misinformation from her boss, Mr. Kennedy. In one of her first big decisions, she ordered agency employees to challenge Pennsylvania’s announcement of two measles deaths, shunning standard procedure.

In its statement, H. H. S. said, “Dr. Schwartz and C. D. C.’s new leadership are evaluating the agency’s structure and operations to ensure C. D. C. can effectively advance the priorities of President Trump and Secretary Kennedy and fulfill its core public health mission.”

Across the C. D. C., the employees who remain are backfilling roles left vacant.

“I’ve never seen such a plethora of acting roles in my life,” the agency’s new chief operating officer, Sean Slovenski, acknowledged to staff members at a meeting in June, a recording of which was obtained by The Times.

Many divisions are struggling to disburse money appropriated by Congress. In an email in May viewed by The Times, an official asked for volunteers from other offices to help the Division of Population Health, which had lost 88 percent of its staff, write notices of funding opportunities for diseases like lupus and epilepsy.

“We are overseeing millions of dollars in funded work, but how can we do this in a responsible way when we just don’t have enough people to really oversee the work well?” said one official at the agency’s chronic disease center.

The agency’s dysfunction is alarming public health experts even outside the country, who had long relied on the C. D. C.’s expertise during global crises. At a recent meeting of global flu experts, Dr. Jernigan said, “people truly believe that we are less prepared now and less capable of having a coordinated response than we were before the pandemic.”

By this time of year in 2024, the C. D. C. had published detailed recommendations for vaccines against respiratory diseases, with endorsements from the director at the time, Dr. Mandy Cohen, and notes from a meeting of its vaccine advisers.

But because of a federal court ruling, the C. D. C.’s vaccine advisers have not met since December, and the agency has not issued updated recommendations for the vaccines. Some employees at the agency wanted to post clear recommendations for flu vaccines, but did not want to get into a conflict with political appointees, Dr. Jernigan said.

After controversy erupted over the Covid vaccine study, Dr. Bhattacharya demoted the previous acting director of the respiratory disease center, Dr. Brandi Limbago, and replaced her with Rebecca Greco Koné, an operational leader who is not a scientist.

The lack of experienced staff members is also affecting one of the C. D. C.’s primary functions: helping state and local governments.

The C. D. C.’s public health infrastructure grant, which helps health departments train employees and build systems, was managed by 20 project officers but it now has just three. As a result, the team’s response time for requests from local departments has increased from less than a day to more than 10, and some requests have been missed entirely. One county health department requested help on Aug. 7 with submitting data for its annual report but as of Sept. 21, the request was unanswered.

“We’re seeing a movement away from clinical guidance, from data, and from working with states,” said Dr. Debra Houry, who was the agency’s chief medical officer before resigning in August 2025.

In all, more than 1,200 people retired between March 2025 and May 2026, nearly four times the number in the comparable period in 2023-24. About 270 people are still on administrative leave, being paid but not working, while a lawsuit challenging the layoffs makes its way through the courts.

Aaron Sussell, an epidemiologist in the agency’s office in Spokane, Wash., who studied the health of miners, was placed on administrative leave in April 2025. He and his colleagues were suddenly recalled to work in January with 24 hours’ notice but by then, some had moved out of state and others had taken jobs outside the government.

Dr. Sussell, who worked at the C. D. C. for 37 years, decided to retire at the end of February. He would normally have trained his replacement. Instead, he saw an ad for his job go up five months after he left, then get taken down. His position remains unfilled.

The agency’s global health center was approved to fill 18 critical positions. Officials posted ads, interviewed candidates and made job offers to some. But the offers expired before H. H. S. completed the next steps like background checks, so they had to start the interview process all over again, according to an official with knowledge of the situation.

By law, C. D. C. employees who were laid off have priority to be rehired, but some applicants were told they were ineligible for the very jobs they had previously held for years. In all, the agency hired 108 employees between March 2025 and May 2026, compared with more than 1,500 between March 2023 and May 2024.

The staffing totals do not always tell the full story. One C. D. C. branch that works on vaccine-preventable diseases, such as measles, has lost only seven of its 50 people. But they include the four most experienced scientists from the measles lab team, which is trying to analyze genetic material that will determine whether the United States can still claim to have eliminated measles. And funding cuts to other federal agencies have also affected the C. D. C.’s budget for fighting infectious diseases: The budget for a branch that tackles Ebola and other deadly diseases has dropped by 36 percent.

Some C. D. C. scientists are hesitant to sign up for the Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of Congo because they disagree with the administration’s focus on keeping infected people out of the country rather than on helping to contain the outbreak.

Others are too overburdened to help. About 100 C. D. C. staff members have been deployed to Congo to help with the outbreak, compared with about 2,000 who went to West African countries during the 2014 Ebola outbreak.

“If you’re doing your job and your boss’s job who left, and you also have three staff people who left under you,” said Dr. Fiona Havers, who resigned from the C. D. C. in June 2025, “no one has the spare capacity to help out in something that’s not in their field.”

For more than a year, it’s been obvious that the C. D. C. is in distress. It’s gone through a devastating round of layoffs, was attacked by a gunman and has lost its director and other senior leaders. I’ve covered many of these developments, but I was still shocked when I dug deeper for this story.

Recent numbers show that the agency has lost about a third of its staff altogether, while Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and others he has appointed have stripped it of much of its independence. The employees still at the C. D. C. are doing their best to hold things together, but as one put it, they’re "running out of fingers and toes to plug holes" in a sinking ship.

Apoorva Mandavilli reports on science and global health for The Times, with a focus on infectious diseases and pandemics and the public health agencies that try to manage them.

Sylvester Stallone Hid His Struggles for Decades. Now He’s Coming Clean.

The New York Times September 26, 2026

The Interview

The Interview

Credit... Philip Montgomery for The New York Times

Supported by

By Lulu Garcia-Navarro

Sylvester Stallone has loomed large in our popular imagination for 50 years, ever since he exploded onto the screen playing the iconic underdog boxer Rocky Balboa in a film he wrote and that won the best picture Oscar. Many more “Rocky” films came after that, and also another franchise, “Rambo,” which heralded a new era of action movies in which Stallone and his one-time nemesis Arnold Schwarzenegger modeled a very specific type of masculinity: physically imposing, morally unambiguous and emotionally aloof.

Now 80, and with a new memoir, titled “The Steps” (a nod to the Philadelphia Museum of Art stairs he famously scaled in “Rocky”), Stallone is ready to examine his own life, his work and the impact it has had on our culture. As he told me in our candid and at times shocking conversations, he can “make a castle out of regrets” for what his drive and fame did to his mind and his body. He also explained how his very difficult childhood, with abusive and neglectful parents, motivated the tough-guy image he showed the world.

Subscribe: Apple Podcasts | Spotify | YouTube | Amazon | iHeart

You wrote in “The Steps” that at difficult moments in your life, you told yourself to put those memories “away in a box” and avoid them, just move forward. What was it like to go back and revisit some of these things for this book? It was some mixed emotion. There were some tears, some laughter, some anger and bitterness. And then I thought, Maybe that was the motivation to do something extraordinary as opposed to having no angst inside of me. It’s like, The guy punched you in your mouth, but did he do you a favor? I truly believe that the parents are the sculptors, and they’re sculpting their masterpiece, or their disaster.

How you came into the world was, in many ways, how you have inhabited it, with a lot of turmoil and drama. Can you tell me about the day you were born? My mother also came from a lot of turmoil, and she really wasn’t mother material. She had grandiose plans for her life, so her pregnancy with me was a big-time interruption. I don’t think she wanted to believe it was happening, even though it was in the ninth month. She was finally on a bus and she goes into labor. It was bad. She just happened to be near a medical center, you might call it, like a charity ward.

And the people who delivered you used forceps and partially paralyzed your face. It could have been worse, because sometimes you get brain damage from it, but maybe that happened too. [Laughs] It was a terrible thing growing up because I slurred and I mumbled. It was like 10 times worse than Rocky.

Did you see yourself as having a disability when you were young? Yeah. If you have a lisp or a stutter, you’re so familiar with it. But other people are like: “What? What language is that?”

In the book you seem to suggest that both your parents saw your arrival as having ruined their ambitions in some way. You wrote, “Can you really make people proud who never wanted you in the first place?” And when you were very little, you were sent to go live in a boardinghouse, and your parents only visited you once a month. How did you understand that as a kid? I don’t know if there was some preventive thing or some blockage from being completely abandoned, but I was just raised by strangers and it became a natural environment. My parents were never nurturing, so this was actually a bonus compared to where I was living.

I think if you are emotionally deprived when you’re younger, you learn to lock things away, which is why I started with that quote about you locking things away. Do you think it made you tough? In the wrong way, it did. It made me very tough. And I literally didn’t figure out real, true love until I was 70. To really have unequivocally true love, that total abandonment, that reckless love that you would jump into a volcano for someone, that came late. And that’s a big pity. I was so consumed with not being another bum from the neighborhood. I was very, very competitive, like a pit bull. That’s what got me going. It’s not healthy.

Your parents had this very hostile and violent marriage, and they divorced when you were about 11 years old. What do you remember about that separation? It was traumatic. When my mom goes, “I’m leaving, I won’t be living here anymore,” I remember holding onto her leg, like being literally dragged. And she pulled the leg away, walked out the door and that was it. My brother came home a little bit after that and there was nobody there. I guess my father took me to the shop or something, so he was abandoned and he never got over that. Ever.

That scene of you holding your mother’s leg. I’m so sorry. What was going on? I don’t know because she never was a loving person. But there’s a connection at birth that some people have that is so palpable, that no matter what, you cannot break away from this need to have this person’s attention. It’s electric. And then being deprived and put into the dark, it’s terrible.

It’s 100 percent true: You can never get rid of the connection to your parents. You end up living with your dad. He loved horses and played polo. But what was it like living alone with your dad? Because that didn’t sound like a great time, either. It would be these constant bombastic explosions and then total silence. If he and I were talking and I said, “I don’t know if I agree with that,” he’d start spinning his fork and suck his teeth, and you knew what was coming. The next thing you know, wham! He had very big hands. You learn to duck. I didn’t put a lot of stuff in the book because I didn’t want a pity party, but it was insane. For example, before we go to church he said, “Go to the store and buy some bread.” I bring home sandwich spread, not bread, and he kicked me in the stomach, laid me out, got in the car and went to church. I’m there in the street with mayonnaise. Really, it’s unbelievable.

Your dad was not only abusive, but he was competitive with you. He often tried to one-up you, humiliate you. You became a very good polo player, and at a polo match, he dragged you off the horse and beat you up in front of everyone. Why do you think he was that way with you? I don’t know. His father was like this. His father was a very stoic barber with a mustache. They say a fly sitting on a ton of cow [expletive] thinks himself a king. He had this sort of imperiousness and he was cold as hell, and so my father was very, very cold and tough. There was a cat making noise outside the house. He went out, got the cat, took it into the laundry room, shot it and left it in the wash tub. I think he did that to impress me. Like, You’ll never be as tough as your old man. And I won’t. There is no chance. That’s a whole other league.

You keep using the word “tough.” But I don’t hear tough. I hear messed up. You know, you’re right. I’m using “tough” as a masculine banner for something much more perverse and weird.

And dark. And dark.

With all that drama and all that violence, was there any love between you two? Only on his deathbed. It’s so weird — my mother never hugged me, ever. Kissing? Forget it. It was always an air thing. And my father wasn’t any better. But I’ll never forget, I was maybe 9 years old, and he would have me take care of his horses. We were coming back from the barn. He’s driving, and I fell asleep. So he put my head on his knee and his hands on my head. I never got over that. I went, Wow, that’s what it feels like. Just a simple stroking of your child’s hair. But that was it. It was one and done.

You went to many different schools during this period, including one for kids who needed discipline, a reform school. Devereux.

You write about being put in a psych ward, and this was one of the most chilling things that I have read. Can you tell me that story and why you included it? At this school, there were five different departments for different ages. And in my age group, the teenagers, if you ever snuck out to see a girl or do something like that, you’d be reprimanded by being taken to a place called Park Lodge or the Snake Pit. On the outside it looked like a big, old Tudor home from the ’20s, and then you walked inside and you entered the heart of insanity. The smell, the filth, people running around naked, clawing, hands tied, drooling. This is what they thought would impress you never to break the rules again.

And they left you there for how long? I was there for a couple of weeks. It was wild. But this to me was one of the better things that happened, too. I said, I know they’re going to try to break me. I was attacked there. They tried to rip my groin off ——

What do you mean? There was a guy named Jay Bird. He was the son of an actor named Lloyd Nolan, and he was put in there. He was big, had no hair, always naked, rotten teeth. They called him Jay Bird because he was always naked as a jaybird. And I go into the bathroom on the way to the food mess hall, and he comes in and comes around me and he’s like ripping on my throat and he is going into my pants and grabbing my groin. Then the two guards come in and they’re beating the crap out of him with razor straps. I go, “What the hell is wrong with him?” And they say: “You’re in a crazy house, boy. Nothing’s wrong with him. He’s crazy.” But let me just get to the point. When I came out of there and was standing before the school principal and he said, “You learned your lesson?” I said: “I learned a lot more than that lesson. A much better lesson: You can’t break me.” So when I got to the city and everything that came after that, I always felt I was unbreakable in that way. My heart could be broken, like every human being, but I’m talking about will. [We reached out to Devereux for comment after this interview, and a spokesperson replied that, while they had not read the book, they respect Mr. Stallone’s “right to tell his story his own way,” take his account seriously and are “sorry for any trauma he remembers experiencing.”]

You end up showing up in New York City in your 20s. You’d dropped out of college at this point. You backpacked around Europe and you had no money. You had a dream, though, that you wanted to become an actor, and you take a job as an usher at a movie theater. What comes through is what an obsessive you became. You start writing down dialogue from your favorite films. What were you trying to do there? I was really trying to learn. I said, I’m nonexistent. I put on this monkey suit and people don’t even see you, but I can see what the audience reacts to, where they laugh, where they don’t, who gets up, why they get up. You listen and talk about the film. And then I started to write it down. I lived in a cell. It was very tiny. Maybe an eight-by-nine-foot room. So I’d sit on my bed and I’d have these old Traffic and Blood, Sweat and Tears albums, and those were my desk. And I would just translate notes. Sometimes I’d think, What if this is it, Sly? You’re sitting in the middle of a bed like a fool doing something that sounds so stupid to anyone else. Then the fear would come, and it’s like the thing in the psych ward: Don’t go there. Take the fear, swallow it, move on.

You had an apartment with blacked-out windows, where you would write scripts for days on end. In this period, you were getting into altercations. But you’re also spending your days not only writing but going to MoMA. You wrote in the book, “At my core, there is this simmering cauldron of emotion that can overflow with volatility, but can also be directed toward deep artistic purpose.” Do you think you ever learned how to control that cauldron? It’s very, very explosive. At the end of “First Blood,” there’s a nervous breakdown. It wasn’t written that way, but it came out. I said, “This is coming from that cauldron.” It’s the self-indignation of being run down, dismissed, because that’s the way I felt. You can call me ugly, you call me short, just don’t call me stupid. Because that is what my father used to say. And literally, it would turn me into a maniac to prove I’m not stupid. And I would just work and work and work. For example, I’m 80 years old, and this morning I’m up at 5 a. m. studying my dialogue that I don’t have to do for a month.

That scene in “First Blood” is just iconic. I was just watching it again yesterday. You are filled with rage and grief. The way it was written was, I’m supposed to commit suicide in a very cool manner. I said, Wait a minute, there are thousands and thousands of men missing parts of their bodies who actually thought they were doing something worthwhile. They were following the rules and orders of their country, and then when they came back they’re looked at as aberrations, Frankensteins, monsters. Then I started to identify, that’s what I felt like growing up. And this rage that they must feel, that not their parents but their country is scorning them — their real parents, the ones they literally lost blood and friends and died for — I really identified with this dismissive attitude that I grew up with all the time. And boy, when I look at that footage, I look distorted. I was gone for a few seconds. Sometimes in acting or painting or writing, you just subliminally lose yourself. You do not know where you are. Maybe it happens in sex for two seconds, where you’re literally blanked out. What was that?

Was it one take? It was one take.

To come back to this period when you were in your apartment with the blacked-out windows: You’re trying to make it as an actor. You get a lot of rejections because of the way you look. And you write “Rocky” for yourself. The studios are very excited for the script, and it’s a well-known story that the studio tried to pay you more and more money not to be in the film. They wanted James Caan or Ryan O’Neal, but they give it to you because you held out. Was this because you had a sense that this was your last chance? This was it. I was done. I had less than a hundred bucks in the bank, and I don’t know if it was spiritual, but I said, “God, I know in my heart that I will regret this for the rest of my life, and I will be more of a broken man than if I had never done this in the first place.” I don’t know why I knew this, because I had had no success. I was green, and they had every right not to want to use me. If someone came to me and did the same thing and looked like me and slurred, I’d go: “Come on, man. You’re not acceptable to a lot of different people in this country.” But I just knew that this is the crossroad. This is the bridge. And if you don’t cross it, then jump off it. I’m not going to have someone else do it. I knew I would hate myself. I would kill myself — emotionally, that is. Not for real.

Can I ask you just about this thing that happened during “Rocky?” This is your big break. You have sacrificed everything for it. They give you the part. You’re a nobody. Everything’s riding on the movie. And you cast your dad as the timekeeper who rings the bell in the climactic boxing match. And it turned into a mess! Why did you let him back in? It was like: I just want you to love me for a little bit. Like, look what I did! Share it with me. I know you thought I was a fool my whole life, but here we are. He didn’t ring the bell properly, and I kept fighting and fighting and fighting. Everything’s choreographed. It’s one, two, three, four, bell. Not six, seven, eight, nine, ten. Carl Weathers is like, “What’s going on?” And of course it ended up in an altercation by the end. It got really nasty. A really bad Italian drama. But for a moment I thought, Jesus, he’d be proud.

Later you end up inviting your mom to the Oscars for “Rocky” and she blows you off. As we’ve discussed here, she was difficult. This is putting it lightly. You’re quite scathing about her in the book. And then in the 1990s she becomes a celebrity psychic. How did you manage the dynamics when she sees proximity to your fame as a financial opportunity? It was very hard. She had been married three more times, and then I saw her posing as a psychic with a turban and rhinestones and this buffoonery. Or she would go on “Howard Stern” and mock my father and call him terrible things and then they’d get on the phone. And I had my father and mother fighting on “Howard Stern”! What other guy has to go through this?

Yeah, this was 1992. They had this horrible on-air argument. It’s unbelievable. Why would you go on and humiliate yourself? Why are you humiliating me, my children? Stop! I’ll pay you anything to do whatever you want — the finest restaurants, anything. Just live your life and try to be proud. She goes, “Why aren’t you proud of me?” I’ll never forget. I asked her: “Have you ever done anything wrong? Do you have any regrets?” She goes, “No, why?” Wow. I live on regrets. I can make a castle out of regrets.

Did you go to therapy later in your life? No. It’s not going to help, because this doesn’t go away. You cover it all with subterfuge and ideology and intellectual this and that and breathing and meditation until that moment, late at night, poof. You’re right back there, and now you’re in anxiety. You ever have anxiety?

Oh, yeah. All that anxiety everyone has, it’s coming from something that’s so deep-rooted.

Tell me about when you first suffered anxiety. The first time was when I was 36 and I was watching dailies, and then all of a sudden I stood up and the hair on my neck went up and I started getting hot and I go, I’m dying, this is it, I’m on my way out. And bang, down I went. Took a knee, crawled, rolled over, and now I’m in this dark movie theater. Where the [expletive] did this come from? And then it happened again and again and again. It went away for five years. And then it always seems to happen, like, just as you’re getting ready to go on the “Today” show — boom! Anybody got a Xanax? It’s too late. So you’re just sitting there holding onto a chair.

I think people would find it very heartening that you have experienced that. Oh, big time. Especially as I got older. When I’m in a crowd, I’d be with my wife at an art exhibition and the room is filling up. It’s getting more and more, and then I’d go, “I’m going down,” and she’d be like, “Let’s get out of here.” And literally I just make it to the alley, boom, get down on one knee. So there’s something still bubbling inside, festering. It’s a marvel, for example, that we still have magma and lava four billion years later in the center of the Earth. How long does it take to cool an egg? My god. Our emotions are always on the verge of eruption.

Despite having such an upsetting upbringing, you’ve become a father of five. What did you learn about being a good parent, considering you didn’t have role models for that? I really wasn’t a very good parent. My wife, Jennifer, is the greatest woman ever. And she is the most giving. I don’t have that gear of just abandonment of your own personal self for someone else. She raised my daughters that way. My first marriage wasn’t like that. I was in my warrior mode. Let’s conquer the world. Everything fell by the wayside. It was just a measly manner of existence.

You suffered an unimaginable loss in 2012 when your eldest son, Sage, died. He had an undiagnosed heart condition that killed him when he was only 36. I imagine that must have profoundly changed you. The thing is, you have so many episodes of guilt. Like: What could I have done? Should I have been there? What if I did that? If I went right or went left? I’ll never forget, it was so cold: My mother’s new husband, who I’d never even met, who was a doctor, called me and goes: “Sly, he’s gone. Sage — he’s gone.” I went, “Gone where?” “He died, he’s gone. I’m sorry.” Click.

That’s how you found out? That’s right. Because of the funeral, dealing with the mother, dealing with your life in the present, it just takes you into a whole other world. You go: Wow, I’m holding it together. When’s it going to happen? And then about a week later, I was all alone in my room, and a wail came out of me I’ve never heard before or since. It was just pain and grief and guilt. It was not human. But all I can say is that he was a very kind kid. He had a great mother. He would have done wonderful things in the future. I just had no idea that he had something that you would expect a very advanced adult to have. But no, you don’t get over that.

I’m sorry. [Shakes head]

[Long Pause] Back to “Rocky.” Back to “Rocky.”

It got 10 Oscar nominations. It ended up winning best picture. And you end up capturing the public’s imagination. I’m very interested in you looking back at this transition, from a struggling actor to suddenly becoming the hottest star in Hollywood. Did you look at fame in the same way as the psych ward, like: This isn’t going to change me? Or did you look at it as: This is everything I ever wanted? Because fame breaks some people. It didn’t break me. It made me combative. It made me very I told you so revengeful. Spiteful. I was so insufferable. Even with The New York Times, I was like, “Oh, ‘Madame Bovary,’ anyone could write that.” I became a petulant child. Years later, I despised myself. I’m surprised I’m still here. I managed to alienate the entire press and people who believed in me. I was just not humble. There was no humility whatsoever. Again, it’s just childhood eruptions coming to the surface at the most inopportune time.

Arnold Schwarzenegger, who you’re now friends with, was a huge action star back then, and you’ve said you couldn’t stand to be in the same room. Why did you hate him so much? Because he was a challenge. I thought I had something going on. Then I see this guy, this immovable force, a very confident human being, even more so than me, and more psychological in the way he would manipulate and do things very cunningly. Not in a negative way, but just shrewdly. I was a blunt force; he was Machiavellian cool. He’s winning these awards, and he’s a bodybuilder, and I consider myself somewhat more of a ——

A thespian. A thespian, a peripatetic dramaturg just wandering the country acting. [Laughs] And I went, Wow, this is the guy I’m going to have trouble with. And sure enough, we did. We were just going at each other, which turned out to be fantastic. I’m regretful for some of the things I said about him, but he antagonized me in a creative way, and I did to him. It forced us to keep moving higher, and bigger guns, louder, more action, disemboweled bodies, everything, until we really carved out a niche that will never quite come around again, that ’80s over-the-top action genre that he and I pioneered.

It’s like a creative marriage, in a way. It’s like Ali and Frazier. You need that thing that brings you to the surface more than any other person. It’s not even hatred. It’s this guy, he won’t go away. I dream about him. I’m on his mind. He’s on my mind. It’s very rare. Eventually we end up working together in “The Expendables,” and I go on the campaign trail for him. Unbelievable.

When was the moment that you two put this to rest? Did it just come with age and him moving into politics? Yeah. At first I thought, Come on, actors in politics? This is oil and water, because actors are very self-absorbed, and politicians, if they’re good, should be the opposite. But he was definitely sincere about it, and I don’t know why but he asked me to be at an event. And sure enough, then we hit it off. He’s one of a kind.

I want to ask you about your body. Well, now you’re getting personal.

At several points in your career you were exceptionally muscular, which wasn’t your build before “Rocky.” How has your relationship with your body changed over time? It became very intimate, you might say. It was my armor. I looked at Rocky: very smooth, very normal-looking guy. And then I said, I think the character would start to become a bit more vain. And then in “Rambo,” you’re playing a warrior, so you’d be a little bit more animalistic. You wouldn’t be so smooth. So I started to think: Design your body like a jaguar, a cat. Not big like Arnold, but more feral and aggressive and very limber and athletic. Then it became an obsession. Really bad. It got to the point where I became bulimic. You heard it here first. I got down to 2.6 percent body fat when I was doing “Rocky III,” and I couldn’t hold anything down. Or I didn’t want to keep it down because I became so obsessed with staying at that point of fitness, literally an obsessive body-worship kind of thing. And nobody does it without additives and drugs, period. I don’t care what they say. It isn’t as though you’re a junkie, but if you’re going to work out and try to stay in shape for six months straight, and you’re eating yogurt and pudding, it’s not happening.

So you were taking steroids, you’re saying? Oh, my god, you have to. But you do it in a sensitive way — six weeks on, six weeks off. People go, “Oh, you don’t get that way naturally.” No, you don’t. But that also took a terrible toll. It wasn’t until I did “Cop Land,” when I had to play the weakest guy in the room — partially deaf, overweight — that I felt somewhat liberated. Then things went sideways and I just fell out of grace with Hollywood. But yeah, I’ve abused my body. I’ve had nine back operations, two shoulder operations, three neck fusions. Everything is held together with baling wire, but I still want to stay in good shape.

Do you still see it as your armor? No, no, no.

Because you’re still fit, and you’re 80. I’m sort of fit, but I take a lot of pills to keep going. It’s come at a terrible price. If I could do it over again, I would say, “Let someone else carry the banner and don’t do your own stunts.” I don’t know what it was about hurting myself all the time.

Was it masochistic? Very masochistic. And this is all going back to dad and back there in the polo field: No, you’re not going to break me. But you do get broken a little bit — physically, not mentally.

You said something earlier about regrets, and that you don’t get to be your age in your career without a mountain of them. It’s horrible. It’s the fog of war, the war of trying to succeed, and you can blame it on that or on petty self-absorption, and wow it is painful. But yesterday is dead. Do you forgive yourself for being a bastard? No, you just regret. You denied people your love, but you also did worse to yourself.

Have you forgiven your parents? [Pause] I’ve accepted that they are who they are. I guess you could say, yeah, I do. It’s definitely a delicate peace treaty, but what are we going to do? Walk around yelling at ghosts? Come back here! We’re not finished! No, I can’t. All I can do is cherish every second, because let’s face it, I can see the light at the end of the tunnel.

You have always exuded invincibility. That’s been your persona in your life and in many of your roles. So it’s kind of astonishing to see you be so vulnerable. [Laughs] Even though I put on this facade of having armor, I really have a lot of empathy for people who just didn’t get a break in life. That’s why I think “Rocky” was such a success.

You talked about how no one would return your calls in Hollywood for a period in the late 1990s. And this was when you had movies that didn’t do well: “Judge Dredd,” “Daylight,” “Get Carter,” “Driven,” “D-Tox,” “Avenging Angelo.” I came across an interview you gave to The New York Times in 1992. The article quotes one prominent Hollywood agent who said: “I think he’s a diminishing asset. With every film he does, he goes down a little further. He’s the new Burt Reynolds.” How do you explain this period of not-so-great films? Was it a quality-control issue? It really was. I didn’t apply myself to the actual quality and the components — in other words, the right director, the right co-star, the right advertising, the right theme song. These are things that I used to really apply myself to. And I suppose I just got lazy and started this whirlpool.

What does it do to the soul of an artistic person to make movies that aren’t good? It’s a death in the family. It’s not as though you didn’t sell a vacuum cleaner today. It’s all over the world. And there is a part of human nature that revels in that. I don’t take it personally. I think that quite often, human nature says, OK, he’s had enough time, let’s bring on the new generation. When you reach a certain age in this business, it becomes a very, very competitive, delicate and tenuous career. That’s why I think it’s a very neurotic business at times, because the product is you. It isn’t like, Oh, you’re rejecting my leather jacket. No, we don’t like you. I’ve always said the artist dies twice. The second death is the easiest one, compared to the career death in which you’re being dismissed. But it woke me up and I was so invigorated starting to write. The hardest and the proudest moment by far in my life is “Rocky Balboa,” because nobody wanted it. I was done — and when I say done, I mean, my agent fired me, managers fired me. I go: OK, this sounds very familiar. Let’s start over again. Let’s see if we can do it at 60. So it was a fantastic voyage into the unknown.

I have a question about “Rambo.” As we discussed, the first movie was quite complicated, about this vet who was discarded by his country who had PTSD. But then the character over time turns into this classic action-movie hero, with less depth than the original character had. Absolutely right. And that’s my fault. I didn’t really focus on the depth of what he was still going through while trying to save P. O. W. s. He’s trying to save his own soul. We never got into that. It’s just bravado, bravado, bravado. That’s all me. You realize, flexing your muscles is a lot easier than showing your soul. And it was terrible. It was like a cartoon.

It came to define this projection of American power. And in an interview in 1985, when you were talking about your view of war and your politics, you said, “If you have the power like the United States, if you’re gonna talk tall and carry a big stick, eventually you’ve gotta use it or they’ll think you’re bluffing.” Did “Rambo” represent a part of your worldview at that point? It did. And now I realize all war is futile. It’s a mechanism to make tons of money for the war department and manufacturers, and these kids are just going out there into a gristmill, being chopped up, and then when they come back with no arms it’s, Oh, sorry, you’re on your own. I hate it and I’m bitterly opposed to it. But at one time I was truly gung-ho. I don’t know if I was just trying to go against the current. In Hollywood, there’s a certain dynamic, as you know. I think it was just naïveté, really, because I read a lot, especially after “First Blood,” and I go, Wow, this is brutal, this is horrible, there’s no glory in war. None.

When did you become antiwar? Look, if you’re under attack, of course you have to defend yourself. I don’t want to get into politics now, but all wars basically destroy both sides. It really creates this horrible history. Grudges are held, countries are destroyed and lines are redrawn, for what?

I know you don’t want to talk about politics, but I am interested in something you just said, which is this idea of Hollywood being liberal and you being seen as a political conservative. Did that put you at odds in what was perceived as a liberal industry, or is that perception actually wrong? It is wrong. I totally understand why the perception is indelible. When “Rocky” came out, I was so naïve. I was pushing 30, and I didn’t even know the difference between Democrat and Republican. But Rocky wrapped himself in a flag. Every movie we were up against at that time was very political, extremely erudite, intellectual. And “Rocky” was not that. It was emotional. I think right away that put me over here. And then when I did “First Blood,” me being jingoistic, and he’s a saber-rattler, it caused a major rift. I wish it wasn’t like that, because I really think a lot of these actors have great empathy, great heart, and they’re really more for the working man down in the trenches. And that’s where I live, you know what I mean? But I’m not considered that. And sometimes you say things and you don’t realize the long-range effects.

You said something earlier that really caught my ear. You said that you can “see the light at the end of the tunnel,” which I took to mean the end of your life. And I was wondering how you feel about death and about there being less time in front of you than there is behind you. In panic mode.

Really? Because of what I said before: I built a castle with thousands of stones made of regrets. I’m trying to make up for it in my own petty way, and I don’t know if there’s enough time. There is not enough time. What I have to do is just focus on the ones who really need me and the ones who I want to go on and have their own life and legacy. At 78, that’s where the insurance company goes, That’s the average. So I’m two years into borrowed time, and I’m making up for it as much as I can, because you’re never too old to be in love, never too old to dance with the great memories that you’ve had, and not wallow in the worst swamp of all, which is the swamp of loneliness. That is truly premature burial.

I grew up watching Sylvester Stallone and, in many ways, he exemplified how I understood on screen masculinity and male power: both verbally taciturn and physically bombastic. So I was surprised when I sat down with Stallone to find him deeply contemplative and, at 80, trying to understand his own life. Some parts of our interview are shocking and raw but throughout our conversation Stallone seemed finally ready to reckon with both the pain and the glory of his long life and career.

This interview has been edited and condensed from two conversations. Listen to and follow “The Interview” on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube, iHeartRadio or Amazon Music. Follow us on Instagram and TikTok.

Director of photography (video): Jessica Dimmock

Lulu Garcia-Navarro is a writer and co-host of The Interview, a series focused on interviewing the world’s most fascinating people.
