‘Make Quinceañeras Great Again’: A Texan Singer Puts the G. O. P. on Defense

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Bobby Pulido, a Tejano musician running as a Democrat for the House, has left his Republican opponent struggling to match his star power in a district that President Trump won easily in 2024.

Bobby Pulido, a Tejano musician running as a Democrat for the House, has left his Republican opponent struggling to match his star power in a district that President Trump won easily in 2024.

Bobby Pulido is running for a House seat anchored in the Rio Grande Valley of Texas. President Trump won the district by 18 percentage points in 2024, but it is now seen as competitive. Credit... Gabriel V. Cárdenas for The New York Times

Supported by

By Bayliss Wagner

Bayliss Wagner reported from Edinburg, McAllen, Pharr and Goliad, Texas, where she went to two birthday parties, one wedding, a high school football game and several political events.

No one had announced that he would show up at the Friday night high school football game in South Texas.

But as he ascended the bleachers, a line quickly formed of fans old and young. Two retirees posed for photos with him, while shy-looking teenagers rehearsed what they would say on their turn.

Most U. S. House candidates do not receive such an enthusiastic reception. But for Bobby Pulido, a Tejano singer running as a Democrat, it is commonplace.

Mr. Pulido — a standard-bearer of the Tejano genre, which fuses the traditional Tex-Mex music of accordion and bajo sexto with modern country or pop — is running in a district anchored in the Rio Grande Valley, where entire families grew up listening to his music. Many voters know him, or at least feel as if they do.

That feeling was summed up by the mother of a high school dance coach: “We know him personally,” Yolanda Ozuna, 69, said of Mr. Pulido, before correcting herself. “We’ve not known the family personally — but the family’s been around him.”

At 53, with two Latin Grammy Awards under his belt, Mr. Pulido is bringing the glam and allure of pop music to a new kind of performance: a high-stakes political campaign. Like other entertainers turned politicians before him — including a certain reality TV star who became president — he is wielding his celebrity and keen sense of spectacle on another stage where attention is a crucial currency.

His prominence and his moderate platform have created an unusual challenge for his Republican opponent, Representative Monica De La Cruz. Even though President Trump won the district by 18 percentage points in 2024, limited polling of the race points to a tight contest that Ms. De La Cruz admits is “very competitive.”

Mr. Pulido has tried to expand his popularity by performing for free at more than 70 quinceañeras, weddings and other events in his district, a tactic he adopted in response to a dig from his opponent. (“This election isn’t about who you want performing at your niece’s quinceañera,” Ms. De La Cruz had said in March.)

At each party, his campaign team collects attendees’ contact info, helping to build a database of potential voters. He sings for 10 minutes, then gives a simple pitch in English or Spanish. Before he leaves, he hands the birthday girl a “Make Quinceañeras Great Again” baseball cap and accommodates guests’ requests for photos.

Ms. De La Cruz and her allies have sought to undercut Mr. Pulido’s family-friendly image. She has attacked him for his ties to Frankie Caballero, a former bandmate who is a registered sex offender, and for past offensive comments denigrating the bodies of postpartum women.

“I have been a leader that has brought results home to this community,” Ms. De La Cruz said in an interview at a park in Edinburg, where she and Mr. Pulido both live, “while my opponent has brought scandals to this community.”

Mr. Pulido maintains that voters have “never” asked him about Mr. Caballero or his past controversial comments, and that they are “distractions” from voters’ concerns about affordability and health care.

Mr. Pulido has mostly managed to dodge Republican attacks on policy. Running as a conservative Democrat, he has avoided partisan positions on transgender athletes, immigration and gun control that are unpopular in the district while embracing Democratic calls for government-funded health care and safety net programs.

Mr. Pulido has given his party newfound hope of reversing Republican gains in the predominantly Hispanic congressional district, Texas’ 15th, at a time when polls show that Latino voters are turning on Mr. Trump.

But he still faces an uphill battle.

“Our greatest challenge since we started has been overcoming the stigma of, ‘He’s just a singer and doesn’t know about politics,’” Mr. Pulido said in an interview at a coffee shop in McAllen, adding an expletive.

“Are we overcompensating?” he mused, going over the many podcasts, interviews and events he fills his schedule with. “Maybe.”

Mr. Pulido’s family has deep roots in South Texas’ political and music scene. One uncle was the Hidalgo County district attorney, another the county’s top elected official.

His father was a farmworker before finding success as a pioneer of Tejano music.

Mr. Pulido spoke publicly about aspirations of running for office as early as 2003, when he told the Mexican newspaper El Norte that he wanted to fight for immigrants’ human rights.

Mr. Pulido’s grueling campaign schedule seems designed to counter Ms. De La Cruz’s claims that he is a dilettante and a “corrupt liberal celebrity.”

One Saturday for Mr. Pulido started with a 7 a. m. Spanish-language radio interview, followed by a three-hour drive to Goliad, a ruby-red town best known as the site of a massacre during the Texas Revolution. After hours under the Texas sun at a farmers’ market, he spoke at a local Democratic Party luncheon, trekked back to the Rio Grande Valley, changed clothes at a convenience store and sang at a Sweet 16 before making his final campaign stop of the day at a quinceañera, or 15th birthday party.

Teenage girls squealed and parents recorded on their phones as he descended a staircase, singing one of his hits.

He has been running this way since last fall. The campaign is “the hardest thing I’ve ever done,” he said in the interview.

Mr. Pulido pitches himself as a conservative “Blue Dog” Democrat who supports a secure border, owns guns and loves God. He says he supports creating pathways to citizenship for immigrants who are working and paying taxes, and deporting violent criminals.

Mr. Pulido has also said he opposes transgender girls participating in girls’ sports. But he doesn’t talk about that on the trail. Instead, he says he would expand health care access, push back against tariffs and curb billionaires’ influence in politics.

Democrats “got really fixated on social justice for a long time, but we have to have an economic message,” he said in the interview.

While Mr. Pulido has leaned into unscripted encounters with voters who could disagree with him, Ms. De La Cruz, 51, a former insurance agent seeking her third term, has taken a more cautious tack.

She stayed near her home in Edinburg on the same day this month that Mr. Pulido went to Goliad. She dropped by a park to thank canvassers, then sat for interviews with two reporters in a pavilion. As the volunteers went house-to-house in the blazing heat, she headed downtown for a fund-raiser and meet-and-greet.

Mr. Trump’s mid-decade redistricting push has complicated her run. Last year, when Texas Republicans gerrymandered the state’s House map to make five Democratic-held seats significantly redder, they carved out roughly 60 percent of Ms. De La Cruz’s constituency. Ms. De La Cruz is now pitching herself to many voters who are less familiar with her — and facing a challenger with sky-high name recognition.

At the same time, she has been weighed down by Mr. Trump’s immigration crackdown and the high cost of gas and groceries, all of which have hit voters and businesses hard in her low-income district.

She has sought to distance herself from Mr. Trump’s policies, saying in an interview that she supports “common-sense enforcement that focuses on the cartels and the criminals.” Her campaign aired an ad featuring a testimonial from a woman whose husband, who is part of the Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals program, was detained by ICE while on his way to deliver breast milk to their baby in a neonatal intensive care unit.

“We need to secure our borders to keep our family safe, but this immigration system is broken,” the woman, Stephanie Villareal, says in the ad, adding, “I voted Democrat before, but Monica puts people over politics.”

Ms. De La Cruz’s record on border security could also be a strength in a conservative district.

Mayra Cantu, 46, whose husband is a Border Patrol agent, said she had knocked on thousands of doors for Ms. De La Cruz since 2020. Ms. Cantu’s husband struggled to handle the mental and emotional toll of the influx of migrants during the Biden administration, she said.

“As a Border Patrol family, we know what we see and exactly what happens when we fall off track,” Ms. Cantu said, warning that a “wishy-washy politician” would not be “strong enough for the task.”

As Election Day approaches, the race has become increasingly ugly.

At Republicans’ midterm convention in Dallas, Ms. De La Cruz accused Mr. Pulido of “bringing a convicted child sex predator around our families,” referring to a 2018 middle school benefit concert where Mr. Pulido played alongside Mr. Caballero. She has also slammed him over past sexually explicit social media posts; in one from June 2016, he made a crude remark about women’s genitals after childbirth. In another, from 2014, he asks a fan for a nude photograph.

Super PACs backing Ms. De La Cruz have echoed her attacks with ominous TV spots. One showed a little girl’s silhouette in the dark, then Mr. Caballero’s face.

Mr. Pulido, who has apologized for the explicit posts, has said that he was unaware of Mr. Caballero’s sex-offender status. His campaign said he permanently cut ties with Mr. Caballero in 2021.

Mr. Pulido’s campaign manager, Abel Prado, said the singer “will not be lectured by Monica De La Cruz — a person who has spent her political career cheerleading a president who has publicly attacked women’s appearances.”

Recently, Mr. Pulido and his allies have gone on offense, running ads that point to allegations that Ms. De La Cruz abused her former stepdaughter. Ms. De La Cruz has vigorously denied the claim, which her ex-husband made during their divorce in 2022, and her campaign emphasized that her ex-husband was found guilty of assaulting a police officer that year.

“South Texans have already rejected these smears twice,” said James Shook, Ms. De La Cruz’s campaign manager.

In interviews, voters across the district seemed largely unfazed by the attacks against Mr. Pulido.

Many Democrats dismissed them as irrelevant given Mr. Trump’s past scandals. Republicans were focused on Mr. Pulido’s policy views; one said he was more concerned about the fact that the candidate had previously said he lived part-time in Mexico.

In an era when congressional campaigns largely reach voters through paid television and social media ads, Mr. Pulido is betting that face-to-face encounters can accomplish more.

At a wedding Mr. Pulido stopped by, the bride agreed and said she was thrilled about his performance.

“People want to know who they’re voting for,” the bride, Keilah Patterson, 25, said as she lit a cigarette by the pool. “Now everyone at this party will say, ‘I saw him!’”

It’s odd to find yourself wearing a press badge and street clothes at the wedding of a stranger. But that's where I ended up as I covered Bobby Pulido's unusual campaign in the Rio Grande Valley, where he often performs at quinceañeras and other events. Everywhere he went, people wanted pictures or autographs, and it seemed like everyone knew his family, too.

Bayliss Wagner is a political reporter and a member of the 2026-27 Times Fellowship, a program for journalists early in their careers.

The Homeless Community That Became a Self-Governed Village

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

headway

Portland’s Dignity Village has been a place for people without housing for more than 25 years.

By Brian Barth

Photographs by Ricardo Nagaoka

One evening a few months ago, the awkward details of a love triangle spilled out in a humble plywood structure next door to a municipal composting facility in Portland, Ore.

The building, known simply as the Commons, serves as the communal kitchen, living room and courtroom of Dignity Village, a community of approximately 60 people living in hand-built tiny homes on the site. All previously homeless, they manage the place on their own — likely the only such community in the country that is not just city-sanctioned, but fully self-funded and self-governed.

The village council had gathered that evening in the cluttered, dimly lit Commons to adjudicate a disagreement between a woman, her boyfriend and an ex. The ex had filed an incident report with the village’s security department which stated that the current boyfriend had been harassing and intimidating him.

The meeting was a curious blend of bureaucracy and bickering friends, much like the village itself — part homeless camp, part homeless services agency. After some debate, a compromise emerged: the ex-boyfriend pledged to stop sending the woman a constant stream of texts and the two men agreed to avoid each other for the foreseeable future. The words of village elders sealed the deal.

Dignity Village is an intriguing answer to some of the thorniest questions posed by the homelessness crisis. Encampment sweeps are on the rise, fueled by a 2024 Supreme Court decision that overturned federal protections for those inhabiting public property if they had nowhere else to go.

But the question of where to put those who have been swept remains intractable. The core idea behind Dignity Village is to allow them to figure it out for themselves.

“Welcome to our radical experiment in collective self-empowerment to end homelessness!” exclaims the village manual. Residents are expected to contribute 10 hours of work each week to maintain the village, substance use must be confined to private spaces, and disputes are resolved by an elected council.

“Peer support is the best way to lift yourself up,” says Scott Layman, a longtime resident who credits the “familyship” of the village with helping him coexist with the voices in his head, without medication, and recover from alcoholism.

Dignity Village’s annual budget is also an order of magnitude less than most shelters.

Representatives of villages attempting self-governance in Portland gather once a month as the Village Federation. At a recent gathering, they welcomed Mitch Green, an economist turned city councilor, whose downtown Portland district includes much of the city’s unhoused population. He was flabbergasted by Dignity Village’s annual operating budget: $60,000, or about $1,000 per person. He said Portland’s city-run tiny home villages cost taxpayers approximately $40,000 per person annually.

“I’m inspired by self-governed villages that center folks who are living in the situation,” he told the federation. Noting that spending on shelter programs was the “biggest driver” of the city’s recent $170 million budget shortfall, Mr. Green said, “I am going to be looking for opportunities to take money away from the city’s shelter system and divert it towards enabling more of this.”

Established in 2001, Dignity Village is the nation’s longest running experiment in what happens when the anarchic structure of an encampment gives way to a more permanent community. City leaders have not embraced its self-governed approach, but many homeless advocates hold it up as a reference for how peer-based solutions can sometimes succeed where bureaucratic solutions fall short. Dignity Village’s residents have found ways to survive, and even thrive, despite addiction, mental illness and extreme poverty, crediting the village’s messy, exhausting, small-D democracy as nonetheless critical to their stability.

“What we’re here trying to do is help people, and when we do that, we help ourselves, and everybody rises,” says Mr. Layman. “That’s the theory anyway.”

The vision for Dignity Village emerged among a group of unhoused residents living under bridges in downtown Portland who were fed up with being repeatedly evicted from their camps. After a series of “shopping cart parades” in 2000 captured national media attention, they settled on city-owned land next to the composting facility, where the government has reluctantly allowed them to remain.

What started as a collection of tents slowly grew into solid structures with the help of legions of volunteers. Under an obscure state law, the city designated the place as an urban campground, allowing some flexibility around building codes.

Current infrastructure includes a guard shack, computer lab, communal bathhouse and a greenhouse that doubles as an overnight shelter for people who show up needing relief. The individual tiny homes lack running water, but since 2025 have been powered by roof-mounted photovoltaic panels, a gift from a local solar energy company.

The community accepts donations from the public, but much of their operating revenue comes from monthly dues — currently $100 per resident — and microbusinesses such as a landscaping operation and firewood sales. According to the city, taxpayer costs for the project are minimal, mainly for annual safety checks by the fire marshal.

Tiny home villages for the homeless have spread rapidly across the country in recent years. Like congregate shelters, most have a long list of rules, enforced by nonprofit operators. Consequently, many without housing still reject them in favor of the relative freedom of the street.

But Dignity Village differs radically from its municipally-controlled counterparts.

The community’s governance structure eschews hard and fast rules in favor of strategies to maintain community cohesion and well-being. People are expelled only in extreme instances, usually involving violence. Rules meant to keep the place clean, discourage hoarding and prevent fires are enforced to the extent necessary to satisfy the fire marshal and environmental regulators. Transgressions tend to be met with peer pressure, formal incident reports and collective kindness.

“Your peers hold you accountable if you’re slacking or engaging in negative behaviors, which hits a lot different than if a staff member of a traditional shelter nags you or gets you in trouble,” said Victory Lafara, a social worker and longtime advocate for the community. “It means more and actually motivates people to make the changes they need to make.”

Numerous unhoused communities across the country have attempted to become permanent and self-governing, but they are typically shut down quickly. Several have emerged in Portland in recent years, including Right to Dream Too and Hazelnut Grove, and while the city has not evicted them, it also hasn’t encouraged the approach.

“The City of Portland does not believe independent villages are scalable, replicable models,” said Alison Perkins, a city spokesperson, noting issues with sanitation, fires and water pollution that “pose life-safety, health, equity and infrastructure issues for both residents of the self-operated shelter and the surrounding community.”

Portland’s formal alternative is a network of seven city-run tiny home communities, called Safe Rest Villages, that are heavily rule-based, with a 120-day limit on length of stay. In contrast, Dignity Village’s lack of time limits draws criticisms from the city. Its model “generally does not provide in-depth case management and does not prioritize moving individuals into permanent housing,” Ms. Perkins said.

Jim Hawes, a Dignity Village resident who was previously housed at a Safe Rest Village in Portland, says he was evicted because he had not done enough to procure items like a driver’s license that are necessary to apply for subsidized housing and other benefits. “If you don’t meet all of these milestones that they’ve established, then they kick you out, regardless of whether you were trying or not,” he said.

Elana Pirtle-Guiney, the Portland city councilor for the district in which Dignity Village and Right to Dream Too are located, sees the self-governed and city-governed models as complementary. Ms. Pirtle-Guiney said her district’s self-governed communities prioritize “building community and creating safe spaces for people. And from there, some people choose to move into traditional housing and some don’t. They have a different set of goals.”

But Dignity Village has kept detailed records since 2018 about length of stay and where departing residents go. While the average stay ranges from one to two years for most residents, the percentage who exit to some form of permanent housing is significantly higher than the city-run sites — about 60 percent, compared to 42 percent.

Nellie Herron, 57, became homeless at the age of 11, and has been in and out of Portland’s shelter programs. Ms. Herron recently got into permanent supportive housing after a year at Dignity Village, and credits its self-governed model with motivating her progress. “If you don’t feel good about yourself, then you’re not going to do anything about your situation,” Ms. Herron said. “It all figures into being housed.”

Andrew Heben spent several years researching encampments and tiny home villages for his 2014 book, “Tent City Urbanism.” He believes unhoused communities need external support to make the model widely replicable.

Mr. Heben helped spearhead a community called Opportunity Village in Eugene, Ore., which was modeled on Dignity Village. He also cofounded a likeminded venture called SquareOne Villages. Unlike Dignity Village, whose founders created a nonprofit of their own, Opportunity Village’s associated nonprofit is run by an external board of directors — housed residents who support an elected council of village residents who oversee daily operations.

“You visit these camps and you see all these positive elements of self-organizing, direct democracy and mutual aid, but they’re also far from ideal living situations,” Mr. Heben said. “As soon as you try to formalize them there needs to be some top-down rules.”

The tension between the independence Dignity Village’s residents credit for the community’s success and the city’s disapproval of its anarchic atmosphere hung over the Dignity Village Council meeting. The aroma of decomposing waste penetrated the walls from the compost facility next door, along with the occasional roar of a jet taking off, as the group trudged through the agenda items — bills to be paid, policies for evicting vicious dogs and the delicate work of resolving a love triangle’s domestic disputes. Village elders issued ardent reminders to keep trash from accumulating and to remain vigilant about fire risks, lest the city pull the plug on their 25-year experiment.

Ray Stanczak, a 76-year-old resident, spoke to the perennial paradox the community faces: they may feel like their model trumps the city’s, but they sit on city-owned land. “I don’t think they’re going to shut us down,” he said. “But they might try to run us.”

In five years of editing Headway, homelessness is the issue we’ve come back to more than any other. And there’s one place in particular that we’ve been eager to take a look at: Dignity Village, in Portland, Ore., a self-governed community of people formerly without housing. As cities across the country have cracked down on encampments, Dignity Village stands out as an intriguing answer to the question, What if we gave people without housing available land where they could make a place permanently?

This isn’t the first appearance of Dignity Village in the Times. We last covered the village* 23 years ago, when its permit from the city was about to expire. “Home for the homeless,” our headline noted then, “but can it continue?” More than two decades later, we can now say that it has continued, but the tension with the city remains everpresent. We hope you find this place as interesting as we did.

The Woodcock Foundation is a funder of Headway’s public square. Funders have no control over the selection, focus of stories or the editing process and do not review stories before publication. The U. N. Is Terrible. We Need the U. N.

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Advertisement

Supported by

Nicholas Kristof

By Nicholas Kristof

Opinion Columnist

Quiz question: What country surpasses Haiti, Somalia and the Democratic Republic of Congo as a deadbeat and rogue nation?

Answer: In the halls of the United Nations, it’s the good old U. S. A.

The Trump administration is delinquent in U. N. dues, while 141 countries — including those mentioned above — are fully paid up. And while other countries at least pretend to advance peace in the spirit of the United Nations, President Trump used his U. N. speech to threaten to “annihilate” Iran and “drive them into hell.” It was a rare instance of a world leader taking to the U. N. podium to muse about whether to commit what sounds like genocide.

All this underscores a tragedy of our era: Some 130 armed conflicts are underway around the globe, more than double the number in 2009, according to the International Committee of the Red Cross, and a growing share of the challenges afflicting us are international and require multilateral solutions, yet the major powers are marginalizing the United Nations and rendering it even less effective than usual.

Fuel prices are surging. Trump’s Iran war has spread to Yemen and the Red Sea. Russia is engaging in so-called gray-zone attacks in Europe. There is a risk of war with China over Taiwan or the South China Sea. Drugs, epidemics, artificial intelligence, computer hacking, terrorism, human trafficking, climate change, the toll of war in Ukraine, Sudan and Gaza, looming famine in Somalia — all these challenges demand cooperative responses, and the United Nations is an obvious forum to develop them.

Yet for many of these problems, the United Nations is becoming almost irrelevant.

Trump last year derided the United Nations as full of “empty words,” and he had a point. The United Nations is a timid Tower of Babel that is more effective at issuing paper than at solving conflicts; hell is a U. N. meeting.

Many times over the years I’ve wanted to beat my head against the wall in frustration with U. N. bureaucracy. In 2009, when I was covering the Darfur genocide with George Clooney, the U. N. pulled our security escort, for fear of being associated with any criticism that Clooney might make of Sudan for committing genocide. When Bosnians, Rwandans and Yazidis were slaughtered, the United Nations dithered.

“The cost is measured in lives,” said Nadia Murad, a Nobel Peace Prize winner whose Yazidi region in Iraq was surrounded by ISIS fighters in 2014 for nearly two weeks. “No one came to help us,” she told me, and she ended up kidnapped by ISIS and was raped for months. Her mother and six brothers were murdered.

Yet if the United Nations is periodically paralyzed, it’s also vital and sometimes a godsend.

“I have also seen U. N. staff remain in places after everyone else has left, doing work no one else is willing to do,” Murad said. “That work is indispensable. That is precisely why the U. N. must do it better.”

Critics can denounce United Nations workers as “fatally arrogant parasites,” as President Javier Milei of Argentina put it a few days ago, but I’ve been held at gunpoint alongside courageous U. N. humanitarians in the Central African Republic who were trying to bring assistance to a desperate area after other aid workers had fled. I’ve seen frontline U. N. workers living out of cargo containers in Somalia, sleeping in tents in South Sudan, driving down perilous roads in Congo and standing up to gunmen in Yemen — risking their lives to save children from war, rape and disease.

One of the heroes of the 20th century was James P. Grant, who led UNICEF and in 1982 engineered the child survival revolution. He and his team employed vaccines and better treatment of diarrhea to save 25 million lives in his lifetime, and countless millions since.

When have critics of the United Nations done anything half so noble?

When have critics of the United Nations put their lives on the line for others, like the 136 U. N. employees who died in the line of duty last year? Or like the 73 U. N. staff members currently held prisoner by the Houthis in Yemen?

Today in the Democratic Republic of Congo, United Nations workers are combating the Ebola outbreak. In Somalia, they are feeding starving children. In Gaza, they are distributing aid. If the United States was distinguished during the Gaza war by providing 2,000-pound bombs that Israel used to destroy neighborhoods, the United Nations stood out for trying to achieve peace and get aid through Israeli checkpoints.

What’s the opposite of United Nations multilateralism? It’s Russia’s invasion of Ukraine. It’s Trump’s attack on Iran. It’s Elon Musk “feeding U. S. A. I. D. into the wood chipper,” as he put it, by one count costing more than 750,000 lives. So for all my impatience with plodding U. N. bureaucracy, I’ll take the United Nations any day over great-power jingoism and caprice.

At stake is not just the U. N. itself but the broader global architecture. Trump’s swipes at NATO are a gift to Russia. His assault on the International Criminal Court is a gift to warlords. His withdrawal from the World Health Organization is a gift to viruses.

Sure, bash the United Nations; it often deserves it. But my guess is that millions more children would die every year if it weren’t for UNICEF, the World Food Program, the U. N. Refugee Agency and the U. N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs. On balance, that seems a defensible record, no?

Understand also that the U. N. is a crumbling pillar of what is left of this geopolitical global order that the United States helped create after World War II and that has so benefited us and the world. And note that one reason for the infuriating U. N. paralysis and timorousness is that great powers throw their weight around, often vetoing constructive action and, in the case of the United States, slashing budgets as well.

I fear that the paralysis may get worse.

The United Nations is supposed to choose a new secretary general this year, and this is a moment when the world needs a charismatic, outspoken leader who could use the bully pulpit and tackle the globe’s security and humanitarian crises. Sadly, that seems exactly what the United States, China and Russia are determined to avoid.

There is growing concern that Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin may be unable to agree on any of the current candidates for secretary general, and that they will settle on some innocuous dark horse nonentity so mild and inoffensive that the United Nations will be further marginalized and weakened.

The result would very likely be more Ebola outbreaks, more war, more paralysis in confronting the common threats to humanity — and more darkness descending on our planet.

I sometimes feel I spend half my time cursing the United Nations and the other half defending it. But in particular, I think the critics don't appreciate the frontline work of U. N. humanitarians in difficult and dangerous places, separated from families, negotiating with warlords, avoiding bandits, trying to protect civilians. We ask them to do the impossible and they often fail at it, but I admire both their sacrifices and their achievements, measured in children's lives saved.

A 7-Day Standoff That Said So Much About Trump and the Media

The New York Times September 26, 2026

Trump’s Media Ban

Advertisement

Supported by

media memo

An abrupt decree, a network boycott, a legal intervention and an uneasy détente: This was no typical battle between a president and his press corps.

By Michael M. Grynbaum

Michael Grynbaum has reported on Donald J. Trump’s relationship with the news media since 2016.

A week ago Friday, at 3:04 p. m., with his chief of staff in Florida and the West Wing winding down for the weekend, President Trump signed off on a 130-word message that sent the Washington press corps into a tailspin.

“Effective immediately,” the president wrote on Truth Social, he was “banning” CNN, MS NOW and Politico from the White House “as a result of their constant ‘reporting’ FAKE NEWS!”

Mr. Trump says this kind of thing all the time. But the idea of a “ban” caught reporters — and the president’s own advisers — by surprise. How would a ban work? Was it legal? Was this for real?

Amid a dragging war effort in Iran, soaring gas prices and higher interest rates, Mr. Trump had managed to generate a media tempest out of thin air.

When Kelly O’Donnell of NBC, an hour later, asked Mr. Trump about the First Amendment and its promise of freedom of the press, the president shrugged. “That’s fine,” he said. “But I don’t have to let them into my — into the people’s house.”

Lawyers for the barred news outlets disagreed, and eventually, so did a federal judge. But the seven-day saga that unfolded — a frenzied news cycle in itself, born of a single social media post — illustrated quite a bit about Mr. Trump’s complicated relationship with the press.

Since his earliest candidate days, when chants of “CNN sucks!” rang out at rallies, Mr. Trump has used the media as a reliable punching bag. And in his second term, he has drastically escalated his attacks, drawing on the levers of government — issuing subpoenas, seizing devices and using regulatory pressure — to intimidate outlets that displease him. Mr. Trump has also sought to bar The Associated Press from parts of the White House and started handpicking which journalists can attend certain events.

His abrupt White House ban was another novel effort to micromanage his coverage. And with Republicans worrying about a bleak midterm outlook, Mr. Trump’s allies seized the moment to rehash the usual complaints about a corrupt liberal media — perhaps a soothing topic for a president whose poll numbers have dipped.

But Mr. Trump, inadvertently or not, had also threatened something he deems precious: his own television coverage.

By barring CNN outright, Mr. Trump threw a wrench into the White House TV pool, a group of five networks that share the responsibility of broadcasting the president’s daily events. On Monday, after a weekend of discussion, the networks, Fox News included, suspended their footage of Mr. Trump until CNN was reinstated, an exceedingly rare collective action by a famously rivalrous group.

Television is Mr. Trump’s oxygen — he regularly scans the news channels with the aid of a DirecTV Genie HD DVR in his dining room — and his absence from the screen was notable. When he held an elaborate ceremony on the South Lawn on Monday to unveil a new helipad, one of his primary home improvement projects, audio problems marred the official White House video feed; Mr. Trump was stuck pantomiming as viewers heard only white noise.

The president got himself back on TV by joining Mayor Zohran Mamdani of New York at a Monday news conference, which local TV crews captured. “They said they’re going to boycott me, but they never boycott me,” Mr. Trump said. Gesturing toward the cameras, he added, “Look at all that press.”

His return was short-lived. By Wednesday, the TV pool was still dark, and no major network carried footage of that day’s pomp-filled event: Mr. Trump welcoming President Xi Jinping of China with a red carpet at Joint Base Andrews.

As for the locked-out journalists, they argued their case to viewers — that a ban on the press was a disservice to the public — while their lawyers argued their case in court, calling the move unconstitutional. Around 1 a. m. on Thursday, a federal judge in Washington ordered the White House to “immediately” reinstate the barred outlets.

It took nearly 12 hours for the administration to comply. And without an assurance that CNN would be restored to the pool, the major networks kept up their boycott. The result was an ironic spectacle: American journalists locked out of the White House as Mr. Trump feted Mr. Xi, a dictatorial leader who has suppressed free speech.

“CNN and MSDNC, to show you how fake they are, today refused to cover one of the Biggest and Most Beautiful Events to take place in many years,” the president complained on Thursday, using a nickname for MS NOW. He did not mention that his administration had barred the outlets from the White House grounds.

On Friday, both sides climbed down.

After the White House indicated that CNN could provide the pool camera for a midday event, the TV networks resumed normal operations. Shortly before noon, a CNN crew was rolling as Mr. Trump guided Mr. Xi, along with their wives, around the National Archives.

Among the documents that Mr. Trump pointed out: the original articles of the Constitution and the Bill of Rights.

By Saturday, tensions had resumed: The White House declined to let CNN travel aboard Air Force One with Mr. Trump, who planned to attend a college football game in Tennessee. Once again, the TV pool went dark.

Michael M. Grynbaum writes about the intersection of media, politics and culture. He has been a media correspondent at The Times since 2016.

Anonymous Men Have Turned Cyberharassment Into a Group Sport—Here’s One Woman’s Side of the Story

Wired September 24, 2026

Last year, Maddie Kowalski was a regular sophomore attending the University of Florida. Then a series of burner accounts on X started proliferating explicit, nonconsensual videos of her. This week, Zoë Schiffer sits down with WIRED senior writer EJ Dickson to discuss the burnerverse, a sprawling, loosely organized network of anonymous accounts that have turned the sexual humiliation of young women into an online participatory sport.

You can follow Zoë Schiffer on Bluesky at @zoeschiffer and EJ Dickson on Bluesky at @ejdickson. Write to us at uncannyvalley@wired. com.

You can always listen to this week's podcast through the audio player on this page, but if you want to subscribe for free to get every episode, here's how:

If you're on an iPhone or iPad, open the app called Podcasts, or just tap this link. You can also download an app like Overcast or Pocket Casts and search for “Uncanny Valley.” We’re on Spotify too.

Note: This is an automated transcript, which may contain errors.

Zoë Schiffer: A quick content warning before we dive in. This conversation includes descriptions of nonconsensual sexual content and references to self-harm. Please take care while listening.

Maddie Kowalski: When I heard that someone had sent a nude photograph of me to his friends at FSU, and in this picture I was heavily intoxicated.

Zoë Schiffer: This is Maddie Kowalski.

Maddie Kowalski: So right after this, I started getting flooded with messages that I was being talked about all over my school's Yik Yak.

Zoë Schiffer: Yik Yak is a platform popular among college students where you can post anonymously if you're within a specific geographic radius.

Maddie Kowalski: Everything was just happening really fast, and I couldn't comprehend any of it.

Zoë Schiffer: What Maddie had heard about was a single photo, but there were a series of videos in which she was visibly out of it, naked, and performing sexual acts. Maddie remembers, well, she was really drunk that night.

Maddie Kowalski: I felt really detached from the girl in the videos because I had so little memory of the events.

Zoë Schiffer: Obviously, she hadn't consented to any of this, not to being filmed, and certainly not to those films being posted online. But now, it was all over X.

Maddie Kowalski: And at this moment, I just felt my whole world collapse. Everything was being shared and reposted so fast, and I couldn't do anything to stop it.

Zoë Schiffer: The videos had officially gone viral. #MaddieKowalski was trending on X nationwide, and it was viewed more than 8.5 million times. For the next 24 hours, Maddie sat paralyzed on her couch while anonymous internet people harassed her. They posted old photos from before the night the videos were taken. They called and texted her parents all throughout the night. One anonymous man told her father that he'd had sex with her and had since tested positive for HIV. People on X were placing bets on whether by the end of the week she would either start an OnlyFans or kill herself. Here's the thing. The people behind this weren't strangers in some far-off corner of the internet. In many cases, they were her literal classmates hiding behind anonymous burner accounts, mostly used to celebrate college sports. From WIRED's Uncanny Valley, I'm Zoë Schiffer, contributing editor. WIRED senior writer EJ Dickson spent months following Maddie's story and what's become known as the burnerverse, a sprawling, loosely organized network of anonymous accounts that has turned the sexual humiliation of young women into a kind of participatory sport. EJ, thank you so much for coming on.

EJ Dickson: Thank you for having me.

Zoë Schiffer: Can you talk us through what exactly is the burnerverse? How is it organized? Who exactly is part of it?

EJ Dickson: So, the burnerverse is a very loosely organized network. It's unfair to even say network because it's just kind of an amorphous community of college sports fan burner accounts. So, they're all anonymous or mostly anonymous accounts. And I think it's important to note that a lot of them are pretty innocuous, but there is a segment of this community that has emerged that is pretty violently racist and misogynistic and antisemitic. And this is the corner of the subculture that has sort of made a sport out of systemically doxing women. So, I initially found out about the burnerverse in February 2025, a few months, about nine months, before Maddie went viral. And I found out about it because I saw this young woman's name trending on X, and her name was Mary Kate Cornett. And I was really curious. I was like, who is this person? And it turned out to be an Ole Miss college student who there was a campus rumor, a salacious, defamatory rumor, about her sex life that had gone viral on campus that had been elevated to the mainstream and was going viral on X nationally because a bunch of prominent people had picked it up. Barstool Sports personalities, Pat McAfee, talked about it on his podcast. So, I was like, how does this happen? How does a girl's name trend nationally based on a completely unverifiable rumor? This is a private citizen. There's no real news interest here. How does this happen? And that's how I started digging into the burnerverse and how burner accounts made her name go viral.

Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, she gets alerted to the fact that these images and videos are going viral on campus. What was her immediate response? What avenues were available to her, I guess, in terms of reporting or getting the content taken down?

EJ Dickson: So, she had the presence of mind to go to the police department in Gainesville, where she went to school, fairly early. And she was receiving harassing phone calls basically every second of the day at that point from these burner accounts, calling her slut, calling her parents, telling that she had AIDS, that she was a crack whore. Just the most horrible things you can possibly imagine. She couldn't even turn off her phone, she told me, because her phone was ringing so much. She couldn't even press the button to turn it off. And so, she went to the Gainesville Police Department to complain about this, and they basically just told her, "Change your phone number." And she was like, "Oh, OK. Well, that's not really going to do anything." Also, the university contacted her because the university found out about the images going viral before she did, even. That's how massively widespread they were. And they opened up a Title IX investigation, but it was closed after about a month because she says the university told her that there was no evidence that the videos had been filmed on campus, so it was not within their jurisdiction. So, her initial options for recourse were pretty limited, at least at first.

Zoë Schiffer: I'm curious, can you talk through her sorority's response? Were they helpful?

EJ Dickson: I think she considered that one of the biggest betrayals is how her sorority sisters responded to all of this. Her sorority basically disavowed her immediately. They allegedly held meetings discussing how this incident would reflect on them. Many of her sorority sisters blocked her, unfollowed her. Again, I mean, this was a girl who was struggling. She was in her second year of college, 19 years old, drinking heavily, needed support, and your sorority sisters are supposed to stick with you through thick and thin. I mean, you're supposed to be bonded for life. And basically the second that this happens, they completely abandoned her is the way she tells it.

Zoë Schiffer: And eventually, she and her family try and find a lawyer, and you write in the story that it was difficult for them to find someone who could understand the scope of the problem. I believe the line in the story is like, "This wasn't a typical revenge porn case. This was much bigger than that."

EJ Dickson: Yeah, I think that's what was confusing to law enforcement and to the lawyers that the Kowalskis consulted as well. If this had been a simple case of a spurned ex-boyfriend posting a nude or a pornographic video nonconsensually, that would've been much easier to prosecute. That's something that law enforcement has seen before, but this wasn't that. This was a network of total strangers posting the nonconsensual intimate images of a girl they didn't even know, for no apparent reason. And there were so many obstacles in the way. They didn't know who was behind these accounts. They didn't know why they were posting them. They didn't know how they had obtained these videos. To this day, Maddie is not sure how her video was leaked. And I also think it really speaks to the real chasm between the speed with which the viral news cycle evolves and the speed with which our legislation evolves. It simply can't keep up.

Zoë Schiffer: So, there's a moment where I believe it's when she's starting to consult with lawyers. What does she ultimately decide?

EJ Dickson: She ultimately decides to go after the burner accounts, the anonymous men who shared her nonconsensual videos. My understanding is that it took a couple of months for the Gainesville Police Department to subpoena X for these guys' records. Two freshmen boys in a fraternity, Theta Chi, who she did not know. And a third man was also charged, who I believe was a former UF student who had transferred at that point.

Zoë Schiffer: You also write that people don't have a lot of recourse in terms of getting X to take immediate action. This is happening years after Elon Musk has purchased the platform formerly known as Twitter. He famously got rid of much of the trust and safety team. The content policies have been relaxed from what they used to be. And so, how responsive was the platform in getting the content to go away?

EJ Dickson: Well, I mean, the platform didn't respond to me when I asked for comment, and I had a lot of questions for them. I mean, I don't think that this would've happened were it not for Elon Musk acquiring X and dismantling the regulations because X's algorithm amplifies divisive or inflammatory content in such a way that it doesn't really matter what's trending. It's just going to be broadcast nationwide. And it's like a game of whack-a-mole. You can file a take-down request, and apparently the Kowalskis said that X was pretty responsive in terms of actually getting the videos down individually once they filed the request because they're legally required to do that because of the Take It Down Act. But, if you remove one, 10 more pop up in their stead. That's just the way the internet works.

Zoë Schiffer: As things stand now, has anyone specifically been held accountable for what happened to Maddie?

EJ Dickson: So, the men are being charged with sexual cyberharassment which is a misdemeanor that is punishable by up to one year in prison and an $1,000 fine. I believe one of them is ... The police department is alleging that he'd financially profited off of her humiliation. When I reached out to Theta Chi, their fraternity, they said that they were on interim suspension and completely disavowed their activities and said, "This is not what Theta Chi is about." I don't know if that was prompted by my reaching out or if that had already been underway prior. I don't want to speculate, but I had said that she will see them posting from parties and stuff.

Zoë Schiffer: And where does this leave Maddie?

EJ Dickson: She's traumatized. I mean, can you imagine the worst moment of your life goes viral when you're 19 years old, and you don't even remember it? She doesn't think she'll be able to date and find love. She thinks this is going to follow her wherever she goes for the rest of her life. And the first time I met her, she wasn't even particularly emotional about it. It was just fact for her. And I was just sitting there. I'm a parent. It broke my heart. And that's the thing that really haunted me after reporting this and what really stuck with me when I spoke to her best friend who's quoted in the article. They stole her youth. They stole her girlhood. They stole her optimism and her sense of hope and belief that she could do something great with her life. Because that's what college is all about, right? You're kind of on the precipice of all of that. And that just seems like the most egregious theft of all.

Zoë Schiffer: Her experience also isn't an isolated incident, right? How far-reaching is this? How many people has this happened to?

EJ Dickson: So, there are degrees of it. All told, I was able to identify about a little less than a dozen women across the country who had been doxed in this fashion and on this scale. They were all young women in their late teens, early 20s, college students or recently graduated from college, conventionally attractive, and they had all been subject to some sort of salacious rumor or had nonconsensual videos or images of them circulating and were perceived to have transgressed the boundaries of sexual norms, I guess, in some way was kind of the unifying criteria. But, the burner accounts were also doing this on a much smaller scale to teenage girls whose photos were posted on college's incoming students' Instagram pages. They were taking their photos and posting them and making fun of their bodies and the way they looked and posting their full names. Girls who weren't even in college yet, incoming freshmen, they were doxing on a much smaller scale. And they do that pretty regularly. Or, they'll take photos of somebody's dating profile, some girl's dating profile or a message, and they'll post it, and they'll release her name and make fun of her. So, it happens all the time. I think that it's really the scale that differs, but the exposure aspect of it happens all the time.

Zoë Schiffer: Going back to Maddie's story, I'm curious how she felt. Like you said, you talked to her after the article came out. Obviously, it's this decision that I think a lot of sources face where it's like, do you not speak out and hope that the story kind of goes away? Or, do you take the chance and try and take back a little of the narrative?

EJ Dickson: That was really difficult. That was something I was really concerned about because I thought that there was a possibility that it could renew the harassment against her. And we had a number of conversations about that. And I think she understood and understands the impact that her story has and that she has an opportunity to speak for other women who have been through this and to sort of ensure that shame switches sides, that she doesn't need to be ashamed of what happened to her. I think she was a little overwhelmed, but she's a very strong person.

Maddie Kowalski: I'd like to end this with something really important. Although I don't have control over what happened to me, I can control what I do moving forward, and I want to move forward with healing.

Zoë Schiffer: Here's Maddie again. We thought she should close out the story in her own words.

Maddie Kowalski: These last few weeks have been the darkest and hardest moments of my life, but I'm still here, and that's something that I'm really learning to be proud of. I'm taking steps to rebuild myself, to feel safe again, and to understand that what happened to me doesn't define me. And I know that this is a long path. I've unfortunately also realized that there are so many women and girls as well as men who go through things like this in silence, feeling alone or ashamed or afraid to speak. And if sharing my story can help even one person feel seen or teach one person why consent and decency matter, then it's worth it.

Zoë Schiffer: That's our show for today. We'll link to all the stories we spoke about in the show notes. Adriana Tapia produced this episode. It was fact-checked by Matt Giles and Daniel Roman. Kate Osborn is our executive producer, and Katie Drummond is WIRED's global editorial director.

I Think I Found an AI Agent Worth the Risk

Wired September 24, 2026

One of the first things I did when I left my full-time job at WIRED was give Claude Cowork access to my email and calendar. After reporting on artificial intelligence for years, I was curious about what the technology could do for me. I had imagined Cowork as a hyper-capable digital assistant, but was let down to discover that it was more like interacting with a regular chatbot, albeit one with extra tools. What did I want it to do? I had no idea.

Then Instinct, an invite-only AI agent that communicates with users through iMessage and WhatsApp, started popping off in the Bay Area. It connects to your email, calendar, and messaging apps. Think of it as OpenClaw for normies. The company, which launched in private beta in February, is reportedly in talks to raise $1 billion on top of the $350 million it’s already raised, bringing its valuation to $10 billion, according to The Information.

Instinct’s moment in the spotlight comes as Meta is experiencing its own unexpected burst of popularity thanks to Muse, an AI assistant the tech giant launched earlier this month. As of writing, Muse is the most popular free app in Apple’s App Store, with more than 900,000 downloads, according to third-party estimates. The commentator class on X seems genuinely excited about it, despite the fact that it rolled out with a serious security vulnerability that would have “let attackers do ‘whatever’ they wanted on a victim’s Mac,” according to Ars Technica. I’m not about to give Meta a ton of my personal information, but if Muse can keep me logged into Bloomberg or unsubscribe me from Hot Yoga São Paulo, which has been emailing me once a week since 2017, I’ll reconsider.

The divide between people who use AI agents for everything and those who have never tried one has never been wider. It explains, in part, why tech CEOs were largely caught off guard by the data center backlash. If you think agents can automate the majority of people’s administrative drudgery and turbocharge their productivity, the costs and disruptions associated with building data centers might look like an acceptable trade-off. But if you’re using chatbots as a fancy form of Google, that deal is probably much less appealing.

The overarching problem, as technology journalist Jasmine Sun writes, is that “most people’s problems are not software-shaped, and most won’t notice even when they are.” AI agents, like chatbots, still require a lot of input and direction from users. If you know what you want—help with your homework, a virtual girlfriend—the tools are eager to provide. But if you don’t, well, welcome to the permanent underclass.

I was eager to avoid such a fate. I may not be agentic, but I like to think I’m action-oriented. Surely I could identify a software-shaped problem in my life. I had used Claude previously to generate a few freelance invoices, saving me approximately 10 minutes. It was nice, but not life-changing. I decided to give Instinct a try.

If you talk to AI researchers about Instinct, you’ll hear the phrase “form factor” a lot. Instinct got the form factor right—no open text box, just iMessage, WhatsApp, and a few helpful prompts. It’s hard to overstate how important this is. Rather than trying to figure out for yourself how to make the chat experience more useful, you’re texting with an agent that’s suggesting things it can do for you, and then actually doing them. And unlike other agents in this space, it doesn’t text too much. I tried a competing agent called Lindy for a week and deleted it after it texted me each morning and started popping into Zoom meetings without my approval.

For its first project, I gave Instinct my itinerary for a work trip to Venice, Italy. I had it book reservations based on where I was going to be, including WhatsApping hole-in-the-wall spots. Success! Restaurant reservations appear to be a gateway drug for many agent-curious people, and I was no exception. (It’s worth noting that while Muse can also call restaurants to book reservations on your behalf, some of those calls are reportedly made by humans in call centers, according to reporting in 404 Media).

Next, I gave Instinct a more complicated task. I had already booked a trip to New York in November with my sister when WIRED asked me to attend the WIRED World Fair, which was taking place in Miami the day before. Unfortunately, I’d booked a saver fare, meaning I couldn’t move the ticket, and if I missed the first leg of the trip it would automatically cancel the whole thing.

Could Instinct cancel my trip and get a refund? To my surprise, it could. The agent detected that Alaska had moved my flight 90 minutes earlier, a fact I’d completely missed, which qualified me for a full refund. It canceled my ticket, saving me roughly $550, and rebooked my one-way return to San Francisco. I don’t know about you guys, but I’m starting to feel the AGI.

This is where I have to pause and acknowledge the risks of using Instinct. There are a lot. People have reported that when they tried to disconnect the agent from their email, they found out it was retaining a copy of their inboxes anyway. One venture capitalist said he was banned from Resy after the bot pinged its API roughly 200 times per hour while trying to make a reservation. Another tech investor said he deleted the app after determining that it would be trivially easy for Instinct to be phished.

Instinct’s Terms of Service are pretty far-reaching, allowing the company to use at least some of your conversations to train its AI models. I also experienced an annoying (if minor) snafu: One day, Instinct canceled a DoorDash order that was seriously delayed, forcing me to forfeit $64. (I’d explicitly told it to cancel only if I could get a refund.) This alerted me to another thing Instinct is very, very good at: profusely apologizing without offering to pay for its mistakes.

The company Instinct, which shares the same name as its flagship AI agent, did not respond to requests for comment from WIRED.

Instinct feels like a mildly chaotic personal assistant, and since I’ve never had a real human assistant, I’m sticking with it. Last week it told me “NOT TO OPEN” an email from a friend inviting me to a backyard BBQ—it turned out to be a phishing scam. Agents are a security nightmare. I get it! But I’m busy. I’m a mom. Everything feels like a security nightmare these days. For now, I’m willing to take the risk.

This is an edition of the Model Behavior newsletter. Read previous newsletters here.

Google’s Gemini Can Now Make Calls for You on Pixel Phones

Wired September 24, 2026

Google has been trying to have its AI assistant make phone calls on your behalf for almost 10 years. Remember Duplex? It enabled the now-defunct Google Assistant to call restaurants and book tables. That service was shuttered a few years ago, but now comes round two, powered by modern large language models.

On Thursday, Google announced Call for Me, an experimental beta feature exclusive to its latest Pixel 11 smartphones in the US (and in English). Pixel 11 owners need a Gemini subscription and have to be enrolled in the Phone by Google app’s public beta. Google has instructions on how to participate here.

These calls are designed to reach businesses. Gemini can call your local hardware store to ask if they stock a specific tool, or chat with a barber to schedule a haircut. Just tell Gemini to make the call—it may ask you follow-up questions for more context—and the chatbot will introduce itself and can have a back-and-forth conversation to ensure your request is handled. If it runs into an automated phone menu, it can navigate it and even wait on hold. On your end, you can view a live transcript on the Pixel and take over at any point.

Google says it works best with businesses, but there are some establishments Gemini won't call, like emergency services. That said, you can ask Gemini to call specific numbers. For example, if your tattoo artist doesn't have much of a web presence, “Gemini will try to search for a phone number, but you may provide one as well,” a Google spokesperson tells WIRED. During these calls, the assistant's voice will be the same one used in Gemini Live interactions, even if your preferred Gemini voice has an accent.

Call for Me expands on Google’s suite of smart calling features on Pixels and Android. The Phone app can already screen incoming calls and block robocalls and telemarketers. Hold for Me lets the assistant listen for when the hold music ends and a live person is on the other end; it alerts you to pick up the phone when it’s finally your cue. Direct My Call can display the different choices in an automated phone menu before they’re spoken, so you can tap nine to reach a live person and skip the recorded voice reading out the whole list. It even has real-time Scam Detection, alerting you when it thinks the person on the other end is scamming you.

Voice assistants handling phone calls is a little more accepted today than back in the Duplex days. Call screening features abound—whether on a Pixel, Samsung, or iPhone, onboard assistants routinely intercept unknown callers to ask why they’re calling.

But these kinds of features—much like hyped-up AI translation features—can often fall short. Calls are unpredictable, and the person on the other end may hang up, assuming it’s just another spam call. What happens if Gemini doesn’t understand a person’s accent all that well? Will it trap the clerk in an endless loop of asking them to repeat themselves? And if the shop doesn’t have the tool you need, does the bot know how to bow out politely—or just cut the line?

“That is exactly what we want to continue testing,” the Google spokesperson says. “With this experiment, we look forward to users testing a variety of cases, so that we can continue to improve the feature across accents and noisy environments.” And yes, Google says Gemini will “politely” hang up if the business can't accommodate your needs.

It still points to a future where robots may take over these kinds of business phone calls altogether. Businesses are also experimenting with artificial-intelligence tools to interface with customers, like local California pizza chain Pizza My Heart, which lets you text its Jimmy the Surfer chatbot to order pizza.

It doesn’t seem too far off that you’ll ask your phone to call a restaurant, and the restaurant’s AI will answer. The machines are talking to each other, except they’re just debating whether you want the stuffed crust.

An OpenAI Agent Hacked Australia’s Health Service. Their Government Found Out Months Later

Wired September 24, 2026

Australia is investigating whether OpenAI broke the law after an agent hacked into its health statistics portal in the first widely known incident of an AI agent hacking a government website.

The Australian government is reviewing whether it should involve the federal police after the agent accessed non-public files from the social and health services agency, Services Australia, in June.

Australia only found out about the incident when OpenAI alerted the government on September 10—almost three months after the hack—by sending an email to a public mailbox. Sam Altman had reportedly not mentioned the incident when he met Australia’s deputy prime minister, Richard Marles, earlier this month, even though OpenAI had been aware since August. The company took “way too long” and the notification should not have just gone through a public inbox, Prime Minister Anthony Albanese said in a press conference in New York on Wednesday. There will also be an inquiry into why Services Australia then took five days to escalate the email to Australia’s Cyber Security Centre.

OpenAI’s agent had been conducting internet based research into health statistics in a development project by an internal OpenAI research team. When it could not access certain information, the agent attempted alternative ways until it found a work around and gained unauthorized access. It also wrote files to the internal server, which the government is waiting on OpenAI for more technical information on. The government is also investigating whether the agent gained unauthorised access to three additional government websites it interacted with.

“There will obviously be legal consequences on it,” Albanese said as he disclosed the “unacceptable” incident. He said he had spoken with Altman over the phone earlier that day about his “extreme concern” about the incident and “disappointment” with the nature and length of time the company took to inform the government. While Albanese did not answer whether he had apologised, Altman “clearly accepted that the company had not done good enough,” he said.

The Australian government currently believes no one’s personal data was accessed, though investigations are ongoing. The website in question is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics such as spending. It was therefore behind much lower levels of security than personal data would have been, Marles said in Sydney. “The impact of the incident is actually relatively minor, but this is a serious incident, obviously, and one that is completely unacceptable,” he cautioned.

A number of incidents over the summer, including OpenAI agents’ hacking of HuggingFace—highlighting the threat of frontier model agents acting rogue—were raised at the United Nations General Assembly this week, with Secretary General António Guterres welcoming calls to control AI. Altman himself had warned the United Nations Security Council earlier on Wednesday about his concern that humans could lose control of these systems.

“It was a shock that it occurred, because it was real and serious,” Albanese said about the incident. “But it also, I think, was something that had been predicted, including by the AI companies themselves.”

Australia is establishing a task force to look at the incident and emerging AI cyber threats. It will consider possible law enforcement and legislative responses to ensure that incidents like this don’t happen again.

The Ovary Is Surprisingly Active After Menopause. Scientists Are Trying to Figure Out Why

Wired September 24, 2026

When Francesca Duncan decided to take a look at what was going on in postmenopausal ovaries, she assumed she wouldn’t find much of interest. In a woman’s reproductive years, the ovary is exceptionally dynamic, shifting form and function from day to day throughout her cycle. But after menopause, when egg supply has dwindled and hormone production has waned, the ovaries are often thought of as little more than empty sacks.

“I assumed it was just sitting there inert,” says Duncan, a reproductive biologist at Northwestern University, who was only looking at postmenopausal ovaries as part of a project to map a cellular aging process called senescence throughout the body.

Instead, Duncan found that aged ovaries were anything but stagnant. When looking at the protein composition of ovaries of postmenopausal women between the ages of 50 and 75 years old, her team found that the molecular signatures differed significantly across the decades. The oldest ovary looked nothing like a 60- or 70-year-old organ at the molecular level. She was shocked. “Clearly something is still happening,” says Duncan.

The question is: what?

A new wave of discovery is forcing researchers to recast the ovary not as an egg factory with an expiration date, but as an organ that impacts a woman’s overall health and may shape the trajectory of aging long after the fertile years have passed. What they are only beginning to understand is whether changes to the ovary after menopause are harmful, protective, or some combination of the two, shifting over time.

This isn’t the first time the ovary’s role in maintaining health has been underestimated. For decades, surgeons removed healthy organs during hysterectomies, figuring they weren’t doing much besides posing cancer risks. But 20 years ago, evidence began accumulating that removing healthy ovaries actually harms a woman’s overall health, finding an increased risk of dementia, cardiovascular disease, and premature death.

Because the ovary has historically been understood primarily as a reproductive organ, though, research has largely ignored what might be happening once those functions decline. “We don’t even know much about what the premenopausal ovary is doing outside of fertility,” says Jennifer Garrison, an ovarian aging expert and founder of a women’s health biotech company currently in stealth mode. After menopause, the extent of what we know about the ovary basically boils down to “it’s important,” she adds.

Biologists have known for decades, for instance, that after menopause, ovaries continue producing hormones, including testosterone and small amounts of estrogen. But arguments continue over the clinical significance of those hormones. And hormones are only part of a complex signaling system.

Generally, the hormones the ovary produces postmenopause are known to help maintain libido, bone, and muscle, among other things, although it’s not clear how much the relatively small amounts produced by the postmenopausal ovary contribute to those effects. Multiple studies demonstrate that women who undergo oophorectomies fare worse than those who do not, particularly when having their ovaries removed before going through menopause naturally.

Recent brain-imaging work by Pauline Maki at the University of Illinois at Chicago shows that even low levels of estrogen circulating postmenopause may matter: Women with higher levels had better-functioning memory circuits when performing memory tasks. Where that estrogen comes from—and how much the ovary contributes—isn’t as clear. After menopause, evidence suggests the brain reorganizes, possibly to compensate for declining estrogen levels. Maki hypothesizes that ovarian signaling may contribute to that adaptation, and that hormone therapy could alter the relationship between the ovary, the body’s circulating estrogen, and the brain.

The significance of residual hormone production may decrease over time. Still, says Walter Rocca, a professor of epidemiology and neurology at the Mayo Clinic, that doesn’t mean the ovary has become unimportant.

“I am convinced until proven otherwise that removing ovaries even after menopause is not advisable,” he says, with a caveat for women at an increased risk of ovarian cancer.

Just how long that importance persists after menopause is still an open question, says Stephanie Faubion, medical director of the Menopause Society. It’s also unclear, she says, how much the answer may vary from woman to woman. “We just have huge gaps,” she says.

Duncan’s work suggests one reason the importance of the postmenopausal ovary may change over time. In analyzing human ovaries, the team found that protein patterns in older ovaries suggested that the ovary becomes a more inflammatory environment. To better understand what may be driving those changes, they looked more closely at the ovaries of mice. The research, published in June in the journal Molecular Human Reproduction, suggests that the ovary may eventually take on a completely new identity after menopause.

The team compared the ovaries of two-month-old mice, reproductively old 18-month-old mice, and post-reproductive 24-month-old mice, and found that over time, the genes linked to inflammation and immune activity became far more active. The number of immune cells in the ovary also increased. While research on mice does not always translate to humans, it could help to explain the molecular changes Duncan observed in human ovaries.

“We think that a lot of those changes may make the ovary more prone to age-related diseases like ovarian cancer,” says Birgit Schilling, an aging researcher at the Buck Institute for Research on Aging who collaborated with Duncan on the human ovary work, which has been published as a preprint. After menopause, the risk of a host of conditions goes up, including stroke, heart disease, and osteoporosis.

Other organs undergo immune remodeling with time, but the ovary ages long before most other organs. Duncan’s work raises the question of whether at some point, the benefits of keeping the ovaries may be outstripped by the risk: As the aging ovary becomes more inflammatory, she wonders whether it may begin broadcasting inflammatory signals to other parts of the body.

David Pépin is probing another possibility: that as follicles that house growing eggs disappear, the ovary may also reorganize to preserve hormone production. Pépin, a reproductive biologist at Massachusetts General Hospital and Harvard Medical School, found that years after cats were given an experimental birth-control gene therapy that prevented their follicles from maturing, the cats were still producing the hormones estrogen, testosterone, and inhibin at completely normal levels.

Follicles drive much of the hormone production during a reproductive cycle; without them, hormone levels should have fallen. In preliminary work he has publicly presented but not yet published, Pépin’s team found that when the ovaries were eventually removed, other cells in the ovary—the stroma—appeared to have taken over hormone production. Pilot studies in mice suggest a similar effect. Pépin thinks he may have tapped into a natural mechanism that helps maintain hormone production as follicles wane. It's long been hypothesized that the stroma may be responsible for some of the human ovary's postmenopausal hormone production.

Estrogen, he says, is not the only hormone that plays a role in menopause. “We know so little about how the other ovarian hormones that are disrupted at menopause may contribute to health,” he says. “It is not a dead organ.”

Why This Week’s Nor’easter Might Be Like a Hurricane

Wired September 24, 2026

A powerful nor’easter developing this week will bring wicked winds, rough surf, and heavy rains to coastal communities from North Carolina to Nova Scotia.

These types of storms are more synonymous with mid-winter than mid-fall. And true to form, this storm is a little different. It won’t drop snow or ice like a classic winter nor’easter. In fact, this system may bring a tease of tropical weather to an Atlantic basin that’s been devoid of hurricane activity so far this year.

Nor’easters are special types of low-pressure systems that earn their name from the fierce northeasterly winds that can lash coastlines.

The seed that’ll grow into this weekend’s nor’easter started developing on Wednesday a few hundred miles off North Carolina’s Outer Banks. The system will meander toward New England into this weekend before slowly winding down into early next week.

Forecasters expect strong, persistent winds to hit coastal locations from North Carolina to Nova Scotia. The strongest gusts will buffet New England through Friday and Saturday, when winds may reach 60 to 70 mph.

Communities throughout the region can expect coastal flooding, beach erosion, life-threatening rip currents, and dangerously rough surf. Isolated power outages are possible. Flight delays at New York's and Boston’s airports are also likely due to blustery winds and rain.

Computer models still don’t entirely agree on how close to the coast this storm will track, or how long it’ll linger in the area—both factors that are crucial to determining exact impacts. A slower track closer to the coast will plaster the region with stronger winds and heavier rainfall than a faster path or one that keeps the center of the storm farther out to sea.

Nor’easters are most common between October and April as powerful jet streams sweep across North America. It’s unusual for such a potent nor’easter to develop this early in the season.

Nor’easters are considered non-tropical—or as meteorologists call them, extratropical—systems that typically draw most of their energy from intense upper-level winds. That’s different from hurricanes, which tend to feed on warmer-than-normal oceans. But low-pressure systems exist on a spectrum that sometimes makes it difficult to neatly define them as tropical or extratropical, and this storm is a prime example.

Some computer models suggest that this week’s nor’easter may acquire some tropical characteristics as it intensifies off the Northeast coastline. Fully extratropical systems feature cold air throughout the entire core of the storm. This nor’easter, on the other hand, may briefly develop a shallow warm core, a phenomenon found in tropical storms and hurricanes. Cloud structure, the storm’s overall wind field, and thunderstorm activity near its center are other tropical characteristics to watch out for.

Even though it’s not likely to earn a name as a hurricane would, it’s important for residents throughout the region to pay attention to the threat of flooding, wind damage, and power outages.

It’s strangely fitting that a nor’easter may prove to be the most hurricane-like non-hurricane we’ve seen across the Atlantic basin this season. We’re now past the peak of hurricane season and the year remains historically quiet. Tropical activity here is running at less than 10 percent of normal for this point in the year. This is also the latest the season has gone without producing a hurricane since the satellite era began in 1966. A quiet hurricane season is a hallmark of an El Niño, when hot waters in the tropical Pacific create conditions in the atmosphere unsuitable for tropical storms to form in the Atlantic.

But winter is a different story, and this week’s storm is also a potential preview of what’s to come as El Niño gains strength. Strong El Niño events tend to influence an active storm track across the southern US during the cooler months, which may in turn lead to more coastal storms along the Eastern Seaboard.
